The step
\mathcal{L}_{6}\dashrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{7}
is the deepest open
construction in the monograph; experimental signatures of
\mathcal{L}_{7}

(ortho/para statistics, nuclear tunnelling) are beyond dispute,
but assembly of the
C^{*}
-algebraic framework remains a research
programme.

The motivating axis throughout is
reaction networks
, not
isolated reactions.
A network at level
k
is a finite directed graph whose vertices
are complexes and whose edges are labelled by morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{k}
;
open networks, exposed to their environment at specified interface
species, compose by pushout.
This is the framework of Baez and Pollard
[
28
]

at the kinetic level, extending the symmetric monoidal Petri-net
language of Meseguer and Montanari
[
221
]
;
the present work applies it at every tower level.
The forcing pairs are always parallel reactions that the previous
level cannot distinguish: parallel reactions with different

\Delta H
force
\mathcal{L}_{0}\to\mathcal{L}_{1}
; same
\Delta H
but different

\Delta S
forces
\mathcal{L}_{1}\to\mathcal{L}_{2}
; same
\Delta G
but different
rate forces
\mathcal{L}_{2}\to\mathcal{L}_{3}
; same rate law but different mechanism
forces
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
, and so on up the tower.
Each chapter closes with worked examples drawn from systems where
the new datum at that level is most cleanly exhibited; the
examples are deliberately level-specific, since no single reaction
sharpens every transition equally and forcing one to do every job
would flatten what each is meant to show.
Table
2
records, for each transition

\mathcal{L}_{k-1}\to\mathcal{L}_{k}
, the concrete pair of physically distinct
reactions that
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
conflates and
\mathcal{L}_{k}
separates; the
corresponding worked example is given in the chapter introducing

\mathcal{L}_{k}
.

§1.3. The chapters at a glance

Each summary below records the categorical structure added at
\mathcal{L}_{k}

and closes with the forcing pair that opens
\mathcal{L}_{k+1}
.

Chapter
2
—
\mathcal{L}_{0}
, stoichiometry.

The base level is the free permutative category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
on a Petri
net
P
: objects are complexes in the free commutative monoid

\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
over chemical species, morphisms are formal reactions,
composition is sequential chaining, and the monoidal product is
mixture.
The language is that of Meseguer and
Montanari
[
221
]
; its universal property
determines every strict symmetric monoidal functor out of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

by its values on generating reactions, so each higher-level datum
(enthalpy, free energy, rate) reduces to a single number per
elementary reaction.
The combinatorial invariants of chemical reaction network theory
(stoichiometric matrix
N
, linkage classes
\ell
, stoichiometric
subspace
s
, deficiency
\delta=n-\ell-s
) are
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data.

Forcing
\mathcal{L}_{1}
.

Two reactions with identical stoichiometric matrices can carry
different heats of reaction; Hess additivity is a new datum above
the bare bookkeeping of species in and species out.

Chapter
3
—
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, thermochemistry.

\mathcal{L}_{1}
equips
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
with a strict symmetric monoidal functor

F_{\!H}\colon\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to(\mathbb{R},+)
into the additive reals.
Hess’s Law is not a postulate but the functoriality of
F_{\!H}
: the
heat of a composite reaction is the sum of the heats of its parts
because composition in
\mathcal{L}_{0}
goes to addition in
\mathbb{R}
.
Thermochemical cycles — calorimetric summation, bond-energy
estimates, Born–Haber loops — become commuting diagrams in
\mathbb{R}
.

Forcing
\mathcal{L}_{2}
.

Two reactions with identical
\Delta H
can carry different
\Delta S
, and
their equilibrium positions then shift differently with temperature
— a distinction
\mathcal{L}_{1}
cannot make.

Chapter
4
—
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, equilibrium.

\mathcal{L}_{2}
adds the entropy functor
F_{\!S}
and, for each temperature

T>0
, the Gibbs functor
F_{G}^{T}:=F_{\!H}-TF_{\!S}
; its kernel is the
equilibrium locus,
F_{G}^{T}(r)=0
iff
r
lies at equilibrium at
temperature
T
.
Detailed balance appears as the condition that reverse reactions
carry opposite
F_{G}^{T}
-values; Wegscheider’s cycle relations become
cohomological conditions on free energies across a reaction network.

Forcing
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

Two reactions with identical
\Delta G
can proceed at rates differing by
many orders of magnitude (uncatalysed versus carbonic-anhydrase
catalysed
\mathrm{CO_{2}}
hydration): kinetics is invisible
at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
.

Chapter
5
—
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, kinetics.

\mathcal{L}_{3}
is a Markov category equipped with a functor

F_{P}\colon\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathbf{Stoch}
into the Markov category of
stochastic kernels: every reaction carries a rate law, and mass-action
kinetics together with the chemical master equation fit into this
framework as morphism-level data.
The Baez–Pollard
[
28
]
compositional structure for
open reaction networks lives here.
Feinberg’s Deficiency Zero and Deficiency One theorems appear in
their correct stratified form: the hypotheses (
n
,
\ell
,
s
,

\delta
) are
\mathcal{L}_{0}
invariants, but the conclusions (existence,
uniqueness, and asymptotic stability of a positive complex-balanced
steady state under mass-action) are statements at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

Forcing
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.

The
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
and
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
mechanisms, tuned to identical
rate laws, are the same morphism at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
but carry non-isomorphic
electron-pushing graphs.

Chapter
6
—
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, mechanism.

\mathcal{L}_{4}
is the free symmetric monoidal category on double-pushout
(DPO) spans in
\mathbf{LGraph}
, the category of labelled molecular
graphs: a morphism is an equivalence class of DPO derivations built
from rules
L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R
that rewrite a left-hand
graph
L
into a right-hand graph
R
while preserving the bond
accounting of the invariant subgraph
K
.
A minimal set of six elementary generators covers organic
reactivity at the arrow-pushing level; the chapter proves both substitution
(
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
/
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
) and elimination (
\mathrm{E_{1}}
/
\mathrm{E_{2}}
)
pairs to be distinct morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, and exhibits the
Briggs–Rauscher oscillating reaction as the first example in the
monograph where a global property of a reaction network (the
structural prerequisite for oscillation: two mechanism families
composing into a cyclic trajectory) is an
\mathcal{L}_{4}
predicate
invisible at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.
The same Briggs–Rauscher network reappears at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
–
\mathcal{L}_{3}
as
the running example of Chapter
12
.

Forcing
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.

The
(R)
- and
(S)
-enantiomers of a chiral substrate share the
same DPO derivation graph — chirality is invisible to
bond-rearrangement data alone.

Chapter
7
—
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, stereochemistry.

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
enriches
\mathcal{L}_{4}
with a
G^{*}
-equivariant structure,
where
G^{*}
is the Longuet-Higgins permutation-inversion group
generated by feasible nuclear permutations and space inversion.
Stereochemical content is carried by the action groupoid

\mathfrak{G}=G^{*}\ltimes\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)
on the nuclear
configuration space that the next level will construct formally.
Chirality appears as a non-trivial orbit of the
\mathbb{Z}/2

subgroup of
G^{*}
generated by inversion; Walden inversion at an

\mathrm{S_{N}2}
carbon is a non-trivial element of

\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})
.

Forcing
\mathcal{L}_{5}
.

\mathrm{CH_{3}Br}
and
\mathrm{CD_{3}Br}
undergoing the same

\mathrm{S_{N}}2
reaction are isomorphic at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
(same labelled
graph, same DPO rule, no stereocentre) yet react at measurably
different rates (
k_{H}/k_{D}\approx 1.3
, a secondary kinetic
isotope effect): explaining the gap requires Hessians at the
minimum and at the transition state, and therefore a mass-weighted
Riemannian metric on a configuration space — the geometric data
of
\mathcal{L}_{5}
, absent at every preceding level.

Chapter
8
—
\mathcal{L}_{5}
, the potential energy surface.

\mathcal{L}_{5}
attaches to each molecular graph
G
the configuration
orbifold
\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)
of nuclear geometries modulo rigid motions
and graph automorphisms, together with a smooth potential-energy
function
V\colon\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)\to\mathbb{R}
, the mass-weighted
Riemannian metric
g
, and the
\mathrm{SO}(3)
gauge connection
inherited from the orbifold quotient.
Transition-state theory, minimum-energy paths, and intrinsic reaction
coordinates all live here as geometric objects on
\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)
.
A revised KIE stratification (Bigeleisen–Mayer in the harmonic
limit, semiclassical tunnelling on the minimum-energy path, and
vibronically nonadiabatic PCET for enzymatic systems with kinetic
isotope effects up to
\sim\!700
) places the entire textbook
catalogue of isotope effects inside this single level.

Forcing
\mathcal{L}_{6}
.

Photochemical pathways branch at conical intersections — seams of
nuclear geometry where two electronic surfaces meet — and a single
smooth
V(R)
cannot distinguish a thermal reaction (no seam
encircled) from an ultrafast photochemical one (
\sim\!200\,\mathrm{fs}

in retinal); the canonical molecular witness is the half-integer
pseudorotational quantisation in the
\mathrm{Na_{3}}

2^{2}E^{\prime}
state, an obstruction class in

H^{1}(\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)\setminus X_{\mathrm{seam}},\mathbb{Z}/2)
that
no scalar correction to
V
can produce.

Chapter
9
—
\mathcal{L}_{6}
, electronic structure.

\mathcal{L}_{6}
replaces the single surface
V(R)
with a Hilbert bundle

\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{el}}\to\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)
whose fibre at
R

is the electronic Hilbert space, together with the Berry connection

A_{mn}
on the adiabatic eigenbundles.
For real molecular Hamiltonians the primary topological invariant is
the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-valued Berry phase

[\gamma_{B}]\in H^{1}(\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)\setminus X_{\mathrm{seam}},\mathbb{Z}/2)
, which records the parity of conical-intersection
encirclements of a loop and thereby distinguishes thermal from
photochemical pathways.
Non-adiabatic couplings, avoided crossings, and geometric-phase
effects are all morphism-level structure at
\mathcal{L}_{6}
.

Forcing
\mathcal{L}_{7}
.

The ortho/para statistical split of
\mathrm{H}_{2}
, and more
generally the superselection structure distinguishing identical
nuclei by spin, is absent from any electronic bundle over a classical
nuclear configuration space; nuclear indistinguishability demands a
quantum treatment of all particles.

Chapter
10
—
\mathcal{L}_{7}
, full quantum structure.

\mathcal{L}_{7}
is the target of a candidate
object-level
functor

F_{7}^{\mathrm{obj}}\colon\mathcal{L}_{6}(P)\to\mathbf{C}^{*}\mathbf{Alg}_{\mathrm{cont}}

into continuous fields of
C^{*}
-algebras: states live on

\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{full}})
, nuclear statistics are
enforced by a groupoid
C^{*}
-algebra
C^{*}(\mathfrak{G})
for

\mathfrak{G}=G^{*}\ltimes\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)
, and the
Born–Oppenheimer approximation becomes the
\varepsilon\to 0

fibre of a continuous field
\{A_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon\in[0,1]}

in the parameter
\varepsilon=(m_{e}/M)^{1/2}
, in the sense of
strict deformation quantisation.
This chapter is different in character from its predecessors: the
physical necessity of
\mathcal{L}_{7}
is established beyond doubt, but its
mathematical construction as a complete categorical level is a
research programme rather than a completed theory.
Four constructions (C1–C4) are stated as formal conjectures; the
chapter separates what is proved, what is formal, and what is
genuinely open, and identifies the tools from the existing literature
that wait to be assembled.
The Woolley–Primas problem of recovering molecular identity as an
effective superselection or correlation-sector label is developed
in depth (§
10
) as the tower statement of C4.
A careful warning records what large kinetic isotope effects can
and cannot serve as forcing evidence for
\mathcal{L}_{7}
: anomalous primary
KIEs of order
10^{2}
–
10^{3}
, although routinely cited as evidence
for “quantum nuclei,” are reproducible by semiclassical or
path-integral approximations built from
\mathcal{L}_{5}
-level geometric
data and so do not by themselves force the full
\mathcal{L}_{7}
structure.

Chapter
11
— the Para enrichment (perpendicular dimension).

Running perpendicular to the exact tower is a second axis: every
level
\mathcal{L}_{k}
admits a Para enrichment

\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}:=\mathrm{Lax\text{-}Alg}_{M_{k}}(\mathrm{Para}(\mathcal{L}_{k}))

of parametric
M_{k}
-equivariant maps in the sense of Gavranović
et al.
[
112
]
.
The Para enrichment is
not
an additional tower level — it
runs alongside every level simultaneously — and every
machine-learning model for chemistry is a morphism in exactly one

\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}
: yield predictors at
\mathcal{L}_{0}^{\mathrm{Para}}
,
neural-ODE kinetic surrogates at
\mathcal{L}_{3}^{\mathrm{Para}}
,

E(3)
-equivariant force fields at
\mathcal{L}_{5}^{\mathrm{Para}}
, neural
wavefunctions at
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para}}
.
Equivariance and thermodynamic-consistency constraints are thereby

theorems
at the relevant level, not architectural choices;
a model violating them is not an object of the corresponding

\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}
.
The chapter organises around three structural questions an
architecture poses to the tower: whether its equivariance is a
theorem or a design choice, what it can represent independently of
its training data (
categorical completeness
at level
k
),
and which tower-coherence conditions it enforces.
Three architectural incompleteness results for the current
published literature follow: the Eyring transition-state-theory
coherence gap (no model couples its learned rate law to the
activation barrier of its own potential surface;

\mathcal{L}_{3}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{5}
), the Wegscheider consistency gap
(forward and reverse rate constants unconstrained by the model’s
own
\Delta G
;
\mathcal{L}_{2}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{3}
), and the
topological output-type gap (a scalar-energy output cannot carry
the Berry-phase invariant
[\gamma_{B}]
regardless of training,
body order, or receptive field;
\mathcal{L}_{5}\to\mathcal{L}_{6}
).
MACE serves as the primary worked example at
\mathcal{L}_{5}^{\mathrm{Para}}
,
So3krates and SO3LR as a paired comparison of architectural designs
at the same level, and the QIM triply-directed encoder of Fallani
et al.
[
89
]
as the running case study at the

\mathcal{L}_{5}
–
\mathcal{L}_{6}
boundary.

Chapter
12
— the simulation functor.

The final chapter delivers a single operational functor

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}\colon\mathbf{Para}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{0}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{2}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{3}\bigr)\;\longrightarrow\;\mathbf{Kl}(\mathsf{IO})

into the Kleisli category of the probabilistic sub-monad of Haskell

IO
, instantiated as a working stochastic simulator of the
Briggs–Rauscher oscillating reaction in the De Kepper–Epstein
twelve-channel formulation
[
74
]
.
Each modelling choice in the source is a morphism in a named tower
category: species populations are elements of the free commutative
monoid at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
; atom and charge balance are
\mathcal{L}_{0}
structural
checks on the stoichiometric matrix; Wegscheider’s relations on the
paired forward/reverse channels (R3/R3-rev and R4/R4-rev) enforce

\mathcal{L}_{1}
–
\mathcal{L}_{2}
thermochemistry; and the scalar rate constants together
with the rate-law saturation forms feed a Markov kernel
F_{P}
at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
,
realised twice from the same network value — by the Gibson–Bruck
next-reaction method (SSA) and, in the large-volume limit, by the
implicit-midpoint mass-action ODE.
The ionic Process A versus radical Process B distinction — the
canonical
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
forcing pair of the Briggs–Rauscher
system, sharing the same overall stoichiometry and the same bulk
HOI-production rate form — lives at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
and is provably
invisible to the simulator by construction: the chemical motivation
for locating the simulation precisely at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
–
\mathcal{L}_{3}
and no
higher.
Three lax cells of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
—
\alpha
(parameter unit),

\phi_{\mathrm{SSA}}
(IO non-commutativity, vanishing in total
variation), and
\phi_{\mathrm{ODE}}
(Kurtz-limit deviation,
non-trivial in the low-copy quiescent phase) — are identifiable
line-by-line in the source.
A denotational companion
\Phi_{\mathrm{den}}:=F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}

marginalises over the pseudorandom seed and lands in the Markov
category
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
, restoring the Markov structure that

\mathbf{Kl}(\mathsf{IO})
does not itself support.
To our knowledge this provides both the first published Kleisli
semantics of the Gillespie next-reaction method and the first
application of the Para construction outside machine learning.
A separate
\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{3}
parameter projection
\pi_{4}
embeds
bond-level mechanism data into scalar rate constants plus rate-law
saturation forms, making the chapter’s several network variants
(canonical De Kepper–Epstein, buffered-
\mathrm{H}^{+}
, Furrow-like
pooled) different
\mathcal{L}_{3}
reductions of the same underlying
mechanism, comparable as Markov kernels in
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
.
The simulation results verify three structural predictions of the
framework: the relaxation-oscillator dynamics emerge from both the
SSA samples and the ODE Kurtz limit; the two simulators agree in
the high-copy spike phase and diverge in the low-copy quiescent
phase, making the
\phi
-cell distinction operationally visible;
and the form of the divergence is interpretable through the Kurtz
theorem rather than as numerical accident.
The framework’s deliverable is not a validation of the tower but
the discipline of distinguishing, in a working simulator, which
features are essential, which are tunable parameters of
\Theta_{\mathrm{sim}}
,
and which are scale-dependent fictions of the chosen
representation.

Four coloured environments serve mathematical and chemical audiences
simultaneously throughout: green for chemical content, blue for
categorical statements, orange for forcing pairs, and purple for the
conceptual connections between them.

§1.4. A brief guide to categorical language

This subsection introduces the categorical vocabulary;
readers comfortable with enriched category theory may proceed directly
to Chapter
2
.

Category theory provides the mathematical grammar of this programme.
The compact dictionary below is aimed at readers fluent in chemistry
or physics but new to categorical ideas; every term is paired with
its chemical meaning and a concrete example.

Category.

A
category

\mathcal{C}
consists of:

•

a collection of
objects
— the states or species pools
under study;

•

for each ordered pair of objects
X,Y
, a set
\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)
of

morphisms
from
X
to
Y
, i.e. all processes or
transformations that lead from state
X
to state
Y
;

•

a
composition law
: if
f\in\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)
and

g\in\mathrm{Hom}(Y,Z)
, their composite
g\circ f\in\mathrm{Hom}(X,Z)
is the
process obtained by performing
f
first and then
g
;

•

for each object
X
, an
identity morphism

\mathrm{id}_{X}\in\mathrm{Hom}(X,X)
— the trivial “do-nothing” process;

satisfying
associativity

(h\circ g)\circ f=h\circ(g\circ f)

and
unitality

\mathrm{id}_{Y}\circ f=f=f\circ\mathrm{id}_{X}

[
253
,
187
]
.

Chemical meaning.

Objects are
complexes
— formal non-negative integer combinations
of chemical species such as
\mathrm{CH_{4}}+2\,\mathrm{O_{2}}
.
The term
complex
is standard in chemical reaction network
theory
[
96
]
: it denotes precisely one side of a balanced
reaction equation.
Morphisms are
reactions
or multi-step pathways between complexes.
The identity
\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}}
is the “no reaction” process on complex

\mathbf{u}
; composition
r_{2}\circ r_{1}
chains two steps sequentially.

A key example:
B\mathbb{R}
.

The real line forms a one-object category
B\mathbb{R}
with a single object

*
and one morphism
a\in\mathbb{R}
for each real number, with composition

b\circ a:=a+b
.
Think of
B\mathbb{R}
as a single node with one directed arrow per real number:
concatenating two arrows means adding their labels.
A functor
F_{H}\colon\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
assigns to every reaction a real
number (e.g. enthalpy
\Delta H
) that is automatically additive along
sequential and parallel steps — this is the categorical formulation of
Hess’s Law, developed fully at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
.

Functor.

A
functor

F\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
is a
structure-preserving map between categories: it sends each object
X

to an object
F(X)
and each morphism
f\colon X\to Y
to a morphism

F(f)\colon F(X)\to F(Y)
, respecting composition
(
F(g\circ f)=F(g)\circ F(f)
) and identities
(
F(\mathrm{id}_{X})=\mathrm{id}_{F(X)}
).

Chemical meaning.

A functor from the reaction category into
B\mathbb{R}
is a
consistent
numerical scoring
of reactions: it assigns a real number to each
elementary step in a way that the score of any sequential or parallel
combination is the sum of the individual scores.
Enthalpy (
\Delta H
), Gibbs free energy (
\Delta G
), and entropy
change (
\Delta S
) are all consistent scorings of this kind — each
is a functor from the appropriate tower level into
B\mathbb{R}
.
The functoriality conditions (
F(g\circ f)=F(g)\circ F(f)
and

F(\mathrm{id})=0
) are precisely the additivity and trivial-process conditions
these thermodynamic quantities must satisfy.

Monoidal category.

A
monoidal category

(\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
is a category
equipped with a
tensor product

\otimes\colon\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
combining two
objects or morphisms “in parallel”, a
unit object

I

satisfying
I\otimes X\cong X\cong X\otimes I
, and coherent
isomorphisms
(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z\xrightarrow{\sim}X\otimes(Y\otimes Z)
(associator) and
I\otimes X\xrightarrow{\sim}X
,

X\otimes I\xrightarrow{\sim}X
(unitors).
When the associator and unitors are identity maps, the category is

strict monoidal

[
187
]
.

Chemical meaning.

X\otimes Y
is the
mixture
of
X
and
Y
:

\mathrm{CH_{4}}\otimes 2\,\mathrm{O_{2}}
is the mixture

\mathrm{CH_{4}}+2\,\mathrm{O_{2}}
.
The unit object is the empty mixture
\mathbf{0}\in\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
.
Since addition in
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
is already strictly associative and

\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}
, the associator and unitors are
identity maps: the tensor is
strict
monoidal for chemical
mixtures.

Symmetric monoidal category.

A monoidal category is
symmetric
if there is a coherent family
of isomorphisms
\sigma_{X,Y}\colon X\otimes Y\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}Y\otimes X
.
In chemistry: a solution “of
A
and
B
” is the same system as one
“of
B
and
A
”; no experiment distinguishes the two descriptions,
so the symmetry isomorphism is physically mandatory.
All symmetric monoidal categories in this chapter are

permutative
: symmetric
strict
monoidal.
In this manuscript an acronym “SMC” is used for symmetric monoidal category and “permutative” for symmetric strict monoidal.
Theorem
2.14
holds for any strict SMC codomain; the primary
application uses
B\mathbb{R}
, which is permutative.

Free construction.

A
free
object on given generators is the most general object of
its type built from those generators, subject to
no
relations
beyond those forced by the axioms of the type.

Example.

The free group on one generator is
\mathbb{Z}
— the integers with addition.
Starting from the generator
+1
and its inverse
-1
, all combinations
by addition are formed; no shortcut is imposed (“
+1
applied three
times” is never identified with “
+2
applied twice” unless the group
axioms force it, which they do not).
The result is the smallest group containing the generator, with no
redundant identifications
[
187
]
.
The key property is
universality
: once
+1
is sent to any
element
g
of a target group
G
, the entire homomorphism
\mathbb{Z}\to G

is uniquely forced (
n\mapsto ng
).

Chemical meaning.

No equivalences
between distinct reaction labels are imposed beyond
those forced by the permutative axioms.
Two routes
r_{1},r_{2}
with the same reactant and product complexes are
kept as distinct morphisms at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
: no physical identification —
same
\Delta H
, same rate, same mechanism — is made until the tower
level at which that information first becomes available.
Once you fix where each species and each reaction label map in a target
category, the entire strict symmetric monoidal functor out of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

is uniquely forced (Theorem
2.14
): there is no modelling
choice left.

Commutative diagram.

A diagram of objects and morphisms
commutes
when every directed
path between the same two objects yields the same composite morphism.
The following example shows what this means in stoichiometric terms.

Commutative diagrams in stoichiometry: nitrogen oxidation

Consider two routes from
\mathrm{N_{2}}+2\,\mathrm{O_{2}}
to

2\,\mathrm{NO_{2}}
, with species ordered

(\mathrm{N_{2}},\mathrm{O_{2}},\mathrm{NO},\mathrm{NO_{2}})
:

where
r_{1}\colon\mathrm{N_{2}}+\mathrm{O_{2}}\to 2\,\mathrm{NO}

and
r_{2}\colon 2\,\mathrm{NO}+\mathrm{O_{2}}\to 2\,\mathrm{NO_{2}}
.
The functor
F_{\Delta\nu}\colon\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to(\mathbb{Z}^{4},+)
assigns each
reaction its net stoichiometric change vector:

\Delta\nu(r_{1})=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\
-1\\
+2\\
0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Delta\nu(r_{2})=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
-1\\
-2\\
+2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Delta\nu(r_{\mathrm{direct}})=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\
-2\\
0\\
+2\end{pmatrix}.

The diagram commutes in
(\mathbb{Z}^{4},+)
if and only if

\Delta\nu(r_{\mathrm{direct}})=\Delta\nu(r_{1})+\Delta\nu(r_{2})
,
which holds: both sides equal
(-1,-2,0,+2)^{\top}
.
This is
atom balance
— the net species change is the same
whether the reaction proceeds directly or via the nitric oxide
intermediate.
Functoriality
F_{\Delta\nu}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})=F_{\Delta\nu}(r_{2})+F_{\Delta\nu}(r_{1})

is
atom balance: it encodes a column of
the stoichiometric matrix
N
as commutativity of a triangle.
Any violation would mean atoms are created or destroyed along one route,
i.e.
F_{\Delta\nu}
is not a functor.

Petri net.

Petri nets
were introduced by Carl Adam Petri in 1962 as a
mathematical framework for concurrent processes
[
240
]
.
Places hold tokens (molecular populations of species) and transitions
represent reactions, consuming tokens from input places and depositing
tokens into output places according to stoichiometric arc multiplicities.
This is exactly the combinatorial skeleton of stoichiometric
chemistry
[
221
,
172
]
.
The precise definition, a worked chemical example, and the construction
of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
from a Petri net are given in §
2.2
.

The central gain of the categorical framework

A category is a precise language for processes that compose sequentially
and run in parallel.
A functor is a consistent numerical scoring of those processes.
Once a thermodynamic or kinetic quantity is identified as a functor from
the reaction category into an appropriate target, its core properties
— additivity along sequences, additivity over parallel reactions —
become
theorems
rather than separate postulates.

Each higher tower level adds a specific categorical extension to
the previous level: a new functor, an enrichment of the morphism
category by a symmetry, a geometric decoration, a topological
invariant, or (at the final step) a deformation of the algebraic
structure itself.
The taxonomy of the six extension types that arise across the
present tower is recorded in §
10.8
;
each is forced at its level by a concrete pair of reactions the
previous level cannot distinguish.
Freeness means no equivalences between reactions are imposed beyond
those forced by the algebra of mixtures; every reaction is kept
distinct unless explicitly identified for a physical reason.

Reading the tower as an ML foundation.

Each level
\mathcal{L}_{k}
admits a perpendicular Para enrichment

\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}
of parametric equivariant maps
(Chapter
11
).
The exact level
\mathcal{L}_{k}
is recovered as the zero-parameter limit of

\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}
; architectures for machine-learning models of
chemistry — yield predictors, equivariant force fields, learned
wavefunctions — are lax algebra morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}
,
with equivariance and thermodynamic-consistency constraints
following from universal properties rather than from architectural
choices.

In summary: a stoichiometric scheme equipped with sequential
composition (one reaction following another), parallel composition
(reactions in independent mixtures), and order-independence of
mixtures is the defining data of a
symmetric monoidal
category
; assigning numerical chemical content is providing a

functor
; starting from the most general such structure is
taking the
free
construction.

Monad.

A
monad
on a category
\mathcal{C}
is an endofunctor

T\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
(a functor whose source and
target are the same category) equipped with two natural
transformations (coherent families of morphisms, one per object):
a
unit

\eta\colon\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{C}}\Rightarrow T
that injects
each object
X
into a
T
-decorated version
T(X)
, and a

multiplication

\mu\colon T\circ T\Rightarrow T
that
collapses two layers of decoration into one.
These satisfy associativity (
\mu\circ T\mu=\mu\circ\mu T
) and unit
laws (
\mu\circ T\eta=\mu\circ\eta T=\mathrm{id}_{T}
)
[
187
,
253
]
.

Operational meaning.

A monad packages a kind of “effect” or “extra structure” that
maps can carry while remaining composable — randomness, state,
partial information, time, or symmetry.

T(X)
is to be read as “a computation that ultimately yields a
value of type
X
while carrying the effect of
T
”;
\eta

produces a trivially-decorated value, and
\mu
is what makes two
effectful computations compose into a single one.

The Kleisli category.

The natural setting for
T
-effectful computations is the

Kleisli category

\mathbf{Kl}(T)
, which has the same
objects as
\mathcal{C}
but takes morphisms
X\to Y
to be

\mathcal{C}
-morphisms
X\to T(Y)
.
The composite of
f\colon X\to T(Y)
and
g\colon Y\to T(Z)
is

g\bullet f\;:=\;\mu_{Z}\circ T(g)\circ f\;\colon\;X\to T(Z),

lifting
g
to act on
T(Y)
via
T
’s functoriality, then
flattening the resulting
T(T(Z))
via
\mu
.

Key example:
\mathbf{Kl}(\mathsf{IO})
.

Haskell’s
\mathsf{IO}
monad packages every interaction with the
outside world — file reads, terminal output, random-number
generation — into the type
\mathsf{IO}(X)
of computations that
eventually produce an
X
, possibly with side effects on the way.
A morphism in
\mathbf{Kl}(\mathsf{IO})
from
X
to
Y
is then a
function
X\to\mathsf{IO}(Y)
: a procedure that, given an input,
may consume random bits or perform other side effects and yields an
output.
Stochastic simulation of a reaction network is exactly such a
procedure: the operational functor
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
of
Chapter
12
lands in the Kleisli category of the

probabilistic sub-monad
of
\mathsf{IO}
— the sub-monad
generated by pseudo-random-number sampling.

§2.
\mathcal{L}_{0}
: The Stoichiometric Level

The simplest possible question about a chemical reaction is:

what goes in and what comes out?

Before energy, before time, before geometry, before mechanism —
purely the bookkeeping of species consumed and produced.

Three structural features are present at this barest level of description:

(a)

Steps compose.

If reaction
r_{1}
produces a species that reaction
r_{2}
consumes,
the two steps together form a new composite reaction
r_{2}\circ r_{1}
.

(b)

Steps run in parallel.

Two reactions that do not interfere with each other can be combined
into a joint process
r_{1}\otimes r_{2}
, run simultaneously.

(c)

The ordering of independent species is irrelevant.

There is no intrinsic left-to-right order in a mixture;

A+B
and
B+A
describe the same physical system.

Expressing these structural features in a precise mathematical language
— rather than leaving them as implicit chemical common sense —
makes it possible to prove rigorously which properties follow from
which hypotheses and to compare different levels of chemical description
on equal footing.
The language appropriate to features (a)–(c) is that of

symmetric monoidal categories
: mathematical structures carrying
exactly the sequential, parallel, and order-irrelevant composition
grammar those features demand.
This language was established by Meseguer and
Montanari
[
221
]
for Petri nets, and extended
into a compositional framework for open reaction networks by Baez and
Pollard
[
28
]
.
The exact tower backbone developed in this chapter and the
subsequent ones admits a perpendicular Para-enrichment dimension
(Chapter
11
, building on
Gavranović et al.
[
112
]
) which places
machine-learning models for chemistry
[
7
,
98
]

on an exact mathematical foundation as parametric equivariant maps
over the same tower levels.

A brief categorical glossary, aimed at readers fluent in chemistry
or physics but new to category theory, is provided in §
1.4
.

§2.1. Species, complexes, and the stoichiometric monoid

Stoichiometry
is the branch of chemistry concerned with the
quantitative relationships between species in a chemical reaction:
how many molecules of each substance are consumed, and how many are
produced.
For a mathematician, it is the study of the additive structure of
molecular populations — which integer combinations of named species
can appear as the left- or right-hand side of a balanced equation,
and how those combinations pool together.
No energy, no dynamics, no geometry: purely the arithmetic of
molecular counts.

The algebraic object capturing this arithmetic is the
free
commutative monoid
on the set of species.

Definition 2.1

(Species and the stoichiometric monoid)
.

Fix a finite set
\mathcal{S}
of
chemical species

(e.g.
\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{H_{2}O,\,CH_{4},\,O_{2},\,CO_{2}}\}
).
Species are abstract labels at this level; no geometric, electronic,
or energetic information is attached.

The
stoichiometric monoid
is the free commutative monoid on
\mathcal{S}
:

\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\;:=\;\Bigl\{\,\textstyle\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}n_{S}\cdot S\;\Big|\;n_{S}\in\mathbb{N},\;\text{all but finitely many }n_{S}=0\,\Bigr\},

(1)

with binary operation

\bigl(\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot S\bigr)+\bigl(\sum_{S}m_{S}\cdot S\bigr):=\sum_{S}(n_{S}+m_{S})\cdot S

and identity element
\mathbf{0}
(the empty complex, “vacuum”).
Elements of
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
are called
complexes
.

Remark 2.2

(Relation to prior mathematical treatments of stoichiometry)
.

The stoichiometric matrix
N\in\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|\times|\mathcal{R}|}
, which encodes
the net change in species counts per reaction, has been the standard
mathematical representation of stoichiometry since the foundational work
of Feinberg
[
92
,
96
]
and
Horn–Jackson
[
146
]
.
Meseguer–Montanari
[
221
]
recognise that Petri
net semantics naturally produces free commutative monoids, and
Baez–Master
[
27
]
exploit this structure for open Petri
nets.
The present treatment differs in making the
universal property
of

\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
the primary organising principle of the stoichiometric level,
rather than a computational convenience: every additive species
observable — mass, atom count, enthalpy, any additive potential —
is exactly a function out of
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
induced by the universal
property, and the entire tower of functors in Chapters 3–10 is built
by iterating this observation upward.
The stoichiometric matrix
N
is recovered as the linear-algebraic
shadow of this structure in §
2.6
.

The claim that
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
as defined above
is
the free
commutative monoid on
\mathcal{S}
— not merely a commutative monoid
containing
\mathcal{S}
— is a theorem whose proof is immediate but worth
making explicit, since the universal property it establishes is the
algebraic engine of everything that follows.

Proposition 2.3

(
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
is the free commutative monoid on
\mathcal{S}
)
.

For any commutative monoid
(M,+,0)
and any function
f:\mathcal{S}\to M
,
there exists a
unique
monoid homomorphism

\bar{f}:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to M
satisfying
\bar{f}(S)=f(S)
for all

S\in\mathcal{S}
, given concretely by

\bar{f}\!\Bigl(\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}n_{S}\cdot S\Bigr)\;=\;\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}n_{S}\cdot f(S),

where
n\cdot m
denotes the
n
-fold sum
m+\cdots+m
in
M
.

Proof.

Existence.

Define
\bar{f}
by the displayed formula.
Since only finitely many
n_{S}
are non-zero, the sum is finite and

\bar{f}
is well-defined.
It is a monoid homomorphism:

\displaystyle\bar{f}(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})

\displaystyle=\bar{f}\!\Bigl(\sum_{S}(n_{S}+m_{S})\cdot S\Bigr)=\sum_{S}(n_{S}+m_{S})\cdot f(S)

\displaystyle=\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot f(S)+\sum_{S}m_{S}\cdot f(S)=\bar{f}(\mathbf{u})+\bar{f}(\mathbf{v}),

and
\bar{f}(\mathbf{0})=\sum_{S}0\cdot f(S)=0_{M}
.

Uniqueness.

Any monoid homomorphism
g:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to M
extending
f
must satisfy,
by the homomorphism property applied
n_{S}
times,

g(n_{S}\cdot S)=n_{S}\cdot g(S)=n_{S}\cdot f(S)
.
Additivity then forces

g\bigl(\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot S\bigr)=\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot f(S)=\bar{f}\bigl(\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot S\bigr)
,
so
g=\bar{f}
.
∎

What is a complex?

A complex is what chemists call one “side” of a balanced equation.
For
\mathrm{CH_{4}}+2\,\mathrm{O_{2}}\to\mathrm{CO_{2}}+2\,\mathrm{H_{2}O}
,
the reactant complex is
1\cdot\mathrm{CH_{4}}+2\cdot\mathrm{O_{2}}

and the product complex is
1\cdot\mathrm{CO_{2}}+2\cdot\mathrm{H_{2}O}
,
both elements of
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
.

The monoid operation is simply
pooling
:

(1\cdot\mathrm{CH_{4}}+2\cdot\mathrm{O_{2}})+(1\cdot\mathrm{CO_{2}}+2\cdot\mathrm{H_{2}O})=1\cdot\mathrm{CH_{4}}+2\cdot\mathrm{O_{2}}+1\cdot\mathrm{CO_{2}}+2\cdot\mathrm{H_{2}O}.

This is the mathematical version of mixing two portions together.
The reaction arrow says: this pool transforms into that pool.
The monoid carries no information about whether or how the transformation
occurs; that belongs to later levels of the tower.

Proposition
2.3
makes precise something a chemist already
knows: once you decide what numerical value to assign to each individual
species (its mass, its atom count, its standard enthalpy of
formation, …), the value for any complex is completely forced —
there is no choice.
The total mass of
1\cdot\mathrm{CH_{4}}+2\cdot\mathrm{O_{2}}
is

M(\mathrm{CH_{4}})+2\,M(\mathrm{O_{2}})
and nothing else; the universal
property is precisely the theorem that says this.

Universal properties are one of the central organising tools of category
theory: MacLane
[
187
]
identifies them as the concept that
unifies free constructions, adjunctions, and limits, and
Riehl
[
253
]
shows systematically how they eliminate arbitrary
choices from mathematical definitions.
The stoichiometric monoid
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
is the
universal
receptacle
for additive species data: any quantity that is additive over species —
mass, elemental composition, standard enthalpy of formation — extends
uniquely to all complexes via Proposition
2.3
, with no
modelling freedom left.
Moreover, the universal property of
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
is the first in a chain:
the universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
(Theorem
2.14
) extends
it one step further, from species and complexes to reactions and their
composites, and every subsequent tower level adds one more universal
property governing the next kind of chemical data.

Universal property of
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]

Let
(M,+,0)
be any commutative monoid — for instance

(\mathbb{R},+,0)
,
(\mathbb{N}^{|\mathsf{E}|},+,\mathbf{0})
, or

(\mathbb{R}_{>0},\times,1)
— and let
f:\mathcal{S}\to M
be any function
assigning an element of
M
to each species.
Proposition
2.3
guarantees two things:

(i)

Existence.
There is a monoid homomorphism

\bar{f}:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to M
extending
f
, given by

\bar{f}\!\bigl(\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot S\bigr)=\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot f(S)
.

(ii)

Uniqueness.

\bar{f}
is the
only
monoid
homomorphism
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to M
that agrees with
f
on individual
species.

Concretely: once you decide what value each species receives, the value
of every complex is completely determined — there is no freedom left.
This universal property is invoked at every level of the tower:
atom-balance maps (
f(S)=
elemental composition of
S
) extend to
all complexes and reaction stoichiometries (§
2.6
);
enthalpy assignments (
f(S)=\Delta H^{\circ}_{f}(S)
) extend to Hess
networks (
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, §3); and rate assignments extend to kinetic
networks (
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, §5).

Remark 2.4

(Rate constants are not species data)
.

Rate constants are associated with
reactions
, not with individual
species, and so lie outside the scope of Proposition
2.3
.
The universal property of
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
applies to species-level
assignments only.
Rate-constant data enters at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
as part of the kinetic functor

F_{P}
, whose domain is the category of reactions
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, not the
monoid of complexes
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
; its universal property is
Theorem
2.14
.

§2.2. Petri nets: the categorical input data

This subsection gives the precise definition of a Petri net and
establishes the category
\mathbf{Petri}
of all Petri nets.
The raw data of a stoichiometric scheme is a finite list of species and a
finite list of reaction labels, each label carrying a source complex (reactants) and
a target complex (products) in
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
This structure is a
Petri net
, introduced by Carl Adam Petri in
1962 as a mathematical framework for concurrent
processes
[
240
]
, and recognised by Meseguer–Montanari to be
the natural input data for free symmetric monoidal
categories
[
221
]
.
The stoichiometric category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is the free categorical structure
generated by a Petri net
P
: one imposes no relations beyond those
forced by the axioms of a symmetric monoidal category.
The free construction occupies §
2.3
.

Definition 2.5

(Petri net
[
240
,
221
,
172
]
)
.

A
Petri net
is a quadruple
P=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},s,t)
where

\mathcal{S}
is a finite set of
species
,

\mathcal{R}
is a finite set of
reaction labels
,
and
s,t:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
assign to each label
r\in\mathcal{R}
its

source complex

s(r)
and
target complex

t(r)
, with
s(r)\neq t(r)
in general.

A Petri net in chemistry: hydrogen combustion

Consider the net stoichiometry of hydrogen combustion:

2\,\mathrm{H_{2}}\;+\;\mathrm{O_{2}}\;\xrightarrow{\;r\;}\;2\,\mathrm{H_{2}O}.

As a Petri net:
\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{H_{2}},\,\mathrm{O_{2}},\,\mathrm{H_{2}O}\}
,

\mathcal{R}=\{r\}
, with

s(r)=2\cdot\mathrm{H_{2}}+1\cdot\mathrm{O_{2}}\;\in\;\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|},\qquad t(r)=2\cdot\mathrm{H_{2}O}\;\in\;\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}.

In the standard Petri net picture, each species is a
place

(a pool holding molecular tokens) and each reaction is a

transition
(consuming tokens from its input places and depositing
tokens into its output places according to the stoichiometric
coefficients).
The arc multiplicities
(2,1,2)
encode stoichiometry; the transition

r
has no internal structure beyond its input and output counts.

What the Petri net captures.

The stoichiometric ratios
(2{:}1{:}2)
, the direction of transformation,
and the connectivity between species and reaction.
Conservation vectors can be computed from the stoichiometric matrix

N
alone (see §
2.6
): here, hydrogen-atom balance gives

w_{\mathrm{H}}=(2,0,2)^{\top}
, confirming two H atoms in each

\mathrm{H_{2}}
and two H atoms in each
\mathrm{H_{2}O}
.

What the Petri net deliberately omits.

•

Energy
: the standard enthalpy of combustion

\Delta H^{\circ}=-484\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

[
60
]

is not part of
P
; it enters at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
.

•

Rate
: the pre-exponential factor and activation energy are
absent; they enter at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

•

Mechanism
: whether the reaction proceeds via radical
intermediates (
\mathrm{H}
,
\mathrm{OH}
,
\mathrm{HO_{2}}
) or in
a single elementary step is invisible at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
; mechanism enters
at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.

•

Geometry
: bond lengths, angles, and three-dimensional
structure are absent; they enter at
\mathcal{L}_{5}
.

The Petri net is the
skeletal
description: the minimal
combinatorial input from which the categorical construction
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

is built. Every additional piece of chemical information corresponds to
additional structure at a higher tower level.

Remark 2.6

(Reaction labels are named generators)
.

\mathcal{R}
is a set of named generators, not a set of ordered pairs of
complexes.
Two distinct labels
r_{1},r_{2}\in\mathcal{R}
with
s(r_{1})=s(r_{2})
and

t(r_{1})=t(r_{2})
represent two different reactions between the same
complexes — for instance, two mechanistically distinct routes with the
same net stoichiometry.
The free construction of §
2.3
keeps them as
distinct generators; no physical identification is imposed until a later
level.

Petri nets assemble into a category: one can map one network into
another by translating species and reaction labels while respecting
stoichiometry, and these translations compose in the obvious way.
This categorical structure on Petri nets is established in
Meseguer–Montanari
[
221
]
and is needed for two
reasons: it allows chemical networks to be compared and translated
systematically, and it ensures that the construction

P\mapsto\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is itself a functor between categories rather than
an ad hoc assignment.

Definition 2.7

(The category
\mathbf{Petri}
)
.

\mathbf{Petri}
is the category whose objects are Petri nets and whose
morphisms
f:P\to P^{\prime}
are pairs
(f_{\mathcal{S}},f_{\mathcal{R}})
of functions

f_{\mathcal{S}}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\qquad f_{\mathcal{R}}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{R}^{\prime},

satisfying the
source–target compatibility conditions

s^{\prime}\circ f_{\mathcal{R}}=\bar{f}_{\mathcal{S}}\circ s,\qquad t^{\prime}\circ f_{\mathcal{R}}=\bar{f}_{\mathcal{S}}\circ t,

where
\bar{f}_{\mathcal{S}}:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}^{\prime}|}
is the unique monoid
homomorphism extending
f_{\mathcal{S}}
(Proposition
2.3
).
Composition is componentwise; the identity on
P
is
(\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{S}},\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{R}})
.

Remark 2.8

(What a Petri morphism does)
.

A morphism
f:P\to P^{\prime}
translates species to species and reaction
labels to reaction labels, in a way that respects stoichiometry: if

r
has source complex
\mathbf{u}
in
P
, then
f_{\mathcal{R}}(r)
has source
complex
\bar{f}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathbf{u})
in
P^{\prime}
, and similarly for targets.
Non-injectivity is permitted: a non-injective
f_{\mathcal{S}}
coarsens species
(merging two species into one); a non-injective
f_{\mathcal{R}}
equates two
distinct reaction labels at the stoichiometric level.
The compatibility conditions are exactly what is needed for

\bar{f}_{\mathcal{S}}
— the unique extension supplied by
Proposition
2.3
— to be well-defined on complexes built
from the translated species.

§2.3. The stoichiometric category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

The categorical language of §
1.4
now assembles into
a single construction.
A
permutative category
is a strict symmetric monoidal category:
associativity and unit hold as strict equalities, while the symmetry

\sigma_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\to Y\otimes X
remains a (possibly
non-trivial) isomorphism between two distinct objects.
The category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
we construct is a
skeletal
permutative
category: in addition to the strict associativity and unit, the
underlying object monoid
(\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|},+,\mathbf{0})
is itself
strictly commutative, so
\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}

holds as an equality of objects, not merely as an isomorphism.
This skeletal structure is forced on us by chemistry: a mixture has
no intrinsic ordering, so
A+B
and
B+A
must literally name the
same complex.
The non-trivial symmetry
\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}:\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\to\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}
then becomes an
endomorphism encoding the permutation data that a non-skeletal
permutative category would store in distinct objects.

A Petri net
P
provides the chemical generators of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
: the
species
\mathcal{S}
generate the objects (via
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
), and the
reaction labels
\mathcal{R}
become the basic morphisms, each typed by its
source and target complex.
The
free
skeletal permutative category on
P
is built from
these generators by closing under sequential composition, parallel
tensor, and the structural morphisms (identities and symmetries),
imposing
only
the permutative axioms and no additional chemical
identifications.
This is
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

Definition 2.9

(Stoichiometric category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
)
.

Let
P=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},s,t)
be a Petri net.
The
stoichiometric category

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is the
free
permutative category
on
P

[
221
,
172
]
:
the unique (up to strict symmetric monoidal equivalence) permutative
category satisfying the following.

(i)

Objects.

The object set is
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, with monoidal product

\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{v}:=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}

and monoidal unit
\mathbf{0}
.
Since
+
is commutative in
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, the tensor is strictly
commutative:
\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}\otimes\mathbf{u}
as the same object.
Associativity and unitality are also strict.

(ii)

Generating morphisms.

The morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
have two distinct origins.

•

Chemical generators (input data).

The reaction generators
r:s(r)\to t(r)
for each

r\in\mathcal{R}
, supplied by the Petri net
P
.
These are the only chemical input.

•

Structural morphisms (forced by the skeletal
permutative structure).

The identity morphisms

\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}}:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{u}
for each

\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, and the symmetry endomorphisms

\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}:\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\to\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}
for each pair

\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
These are not chemical input; they are forced on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

by the requirement that it be a skeletal permutative category
at all.

The symmetry
\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}
is an endomorphism —
not an isomorphism between two distinct objects — because

\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}
as the same element
of
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, the skeletal property of item (i) above.

(iii)

All morphisms.

Closed under sequential composition
g\circ f

(when
\operatorname{cod}(f)=\operatorname{dom}(g)
, which holds in general as chemistry demands it)
and parallel tensor
f\otimes g
.

(iv)

Relations.

Morphisms are equivalence classes under the smallest congruence
compatible with
\circ
and
\otimes
generated by the

permutative axioms
:
identity laws; associativity of
\circ
; interchange

(g_{1}\otimes g_{2})\circ(f_{1}\otimes f_{2})=(g_{1}\circ f_{1})\otimes(g_{2}\circ f_{2})
;
tensor unit; involutivity of
\sigma
; naturality of
\sigma
;
and the hexagon axiom (all defined in
Remark
2.10
below).

No
equation
r_{1}\equiv r_{2}
is imposed for distinct

r_{1},r_{2}\in\mathcal{R}
, even if
s(r_{1})=s(r_{2})
and

t(r_{1})=t(r_{2})
.

(v)

Functoriality.

A Petri morphism
f=(f_{\mathcal{S}},f_{\mathcal{R}}):P\to P^{\prime}
induces a strict
symmetric monoidal functor
\mathcal{L}_{0}(f):\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{0}(P^{\prime})
,
acting as
\bar{f}_{\mathcal{S}}
on objects and by
r\mapsto f_{\mathcal{R}}(r)

on generators, making
\mathcal{L}_{0}:\mathbf{Petri}\to\mathbf{PermCat}

a functor.

Here
\mathbf{PermCat}
denotes the category whose objects are small

skeletal permutative categories
(strict symmetric monoidal
categories whose object monoid
(\mathrm{Ob}\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
is
itself strictly commutative, matching the structure of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
)
and whose morphisms are strict symmetric monoidal functors.

Remark 2.10

(The permutative axioms: involutivity, naturality, hexagon)
.

The three axioms governing the symmetry morphisms
\sigma
in
Definition
2.9
(iv) are standard in the theory of symmetric
monoidal categories
[
188
,
187
]
; we spell them out
explicitly for readers encountering them for the first time.

•

Involutivity.

\sigma_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u}}\circ\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}}
.
Swapping the order of
\mathbf{u}
and
\mathbf{v}
twice returns to
the original arrangement.

Chemically: reordering a mixture and then reordering it back leaves
it unchanged.

•

Naturality.

For any morphisms
f:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{u}^{\prime}
and

g:\mathbf{v}\to\mathbf{v}^{\prime}
,

\sigma_{\mathbf{u}^{\prime},\mathbf{v}^{\prime}}\circ(f\otimes g)\;=\;(g\otimes f)\circ\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}.

Reordering before or after running two reactions in parallel gives
the same result.

Chemically: it does not matter whether you relabel species before or
after performing the reactions — the stoichiometric outcome is
identical.

•

Hexagon axiom.

For all complexes
\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}
,

\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}}\;=\;(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{v}}\otimes\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}})\circ(\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{w}}).

The name comes from the hexagonal commutative diagram the equation
generates.
It says that swapping
\mathbf{u}
past the combined pool

\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}
is the same as swapping
\mathbf{u}
past

\mathbf{v}
first and then past
\mathbf{w}
.

Chemically: reordering one component past a mixture of two others
can be done in a single step or two sequential steps with the same
result.

In a non-skeletal permutative category, the symmetry

\sigma_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\to Y\otimes X
runs between distinct
objects, and involutivity composes the two arrows to land back at

X\otimes Y
.
In the skeletal
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, where
\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}
as the same object,
\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}

becomes an endomorphism and involutivity says it is its own inverse:

\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}
generates a
\mathbb{Z}/2
-action on

\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})
rather than
collapsing to the identity.

Remark 2.11

(The symmetry morphisms and coherence)
.

In a non-skeletal symmetric monoidal category, the symmetry

\sigma_{A,B}:A\otimes B\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}B\otimes A

is an isomorphism between two
distinct
objects
A\otimes B

and
B\otimes A
.
In
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, because
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
is strictly commutative,

\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}
and
\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}
are literally the
same object, so
\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}
is an endomorphism
— an arrow from a complex back to itself — rather than an
isomorphism between two different complexes.

Despite living in
\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v},\,\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})
,

\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}
is
not
the identity morphism

\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}}
: it is a non-trivial endomorphism, the
involutive generator of a
\mathbb{Z}/2
-action on the hom-space.
This distinction matters for functors: a strict symmetric monoidal
functor
F:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\mathcal{C}
into a target satisfying the
hypothesis of Theorem
2.14
(object monoid strictly
commutative) must send
\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}
to the
symmetry
\sigma^{\mathcal{C}}_{F(\mathbf{u}),F(\mathbf{v})}
, which
is itself an endomorphism of
F(\mathbf{u})\otimes F(\mathbf{v})
.
That target endomorphism may be trivial (as in the Baez–Master CMC,
Remark
2.17
) or non-trivial;
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
maps
coherently into both kinds of skeletal permutative target.

Remark 2.12

(No additional chemical relations)
.

The only relations in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
are the permutative axioms of
Definition
2.9
(iv).
No equation
r_{1}\equiv r_{2}
is ever imposed between distinct reaction
labels: two routes sharing the same source and target complexes remain
distinct morphisms, kept apart by their names alone.
Any physical identification — same enthalpy change, same mechanism,
same rate law — must be imposed explicitly at a higher level of the
tower, where the relevant structure is available to make such an
identification meaningful.
In this sense
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is the
most general
stoichiometric
category consistent with the Petri net
P
: it retains every distinction
that stoichiometry alone cannot collapse.

Example 2.13

(
\mathcal{L}_{0}
of a three-reaction network)
.

Let
\mathcal{S}=\{A,B,C\}
and
r_{1}:A\to B
,

r_{2}:B\to A
,
r_{3}:A{+}B\to C
.

Sequential composition.

r_{2}\circ r_{1}:A\to A
is well-typed (
t(r_{1})=s(r_{2})=B
) and is

not
equal to
\mathrm{id}_{A}
: no permutative axiom identifies a composite
of two generating reactions with an identity.

Type enforcement.

The composite
r_{3}\circ(r_{1}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B})
is ill-typed:

t(r_{1}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B})=B+B=2B\neq A+B=s(r_{3})
.
The category refuses to compose steps whose stoichiometries do not match.

Distinct labels.

Adding a label
r_{1}^{\prime}:A\to B
(a mechanistically distinct
isomerisation) produces
r_{1}\neq r_{1}^{\prime}
as morphisms
A\to B
.
No permutative axiom identifies them; any physical identification
(same
\Delta H
, same rate) must wait for
\mathcal{L}_{1}
or
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

§2.4. The universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}

A
strict symmetric monoidal functor
out of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is the
mathematical notion of a consistent assignment of chemical content to a
network: it sends species to objects of the target category, reaction
labels to morphisms of the correct type, and is required to preserve
both sequential composition and parallel tensor.
The universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
says that any such functor is
completely determined by its values on the elementary generators —
species and individual reaction labels — with no further consistency
conditions to verify.
This is the reaction-level analogue of Proposition
2.3
:
just as a monoid homomorphism out of
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
is fixed by its values
on individual species, a symmetric monoidal functor out of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

is fixed by its values on individual species and individual reactions.

Theorem 2.14

(Universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
)
.

Let
P=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},s,t)
be a Petri net and
\mathcal{C}
a strict
symmetric monoidal category whose object monoid

(\mathrm{Ob}\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
is strictly commutative — i.e.
X\otimes Y=Y\otimes X
as the same object for all

X,Y\in\mathrm{Ob}\mathcal{C}
.
There is a bijection — which varies consistently as
P
and

\mathcal{C}
vary — between:

\left\{\,\begin{array}[]{l}\text{strict symmetric }\\
\text{monoidal functors}\\
F:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\mathcal{C}\end{array}\,\right\}\;\cong\;\left\{\,(g,h)\;\left|\;\begin{array}[]{l}g:\mathcal{S}\to\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C}),\\[2.0pt]
h(r):\bar{g}(s(r))\to\bar{g}(t(r))\\[2.0pt]
h(r)\text{ in }\mathcal{C}\text{ for each }r\in\mathcal{R}\end{array}\right.\,\right\},

(2)

where
\bar{g}:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C})
is the unique monoid
homomorphism extending
g
(Proposition
2.3
), given by

\bar{g}\!\bigl(\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot S\bigr)=\bigotimes_{S}g(S)^{\otimes n_{S}}
,
and
\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C})
stands for the objects of the category
\mathcal{C}
.
Under the bijection,
F(S)=g(S)
for each species
S\in\mathcal{S}
and

F(r)=h(r)
for each
r\in\mathcal{R}
; all remaining values of
F
are
then forced by strict functoriality and monoidality.

Proof.

Given a strict symmetric monoidal functor
F:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\mathcal{C}
,
define
g(S):=F(S)
and
h(r):=F(r)
.
Strict monoidality forces
F(\mathbf{u})=\bar{g}(\mathbf{u})
for all

\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
(both sides are monoid homomorphisms

\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C})
agreeing on generators, so they agree
everywhere by Proposition
2.3
), and strict functoriality
forces all values on composites and tensors.
Conversely, given any pair
(g,h)
, define
F
on objects by
\bar{g}

and on generators by
h
, extending to all morphisms by

F(f\circ k):=F(f)\circ F(k)
,

F(f\otimes k):=F(f)\otimes F(k)
, and

F(\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}):=\sigma^{\mathcal{C}}_{F(\mathbf{u}),F(\mathbf{v})}
.
This is well-defined on equivalence classes (Definition
2.9
(iv))
because each permutative axiom in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
maps to the corresponding
axiom of
\mathcal{C}
, which holds since
\mathcal{C}
is a strict
symmetric monoidal category.
The bijection varies consistently with
P
and
\mathcal{C}
because
a Petri morphism
f:P\to P^{\prime}
precomposes
(g,h)
by

(g\circ f_{\mathcal{S}},\;r\mapsto h(f_{\mathcal{R}}(r)))
, which is exactly how

\mathcal{L}_{0}(f)
acts.
∎

Remark 2.15

(Why the strict-commutativity hypothesis on
\mathcal{C}
is harmless in practice)
.

The hypothesis that
(\mathrm{Ob}\mathcal{C},\otimes,I)
is strictly
commutative is forced by the skeletal nature of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
:
because
\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}
as the same
object in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, any strict symmetric monoidal functor must
send these to the same object of
\mathcal{C}
, and this is only
guaranteed when the object monoid of
\mathcal{C}
is itself strictly
commutative.
Every target category used in this monograph satisfies this
condition automatically:
B\mathbb{R}
(Corollary
2.16
),

B\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathsf{E}|}
(Example
2.38
), and more
generally
BM
for any commutative monoid
M
are one-object
categories, so strict commutativity on objects holds vacuously.
For target categories with multiple objects and genuinely
non-commutative tensor (where
X\otimes Y
and
Y\otimes X
are
distinct objects), one must replace strict symmetric monoidal
functors by
strong
ones, equipped with coherence isomorphisms

F(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})\xrightarrow{\sim}F(\mathbf{u})\otimes F(\mathbf{v})

that absorb the object-level reordering.
The strong version is not needed in this chapter and is not pursued.

Corollary 2.16

(Additive functors into
B\mathbb{R}
)
.

The real line
\mathbb{R}
carries the structure of a one-object category

B\mathbb{R}
: there is a single object
*
, and the morphisms from
*
to
itself are the real numbers, with composition defined by addition

b\circ a:=a+b
.
Every real number is an arrow, and composing two arrows means adding
their labels; the identity morphism on
*
is the number
0
.
This is a permutative category with trivial symmetry

\sigma_{*,*}=0
(the zero element of
\mathbb{R}
, since swapping a
one-element tensor with itself leaves the number unchanged).

By Theorem
2.14
, strict symmetric monoidal functors

F:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
correspond bijectively to arbitrary maps

h:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R}
(one real number per reaction label), since the
unique species assignment is
g(S)=*
for all
S
.
The extension to all morphisms is forced:

F(f\circ k)=F(f)+F(k),\qquad F(f\otimes k)=F(f)+F(k),\qquad F(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}})=0,\qquad F(\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}})=0.

Such a functor assigns an additive numerical weight to every composite
and parallel process.
For
F
to model thermodynamic enthalpy as a state function — i.e. for
h(r)
to depend only on
s(r)
and
t(r)
, not on the particular
label
r
— the additional condition that
h
factor through an object
potential
\Delta H:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}
via

h(r)=\Delta H(t(r))-\Delta H(s(r))
must be imposed separately.
This state-function condition is
not
part of the
\mathcal{L}_{1}

structure, which supplies only the additivity condition

h:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R}
; it is a further constraint on the particular functor

F_{H}
, discussed in §
2.8
.

Remark 2.17

(Relation to the Baez–Master free CMC)
.

A
commutative monoidal category
(CMC)
[
27
]
is a
symmetric monoidal category in which every symmetry morphism is the
identity:
\sigma_{A,B}=\mathrm{id}_{A\otimes B}
.
Baez and Master
[
27
]
construct the free CMC

F_{\mathrm{Petri}}(P)
on a Petri net
P
; it is the quotient of

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
by the congruence
\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}}
, and Theorem
2.14
specialises
to their result when the target
\mathcal{C}
is a CMC.
We use
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
rather than
F_{\mathrm{Petri}}(P)
as the base of
the tower because the higher levels
\mathcal{L}_{2}
(
\dagger
-SMC),
\mathcal{L}_{3}

(Markov category), and
\mathcal{L}_{4}
(DPO spans in
\mathbf{LGraph}
) all
carry non-trivial symmetry structure: a functor out of a CMC, where all
symmetries are identities, cannot map coherently into a target where they
are not.

What the universal property means for chemists

Any consistent additive assignment of chemical content to species and to
individual reaction labels extends uniquely to all composites and parallel
combinations.
The extension is forced by the requirement of being a strict symmetric
monoidal functor; it is not a modelling choice.

Examples.

Assigning enthalpies
h(r)\in\mathbb{R}
to generators and demanding
functoriality gives Hess’s Law (additivity over sequences and parallel
reactions) as a consequence of Corollary
2.16
: not a separate
postulate but a theorem.
Assigning per-species atom counts and demanding functoriality
(Example
2.38
) extends each generator’s atom
imbalance additively along all sequential and parallel composites,
giving atom conservation as a theorem whenever every generator is
balanced.
Rate constants at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
require different machinery: rates are not
path-additive, so they enter via a kinetic functor into a Markov
category, not via the additive universal property of
B\mathbb{R}
.

What is not forced.

The state-function condition — that
h(r)
depends only on the
complexes
s(r)
and
t(r)
, not on the particular reaction label
r

— is an additional physical constraint, not a consequence of
functoriality alone.
Two distinct reaction labels
r_{1},r_{2}
with the same source and target
can carry different enthalpies
h(r_{1})\neq h(r_{2})
, and the functor
axioms do not prohibit this.
The distinction between functorial additivity (supplied by
\mathcal{L}_{1}
)
and the state-function condition (a separate physical constraint
on the particular functor
F_{H}
) is developed in
§
2.8
.

§2.5. The automorphism exact sequence and the forcing principle

Theorem
2.14
establishes
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
as the free skeletal
permutative category on the Petri net
P
: once species are assigned to objects of
a target category and reaction labels to morphisms of the correct type,
the extension to all composites and tensors is uniquely determined.
This universal property now gives us a precise handle on the
automorphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
itself, and — more importantly — on
what they cannot see.

As previewed in §
1.2
, the tower

\mathcal{L}_{0}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{1}\hookrightarrow\cdots\hookrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{7}

is built bottom-up: at each step there exist pairs of reactions that
are physically distinct yet indistinguishable at the previous level.
The tool that makes “indistinguishable” mathematically precise is
the
automorphism sequence
, an adaptation to the categorical
setting of a classical algebraic device.
For a homomorphism
\varphi:G\to H
of groups, the kernel

\ker\varphi
measures what
\varphi
collapses, and the coset space

H/\mathrm{im}\varphi
measures what lies outside its image
[
253
,
214
]
.
Applied to the restriction map between the automorphism groups of
adjacent tower levels, the kernel records new symmetries that level

k
adds beyond level
k-1
, and the coset space records symmetries
of
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
that fail to lift to
\mathcal{L}_{k}
— precisely the
distinctions a given level cannot express, and that the next level
must add.
We do not assume the image of the restriction map to be a normal
subgroup, so the coset space is in general only a pointed set, not a
group; this is sufficient for the forcing diagnostic developed below.

Presentation-preserving automorphisms and the restriction map.

A
presentation-preserving automorphism
of
\mathcal{L}_{k}
is a strict
symmetric monoidal autoequivalence
\phi:\mathcal{L}_{k}\to\mathcal{L}_{k}
that preserves
the chemical input data — species set
\mathcal{S}
and reaction labels

\mathcal{R}
— as subsets of objects and morphisms respectively.
We write
\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k})
for the group of all such
automorphisms under composition.
The presentation-preserving qualifier is essential: an arbitrary
categorical autoequivalence might rearrange composites and tensor
products in ways unrelated to any Petri-net relabelling, and the
results below would not apply to it.

If some
\phi\in\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k})
swaps two reactions

r_{1},r_{2}\in\mathcal{R}
, then the two are indistinguishable by every

\mathcal{L}_{k}
-level observable: any functor out of
\mathcal{L}_{k}
must commute
with
\phi
and therefore cannot separate them.
The converse fails in general — two reactions can agree under every

\mathcal{L}_{k}
-functor without there being a global presentation-preserving
automorphism realising the swap — so a swapping automorphism is a

sufficient diagnostic
for indistinguishability, not a
characterisation.
This is exactly what the forcing argument needs: a swap that fails
to lift to
\mathcal{L}_{k+1}
exhibits a real distinction
\mathcal{L}_{k}
misses.

Each tower inclusion
\iota_{k}:\mathcal{L}_{k-1}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{k}
induces a

restriction homomorphism

\varphi_{k}\;:\;\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k})\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k-1}),\qquad\phi\;\longmapsto\;\phi\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}_{k-1}},

sending each presentation-preserving automorphism of the richer
level to its restriction to the simpler one.
Not every element of
\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k-1})
arises this
way: those that do not are symmetries present at level
k-1
that
level
k

breaks
, precisely because the extra structure at
level
k
distinguishes what level
k-1
could not.

The automorphism sequence and the forcing principle

For each tower step, the restriction map
\varphi_{k}
yields an exact
sequence of pointed sets

1\;\longrightarrow\;\ker\varphi_{k}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k})\;\xrightarrow{\;\varphi_{k}\;}\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k-1})\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{k}\;\longrightarrow\;1,

(3)

where
\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{k}:=\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k-1})/\mathrm{im}\varphi_{k}

is the set of left cosets, with basepoint the trivial coset.
The first three terms carry group structure (kernel of a group
homomorphism, the two automorphism groups themselves), but

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{k}
is in general only a pointed set: we do not assume

\mathrm{im}\varphi_{k}
to be a normal subgroup of

\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k-1})
.
Exactness at each term means the image of the incoming map equals
the preimage of the basepoint of the outgoing one.
The three terms carry distinct chemical content.

•

\ker\varphi_{k}
: presentation-preserving automorphisms of

\mathcal{L}_{k}
restricting to the identity on
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
—

new symmetries first visible at level
k
.
Example: time-reversal
\dagger
(sending each reaction to its
reverse) is an automorphism of
\mathcal{L}_{2}
invisible at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
,
where no reverse reaction exists.

•

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{k}
: cosets of presentation-preserving
automorphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
modulo those that lift to
\mathcal{L}_{k}
.
A non-trivial coset is represented by an automorphism of

\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
that fails to lift — a symmetry that
\mathcal{L}_{k}

breaks.
A non-trivial cokernel is the precise statement that
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}

conflates objects (reactions, complexes, or configurations) that

\mathcal{L}_{k}
separates.

•

\varphi_{k}
itself: records how much symmetry survives when
the extra structure of level
k
is forgotten.

Forcing principle (diagnostic direction).

If
\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{k}
is non-trivial, then
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
admits a genuine
symmetry that
\mathcal{L}_{k}
breaks:
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
cannot distinguish reactions
that
\mathcal{L}_{k}
separates, so the extension is necessary — i.e., no
reformulation within
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
can capture the distinction.

Forcing principle (constructive direction).

At each observed non-trivial
\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{k}
, an explicit minimal
extension
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}\to\mathcal{L}_{k}
that breaks the cokernel class is
exhibited — adding exactly the new functor, enrichment, or
deformation required and no more.
That this extension is the
unique
minimal extension breaking
the cokernel class is claimed level by level on construction, not as
a general theorem about categorical extensions; the full taxonomy of
the six extension types that occur across the present tower is given
in §
10.8
.

What the exact sequence means for a chemist

An automorphism is a relabelling of the mathematical structure that
leaves every observable at that level unchanged.
If a relabelling swaps two reactions
r_{1}
and
r_{2}
, then no
measurement available at level
k-1
can tell them apart.

The cokernel
\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{k}
collects exactly those relabellings of

\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
that swap reactions which are genuinely distinct in
physical reality.
A non-trivial cokernel means
\mathcal{L}_{k-1}
is
blind
to a real
distinction: it lacks the vocabulary to express it.
Adding the minimal structure needed to break that spurious symmetry
yields
\mathcal{L}_{k}
, and nothing more.

This is the categorical formalisation of a familiar experience:
every time a chemical rule has an exception, the exception reveals
that a finer level of description was implicitly being assumed.
The automorphism exact sequence turns this intuition into a working
mathematical diagnostic.

\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{k})

The sequence at
k=0
: identifying the cokernel.

At the base level,
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is the free skeletal permutative
category on
P
(Theorem
2.14
), so its
presentation-preserving automorphisms are determined by their action
on the two families of chemical generators: species
\mathcal{S}
(generating
the object monoid via Proposition
2.3
) and reaction
labels
\mathcal{R}
(the morphism generators).

•

Species permutations.

A permutation
\pi\in\mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{S})
that
preserves the
Petri net
— i.e., whose induced action on
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
sends

\{(s(r),t(r)):r\in\mathcal{R}\}
back to itself — extends
(via Proposition
2.3
on objects and the universal
property on morphisms) to an element of

\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P))
.
We write
\mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{S})_{\!P}
for this stabiliser subgroup.

•

Label permutations within fibres.

For any pair

(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\times\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
,
a permutation of the fibre

(s,t)^{-1}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=\{r\in\mathcal{R}:s(r)=\mathbf{u},\;t(r)=\mathbf{v}\}
— a relabelling that sends
each reaction to another with identical source and target —
extends to an element of
\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P))
.

The second family suffices for the
k=0
forcing argument.
Let
r_{1},r_{2}\in\mathcal{R}
be two distinct labels with

s(r_{1})=s(r_{2})=\mathbf{u}
and
t(r_{1})=t(r_{2})=\mathbf{v}
,
carrying distinct enthalpies
\Delta H_{1}\neq\Delta H_{2}

(an instance exhibited concretely in
§
2.8
for the

\mathrm{N_{2}}+\mathrm{O_{2}}\to 2\,\mathrm{NO}
system).
The swap
r_{1}\leftrightarrow r_{2}
extends to an element of

\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P))
:
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
carries no numerical
data to distinguish the two labels, so no information at this level
is disturbed by the swap.

It is
not
the restriction of any automorphism of
\mathcal{L}_{1}
: at

\mathcal{L}_{1}
, the functor
F_{H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
assigns

F_{H}(r_{1})\neq F_{H}(r_{2})
, and any
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-automorphism must commute
with
F_{H}
, ruling out the swap.
The label swap therefore represents a non-trivial class in

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
,

[\,r_{1}\leftrightarrow r_{2}\,]\;\in\;\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1},

(4)

demonstrating that
\mathcal{L}_{1}
is necessary.
The minimal extension resolving the conflation is to equip

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
with a strict symmetric monoidal functor

F_{H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
assigning a real enthalpy to each reaction
label — the content of
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, no more and no less.
The full development of this extension, including the distinction
between the additivity condition (which
F_{H}
satisfies by
functoriality) and the state-function condition (an additional
physical requirement), is given in §
2.8
.

The full tower, forced level by level.

The same argument at every subsequent tower step yields the
automorphism groups and forcing cokernels recorded in
Table
3
.
The following tour lists the levels in order; full developments
occupy Chapters 3–10.

At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, the automorphisms are isoenthalpic permutations, and
the cokernel detects reactions sharing
\Delta H
but differing in

\Delta S
, which shift their equilibria differently with
temperature and are therefore genuinely distinct at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, adding the
\dagger
-structure (time-reversal,
encoding detailed balance) breaks the remaining isothermodynamic
symmetry; the cokernel witnesses reactions with identical

\Delta G
but different rates, forcing
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, rate-preserving permutations are the surviving
symmetries, and the cokernel is generated by the swap

\mathrm{E}2\leftrightarrow\mathrm{S_{N}}2
: two reactions with
identical empirical rate laws but mechanistically distinct
electron-pushing graphs, forcing
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, once full bond-graph structure is present, the residual
symmetry is
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
on typed molecular graphs; the cokernel
detects the same bond changes realised in different
three-dimensional embeddings, forcing
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, the full permutation-inversion group
G^{*}
governs
enantiomeric and diastereomeric distinctions, including
symmetry-forbidden versus symmetry-allowed pathways under the
Woodward–Hoffmann rules; the cokernel forces
\mathcal{L}_{5}
by exhibiting
reactions whose transition states occupy geometrically distinct
points on a potential energy surface.
At
\mathcal{L}_{5}
, isometries of the configuration orbifold
{C_{e}}(G)

preserving the PES
V
are the automorphisms; the cokernel
distinguishes reactions with the same geometry but different
topological Berry class, separating photochemical from thermal
pathways and forcing
\mathcal{L}_{6}
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{6}
, the real adiabatic eigenbundle admits a

\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-valued gauge freedom (the overall sign of the real
eigensection in a simply connected patch), and its cokernel
captures loops encircling the conical-intersection seam on which
the sign cannot be chosen globally; the invariant is the mod-2
Berry holonomy class
[\gamma_{B}]\in H^{1}({C_{e}}(G)\setminus\mathcal{X}_{01},\mathbb{Z}_{2})
, and the cokernel
separates CI-crossing reactions from adiabatic ones, forcing

\mathcal{L}_{7}
.
Finally, at
\mathcal{L}_{7}
, the symmetry group
S_{N}\times S_{M}
encodes
all-particle exchange statistics (electrons and nuclei
respectively); the cokernel witnesses distinctions invisible at
every earlier level, exhibited by concrete forcing pairs —
hydrogen versus deuterium (isotope permutation), and ortho- versus
para-
\mathrm{H_{2}}
(identical-particle exchange forbidden by Pauli
antisymmetry).
The former produces distinct dynamical algebras through the

\varepsilon
-dependent Born–Oppenheimer expansion; the latter
splits the compact ideal of
\mathcal{K}(L^{2}({C_{e}}(G)))
into disjoint
nuclear-spin superselection sectors, neither of which an earlier
level can express.
