With the automorphism diagnostic in hand, the remaining combinatorial
content of
\mathcal{L}_{0}
— the stoichiometric matrix, Feinberg’s
deficiency invariants, the Deficiency Zero Theorem, and open-network
composition — is the subject of the following subsection.

§2.6. The stoichiometric matrix, conservation laws, and deficiency

The previous subsections built
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
as a categorical object.
This subsection extracts its classical linear-algebraic content — the
stoichiometric matrix
N
, the conservation-law space, and the deficiency

\delta
— and shows precisely which of these arise from the
universal-property machinery already established, and which are purely
presentational invariants of the Petri net
P
.
In every case the derivation uses only Proposition
2.3
,
Theorem
2.14
, and Corollary
2.16
.
The dynamical significance of
\delta
— the Deficiency Theorems —
requires mass-action kinetics and belongs to
\mathcal{L}_{3}
; we state the
theorems here and mark the level boundary throughout.

The notion of a chemical reaction network used throughout the CRNT
literature goes back to Horn, Jackson, and
Feinberg
[
147
,
146
,
92
,
96
]
.
The following definition adapts their framework to the Petri-net
presentation of
\mathcal{L}_{0}
, retaining named reaction labels so that
mechanistically distinct routes between the same complexes remain
distinct morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

Definition 2.18

(Chemical Reaction Network at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
)
.

A
chemical reaction network (CRN)
at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
is a quintuple

(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R},s,t)
where
\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
is a finite set
of
complexes
,
\mathcal{R}
is a finite set of
reaction labels
,
and
s,t:\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{C}
assign source and target complexes.
The
underlying Petri net
is
P=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},s,t)
with
s,t

viewed as maps into
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, and the stoichiometric category of the
CRN is
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
The
reaction multigraph

G(\mathcal{R})
is the directed multigraph with
vertex set
\mathcal{C}
and one directed edge per element of
\mathcal{R}
.

Remark 2.19

(Relation to the classical Feinberg CRN)
.

The classical CRNT triple
[
147
,
146
,
92
,
96
]

(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{E})
uses a set of directed edges

\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}
, collapsing two reactions with
the same source and target to a single edge.
The label-preserving quintuple is necessary for the Petri-net
presentation: distinct labels must remain distinct morphisms in

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
The classical triple is recovered by replacing
\mathcal{R}
with

\{(s(r),t(r)):r\in\mathcal{R}\}
.

Every generating morphism
r\in\mathcal{R}
of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
has a source
complex
s(r)\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
and a target complex
t(r)\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
Their difference
t(r)-s(r)
lives in the group completion

\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{S}]\cong\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
of
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
Collecting these differences as columns, after choosing linear orderings
of
\mathcal{S}
and
\mathcal{R}
, gives the stoichiometric matrix.

Definition 2.20

(Stoichiometric matrix
[
146
,
92
]
)
.

Let
P=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},s,t)
be a Petri net.
Fix a linear ordering of
\mathcal{S}
(identifying
\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{S}]\cong\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
)
and of
\mathcal{R}
.
The
stoichiometric matrix

N\in\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|\times|\mathcal{R}|}
has

(i,r)
-entry

N_{i,r}\;:=\;(t(r))_{i}-(s(r))_{i},

the net change in species
S_{i}
produced by reaction
r
.
Column
r
of
N
is the image of
t(r)-s(r)
in
\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.

Remark 2.21

(
N
as a presentational invariant of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
)
.

Different orderings of
\mathcal{S}
and
\mathcal{R}
give the same
N
up to row and
column permutations, so
\mathrm{rank}_{\mathbb{R}}(N)
and
\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{R}}(N)
are independent
of the ordering.
However,
N
depends on which morphisms are
generators
(elements
of
\mathcal{R}
) as opposed to composites or tensors: it is a

presentational invariant
of
P
, not a categorical invariant of

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
up to strict symmetric monoidal equivalence.
Two Petri nets with equivalent stoichiometric categories can have different
stoichiometric matrices.

Notational convention.

Throughout this subsection,
\rho:=\mathrm{rank}_{\mathbb{R}}(N)
and

\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}:=\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{R}}(N)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
denotes the

stoichiometric subspace
.
We reserve
s
for the source map
s:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.

The universal property of
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
(Proposition
2.3
)
and the universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
(Theorem
2.14
,
Corollary
2.16
) together give a complete characterisation of
conservation laws in terms of functors out of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
This is the first place in the monograph where those universal properties
combine to yield a non-trivial chemical result.

Proposition 2.22

(Conservation laws as vanishing functors)
.

Let
P=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},s,t)
be a Petri net with stoichiometric matrix

N
.
For each
w_{0}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}
, Proposition
2.3
provides a
unique monoid homomorphism
\bar{w}:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}
extending
w_{0}
.
Define
h_{w}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R}
by

h_{w}(r)\;:=\;\bar{w}(t(r))-\bar{w}(s(r)),\qquad r\in\mathcal{R}.

By Corollary
2.16
,
h_{w}
determines a unique strict symmetric
monoidal functor
F_{w}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
with
F_{w}(r)=h_{w}(r)
on
each generator, and
F_{w}
extended to all morphisms by

F_{w}(g\circ f)=F_{w}(g)+F_{w}(f),\quad F_{w}(f\otimes g)=F_{w}(f)+F_{w}(g),\quad F_{w}(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}})=0.

The following are equivalent:

(i)

w_{0}\in\ker(N^{\top})
, i.e.
w_{0}^{\top}(t(r)-s(r))=0

for every
r\in\mathcal{R}
.

(ii)

F_{w}\equiv 0
on all morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

(iii)

\bar{w}(t(r))=\bar{w}(s(r))
for every generating morphism

r\in\mathcal{R}
.

Proof.

(i)\Leftrightarrow(iii)
: by definition of
\bar{w}
,

\displaystyle\bar{w}(t(r))-\bar{w}(s(r))

\displaystyle=\sum_{S}(t(r))_{S}w_{S}-\sum_{S}(s(r))_{S}w_{S}

\displaystyle=w_{0}^{\top}(t(r)-s(r)),

so
\bar{w}(t(r))=\bar{w}(s(r))
iff
w_{0}^{\top}(t(r)-s(r))=0

iff column
r
of
N^{\top}w_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|}
is zero.
Since this holds for all
r
, it is equivalent to
N^{\top}w_{0}=0
.

(iii)\Leftrightarrow(ii)
:
F_{w}(r)=h_{w}(r)=\bar{w}(t(r))-\bar{w}(s(r))
, so
F_{w}(r)=0
for all
r\in\mathcal{R}
iff (iii).
By Theorem
2.14
, the functor
F_{w}
is entirely determined by
its values on generators; if
F_{w}(r)=0
for all
r\in\mathcal{R}
, then

F_{w}\equiv 0
on all morphisms by the forced extension

F_{w}(g\circ f)=0+0=0
and
F_{w}(f\otimes g)=0+0=0
.
∎

Conservation laws as a tower concept

Proposition
2.22
gives the categorical
content of conservation laws entirely within
\mathcal{L}_{0}
:

A species potential
w_{0}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}
is a conservation law if and
only if the functor
F_{w}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
it induces (via
Proposition
2.3
and Corollary
2.16
) assigns zero
to every morphism of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

The reason conservation is preserved by
all
compositions and
parallel combinations — not just the generating reactions — is
functoriality:
F_{w}(g\circ f)=F_{w}(g)+F_{w}(f)=0
and

F_{w}(f\otimes g)=0
follow automatically once
F_{w}=0
on
generators.
No separate proof is needed; the functor axioms carry it.

This also explains what
\ker(N^{\top})
is from the tower’s point of
view: it is the set of species potentials for which the induced

\mathcal{L}_{1}
-level functor (Corollary
2.16
) happens to be identically
zero.
Conservation is not an additional axiom imposed on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
; it is a
condition on functors
out of

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, and functoriality does
the work.

Proposition 2.23

(Stoichiometric subspaces)
.

Let
P=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},s,t)
be a Petri net with matrix
N
.

(i)

The
stoichiometric subspace

\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}:=\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{R}}(N)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
is spanned by the net
displacement vectors
\{t(r)-s(r):r\in\mathcal{R}\}
of the
generating morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

(ii)

The
conservation-law space

\ker(N^{\top})
is the
orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}
and equals, by
Proposition
2.22
, the set of species
potentials
w_{0}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}
for which the induced functor

F_{w}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
is identically zero.

(iii)

The
stoichiometric cycle space

\ker_{\mathbb{R}}(N):=\{\bm{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|}\mid N\bm{\nu}=0\}

consists of formal real-linear combinations
\sum_{r}\nu_{r}r
of
generating morphisms whose combined net displacement

\sum_{r}\nu_{r}(t(r)-s(r))
is zero in
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
The role of
\ker_{\mathbb{R}}(N)
in the dynamics of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
requires

\mathcal{L}_{3}
kinetics; at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
it records which weighted combinations
of reactions leave the stoichiometric subspace point-wise fixed.

All three subspaces are computable from
N
alone; no kinetic data is
required.

Proof.

(i) is the definition of
\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{R}}(N)
applied to the column vectors

t(r)-s(r)
.
(ii) follows from Proposition
2.22
and the
standard linear-algebraic fact that
\ker(N^{\top})=(\mathrm{im}(N))^{\perp}
.
(iii) is the definition of
\ker_{\mathbb{R}}(N)
.
∎

The following corollary, which requires
\mathcal{L}_{3}
kinetics, shows why

\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}
and
\ker(N^{\top})
matter dynamically: the stoichiometric
subspace confines every trajectory, and the conservation laws become
exact first integrals.
The compatibility classes that
\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}
cuts out are, however,
already determined at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
, before any kinetics is specified.

Corollary 2.24

(Trajectory confinement; requires
\mathcal{L}_{3}
kinetics)
.

Let
\bm{\nu}:\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|}
be any kinetic rate
function (
\mathcal{L}_{3}
structure
) and let
\mathbf{x}(t)
satisfy

\dot{\mathbf{x}}=N\bm{\nu}(\mathbf{x})
.
Then
\mathbf{x}(t)-\mathbf{x}(0)\in\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}
for all
t\geq 0
.
Moreover, for every
w_{0}\in\ker(N^{\top})
, the quantity

w_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{x}(t)
is constant along every trajectory:

\tfrac{d}{dt}(w_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{x})=0
.

Proof.

\dot{\mathbf{x}}=N\bm{\nu}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}
pointwise, giving
the first claim.

\tfrac{d}{dt}(w_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{x})=w_{0}^{\top}N\bm{\nu}=(N^{\top}w_{0})^{\top}\bm{\nu}=0
since
w_{0}\in\ker(N^{\top})
.
∎

The four combinatorial invariants below are computable from

(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R},s,t)
alone — from
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data.
They were introduced by Feinberg, Horn, and Jackson
[
147
,
146
,
92
,
96
]
and underpin the Deficiency
Theorems.
Recent work has confirmed their centrality: deficiency zero is generic
in random reaction networks
[
20
]
, and the interplay
between deficiency, weak reversibility, and steady states is an active
frontier
[
50
,
155
]
.

Definition 2.25

(Feinberg’s combinatorial invariants
[
92
,
96
]
)
.

Let
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R},s,t)
be a CRN.

•

n:=|\mathcal{C}|
: number of complexes.

•

\ell
: number of
linkage classes
(connected components
of the undirected graph underlying
G(\mathcal{R})
).

•

\rho:=\mathrm{rank}_{\mathbb{R}}(N)
: dimension of
\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}
.

•

\delta:=n-\ell-\rho\geq 0
: the
deficiency
.

A feel for
n
,
\ell
,
\rho
,
\delta

n
counts the distinct molecular pools appearing as complexes.

\ell
counts the reaction islands: groups of complexes linked by some
directed path, with no connection to other groups.

\rho
counts the independent directions in concentration space along
which any trajectory can move.

\delta
counts the independent ways the complex graph can “circulate”
while producing zero net species change: complex-level degrees of
freedom invisible to species-level accounting.
A
\delta=0
network has no such hidden structure.

To give
\delta
a precise meaning in terms of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, we
factor the stoichiometric matrix through the complex level.
The inclusion
\iota:\mathcal{C}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
(each complex
c\in\mathcal{C}

is already an element of
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
) is a function from the set
\mathcal{C}

to the commutative monoid
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
By Proposition
2.3
applied with generator set
\mathcal{C}
and
target monoid
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, this extends to a unique monoid homomorphism

\bar{\iota}\;:\;\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{C}]\;\longrightarrow\;\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|},\qquad c\;\longmapsto\;c\;\text{(viewed as element of }\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\text{)},

from the free commutative monoid on complexes to the free commutative
monoid on species.
Its matrix representation (after choosing orderings) is

Y\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|\times n}
, the
complex composition
matrix
, whose column
c
is the coordinate vector of complex

c\in\mathcal{C}
in
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.

Independently, the reaction multigraph
G(\mathcal{R})
has an

incidence matrix

I_{a}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{n\times|\mathcal{R}|}

defined by:
(I_{a})_{c,r}=+1
if
c=t(r)
,

(I_{a})_{c,r}=-1
if
c=s(r)
, else
0
.
Here
I_{a}
is a purely graph-theoretic object determined by
G(\mathcal{R})
.

Proposition 2.26

(Linear algebraic interpretation of deficiency
[
92
,
96
]
)
.

With
Y
and
I_{a}
as above:

(i)

N=YI_{a}
.

(ii)

\mathrm{rank}(I_{a})=n-\ell
.

(iii)

\delta=\dim_{\mathbb{R}}(\ker(Y)\cap\mathrm{im}(I_{a}))\geq 0
.

(iv)

\delta=0
if and only if
Y\!\restriction_{\mathrm{im}(I_{a})}
is
injective, i.e. every nonzero net complex-flow produces a nonzero
species displacement.

Proof.

(i) Column
r
of
YI_{a}
is

Y(e_{t(r)}-e_{s(r)})=t(r)-s(r)
in
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
,
which is column
r
of
N
.
(ii) Standard: the rank of the incidence matrix of a directed graph
with
n
vertices and
\ell
connected components is
n-\ell
.
(iii) By rank–nullity on
Y\!\restriction_{\mathrm{im}(I_{a})}
:

\mathrm{rank}(YI_{a})=(n-\ell)-\dim(\ker(Y)\cap\mathrm{im}(I_{a}))
,
so
\rho=(n-\ell)-\dim(\ker(Y)\cap\mathrm{im}(I_{a}))
, giving

\delta=n-\ell-\rho=\dim(\ker(Y)\cap\mathrm{im}(I_{a}))\geq 0
.
(iv)
\delta=0
iff
\ker(Y)\cap\mathrm{im}(I_{a})=\{0\}
iff

Y\!\restriction_{\mathrm{im}(I_{a})}
is injective.
∎

Deficiency as a failure of the canonical monoid map

Proposition
2.26
has a direct tower interpretation.

The matrix
Y
is the real-linear extension of the monoid
homomorphism
\bar{\iota}:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{C}]\to\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
induced by
Proposition
2.3
from the inclusion
\iota:\mathcal{C}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
This map sends any formal combination of complexes to the corresponding
combination of species counts.

The matrix
I_{a}
records the net complex-level flows induced by the
reaction labels: each column
r
is
e_{t(r)}-e_{s(r)}
in
\mathbb{R}^{n}
,
the net movement from source complex to target complex.

The factorization
N=YI_{a}
(part (i)) says: the net species
displacement of a reaction factors as

first, compute the net complex-flow
(
I_{a}
),

then project complexes to species counts
(
Y
=
\bar{\iota}
).

Deficiency
\delta
measures exactly the failure of
\bar{\iota}
to
be injective on the image of the complex-flow matrix: it counts the
dimension of the space of complex-level circulations that produce zero
net species change.
When
\delta=0
,
\bar{\iota}
is injective on
\mathrm{im}(I_{a})
:
every complex-graph flow leaves a detectable trace in species space.
The Deficiency Zero Theorem uses this injectivity crucially.
When
\delta>0
, there are “hidden” complex-level circulations that

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, viewed through the species map
\bar{\iota}
, cannot detect.

Weak reversibility is a property of the presentation
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R},s,t)
,
not a categorical invariant of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
up to equivalence
(Remark
2.21
).
It records whether every directed path in the generating graph
G(\mathcal{R})

can be returned to its starting complex by further generators — not by
arbitrary composites, but specifically by further elements of
\mathcal{R}
.
This is a strictly
\mathcal{L}_{0}
datum: no kinetics, no thermodynamics,
no reverse-reaction functor.

It is distinct from the
\dagger
-structure at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, the
\dagger
operator provides an
explicit
reverse
generator
r^{\dagger}:t(r)\to s(r)
for each
r\in\mathcal{R}
, subject to
the categorical axiom
r^{\dagger\dagger}=r
.
Weak reversibility at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
requires only that the reverse direction
is achievable by some directed path of generators in
G(\mathcal{R})
— a
much weaker condition, expressible purely in terms of the multigraph.
Introduced by Horn and Jackson
[
147
,
146
]
, it is
the graph-theoretic hypothesis that, together with
\delta=0
,
guarantees the conclusions of the Deficiency Zero Theorem.
Boros
[
50
]
later showed that weak reversibility alone
(without
\delta=0
) guarantees existence of a positive steady state
in each compatibility class.

Definition 2.27

(Weak reversibility
[
147
,
146
]
)
.

A CRN
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R},s,t)
is
weakly reversible
if for every
directed path
c_{0}\to c_{1}\to\cdots\to c_{k}
in
G(\mathcal{R})
, there
exists a directed path from
c_{k}
back to
c_{0}
in
G(\mathcal{R})
.
Equivalently, every connected component of
G(\mathcal{R})
is strongly
connected.

Remark 2.28

(Level stratification and compatibility classes)
.

The invariants
n,\ell,\rho,\delta
and weak reversibility are
purely
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data: computable from
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R},s,t)
with no
functor into any target category.

For the Deficiency Zero Theorem below, the relevant partition of
concentration space is by
stoichiometric compatibility classes
:
the class of
\mathbf{x}_{0}
is

\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{0}+\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}\bigr)\cap\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}_{>0},

the set of positive concentration vectors reachable from
\mathbf{x}_{0}

by stoichiometric changes.
In tower language,
\mathbf{x}
lies in this class if and only if

\bar{w}(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\bar{w}(\mathbf{x}_{0})\quad\text{for every }w_{0}\in\ker(N^{\top}),

where
\bar{w}:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}
is the unique monoid homomorphism
extending
w_{0}
(Proposition
2.3
), and

\bar{w}(\mathbf{x})=w_{0}^{\top}\mathbf{x}
is its value on a
concentration vector.
The partition of
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}_{>0}
into stoichiometric compatibility
classes is determined entirely at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
; the Deficiency Zero Theorem
says which class contains a unique stable
\mathcal{L}_{3}
fixed point.

Theorem 2.29

(Deficiency Zero Theorem
[
147
,
92
]
)
.

Let
(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R},s,t)
be a CRN with
\delta=0
, endowed with

mass-action kinetics
(
\mathcal{L}_{3}
structure
): the rate
function
\bm{\nu}
takes the specific form

\nu_{r}(\mathbf{x})=k_{r}\prod_{S\in\mathcal{S}}x_{S}^{(s(r))_{S}}

for positive rate constants
k_{r}>0
.

(i)

If not weakly reversible: no positive steady state exists for
any choice of positive rate constants.

(ii)

If weakly reversible: for every choice of positive rate
constants, there is exactly one positive steady state in each stoichiometric
compatibility class
\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{0}+\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}\bigr)\cap\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}_{>0}
(Remark
2.28
);
it is locally asymptotically
stable; and no periodic orbits exist in
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}_{>0}
.

Tower-language breakdown.

•

From
\mathcal{L}_{0}
alone:
the hypotheses
\delta=0
and weak
reversibility; the stoichiometric subspace
\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}
; the conservation
laws
\ker(N^{\top})
(Proposition
2.22
);
and the partition of
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}_{>0}
into stoichiometric
compatibility classes (Remark
2.28
).

•

From
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, specifically:
mass-action kinetics — the
parametric form
\nu_{r}(\mathbf{x})=k_{r}\prod_{S}x_{S}^{(s(r))_{S}}
,
not an arbitrary kinetic rate function.
The DZT fails for general
\mathcal{L}_{3}
kinetics.

•

The conclusion:
within each
\mathcal{L}_{0}
-determined class,
the mass-action dynamics has exactly one fixed point and it is
stable.
The class is an
\mathcal{L}_{0}
object; the fixed point and its stability
are
\mathcal{L}_{3}
statements.

Remark 2.30

(Deficiency One and beyond
[
93
,
95
]
)
.

Feinberg
[
93
,
95
]
proved a Deficiency One
Theorem for
\delta=1
under additional structural conditions on
linkage classes.
Boros
[
50
]
removed the
\delta=0
hypothesis from the
existence part of Theorem
2.29
(i): every weakly reversible
mass-action system has a positive steady state in each stoichiometric compatibility class

\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{0}+\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}\bigr)\cap\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}_{>0}
,
regardless of deficiency.
In all cases, the hypotheses are
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data and the conclusions
require mass-action kinetics at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

Remark 2.31

(Tower framework and Feinberg’s CRNT)
.

The combinatorial backbone is identical to classical CRNT
[
92
,
93
,
96
]
: species, complexes, reaction multigraph,
stoichiometric matrix, and the Deficiency Theorems originate there.
The architectural difference is that classical CRNT does not separate the
stoichiometric layer from the kinetic layer.
The tower makes this explicit:
\mathcal{L}_{0}
carries the hypotheses and the
compatibility-class partition;
\mathcal{L}_{3}
carries the kinetics and the
conclusions.

Example 2.32

(Michaelis–Menten enzyme kinetics)
.

Network:
\mathrm{E+S}\underset{r_{2}}{\overset{r_{1}}{\rightleftharpoons}}\mathrm{ES}\overset{r_{3}}{\to}\mathrm{E+P}
.
Species
\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{E,S,ES,P}\}
;
complexes
c_{1}=\mathrm{E+S}
,
c_{2}=\mathrm{ES}
,

c_{3}=\mathrm{E+P}
.

N=\begin{pmatrix}-1&+1&+1\\
-1&+1&0\\
+1&-1&-1\\
0&0&+1\end{pmatrix},\qquad n=3,\quad\ell=1,\quad\rho=2,\quad\delta=0.

Conservation laws (Proposition
2.22
).

The conservation-law space
\ker(N^{\top})
has dimension
|\mathcal{S}|-\rho=2
.
We find the two vanishing functors by computing:

For
w_{1}=(1,0,1,0)^{\top}
(enzyme):

h_{w_{1}}(r_{1})=\bar{w}_{1}(c_{2})-\bar{w}_{1}(c_{1})=1-(1+0)=0
,

h_{w_{1}}(r_{2})=\bar{w}_{1}(c_{1})-\bar{w}_{1}(c_{2})=1-1=0
,

h_{w_{1}}(r_{3})=\bar{w}_{1}(c_{3})-\bar{w}_{1}(c_{2})=(1+0)-1=0
.
So
F_{w_{1}}\equiv 0
: enzyme conservation

[\mathrm{E}]+[\mathrm{ES}]=\mathrm{const}
.

For
w_{2}=(0,1,1,1)^{\top}
(substrate):

h_{w_{2}}(r_{1})=\bar{w}_{2}(c_{2})-\bar{w}_{2}(c_{1})=1-(0+1)=0
,

h_{w_{2}}(r_{2})=0
by symmetry,

h_{w_{2}}(r_{3})=\bar{w}_{2}(c_{3})-\bar{w}_{2}(c_{2})=(0+1)-1=0
.
So
F_{w_{2}}\equiv 0
: substrate conservation

[\mathrm{S}]+[\mathrm{ES}]+[\mathrm{P}]=\mathrm{const}
.

Both are
\mathcal{L}_{0}
facts derivable from
N
alone.
Not weakly reversible (
r_{3}
has no return path:
c_{3}\to\cdots\to c_{2}

does not exist in
G(\mathcal{R})
).

Compatibility classes (Remark
2.28
).

The stoichiometric compatibility class of
\mathbf{x}_{0}
is the
two-dimensional surface
\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{0}+\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}\bigr)\cap\mathbb{R}^{4}_{>0}
, cut out by fixing
\bar{w}_{1}(\mathbf{x})=e_{0}
and

\bar{w}_{2}(\mathbf{x})=s_{0}
for constants
e_{0},s_{0}>0
.

Anticipating
\mathcal{L}_{3}
:

Theorem
2.29
(i) implies no positive steady state under
mass-action kinetics.

Example 2.33

(Minimal weakly reversible network)
.

A\overset{r_{1}}{\underset{r_{2}}{\rightleftharpoons}}B
,

\mathcal{S}=\{A,B\}
,
n=2
,
\ell=1
,
\rho=1
,
\delta=0
.

For
w=(1,1)^{\top}
:

h_{w}(r_{1})=\bar{w}(B)-\bar{w}(A)=1-1=0
,

h_{w}(r_{2})=\bar{w}(A)-\bar{w}(B)=1-1=0
.
So
F_{w}\equiv 0
:
[A]+[B]=\mathrm{const}
is the unique
conservation law.
Weakly reversible:
G(\mathcal{R})
is strongly connected.
The stoichiometric compatibility class of
\mathbf{x}_{0}
is

\{[A]+[B]=c\}\cap\mathbb{R}^{2}_{>0}
for
c=\bar{w}(\mathbf{x}_{0})>0
,
determined entirely at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
.

Anticipating
\mathcal{L}_{3}
:

Theorem
2.29
(ii) gives exactly one positive mass-action steady
state in each such class.

A single closed CRN models an isolated system.
The category
\mathbf{Petri}
(Definition
2.7
) allows
open systems to be built modularly and assembled by pushout.
A
cospan
in a category
\mathbf{C}
is a diagram

A\xrightarrow{f}C\xleftarrow{g}B
: two morphisms sharing a common
target.
Two cospans with matching right/left boundaries compose by

pushout
: the universal construction that identifies the shared
boundary and takes the union of the bulk.
This is how Baez–Pollard
[
28
]
compose open reaction
networks; we give the
\mathcal{L}_{0}
version here.

Definition 2.34

(Open CRN at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
)
.

Let
\Sigma_{I},\Sigma_{O}\subseteq\mathcal{S}
be finite sets of
input

and
output interface species
: those shared with the environment.
Regard
D_{I}=(\Sigma_{I},\emptyset,-,-)
and

D_{O}=(\Sigma_{O},\emptyset,-,-)
as discrete Petri nets.
An
open CRN
at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
is a cospan

D_{I}\;\xrightarrow{\;i\;}\;P\;\xleftarrow{\;o\;}\;D_{O}

in
\mathbf{Petri}
.
Two open CRNs with
\Sigma_{O}=\Sigma_{I}^{\prime}
compose by pushout in

\mathbf{Petri}
, identifying the output species of the first with the
input species of the second.

Proposition 2.35

(Stoichiometric structure under pushout)
.

Let
P_{1}=(\mathcal{S}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{R}_{1},s_{1},t_{1})
and

P_{2}=(\mathcal{S}_{2},\mathcal{C}_{2},\mathcal{R}_{2},s_{2},t_{2})
be CRNs assembled by pushout
in
\mathbf{Petri}
along a discrete interface

D=(\Sigma,\emptyset,-,-)
with injective species inclusions

f_{i,\mathcal{S}}:\Sigma\to\mathcal{S}_{i}
(
i=1,2
), the standard open-CRN
setup of Definition
2.34
.
Then
P_{12}=P_{1}\cup_{D}P_{2}
has species set

\mathcal{S}_{12}=\mathcal{S}_{1}\cup_{\Sigma}\mathcal{S}_{2}
(identified with

\mathcal{S}_{1}\cup\mathcal{S}_{2}
via the inclusions) and reaction set

\mathcal{R}_{12}=\mathcal{R}_{1}\sqcup\mathcal{R}_{2}
.

(i)

The stoichiometric matrix of
P_{12}
is

N_{12}\;=\;\bigl[\,N_{1}^{\mathrm{ext}}\;\big|\;N_{2}^{\mathrm{ext}}\,\bigr]\;\in\;\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}_{12}|\times|\mathcal{R}_{12}|},

where
N_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}
denotes
N_{i}
zero-extended to have rows
indexed by all of
\mathcal{S}_{12}
(zero rows for species in

\mathcal{S}_{12}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{i}
).

(ii)

The stoichiometric subspace satisfies

\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}{}_{12}=\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}{}_{1}^{\mathrm{ext}}+\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}{}_{2}^{\mathrm{ext}}
,
the sum of the extended subspaces in
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}_{12}|}
.

(iii)

A species potential
w_{0}:\mathcal{S}_{12}\to\mathbb{R}
satisfies

w_{0}\in\ker(N_{12}^{\top})
— equivalently, by
Proposition
2.22
, the functor

F_{w}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P_{12})\to B\mathbb{R}
is identically zero — if and only
if both of the following hold:

w_{0}\!\restriction_{\mathcal{S}_{1}}\in\ker(N_{1}^{\top}),\qquad w_{0}\!\restriction_{\mathcal{S}_{2}}\in\ker(N_{2}^{\top}),

where
w_{0}\!\restriction_{\mathcal{S}_{i}}:\mathcal{S}_{i}\to\mathbb{R}
denotes the
restriction of the single function
w_{0}
to the coordinates
indexed by
\mathcal{S}_{i}
.
Note that both restrictions automatically agree on
\Sigma
since
they are restrictions of the same
w_{0}
.

Proof.

(i) The generating morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P_{12})
are
\mathcal{R}_{1}\sqcup\mathcal{R}_{2}
,
with
s_{i}(r)
and
t_{i}(r)
in
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}_{i}]\subset\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}_{12}]
.
The
(j,r)
-entry of
N_{12}
for
r\in\mathcal{R}_{i}
is

(t_{i}(r))_{j}-(s_{i}(r))_{j}
, which is
(N_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}})_{j,r}
.

(ii)
\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}{}_{12}=\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{R}}(N_{12})=\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{R}}(N_{1}^{\mathrm{ext}})+\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{R}}(N_{2}^{\mathrm{ext}})=\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}{}_{1}^{\mathrm{ext}}+\mathcal{S}_{\!\mathrm{sto}}{}_{2}^{\mathrm{ext}}
.

(iii) By Proposition
2.22
applied to
P_{12}
:

F_{w}\equiv 0
on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P_{12})
iff
h_{w}(r)=0
for all

r\in\mathcal{R}_{12}
.
For
r\in\mathcal{R}_{1}
:
h_{w}(r)=\bar{w}(t_{1}(r))-\bar{w}(s_{1}(r))=(w_{0}\!\restriction_{\mathcal{S}_{1}})^{\top}(t_{1}(r)-s_{1}(r))
, which is zero for
all
r\in\mathcal{R}_{1}
iff
w_{0}\!\restriction_{\mathcal{S}_{1}}\in\ker(N_{1}^{\top})
,
and analogously for
r\in\mathcal{R}_{2}
.
Both conditions involve restrictions of the same
w_{0}
, which agrees on

\Sigma
by definition.
∎

Remark 2.36

(Conservation laws are modular; deficiency is not)
.

Proposition
2.35
(iii) is a positive result: a species
potential
w_{0}
on the assembled network is a conservation law if and
only if it is a conservation law for each sub-network independently.
This follows cleanly from Proposition
2.22

applied to
P_{12}
, and is an instance of the tower language doing
genuine work.

Deficiency, by contrast, does not behave well under pushout.
Writing
\delta_{12}=n_{12}-\ell_{12}-\rho_{12}
: the number of
complexes satisfies
n_{12}=n_{1}+n_{2}-|\mathcal{C}_{1}\cap\mathcal{C}_{2}|
(shared
complexes are merged); the number of linkage classes satisfies

\ell_{12}\leq\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}
with strict inequality when the
interface creates new connections; and
\rho_{12}=\mathrm{rank}(N_{12})\leq\rho_{1}+\rho_{2}
with strict inequality when interface species create
linear dependencies.
Each of these quantities can change in a way not determined by
\delta_{1}

and
\delta_{2}
alone, so
\delta_{12}
is not controlled by
\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}
: two
\delta=0
sub-networks can assemble into a

\delta>0
network, and vice versa.
In particular, the DZT conclusion — unique stable steady state per
compatibility class — does not compose under pushout.

Open networks as composable chemical systems

An open CRN is a chemical system with designated
inlet species

(
\Sigma_{I}
) and
outlet species
(
\Sigma_{O}
).
Pushout composition connects two such systems in series.

Proposition
2.35
tells us what
\mathcal{L}_{0}
knows about
the assembly: the stoichiometric matrix is the column-concatenation of
the two sub-matrices, and a potential is conserved in the assembly if
and only if it is conserved by both sub-networks.
Conservation laws are therefore modular at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
.

What is not modular is deficiency: the assembly can create or destroy
linkage-class connections and stoichiometric dependencies in ways

\delta_{1}
and
\delta_{2}
alone cannot predict.
The DZT therefore does not compose, and the kinetic composition
(gray-boxing) that Baez–Pollard
[
28
]
develop at

\mathcal{L}_{3}
must handle this non-modularity directly.

§2.7.
\mathcal{L}_{0}
as a working tool

The previous sections established
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
as a mathematical object.
This section demonstrates it as a working tool.
The three examples below correspond to the three main structural
components introduced above: §
2.3
(morphism
calculus), §
2.4
(universal property), and
Definition
2.34
(open composition).
Each derives a non-trivial fact from
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data alone — no energy,
no rates, no geometry.

Example 2.37

(The catalytic cycle as a single composite morphism)
.

Consider the Michaelis–Menten network

E+S\;\underset{r_{2}}{\overset{r_{1}}{\rightleftharpoons}}\;ES\;\overset{r_{3}}{\longrightarrow}\;E+P,

with
\mathcal{S}=\{E,S,ES,P\}
.
The three generating morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
are

r_{1}:E{+}S\to ES
,
r_{2}:ES\to E{+}S
, and
r_{3}:ES\to E{+}P
.

The catalytic cycle.

The composite

r_{3}\circ r_{1}\;:\;E{+}S\;\longrightarrow\;E{+}P

is a well-formed morphism in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, since
t(r_{1})=ES=s(r_{3})
.
It represents the full catalytic event — substrate binding followed by
product release — as a single process in the stoichiometric calculus.
This composite is a distinct morphism
E{+}S\to E{+}P
from any
hypothetical direct reaction generator
r^{\prime}:E{+}S\to E{+}P
that one
might add to the Petri net: no permutative axiom identifies a composite
of two generating reactions with a fresh generator, so
r_{3}\circ r_{1}

and
r^{\prime}
remain distinct morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

Running binding and release in parallel.

The tensor product

r_{1}\otimes r_{2}\;:\;(E{+}S)+ES\;\longrightarrow\;ES+(E{+}S)

is a morphism representing simultaneous substrate binding in one part
of the system and enzyme–substrate dissociation in another.
It is not equal to
\mathrm{id}_{E+S+ES}
: the two processes happen at
different molecular sites and are kept as a non-trivial parallel process.

A type error.

The composite
r_{3}\circ r_{2}
is
ill-typed
:

t(r_{2})=E{+}S
while
s(r_{3})=ES
, and
E{+}S\neq ES
in

\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
since
E+S
(the unbound enzyme–substrate pair) and
ES

(the enzyme–substrate complex) are distinct species.

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
refuses to form this composite, encoding at the categorical
level the mechanistic fact that
ES
must form before it can release
product: product release cannot follow dissociation.

Example 2.38

(Atom balance via the imbalance functor)
.

Chemical balancedness — the requirement that every reaction
preserves atom counts — is not an axiom of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
It is expressed by a functor out of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
: every Petri net,
balanced or not, admits an
atom-imbalance functor
that
records the elemental discrepancy of each reaction, and balancedness
is the condition that this functor takes value zero on every generator.
The construction uses two successive applications of the universal property.

Setup.

Consider the hydrogen combustion reaction

r:2\,\mathrm{H_{2}}+\mathrm{O_{2}}\to 2\,\mathrm{H_{2}O}
,
with
\mathcal{S}=\{H_{2},O_{2},H_{2}O\}
.

Step 1: species-level atom counts
(Universal Property of
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, Proposition
2.3
).

Define the
atomic composition map

a:\mathcal{S}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathbb{N}^{2},\qquad a(H_{2})=(2,0),\quad a(O_{2})=(0,2),\quad a(H_{2}O)=(2,1),

where the two coordinates record H and O atom counts.
By Proposition
2.3
,
a
extends to a unique monoid
homomorphism
\bar{a}:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{N}^{2}
, given by

\bar{a}\!\bigl(\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot S\bigr)=\sum_{S}n_{S}\cdot a(S)
.
Applied to the complexes of this reaction:

\displaystyle\bar{a}(2\,H_{2}+O_{2})

\displaystyle=2(2,0)+(0,2)=(4,2),

\displaystyle\bar{a}(2\,H_{2}O)

\displaystyle=2(2,1)=(4,2).

The source and target complexes carry the same atom count.

Step 2: the morphism-level extension
(Universal Property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, Theorem
2.14
).

Let
B\mathbb{Z}^{2}
be the one-object category with morphisms
\mathbb{Z}^{2}
and
composition given by vector addition; this is a strict symmetric
monoidal category whose object monoid is trivially commutative
(one object), so Theorem
2.14
applies.
Define the generator assignment
(a^{\mathrm{obj}},h)
by

a^{\mathrm{obj}}(S):=*\quad\text{for every }S\in\mathcal{S},\qquad h(r):=\bar{a}(t(r))-\bar{a}(s(r))\in\mathbb{Z}^{2},

where
*
is the unique object of
B\mathbb{Z}^{2}
.
The species-level atom counts
\bar{a}(S)
enter only through the
morphism assignment
h(r)
, which records each reaction’s

atom imbalance
; they are not objects of
B\mathbb{Z}^{2}
, which has
only one.
For the hydrogen combustion reaction,

h(r)=(4,2)-(4,2)=(0,0)
.
Theorem
2.14
provides a unique strict symmetric monoidal
functor

F_{a}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\;\longrightarrow\;B\mathbb{Z}^{2},

the
atom-imbalance functor
of the assignment
a
.

What the functor asserts.

Strict functoriality forces, for every morphism
f
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
:

•

F_{a}(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}})=(0,0)
: the trivial process changes
no atom counts.

•

F_{a}(g\circ f)=F_{a}(g)+F_{a}(f)
: atom changes add along
sequential steps.

•

F_{a}(f\otimes g)=F_{a}(f)+F_{a}(g)
: atom changes add over
parallel processes.

Since
F_{a}(r)=(0,0)
, every composite and tensor product of
r
with
itself also maps to
(0,0)
.
Running a cascade of balanced reactions therefore produces zero net atom
change: additivity of atom counts along reaction sequences is a theorem,
not a postulate.

Balancedness as a vanishing condition on
F_{a}
.

For a general Petri net
P^{\prime}
and atom map

a:\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{N}^{|\mathsf{E}|}
, the imbalance functor

F_{a}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P^{\prime})\to B\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathsf{E}|}

always exists
: the
assignment
h(r):=\bar{a}(t(r))-\bar{a}(s(r))
is well-defined
for every generator regardless of whether atoms balance, and
Theorem
2.14
extends it uniquely to all morphisms.
Balancedness is the condition that
F_{a}
takes value zero on every
generator — equivalently, by strict functoriality, that
F_{a}
is
the zero functor on every morphism of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P^{\prime})
.
An unbalanced Petri net is a perfectly valid stoichiometric category
equipped with a non-zero imbalance functor; the values

F_{a}(r)\neq 0
record exactly which reactions fail to conserve atoms
and by how much.
Balancedness is therefore not a condition on the
existence
of

F_{a}
, but a vanishing condition on its values — a condition on a
functor out of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P^{\prime})
, not an axiom of
\mathcal{L}_{0}
itself.

Example 2.39

(Open composition: assembling a network from sub-networks)
.

We decompose the Michaelis–Menten catalytic cycle into two modular
sub-networks and reassemble it via pushout in
\mathbf{Petri}
, in the
sense of Definition
2.34
.

Sub-network 1 (binding and dissociation).

P_{1}=(\{E,S,ES\},\;\{r_{1},r_{2}\},\;s_{1},t_{1})

with
r_{1}:E{+}S\to ES
and
r_{2}:ES\to E{+}S
.
The
output interface
is
D_{O}=(\{ES\},\emptyset,-,-)
,
embedded by
o_{1}:D_{O}\to P_{1}
sending
ES
to
ES
.
The species
E
and
S
are treated as background, not exposed at the
interface.

Sub-network 2 (catalysis).

P_{2}=(\{ES,E,P\},\;\{r_{3}\},\;s_{2},t_{2})

with
r_{3}:ES\to E{+}P
.
The
input interface
is
D_{I}^{\prime}=(\{ES\},\emptyset,-,-)
,
embedded by
i_{2}:D_{I}^{\prime}\to P_{2}
sending
ES
to
ES
.

Pushout in
\mathbf{Petri}
.

Both interfaces are
D=(\{ES\},\emptyset,-,-)
, so we form the
pushout

P_{1}\;\cup_{D}\;P_{2}

in
\mathbf{Petri}
.
The pushout identifies the two copies of
ES
, takes the disjoint union
of the remaining species and all reaction labels, and gives

P_{1}\cup_{D}P_{2}\;=\;(\{E,S,ES,P\},\;\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\},\;s,t),

the full Michaelis–Menten network of Example
2.37
.
The free construction
\mathcal{L}_{0}:\mathbf{Petri}\to\mathbf{PermCat}
is
a left adjoint and therefore preserves pushouts; the pushout in

\mathbf{Petri}
maps to the pushout in
\mathbf{PermCat}
,

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P_{1}\cup_{D}P_{2})\;\cong\;\mathcal{L}_{0}(P_{1})\;+_{\mathcal{L}_{0}(D)}\;\mathcal{L}_{0}(P_{2}),

under the hypotheses of Proposition
2.35
on the
interface (discrete, injective on species, no reaction-label
identifications), all of which hold here.
Any strict symmetric monoidal functor out of the assembled category
into a strictly commutative target — the atom-imbalance functor
of Example
2.38
, or an enthalpy assignment at
\mathcal{L}_{1}

— decomposes into compatible sub-network assignments glued along the
shared interface, by the universal property of the pushout.

What the decomposition gives.

The composite morphism
r_{3}\circ r_{1}:E{+}S\to E{+}P
is visible in
the assembled category but not in either sub-category alone:
r_{1}

belongs to
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P_{1})
and
r_{3}
belongs to
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P_{2})
, and only
the pushout assembles them into a composable pair.
This is the categorical content of modular network assembly: the
assembled category contains morphisms not present in any single module,
but these morphisms are entirely determined by the sub-network data
and the interface identification.

The limits of
\mathcal{L}_{0}

The three examples above exhaust what
\mathcal{L}_{0}
can do: track
stoichiometric type, extend additive assignments from generators to
all processes via the universal property, and assemble networks from
modular parts via pushout.
What
\mathcal{L}_{0}
cannot do is distinguish two reactions with the same source
and target by any numerical criterion, because
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
carries no
numerical data as part of its structure.
The next section identifies this gap precisely and shows that
extending
\mathcal{L}_{0}
by exactly one additional piece of data — a functor

F_{H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
— is the minimal and canonical next step.

§2.8. What
\mathcal{L}_{0}
cannot express: the forcing of
\mathcal{L}_{1}

Section
2.5
established, via the automorphism
sequence (
3
) at
k=0
, that any two reaction
labels
r_{1},r_{2}\in\mathcal{R}
with identical source and target complexes
— whenever
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
contains such a pair — represent a class

[r_{1}\leftrightarrow r_{2}]\in\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
that
\mathcal{L}_{0}

cannot break, forcing the existence of
\mathcal{L}_{1}
.
This subsection gives the chemical realisation of that abstract
argument using the nitrogen–oxygen–nitric oxide system, and then
develops the subtler content of
\mathcal{L}_{1}
itself: the distinction
between the
additivity
condition (satisfied by any strict
symmetric monoidal functor into
B\mathbb{R}
) and the
state-function

condition (satisfied only by functors induced by an object potential).
The first is the categorical content of
\mathcal{L}_{1}
; the second is an
additional physical constraint that only some
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-functors
satisfy.

The gap at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
: a worked chemical instance

A single reaction.

Consider the oxidation of nitrogen,

r:\mathrm{N_{2}(g)}+\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\;\longrightarrow\;2\,\mathrm{NO(g)},\qquad\Delta H^{\circ}=+180.5\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}~\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{Chase1998}{}{}]}.

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
contains the generating morphism

r:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{v}
with
\mathbf{u}=\mathrm{N_{2}}+\mathrm{O_{2}}
and
\mathbf{v}=2\,\mathrm{NO}
.
It does not contain the scalar
+180.5
:
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
carries no
real-valued functor as part of its data, so there is no structure
at this level in which the enthalpy can reside.

Parallel routes — the forcing instance.

In practice, a reaction network frequently contains two distinct
reaction labels
r_{1},r_{2}\in\mathcal{R}
sharing source and target
complexes:

s(r_{1})=s(r_{2})=\mathbf{u},\qquad t(r_{1})=t(r_{2})=\mathbf{v},

for example, two experimentally identified pathways with the same
gross stoichiometry, or the same reaction studied under different
catalytic conditions.
Both appear as distinct generating morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

(Remark
2.6
); the free construction imposes no
identification on them.

Suppose these two reaction labels carry distinct enthalpies:

\Delta H_{1}\neq\Delta H_{2}
.
The label swap
r_{1}\leftrightarrow r_{2}
extends to an element of

\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P))
— specifically, a label
permutation within the fibre
(s,t)^{-1}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})
,
the second family identified in §
2.5
.
It preserves every structure of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
: source and target
complexes are unchanged, and no numerical data exists at
\mathcal{L}_{0}

to be disturbed.
Yet this swap is not the restriction of any element of

\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{1})
: every presentation-preserving
automorphism at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
must commute with the enthalpy functor

F_{H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
whose existence defines
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, and

F_{H}(r_{1})\neq F_{H}(r_{2})
prevents the swap from preserving the

\mathcal{L}_{1}
-structure.
By (
4
), the swap represents a non-trivial class in

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
.
The minimal extension resolving this conflation is to equip

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
with the functor
F_{H}
itself:
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, developed
in Chapter 3.

Remark 2.40

(The additivity condition: equipping
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

with
F_{H}
)
.

Passing to
\mathcal{L}_{1}
means equipping
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
with a strict
symmetric monoidal functor

F_{H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\;\longrightarrow\;B\mathbb{R}.

By Corollary
2.16
, such a functor is uniquely determined by
specifying one real number
F_{H}(r)\in\mathbb{R}
for each generating
reaction
r\in\mathcal{R}
; the values on composites and tensors are then
forced:

F_{H}(g\circ f)=F_{H}(g)+F_{H}(f),\qquad F_{H}(f\otimes g)=F_{H}(f)+F_{H}(g),\qquad F_{H}(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}})=0.

These are the
additivity conditions
on
F_{H}
.
The first is the additivity form of Hess’s Law — enthalpy changes
add along sequential reaction steps; the second is additivity over
independent parallel processes.
Both follow from functoriality, not from any separate physical
postulate.

In terms of the automorphism sequence, equipping
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
with
F_{H}

breaks the spurious label-swap symmetry in
\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
: once
distinct real values
F_{H}(r_{1})\neq F_{H}(r_{2})
are assigned, the swap

r_{1}\leftrightarrow r_{2}
no longer preserves structure, and the two
reaction labels are numerically distinguishable.

The values
\{F_{H}(r)\}_{r\in\mathcal{R}}
are free parameters: any
assignment of real numbers to reaction generators extends to a valid
strict symmetric monoidal functor.
This is the
additivity condition
for
\mathcal{L}_{1}
: it adds
exactly one real parameter per reaction label, and no other
structure.

Remark 2.41

(The state-function condition)
.

The physical fact that enthalpy is a
state function
— that
the enthalpy change of a reaction depends only on its initial and
final complex, not on the reaction label — is strictly stronger
than the additivity condition of Remark
2.40
.
It requires
F_{H}
to be induced by an
object potential
: a
monoid homomorphism

h:(\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|},+,\mathbf{0})\to(\mathbb{R},+,0)
satisfying

F_{H}(r)\;=\;h(t(r))-h(s(r))\qquad\text{for every generating }r\in\mathcal{R}.

By the universal property of
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
(Proposition
2.3
),
any function
h_{0}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}
— one real value per species,
typically the standard enthalpy of formation
\Delta H^{\circ}_{f}(S)

— extends to a unique such
h
, and then to a valid
F_{H}
via
Corollary
2.16
.
When such an
h
exists, the enthalpy change of any morphism

f:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{v}
(whether a single generator, a
composite, or a tensor product) equals
h(\mathbf{v})-h(\mathbf{u})
, depending only on the source and target and not on
the particular morphism.
Path independence then holds automatically: for any two morphisms

f,g:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{v}
,

F_{H}(f)=h(\mathbf{v})-h(\mathbf{u})=F_{H}(g)
.

The two conditions are distinct.

The additivity condition (Remark
2.40
) provides
a real number per reaction label, allows

F_{H}(r_{1})\neq F_{H}(r_{2})
for two labels with identical source and
target, and is the categorical content of
\mathcal{L}_{1}
.
The state-function condition imposes
F_{H}(r_{1})=F_{H}(r_{2})
whenever

s(r_{1})=s(r_{2})
and
t(r_{1})=t(r_{2})
, by requiring
h
to be
well-defined on complexes, but
does not
identify
r_{1}
with

r_{2}
as morphisms in the category: the two reaction labels remain
distinct elements of
\mathcal{R}
, they simply receive the same enthalpy
value.
The state-function condition is therefore a constraint on the
particular functor
F_{H}
, not a relation imposed on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

itself.

An
F_{H}
satisfying only the additivity condition but not the
state-function condition is a perfectly valid strict symmetric
monoidal functor, representing a situation in which the same gross
stoichiometry is associated with distinct energetic signatures
across different realisations (e.g., different catalysts, different
solvents, or mechanistically distinct pathways).
Both conditions are of physical interest, and the distinction
between them is central to how
\mathcal{L}_{1}
and
\mathcal{L}_{2}
differ.

Remark 2.42

(Bridge to
\mathcal{L}_{1}
)
.

The pair
(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{H})
, where
F_{H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
is a
strict symmetric monoidal functor satisfying the additivity
condition, is the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-level data associated with
P
.
The complete development of
\mathcal{L}_{1}
— its relationship to
equilibrium thermodynamics via the entropy functor
F_{S}
, the

\dagger
-structure of
\mathcal{L}_{2}
encoding detailed balance, and the
Wegscheider cycle conditions for rate constants — is given in
Chapter 3.

§3.
\mathcal{L}_{1}
: The Thermochemical Level

§3.1. The forcing of
\mathcal{L}_{1}

Section
2.8
exhibited the concrete
\mathcal{L}_{0}\to\mathcal{L}_{1}
forcing instance: two reaction labels

r_{1},r_{2}\in\mathcal{R}
sharing source and target complexes (the

\mathrm{N_{2}}+\mathrm{O_{2}}\to 2\,\mathrm{NO}
system of
Forcing Box
2.8
), and the label-permutation within
the fibre
(s,t)^{-1}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})
representing a
non-trivial class in
\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
.
This section picks up the structural answer:
what exactly
is the minimal extension
\mathcal{L}_{1}
that resolves this class?

After a brief complementary illustration, three physical
observations constrain the answer to a single categorical object:
a strict symmetric monoidal functor

F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
.

A complementary forcing instance for
\mathcal{L}_{1}

The §
2.8
forcing instance used two distinct
reaction labels in the same Petri net, distinguishable by having
different enthalpies.
A second, pedagogically minimal manifestation of the same

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
non-triviality is the following.

Let
P
be any Petri net, and consider two
thermochemical
systems
built on it:

\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),\,F_{H}^{(1)}\bigr)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),\,F_{H}^{(2)}\bigr),

with
F_{H}^{(1)}(r)\neq F_{H}^{(2)}(r)
on at least one generating
reaction
r
— the minimal instance being a single-reaction
Petri net
P=(\{A,B\},\{r\},s,t)
with

r:A\to B
, and
F_{H}^{(1)}(r)=+50
versus
F_{H}^{(2)}(r)=-50

(in
\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
, chosen schematically).
Both decorated pairs have the same image under the forgetful
operation
U_{1}
(Definition
3.1
): dropping the
thermochemical datum yields the same
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
in either case.

At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, however, the two decorated pairs are genuinely
distinct: in this minimal example

\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Petri}}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P))
is trivial, so the only candidate
intertwining
\alpha:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is the identity, and

F_{H}^{(2)}\circ\mathrm{id}=F_{H}^{(1)}
would force

F_{H}^{(2)}(r)=F_{H}^{(1)}(r)
— contradicting the choice.
By the automorphism sequence of §
2.5
, this
separation at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
(invisible at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
) is precisely what
non-triviality of
\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
records: the forgetful
operation
U_{1}
is not injective on decorated pairs — the
underlying
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
alone does not determine
F_{\!H}
.
Distinguishing the two pairs requires at least the

\mathcal{L}_{1}
-decoration data.

The §
2.8
fibre-permutation instance and the
complementary instance above exhibit the same underlying fact —

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
is non-trivial — from two different directions:
the former fixes a single Petri net with two distinct labels and
asks which automorphism of the
\mathcal{L}_{0}
-presentation fails to lift;
the latter fixes a single reaction label and asks which pair of

\mathcal{L}_{1}
-decorated objects projects to the same
\mathcal{L}_{0}
-object.
Both confirm that
\mathcal{L}_{0}
cannot distinguish endothermic from
exothermic realisations, and that a real-valued datum on reactions
is the minimal structure needed to break this ambiguity.

What structure resolves the ambiguity?

Before writing any mathematics, three physical observations
constrain the answer.

(a)

Sequential additivity (Hess’s Law).

If reaction
r_{1}
is followed by
r_{2}
, the total enthalpy
change is
\Delta H(r_{2}\circ r_{1})=\Delta H(r_{1})+\Delta H(r_{2})
.
The label must be compatible with categorical composition.

(b)

Parallel additivity.

If
r_{1}
and
r_{2}
proceed independently,

\Delta H(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})=\Delta H(r_{1})+\Delta H(r_{2})
.
The label must be compatible with the monoidal product.

(c)

No spurious energy.

\Delta H(\mathrm{id}_{\bf u})=0
for every complex
\mathbf{u}
—
unitality.

These three constraints specify a strict symmetric monoidal
functor

F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\;\longrightarrow\;B\mathbb{R}

— the one-object additive category
B\mathbb{R}
introduced in
§
1.4
.
The fit between the three physical axioms and this categorical
structure is exact in both directions.

•

No weaker structure suffices.

A plain (non-monoidal) functor satisfies (a) but misses (b):
functoriality constrains composition, not the tensor product.
A lax monoidal functor weakens (b) to

F_{\!H}(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2})+\phi_{r_{1},r_{2}},

introducing a coherence term
\phi_{r_{1},r_{2}}\in\mathbb{R}
absent
from any physical enthalpy assignment.
Dropping the unit condition loses (c).
Each weakening fails at least one of the three physical axioms.

•

No stronger structure is needed.

The three axioms fix
F_{\!H}
uniquely on all morphisms given its
values on generators (Proposition
3.2
in
§
3.2
).
Any further structure — requiring
F_{\!H}
to be a monoidal
equivalence, an adjunction, or a faithful functor — would
impose conditions (surjectivity, invertibility, injectivity on
morphisms) with no physical interpretation for an enthalpy
assignment.

The extension presented here is the minimal categorical object
resolving the
\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
class identified at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
:
a decorator functor adjoined to
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
without modifying its
underlying category.
That this is the
unique
minimal extension resolving the
cokernel is claimed constructively at the present level, not as a
general theorem about categorical extensions; the full taxonomy of
the six extension types that occur across the tower is recorded in
§
10.8
.
The next subsection makes the construction precise.

§3.2. Definition of
\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)

Definition 3.1

(Thermochemical level
\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)
)
.

Let
P=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},s,t)
be a Petri net.
The
thermochemical level
of
P
is the pair

\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)\;:=\;\bigl(\,\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),\;F_{\!H}\,\bigr),

where
F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
is a strict symmetric monoidal
functor from the stoichiometric category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
into
B\mathbb{R}
.
The notation
\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)
refers to this pair — a decorated
structure, not itself a category.
We write
U_{1}
for the
forgetful operation

U_{1}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{\!H}\bigr)\;:=\;\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),

which returns the underlying stoichiometric category from the
decorated pair, dropping
F_{\!H}
.

Unpacking Definition
3.1

The domain of
F_{\!H}
is
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, the free skeletal permutative
category already constructed in Section
2
.
The pair
(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{\!H})
is
\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)
; it is emphatically

not
the case that
F_{\!H}
maps
\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)
to
B\mathbb{R}
(that
would be circular —
\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)
is the decorated pair, not a
category in its own right).

The target
B\mathbb{R}
is a one-object category, so its object monoid

\{\ast\}
is trivially strictly commutative; this is exactly the
hypothesis on the target required by Theorem
2.14
, and
it is satisfied here without further work.
The action of
F_{\!H}
is therefore entirely determined by its action
on morphisms:

•

Every object
{\bf u}\in\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
maps to the single
object
\ast
.

•

Every morphism
r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
maps
to a real number
F_{\!H}(r)\in\mathbb{R}
.

The “strict symmetric monoidal” conditions then read:

•

Functoriality:

F_{\!H}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})=F_{\!H}(r_{2})+F_{\!H}(r_{1})
.

•

Monoidality:

F_{\!H}(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})=F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2})
.

•

Unitality:

F_{\!H}(\mathrm{id}_{\bf u})=0
for all
{\bf u}
.

The adjective
strict
means that the coherence isomorphisms
of a monoidal functor—the natural transformations

\phi_{A,B}:F_{\!H}(A)\otimes F_{\!H}(B)\to F_{\!H}(A\otimes B)

and
\phi_{0}:I\to F_{\!H}(I)
—are required to be

identity morphisms
, not merely natural isomorphisms

[
187
, Ch. XI, §1]
.
In
B\mathbb{R}
each
\phi_{A,B}
is an endomorphism of the unique object

\ast
, i.e. a real number; strictness requires it to equal
0

(the identity in
B\mathbb{R}
), which is precisely the
monoidality equation above.
These three equations are the
complete content
of the
thermochemical decoration.

The existence and uniqueness of
F_{\!H}
given its values on generating
reactions follows directly from the universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

Proposition 3.2

(Existence and uniqueness of
F_{\!H}
)
.

Let
P
be a Petri net with reaction set
\mathcal{R}
.
Given any assignment
\Delta H_{0}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R}
, there is a unique strict
symmetric monoidal functor

F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}

satisfying
F_{\!H}(r)=\Delta H_{0}(r)
for every generating reaction

r\in\mathcal{R}
.

Proof.

By Theorem
2.14
,
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is the free skeletal
permutative category on
P
: for any strict symmetric monoidal
category
\mathcal{C}

whose object monoid is strictly
commutative
and any morphism-assignment

f:\mathcal{R}\to\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{C})
compatible with source/target
types, there is a unique strict symmetric monoidal functor

\bar{f}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\mathcal{C}
extending
f

[
187
, Ch. XI, §3]
.

Take
\mathcal{C}=B\mathbb{R}
, the one-object category with morphisms

\mathbb{R}
and composition given by addition.
Its object monoid is a singleton, so trivially strictly commutative
— the hypothesis of Theorem
2.14
is satisfied.
The source/target compatibility condition on
f=\Delta H_{0}
is also
trivial since
B\mathbb{R}
has only one object.
The unique extension
\bar{f}=F_{\!H}
satisfies all three conditions
of Definition
3.1
by construction.
∎

One real number per reaction

Proposition
3.2
says: the thermochemical content
of a network at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
is determined by
exactly one real
number per chemical generator
.
The reason is structural: every morphism of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is a finite
composite and tensor product of chemical generators
r\in\mathcal{R}

together with structural morphisms (identities and symmetries

\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}
).
Strictness forces
F_{\!H}(\mathrm{id}_{\bf u})=0
and

F_{\!H}(\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}})=0
(the symmetry of
B\mathbb{R}

is trivial because
B\mathbb{R}
has one object), so for any morphism

f=r_{i_{k}}\circ\cdots\circ(r_{i_{1}}\otimes r_{i_{2}})\circ\cdots
:

F_{\!H}(f)\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{i_{k}})+\cdots+F_{\!H}(r_{i_{1}})+F_{\!H}(r_{i_{2}})+\cdots

F_{\!H}(f)
is a sum of the chemical-generator values
\Delta H_{0}(r_{i})
,
with multiplicities determined by how many times each generator
appears in
f
.
The values
\{\Delta H_{0}(r)\}_{r\in\mathcal{R}}
therefore determine
F_{\!H}

completely and uniquely; no further measurement is needed.

§3.3. Layer 1: the generic additive functor

The functor
F_{\!H}
of Definition
3.1
as stated —
one free real parameter per generating reaction — constitutes

Layer 1
of the thermochemical structure.
The following theorem encodes Hess’s Law and its monoidal
counterpart as the two defining axioms of
F_{\!H}
.
The physical content of Hess’s Law has been understood since 1840

[
139
]
; its formulation as the functoriality condition of a
strict monoidal functor into
B\mathbb{R}
is, to the authors’ knowledge,
original to this work.

Theorem 3.3

(Hess’s Law and parallel additivity — Layer 1)
.

Let
F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
be the thermochemical functor
(Layer 1 data).

(i)

(Sequential additivity / Hess’s Law)

For composable reactions

r_{1}:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
,
r_{2}:{\bf v}\to{\bf w}
:

F_{\!H}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2}).

(ii)

(Parallel additivity)

For any reactions
r_{1},r_{2}
:

F_{\!H}(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2}).

(iii)

(No spurious energy)

F_{\!H}(\mathrm{id}_{\bf u})=0
for every complex
{\bf u}
.

Proof.

Parts (i)–(iii) are the functoriality, monoidality, and unitality
axioms of
F_{\!H}
respectively.
They hold by definition of a strict symmetric monoidal functor;
the content of the theorem is that such an
F_{\!H}
exists and is
unique given values on generators, as established in
Proposition
3.2
.
∎

Remark 3.4

(Two postulates, one equation)
.

Traditional thermochemistry textbooks state Hess’s Law (part (i))
and parallel additivity (part (ii)) as two separate empirical
postulates
[
24
]
.
Categorically, both are instances of the single requirement that

F_{\!H}
is a monoidal functor: sequential additivity is functoriality,
parallel additivity is monoidality.
The classical textbook presentation reflects the same mathematical
structure, stated in the language of experiments rather than of
categories.

Physically, the full
path-independence
form of Hess’s Law
— the enthalpy of a process depends only on initial and final
complexes, regardless of route — is classically derived from the
first law together with the identification of enthalpy as a state
function
[
23
]
.
Theorem
3.3
captures the additive content of Hess’s
Law (along sequential composites and across parallel processes)
directly from functoriality, without invoking the state-function
identification.
The path-independence form proper requires the Layer 2 coboundary
condition
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h
developed in §
3.4
.

What Layer 1 does not enforce: the cycle condition.

Theorem
3.3
guarantees that
F_{\!H}
is additive along
any composable sequence of reactions and across any parallel
combination.
A natural further expectation is that traversing a closed loop of
reactions should accumulate zero net enthalpy — the physical
content of “enthalpy is a state function.”
This is
not
a consequence of Layer 1 alone; it requires
an additional constraint.
The following warning, drawn from a real carbon-combustion cycle,
makes this precise.

Warning 3.5

(Cycle non-closure is consistent with Layer 1)
.

Consider the carbon–oxygen system

\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{C(s)},\,\mathrm{O_{2}(g)},\,\mathrm{CO(g)},\,\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\}

with three generating reactions forming a directed cycle:

\displaystyle r_{1}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{C(s)}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\to\mathrm{CO(g)},

\displaystyle r_{2}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{CO(g)}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\to\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)},

\displaystyle r_{3}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\to\mathrm{C(s)}+\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}.

The thermochemically correct values are

F_{\!H}(r_{1})=-110.5
,
F_{\!H}(r_{2})=-283.0
,

F_{\!H}(r_{3})=+393.5
(all in kJ/mol)
[
68
]
.
Composing
r_{2}
with
r_{1}
requires a spectator

\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}
to bridge the source–target gap, so
the directed cycle from
\mathrm{C(s)}+\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}
back to
itself is

r_{3}\circ r_{2}\circ\bigl(r_{1}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}}\bigr)
.
Functoriality, monoidality, and
F_{\!H}(\mathrm{id})=0
give a cycle sum
of exactly zero:

F_{\!H}\!\Bigl(r_{3}\circ r_{2}\circ\bigl(r_{1}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}}\bigr)\Bigr)\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2})+F_{\!H}(r_{3})\;=\;0.

Now suppose, however, that one assigns the hypothetically inconsistent
value
F_{\!H}(r_{3})=+380.0\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}
(as might arise from a
calibration error or an inconsistent reference state).
Functoriality (Layer 1) then gives:

F_{\!H}\!\Bigl(r_{3}\circ r_{2}\circ\bigl(r_{1}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}}\bigr)\Bigr)\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2})+F_{\!H}(r_{3})\;\neq\;0.

This assignment satisfies all three axioms of Layer 1 — Hess’s
Law for composable morphisms, parallel additivity, and no spurious
energy on identity morphisms — yet the directed cycle does not
sum to zero.
Layer 1 is blind to this inconsistency.
The cycle condition
\sum_{i}F_{\!H}(r_{i})=0
is an independent
constraint; it is
not
derivable from the functor axioms alone.

Why the free category is the right domain

In
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, every type-compatible composite of chemical
generators yields a distinct morphism.
The only equalities that hold are those forced by the axioms of a
skeletal permutative category (associativity, unit laws,
naturality and involutivity of the symmetry endomorphisms

\sigma_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}
) —
never
any equation
among chemical generators.
In particular,

r_{3}\circ r_{2}\circ\bigl(r_{1}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}}\bigr)\neq\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{C(s)}+\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}}
in the free category,
even though the composite’s source and target both equal

\mathrm{C(s)}+\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}
: the free category has no way to
know that going around the cycle “should” be trivial.
The physical interpretation is immediate: a thermochemical
assignment that satisfies Layer 1 but not Layer 2 is the
mathematical model of a calorimetric dataset corrupted by
inconsistent reference states or measurement errors.
Layer 2, introduced in Section
3.4
, is precisely
the condition that eliminates all such inconsistencies.

§3.4. Layer 2: the state-function condition

Warning
3.5
shows that Layer 1 alone permits
thermochemical cycles to accumulate non-zero enthalpy, in conflict
with the first law of thermodynamics.
The culprit is that Layer 1 assigns a real number to each

reaction
independently; it imposes no relationship between
the enthalpy of a reaction and any intrinsic property of the

complexes
it connects.
The first law demands more: enthalpy must be a
state
function
, meaning its value for any process depends only on the
initial and final states, not on the path taken.
Mathematically, this means the enthalpy assignment must be
expressible as a
difference of potentials
defined on the
complexes themselves.
Layer 2 is the additional datum that enforces this.

Definition 3.6

(Layer 2: state-function / coboundary condition)
.

A thermochemical functor
F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
satisfies the

state-function condition
(Layer 2) if there exists a monoid
homomorphism

h\;:\;\bigl(\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}],+,\mathbf{0}\bigr)\longrightarrow\bigl(\mathbb{R},+,0\bigr)

such that, for every generating reaction
r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
,

F_{\!H}(r)\;=\;h({\bf v})-h({\bf u}).

We write this condition as
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h
and call
h
an

object potential
(or
additive potential
) for
F_{\!H}
.

The notation
\delta^{0}
and the term
object potential
require
some comments.
The map
h
assigns a real number (a “height” or “potential”)
to each complex in
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
, and the identity

F_{\!H}(r)=h({\bf v})-h({\bf u})
says that the enthalpy of a generating
reaction is the difference of the endpoint potentials.
This is the discrete analogue of a conservative field on a graph:
individual reactions are directed edges, while sequences of reactions
are directed paths.
For an exact edge-labeling, the total enthalpy along a directed path
depends only on its endpoints, and hence vanishes on directed cycles

[
101
,
280
]
.

The symbol
\delta^{0}
is borrowed from graph cohomology.

Coboundary notation

To explain the notation precisely, let

G_{P}=(V_{P},E_{P})

be the directed reaction graph of the network, where

V_{P}:=s(\mathcal{R})\cup t(\mathcal{R})\subseteq\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}],\qquad E_{P}:=\mathcal{R},

and
s,t:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
are the source and target maps.
For the reaction graph
G_{P}
, the standard graph-cochain spaces are

\widetilde{C}^{0}(G_{P};\mathbb{R}):=\{\phi:V_{P}\to\mathbb{R}\},\qquad\widetilde{C}^{1}(G_{P};\mathbb{R}):=\{\omega:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R}\}.

Thus a
0
-cochain is a real-valued function on vertices and a

1
-cochain is a real-valued function on directed edges

[
201
]
.
The standard degree-zero graph coboundary is

\widetilde{\delta}^{0}:\widetilde{C}^{0}(G_{P};\mathbb{R})\to\widetilde{C}^{1}(G_{P};\mathbb{R}),\qquad(\widetilde{\delta}^{0}\phi)(r):=\phi\bigl(t(r)\bigr)-\phi\bigl(s(r)\bigr).

This is the graph-theoretic analogue of taking the gradient of a
scalar potential
[
201
]
.

In the present thermochemical setting we impose the stronger
requirement that the potential extend additively to all complexes.
Accordingly, we define

C^{0}:=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Mon}}(\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}],\mathbb{R}),\qquad C^{1}:=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(\mathcal{R},\mathbb{R}).

Restriction to the vertex set gives a map

\mathrm{res}:C^{0}\to\widetilde{C}^{0}(G_{P};\mathbb{R}),\qquad h\mapsto h|_{V_{P}},

and we define

\delta^{0}:C^{0}\to C^{1}

by the same endpoint-difference formula,

(\delta^{0}h)(r)\;:=\;h\bigl(t(r)\bigr)-h\bigl(s(r)\bigr).

Thus
\delta^{0}
is the usual graph coboundary, restricted to the
subspace of additive potentials on complexes.

Since
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
is the free commutative monoid on the
species set
\mathcal{S}
, every monoid homomorphism
h:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to\mathbb{R}
is uniquely
determined by its values on species:

h\!\left(\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}n_{S}S\right)\;=\;\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}n_{S}\,h(S).

Hence an additive object potential has at most
|\mathcal{S}|
free parameters,
one for each species.

The state-function condition admits two equivalent algebraic
formulations, together with two immediate consequences.
The equivalence below is the additive-monoid form of Hess’s law:
reaction enthalpies arise from species potentials exactly when they are
linear in the net stoichiometric change.
Path-independence and cycle-vanishing then follow by telescoping

[
101
,
280
]
.

Proposition 3.7

(Equivalent algebraic formulations of Layer 2)
.

Let
F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
be a Layer 1 functor.
The following are equivalent:

(i)

(Coboundary)
There exists an object potential

h\in C^{0}
such that

F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h.

(ii)

(Species-potential form)
There exist real numbers

\eta_{S}\in\mathbb{R}
for each species
S\in\mathcal{S}
such that, for every
generating reaction
r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
,

F_{\!H}(r)\;=\;\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}N_{S,r}\,\eta_{S},

where

N_{S,r}:=\nu_{S}^{({\bf v})}-\nu_{S}^{({\bf u})}

is the net stoichiometric coefficient of species
S
in reaction

r
.

Moreover, either of these equivalent conditions implies:

(iii)

(Path independence)
For any two directed paths of
generating reactions from
{\bf u}
to
{\bf v}
,

p:r_{1},\dots,r_{m}:{\bf u}\leadsto{\bf v},\qquad p^{\prime}:r^{\prime}_{1},\dots,r^{\prime}_{n}:{\bf u}\leadsto{\bf v},

one has

\sum_{i=1}^{m}F_{\!H}(r_{i})\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}F_{\!H}(r^{\prime}_{j}).

(iv)

(Directed-cycle condition)
For every directed closed
loop of generating reactions

r_{1}:{\bf u}_{0}\to{\bf u}_{1},\;r_{2}:{\bf u}_{1}\to{\bf u}_{2},\;\ldots,\;r_{k}:{\bf u}_{k-1}\to{\bf u}_{0},

one has

\sum_{i=1}^{k}F_{\!H}(r_{i})=0.

Proof.

(i)
\Rightarrow
(ii).

Set
\eta_{S}:=h(S)
for each
S\in\mathcal{S}
.
Since
h
is a monoid homomorphism,

h({\bf u})=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\nu_{S}^{({\bf u})}\eta_{S},\qquad h({\bf v})=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\nu_{S}^{({\bf v})}\eta_{S}.

Therefore

\displaystyle F_{\!H}(r)

\displaystyle=h({\bf v})-h({\bf u})=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\bigl(\nu_{S}^{({\bf v})}-\nu_{S}^{({\bf u})}\bigr)\eta_{S}

\displaystyle=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}N_{S,r}\eta_{S}.

(ii)
\Rightarrow
(i).

Define

h\!\left(\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}n_{S}S\right):=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}n_{S}\,\eta_{S}.

Since
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]=\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
is free commutative on
\mathcal{S}
, this defines
a monoid homomorphism
h:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to\mathbb{R}
.
For any generating reaction
r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
,

h({\bf v})-h({\bf u})=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\bigl(\nu_{S}^{({\bf v})}-\nu_{S}^{({\bf u})}\bigr)\eta_{S}=F_{\!H}(r),

so
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h
.

(i)
\Rightarrow
(iii).

If

p:r_{1},\dots,r_{m}:{\bf u}\leadsto{\bf v},

then

\sum_{i=1}^{m}F_{\!H}(r_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl[h({\bf u}_{i})-h({\bf u}_{i-1})\bigr]=h({\bf v})-h({\bf u}),

and the same formula holds for any other path
p^{\prime}
from
{\bf u}
to

{\bf v}
.

(iii)
\Rightarrow
(iv).

Apply path independence to a closed path and the trivial path at the
same basepoint.
∎

Remark 3.8
.

For arbitrary edge-labelings on a directed graph, vanishing on
directed cycles characterises exactness with respect to an arbitrary
vertex-potential.
In the present paper, however, Layer 2 is stronger: the potential must
extend additively to a monoid homomorphism
h:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to\mathbb{R}
.
Accordingly, the directed-cycle condition is a consequence of
Layer 2, but not by itself an equivalent replacement for it.

Why the state-function condition is the first law

The condition
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h
encodes the first law of
thermodynamics in a single equation.
Saying
F_{\!H}(r)=h({\bf v})-h({\bf u})
means enthalpy depends
only on the initial and final complexes, not on which specific
reaction or sequence of reactions connects them.
Going around a closed reaction cycle yields zero net enthalpy
because the potential heights
h
return to their starting values.
Layer 1 alone is the theory of an
additive
reaction label;
Layer 2 additionally demands that this label derives from an
absolute assignment of values to the objects (complexes) of
the network.

Parameter count.

Observation 3.9

(Parameter reduction at Layer 2)
.

The state-function condition reduces the number of free parameters
required to specify a thermochemical network, exchanging
reaction-level freedom for a smaller species-level one.

•

Layer 1
:
|\mathcal{R}|
free parameters (one real number
per generating reaction).

•

Layer 2
:
|\mathcal{S}|
species values
\{h(S)\}_{S\in\mathcal{S}}

specify
h
, hence
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h
; the physically
meaningful content of
h
is its image under
\delta^{0}
, which
has gauge kernel

\ker(\delta^{0})\cap\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Mon}}(\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}],\mathbb{R})\;\cong\;\ker(N^{\top})\;\subseteq\;\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}.

where
N\in\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|\times|\mathcal{R}|}
is the stoichiometric
matrix.
Equivalently, two object potentials
h,h^{\prime}
differ only by an
irrelevant gauge iff
h-h^{\prime}
is a conservation law
(Proposition
2.22
).

•

Net dimension
: the reaction-enthalpy parameter
space
\mathrm{im}(\delta^{0})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|}
has dimension

\rho:=\mathrm{rank}_{\mathbb{R}}(N)
, the dimension of the stoichiometric
subspace (§
2.6
); the gauge kernel is

|\mathcal{S}|-\rho
dimensional.

The reduction from
|\mathcal{R}|
to
\rho
parameters proceeds in two
stages, exposing the role of deficiency.
Graph-cycle conditions on the reaction graph alone — equivalent
to requiring an arbitrary vertex potential, not necessarily
species-additive — reduce
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|}
to
\mathrm{im}(I_{a}^{\top})
of
dimension
n-\ell
, where
n
is the number of complexes and

\ell
the number of linkage classes.
Imposing the further
species-additive
structure of Layer 2
(the potential
h
must be a monoid homomorphism on
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
, not
merely a function on complexes) reduces this to
\mathrm{im}(N^{\top})=\mathrm{im}(\delta^{0})
of dimension
\rho
.
The difference
(n-\ell)-\rho=:\delta\geq 0
is the

deficiency
of the network (§
2.6
);
\rho=n-\ell
holds precisely when
\delta=0
.
The total constraint count
|\mathcal{R}|-\rho
therefore decomposes as

\gamma+\delta
, where
\gamma=|\mathcal{R}|-(n-\ell)
counts the
graph-cycle conditions.

Counting calorimetric experiments

A thermochemical network with
|\mathcal{R}|
generating reactions and
stoichiometric rank
\rho
requires exactly
\rho
independent
calorimetric measurements to fully characterise all reaction
enthalpies; the remaining
|\mathcal{R}|-\rho
values are determined by
the cycle conditions of Proposition
3.7
(iv).
For deficiency-zero networks,
\rho=n-\ell
, recovering the
familiar “
n-\ell
measurements” rule of thumb (where
n
is
the number of complexes and
\ell
the number of linkage classes);
non-zero deficiency requires
\rho<n-\ell
measurements
relative to the rule of thumb.

For the Born–Haber cycle of Example
3.15
, the
cycle constraint relating the direct formation reaction to the
five-step elementary decomposition lets the lattice enthalpy

F_{\!H}(r_{5})
— which is not accessible to direct calorimetry —
be extracted from the four measurable elementary steps and the
net formation enthalpy.

3.4.1. Formation enthalpies as the canonical trivialisation

The object potential
h\in C^{0}
is determined by
F_{\!H}
only up to
addition of a conservation-law potential (
\ker(N^{\top})
); see
Remark
3.12
below.
Chemistry resolves this gauge freedom by a universal convention:
the elemental reference species in their standard states are
assigned enthalpy zero.
The resulting
standard molar enthalpies of formation

\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)
, compiled in thermochemical databases such as the
NIST-JANAF tables
[
60
]
, give the conventionally
canonical choice of object potential.
This is the IUPAC convention
[
249
]
: it picks a
distinguished representative from the gauge equivalence class of
object potentials and is the universally adopted standard in
thermochemical databases.
We now make this precise.

Definition 3.10

(Formation enthalpy and elemental references)
.

Let
\mathcal{E}\subset\mathcal{S}
be the set of
elemental
reference species
in their standard states
(e.g. H
2
(g), C(graphite), Na(s), O
2
(g)).
The
standard molar enthalpy of formation
of species
S\in\mathcal{S}
is the real number
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)\in\mathbb{R}
defined as the
enthalpy change for the reaction that forms one mole of
S
from
its constituent elements in their standard reference states.
By convention,
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(E):=0
for all
E\in\mathcal{E}

[
60
,
23
]
.

Proposition 3.11

(Formation enthalpies give the canonical object potential)
.

Define
h_{f}:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to\mathbb{R}
by extending the formation enthalpies
linearly over complexes:

h_{f}\!\left(\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}n_{S}\,S\right)\;:=\;\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}n_{S}\,\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S).

Then
h_{f}
is a monoid homomorphism (an object potential in the
sense of Definition
3.6
), and for every generating
reaction
r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
with stoichiometric coefficients

\nu_{S}^{({\bf u})}
and
\nu_{S}^{({\bf v})}
counting the
multiplicity of species
S
in complexes
{\bf u}
and
{\bf v}

respectively:

\delta^{0}h_{f}(r)\;=\;h_{f}({\bf v})-h_{f}({\bf u})\;=\;\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}N_{S,r}\,\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S),

where
N_{S,r}:=\nu_{S}^{({\bf v})}-\nu_{S}^{({\bf u})}\in\mathbb{Z}

is the net stoichiometric coefficient of species
S
in reaction

r
(positive for products, negative for reactants).

Proof.

h_{f}
is a monoid homomorphism.

Since
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]=\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
is the free commutative monoid on
\mathcal{S}
,
every monoid homomorphism
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to\mathbb{R}
is uniquely determined by
its values on generators (species), and the extension

h_{f}(\sum_{S}n_{S}S)=\sum_{S}n_{S}h_{f}(S)
is the unique such
homomorphism with
h_{f}(S)=\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)
.
The monoid homomorphism axioms hold by linearity:

h_{f}(\mathbf{0})=0,\qquad h_{f}({\bf u}+{\bf v})=h_{f}({\bf u})+h_{f}({\bf v}).

The formula for
F_{\!H}(r)
.

Direct computation:

\displaystyle h_{f}({\bf v})-h_{f}({\bf u})

\displaystyle=\sum_{S}\nu_{S}^{({\bf v})}\,\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)-\sum_{S}\nu_{S}^{({\bf u})}\,\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)

\displaystyle=\sum_{S}\bigl(\nu_{S}^{({\bf v})}-\nu_{S}^{({\bf u})}\bigr)\,\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)=\sum_{S}N_{S,r}\,\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S).\qed

Remark 3.12

(Gauge freedom and reference state)
.

The object potential
h_{f}
is determined by
F_{\!H}
only up to the
gauge
\ker(N^{\top})\subset\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
: two potentials

h_{f},h^{\prime}_{f}\in C^{0}=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Mon}}(\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}],\mathbb{R})
yield the same
reaction enthalpies
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h_{f}=\delta^{0}h^{\prime}_{f}
if and
only if their difference
g:=h^{\prime}_{f}-h_{f}
lies in
\ker(N^{\top})
,
i.e.
\sum_{S}N_{S,r}g(S)=0
for every reaction
r
.
The space
\ker(N^{\top})
is precisely the space of conservation
laws (Proposition
2.22
); two object
potentials are gauge-equivalent exactly when they differ by a
conservation-law potential.
This is the precise categorical content of the thermodynamic
statement that “absolute enthalpies do not exist, but enthalpy
differences do”
[
23
]
.
The IUPAC convention
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(E)=0
for elemental reference
species
[
249
]
is the standard chemical gauge
fixing: for typical chemical networks, where the conservation
laws are spanned by atomic-composition counters, setting the
