elemental potentials to zero uniquely determines
h_{f}
on the
remaining (non-elemental) species.

The formation table
is
the object potential

A standard thermochemical data table — one entry
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)

per species
S\in\mathcal{S}
— is precisely the specification of the
monoid homomorphism
h_{f}:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to\mathbb{R}
.
From this single table, Proposition
3.11

computes
F_{\!H}(r)=\sum_{S}N_{S,r}\,\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)
for every
reaction
r
in the network, with no further data.
The functor
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h_{f}
follows automatically from the
coboundary structure.
The table
is

h_{f}
; the Layer 2 condition
is
the
statement that every internally consistent thermochemical dataset
has such a table.

§3.5. Worked examples

The three examples below are standard exercises from undergraduate
thermochemistry curricula
[
24
,
60
]
.
Every introductory chemistry student learns to add enthalpies along
reaction pathways, to close thermochemical cycles, and to use
tabulated formation enthalpies to predict unmeasurable quantities.
The categorical language of
\mathcal{L}_{1}
reveals the common mathematical
skeleton behind all three: Hess’s Law is functoriality, cycle closure
is the coboundary condition, and a thermochemical data table is an
object potential.
Nothing new is computed; what is new is the identification of the
precise categorical structure that makes the computations valid.

3.5.1. Hess’s Law as parallel morphisms: carbon combustion

Example 3.13

(Two paths to CO
2
)
.

Species

\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{C(graphite),\,O_{2}(g),\,CO(g),\,CO_{2}(g)}\}
;
three generating reactions, with reaction enthalpies from

[
60
]
:

\displaystyle r_{1}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{C(graphite)}+\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\to\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}(r_{1})=-393.5\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},

\displaystyle r_{2}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{C(graphite)}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\to\mathrm{CO(g)},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}(r_{2})=-110.5\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},

\displaystyle r_{3}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{CO(g)}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\to\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}(r_{3})=-283.0\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.

Remark 3.14

(Fractional stoichiometric coefficients)
.

The coefficient
\tfrac{1}{2}
in
r_{2}
and
r_{3}
appears to
conflict with the definition of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
as a category of
complexes in
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
(free commutative monoid on species,
with non-negative integer multiplicities).
There is no genuine conflict: the coefficient
\tfrac{1}{2}

is chemical shorthand for a scaled version of the reaction.
One may always clear denominators — writing

2r_{2}:2\,\mathrm{C(s)}+\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\to 2\,\mathrm{CO(g)}

and

2r_{3}:2\,\mathrm{CO(g)}+\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\to 2\,\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}

— to obtain integer-coefficient reactions in
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, with

F_{\!H}(2r_{k})=2F_{\!H}(r_{k})
by monoidality.
Fractional coefficients never arise as transcendental or
irrational numbers: stoichiometry is always rational, and rational
coefficients always lift to integer coefficients by scaling by the
least common denominator of all fractions appearing in the network.
Throughout this section we retain conventional chemical notation.

At
\mathcal{L}_{0}
.

The complex
\mathrm{C(s)}+\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}

(where
+
denotes the tensor product
\otimes
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
,
per the chemical-notation convention) is the source of
r_{1}
.
To reach
\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}
via
r_{2}
then
r_{3}
, the spectator

\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}
must be carried along until
r_{3}

consumes it: starting from
\mathrm{C}+\mathrm{O_{2}}=\mathrm{C}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}
, the two-step path is the composite

r_{3}\circ\bigl(r_{2}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}}\bigr)
.
Its source is
\mathrm{C}+\mathrm{O_{2}}
and its target is

\mathrm{CO_{2}}
, matching
r_{1}
.
The direct
r_{1}
and the two-step

r_{3}\circ\bigl(r_{2}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}}\bigr)

are therefore
distinct parallel morphisms
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

with the same source and target.

At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, Layer 1.

Functoriality, monoidality, and unitality
(Theorem
3.3
) give

F_{\!H}\bigl(r_{2}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}}\bigr)=F_{\!H}(r_{2})+0=F_{\!H}(r_{2})
, hence:

F_{\!H}\!\Bigl(r_{3}\circ\bigl(r_{2}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}}\bigr)\Bigr)\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{2})+F_{\!H}(r_{3})\;=\;-110.5+(-283.0)\;=\;-393.5\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{1}).

The two paths agree because the data are thermodynamically
consistent.
Whether this equality is
forced
(a structural consequence)
or coincidental is the Layer 2 question.

At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, Layer 2.

The equality
F_{\!H}(r_{1})=F_{\!H}(r_{3}\circ r_{2})
is path independence
(Proposition
3.7
(iii)): the two parallel morphisms
must have the same
F_{\!H}
value whenever the coboundary condition
holds.
Using standard formation enthalpies

\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(\mathrm{CO_{2}})=-393.5
,

\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(\mathrm{CO})=-110.5
,

\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(\mathrm{C})=\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(\mathrm{O_{2}})=0

(all in
\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
, elemental references at zero

[
60
]
):

h_{f}(\mathrm{CO_{2}})-h_{f}(\mathrm{C}\otimes\mathrm{O_{2}})=-393.5-(0+0)=-393.5\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.

The commutative diagram below displays both levels simultaneously.

At
\mathcal{L}_{0}
, the diagram does
not
commute:
r_{1}
and

r_{3}\circ\bigl(r_{2}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}}\bigr)

are distinct parallel morphisms in the free SMC.
The Layer 2 coboundary condition
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h_{f}
forces the
equality
F_{\!H}(r_{1})=F_{\!H}\bigl(r_{3}\circ(r_{2}\otimes\mathrm{id})\bigr)

in
B\mathbb{R}
, making the diagram commute after applying
F_{\!H}
.
This image-commutativity in
B\mathbb{R}
is the categorical content of
Hess’s Law.

3.5.2. Born–Haber cycle: Layer 2 uniquely determines the unmeasurable step

Example 3.15

(Born–Haber cycle for sodium chloride)
.

The formation reaction

r_{\mathrm{form}}:\mathrm{Na(s)}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)}\to\mathrm{NaCl(s)}

decomposes into five elementary generators (all values at
298 K
[
23
,
60
]
):

\displaystyle r_{1}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{Na(s)}\to\mathrm{Na(g)},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}=+108\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

\displaystyle\quad\text{(sublimation)},

\displaystyle r_{2}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{Na(g)}\to\mathrm{Na^{+}(g)}+e^{-},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}=+496\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

\displaystyle\quad\text{(ionisation)},

\displaystyle r_{3}

\displaystyle:\;\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)}\to\mathrm{Cl(g)},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}=+121\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

\displaystyle\quad\text{(bond dissociation)},

\displaystyle r_{4}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{Cl(g)}+e^{-}\to\mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}=-349\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

\displaystyle\quad\text{(electron affinity)},

\displaystyle r_{5}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{Na^{+}(g)}+\mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)}\to\mathrm{NaCl(s)},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}=\;?\;

\displaystyle\quad\text{(lattice enthalpy)}.

The lattice enthalpy
F_{\!H}(r_{5})
— the enthalpy of converting
the ionic crystal into infinitely separated gas-phase ions —
is not directly accessible by calorimetry.
The experimental obstacle is fundamental: there is no way to carry
out the process
\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\to\mathrm{Na^{+}(g)}+\mathrm{Cl^{-}(g)}
in a single calorimetric step, because this
requires vaporising and fully ionising the crystal into isolated
gas-phase ions with no counter-ions in the vicinity

[
23
]
.
What
can
be measured calorimetrically are the four steps

r_{1}
–
r_{4}
and the net formation enthalpy
F_{\!H}(r_{\mathrm{form}})=-411\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

[
60
]
.
The Born–Haber cycle
[
48
]
was introduced precisely
to extract the lattice enthalpy from these measurable quantities;
the Layer 2 coboundary condition is its mathematical content.

\mathcal{L}_{0}
content.

The composite
r_{4}\circ r_{3}
is ill-typed:
r_{3}
produces

\mathrm{Cl(g)}
but
r_{4}
requires

\mathrm{Cl(g)}+e^{-}
, and the electron is generated by
r_{2}
,
not by
r_{3}
.
The two reduction steps must therefore be sequenced so that
r_{2}

fires before
r_{4}
:

r_{\mathrm{form}}^{\prime}\;:=\;r_{5}\circ\bigl(\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Na^{+}(g)}}\otimes r_{4}\bigr)\circ\bigl(r_{2}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Cl(g)}}\bigr)\circ\bigl(r_{1}\otimes r_{3}\bigr).

Both
r_{\mathrm{form}}
and the composite
r_{\mathrm{form}}^{\prime}

have source
\mathrm{Na(s)}\otimes\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)}

and target
\mathrm{NaCl(s)}
; they are
distinct parallel
morphisms
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, not an equality of morphisms in the free
SMC.

\mathcal{L}_{1}
, Layer 2 (coboundary).

Since
r_{\mathrm{form}}
and
r_{\mathrm{form}}^{\prime}
are parallel
morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, path independence forces:

F_{\!H}(r_{\mathrm{form}})\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{\mathrm{form}}^{\prime})\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2})+F_{\!H}(r_{3})+F_{\!H}(r_{4})+F_{\!H}(r_{5}),

where the second equality uses functoriality, monoidality, and

F_{\!H}(\mathrm{id})=0
to collapse the spectator identities.

Inserting
F_{\!H}(r_{\mathrm{form}})=-411\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
:

-411=F_{\!H}(r_{5})+496+108+(-349)+121\;\implies\;F_{\!H}(r_{5})=-787\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.

The Layer 2 coboundary condition uniquely determines the lattice
enthalpy from the four measurable steps; this is the universal
property statement: the object potential
h_{f}
assigns heights to
all complexes, and closing the cycle is structurally forced.

Layer 1 vs Layer 2.

Layer 1 (functoriality, monoidality, unitality) gives the
additivity of
F_{\!H}
along the composite
r_{\mathrm{form}}^{\prime}
:

F_{\!H}(r_{\mathrm{form}}^{\prime})=\sum_{i=1}^{5}F_{\!H}(r_{i})
.
That
r_{\mathrm{form}}^{\prime}
and
r_{\mathrm{form}}
are parallel
morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is a purely
\mathcal{L}_{0}
fact (matching
source–target pairs).
What Layer 2 adds is that parallel morphisms have equal images
under
F_{\!H}
:
F_{\!H}(r_{\mathrm{form}})=F_{\!H}(r_{\mathrm{form}}^{\prime})
.
Together these give the numerical determination of the lattice
enthalpy.

3.5.3. Organic combustion network: cycle consistency

Example 3.16

(Combustion network: testing Layer 2 consistency)
.

The previous two examples used Layer 2 to
predict
an unknown
quantity.
This example uses it in the opposite direction: to
check

whether a set of experimentally measured enthalpies is internally
consistent, i.e. whether a single object potential
h_{f}
exists
that accounts for all of them.
This is exactly the test a calorimetrist applies when verifying a
new thermochemical dataset.

Consider the alkane combustion network with

\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{CH_{4}(g),\,C_{2}H_{6}(g),\,H_{2}(g),\,O_{2}(g),\,CO_{2}(g),\,H_{2}O(g)}\}

and four generating reactions (all at 298 K, H
2
O(g);
values from
[
60
]
):

\displaystyle r_{1}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{CH_{4}}+2\,\mathrm{O_{2}}\to\mathrm{CO_{2}}+2\,\mathrm{H_{2}O},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}=-802.3\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},

\displaystyle r_{2}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}+\tfrac{7}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}\to 2\,\mathrm{CO_{2}}+3\,\mathrm{H_{2}O},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}=-1428.5\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},

\displaystyle r_{3}

\displaystyle:\;2\,\mathrm{CH_{4}}\to\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}+\mathrm{H_{2}},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}=+65.7\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},

\displaystyle r_{4}

\displaystyle:\;\mathrm{H_{2}}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_{2}}\to\mathrm{H_{2}O},

\displaystyle F_{\!H}=-241.8\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.

Here
r_{3}
is a formal dehydrogenative coupling step (no oxygen
participates) and
r_{4}
is hydrogen combustion.

\mathcal{L}_{0}
parallel morphisms.

At the stoichiometric level,
r_{1}\otimes r_{1}
and the three-step
composite formed from
r_{3}
,
r_{4}
, and
r_{2}
(with spectator

\mathrm{O_{2}}
molecules carried along to balance the oxidant
budget at each step) are
distinct parallel morphisms
in

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
from
2\,\mathrm{CH_{4}}+4\,\mathrm{O_{2}}
to

2\,\mathrm{CO_{2}}+4\,\mathrm{H_{2}O}
, not an equality of morphisms
in the free SMC.
Verbally: two simultaneous methane combustions reach the same
source–target pair as the indirect path (i) couple two methanes
to ethane and
\mathrm{H_{2}}
, (ii) burn the
\mathrm{H_{2}}
,
(iii) burn the ethane.

\mathcal{L}_{1}
, Layer 1 check.

Functoriality, monoidality, and
F_{\!H}(\mathrm{id})=0
collapse the
spectator identities, so each path’s enthalpy is the sum of the

F_{\!H}
values on its non-trivial generators.
Using the values above:

\displaystyle F_{\!H}(r_{3})+F_{\!H}(r_{4})+F_{\!H}(r_{2})

\displaystyle\;=\;65.7+(-241.8)+(-1428.5)\;=\;-1604.6\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},

\displaystyle 2\,F_{\!H}(r_{1})

\displaystyle\;=\;2\times(-802.3)\;=\;-1604.6\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.

The two sums agree exactly because all four values are drawn from
a single internally-consistent compilation
[
60
]
.
A genuine cross-source consistency test — comparing
measurements from independent laboratories with independent
reference states — typically reveals discrepancies of

1
–
3\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
per measurement, the calorimetric
noise floor against which Layer 2 violations would be detectable.

Layer 2 interpretation.

Near-zero cycle sum across measurements from independent sources
means the data lie in (or very close to)
\mathrm{im}(\delta^{0})
: they
are coboundaries of a common object potential
h_{f}
.
This is stronger than a Layer 1 check on a single compilation,
which is internally consistent by construction; cross-source
consistency actively tests whether the four experiments — run
in different laboratories with independent reference states —
admit a unified thermochemical description.
A significant non-closure would signal either measurement error
or use of inconsistent reference states, a violation of the
Layer 2 coboundary condition detectable without knowing which
individual measurement is wrong.
This is the calorimetric analogue of a Kirchhoff consistency
check in an electrical network
(Section
3.6
).

§3.6. Thermochemical networks and the Wegscheider pre-condition

In 1901, Rudolf Wegscheider showed that in a reversible mass-action
reaction network obeying detailed balance, the rate constants — equivalently
the elementary-step equilibrium constants — cannot be chosen independently;
stoichiometric cycle relations impose multiplicative constraints,
now called the
Wegscheider conditions

[
296
]
.
These conditions are the cornerstone of thermodynamic consistency in
chemical kinetics and underpin everything from enzyme network
analysis to the theory of detailed balance

[
234
,
94
]
.

The constraints enter the tower in two stages.
At
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, the full Wegscheider conditions arise as the coboundary
condition for the Gibbs functor
F_{G}^{T}=F_{\!H}-TF_{S}
, restricting
the allowed equilibrium constants via
\ker F_{G}^{T}
(see
Section
4
).
At the present level
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, the same mathematical structure
appears in a purely enthalpic form: any thermochemical network with
directed cycles must satisfy
additive
cycle conditions on the
enthalpy assignment.
This is the
thermochemical pre-condition
— the
enthalpic-additive analogue of the full Wegscheider conditions,
visible already at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
before entropy and free energy enter at

\mathcal{L}_{2}
.
Isolating it here makes the tower structure explicit: the
Wegscheider conditions are not a kinetic accident but a consequence
of the coboundary structure that is already forced at the thermochemical level.

The following definition places this classical notion on the
categorical footing provided by
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
The underlying idea — that a thermochemical network is a reaction
graph decorated by an enthalpy assignment — goes back to Hess

[
139
]
and was made explicit in the cycle-condition language
by Wegscheider
[
296
]
; the formulation below is
new in casting it as a pair
(P,h)
where
h
is a monoid
homomorphism into
\mathbb{R}
and the enthalpy functor is the induced
coboundary
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h
.

Definition 3.17

(State-function thermochemical network)
.

A
state-function thermochemical network
(a Layer 2
thermochemical network) is a pair
(P,h)
where
P
is a Petri
net and
h:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to\mathbb{R}
is a monoid homomorphism (an object
potential in the sense of Definition
3.6
).
The induced functor
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}

automatically satisfies both Layer 1 (functoriality) and Layer 2
(the coboundary condition), and is uniquely determined by
h
.
This is the Layer 2 specialisation of the generic

\mathcal{L}_{1}
-decoration of Definition
3.1
: a generic

\mathcal{L}_{1}
-functor
F_{\!H}
is required only to be strict symmetric
monoidal, while a state-function thermochemical network requires

F_{\!H}
to factor through an object potential.

Thermochemical networks in this sense pervade chemistry.
The Born–Haber cycles of ionic compounds (Example
3.15
),
the Hess cycles for combustion enthalpies
(Examples
3.13
,
3.16
), and the
thermodynamic cycles for ATP hydrolysis coupled to biosynthetic
reactions
[
8
]
are all instances: in each case, the
physically meaningful quantity is the object potential
h
, and the
measurable reaction enthalpies are its coboundary.
The parameter count
\rho=\mathrm{rank}N
of
Observation
3.9
is the number of independent
calorimetric experiments needed to determine
h
up to the

\ker(N^{\top})
gauge (equivalently, up to the choice of reference
state); for deficiency-zero networks this reduces to
n-\ell
.

Proposition 3.18

(Kirchhoff’s cycle condition as a theorem)
.

Let
(P,h)
be a thermochemical network at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
and let

r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}
form a directed closed loop in the CRN graph

G(\mathcal{R})
.
Then
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}F_{\!H}(r_{i})=0
.

Proof.

Immediate from Proposition
3.7
(i)
\Rightarrow
(iv):
the coboundary form of
F_{\!H}
implies the directed-cycle condition.
∎

To the author’s knowledge, the connection between this proposition and
Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law has not previously been stated as a theorem
in the chemical reaction network literature, though the analogy
between thermochemical cycles and electrical circuits has been used
informally since the early network thermodynamics of Oster,
Perelson, and Katchalsky
[
236
]
.
The categorical proof makes the connection exact.

Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law in disguise

In an electrical circuit, Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL) states that
the algebraic sum of voltage drops around any closed loop of
circuit branches is zero
[
169
]
: in a conservative
(electrostatic) network, voltage drops are differences of an
electric scalar potential, so traversing a directed cycle returns
to the starting potential.
Formally: for any directed cycle of circuit branches, the sum of
the voltage drops equals zero.

Proposition
3.18
and KVL are the same mathematical
statement in different physical guises.
In both cases, a functor (the voltage assignment in circuits; the
enthalpy functor
F_{\!H}
in thermochemistry) maps into the one-object
additive category
B\mathbb{R}
and must assign zero to every closed loop.
The reason is identical: both the voltage in a circuit and the
enthalpy of a reaction are coboundaries of a scalar potential
(electric potential
\phi
in circuits; the object potential
h

in thermochemistry).
The Born–Haber cycle, Hess’s Law for formation enthalpies, and the
ATP–ADP free energy cycle in cellular metabolism

[
8
]
are all chemical instances of the same
categorical fact.

The non-coincidence is the point: both laws derive from the
coboundary structure
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h
(or
\Delta\phi=\delta^{0}\phi
in circuits), and the cycle condition

\sum_{r\in\gamma}F_{\!H}(r)=0
is the boundary–coboundary
duality

\sum_{r\in\gamma}(\delta^{0}h)(r)\;=\;\langle h,\partial\gamma\rangle

applied to any directed closed cycle
\gamma
, for which the
boundary
\partial\gamma
vanishes (each complex appears equally
often as source and as target).

Observation 3.19

(The number of independent cycle conditions)
.

The
cycle rank
(first Betti number) of the CRN graph is

\gamma=|\mathcal{R}|-(n-\ell)
, where
n
is the number of
distinct complexes and
\ell
is the number of linkage classes.
The
\gamma
independent directed-cycle conditions reduce the
Layer 1 parameter space
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|}
to
\mathrm{im}(I_{a}^{\top})
of
dimension
n-\ell
— the image of arbitrary, not necessarily
species-additive, vertex potentials on the complex graph.
Imposing the further species-additive structure of Layer 2
reduces this to
\mathrm{im}(N^{\top})=\mathrm{im}(\delta^{0})
of dimension

\rho=(n-\ell)-\delta
, where
\delta\geq 0
is the
deficiency.
This is Observation
3.9
restated in terms of the
topology of the reaction graph:
\gamma
graph-cycle conditions
followed by
\delta
deficiency conditions, totalling
|\mathcal{R}|-\rho
constraints overall.

§3.7. What
\mathcal{L}_{1}
cannot express: forcing of
\mathcal{L}_{2}

Layer 1 assigns a single real number
F_{\!H}(r)
to each generating
reaction and propagates it additively.
The physical question it cannot answer is:
how does a reaction
network respond to changes in temperature?

The temperature dependence of equilibrium is governed by the Gibbs
free energy
\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S
; two reactions with identical
\Delta H

but different
\Delta S
accumulate different free energies at every
temperature, yet are indistinguishable by
F_{\!H}
alone.
The following makes this gap precise.

Forcing empirical result for
\mathcal{L}_{2}
: enthalpy-indistinguishable, entropy-separated

Let
P
be a
coarse-grained
Petri net with species

\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{H},\,\mathrm{I},\,\mathrm{HI}\},

where
\mathrm{H}
denotes Hsp90,
\mathrm{I}
denotes the
aryl-dihydroxyphenyl-thiadiazole inhibitor class, and

\mathrm{HI}
the bound complex.
Consider two generating reactions

r_{E},\,r_{F}:\ \mathrm{H}\otimes\mathrm{I}\longrightarrow\mathrm{HI},

representing, after coarse-graining, the binding of ICPD26 and
ICPD34.
Chemically these are distinct ligands; they become parallel
morphisms only because the label
\mathrm{I}
forgets substituent
identity.

Kazlauskas et al. report that the modification

\mathrm{ICPD26}\to\mathrm{ICPD34}
weakens binding by about

3.1\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
, while the binding enthalpies remain
essentially unchanged within the experimental uncertainty of the
isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) analysis; the observed change
in binding free energy is therefore attributed to entropy

[
164
]
.

This exposes a genuine limitation of the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
description.
At the coarse-grained stoichiometric level, the two binding events
have the same source, the same target, and the same enthalpy label
to experimental resolution:

F_{\!H}(r_{E})\approx F_{\!H}(r_{F}).

Yet they are not thermodynamically equivalent, since their binding
free energies differ measurably.
Thus
F_{\!H}
alone does not contain enough information to separate
them.

Indistinguishability at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
.

If
\mathcal{L}_{1}
records only stoichiometry together with the enthalpy
assignment, then
r_{E}
and
r_{F}
are indistinguishable at that
level: every invariant visible to
\mathcal{L}_{1}
treats them as the same
reaction.

Why
\mathcal{L}_{1}
is not enough.

The Hsp90 example therefore forces an extension of the theory.
There exists thermodynamic information relevant to binding that is
invisible to
\mathcal{L}_{1}
but necessary to explain the experimentally
observed difference in affinity.
In other words, once one reaches this point, an enthalpy-only level of the tower
is no longer adequate: the tower must be refined by adjoining a
further thermodynamic datum.

Methodological caution.

This formulation must be stated at the level of

intrinsic
thermodynamic parameters rather than raw observed
heats.
For protein–ligand binding, calorimetric enthalpies can be
shifted by linked protonation and buffer effects, so comparison of
reaction labels should be made only after such corrections

[
176
,
165
]
.

This forces
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, which must add:

(i)

A second strict symmetric monoidal functor

F_{S}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
recording standard entropy changes

\Delta S^{\circ}_{r}
per generating reaction (one additional real
number per reaction, by the same universal property as
F_{\!H}
);
the level
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
is then the triple
(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{\!H},F_{S})

— a second decoration on the same underlying stoichiometric
category, exactly parallel to how
F_{\!H}
decorates
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
in
Definition
3.1
.

(ii)

A
dagger structure

({\cdot})^{\dagger}
assigning to
each reaction
r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
a formal reverse

r^{\dagger}:{\bf v}\to{\bf u}
, satisfying

F_{\!H}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{\!H}(r)
and
F_{S}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{S}(r)
,
encoding microscopic reversibility
[
234
]
.

(iii)

A temperature-parametric
Gibbs functor

F_{G}^{T}:=F_{\!H}-T\cdot F_{S}
for each
T>0
, with

\ker F_{G}^{T}
characterising the reactions whose standard
Gibbs free energy vanishes at temperature
T
—
equivalently, those with
K_{r}(T)=1
.
Detailed balance in the kinetic sense is a stronger condition,
requiring rate data and equilibrium concentrations beyond the
thermodynamic content of
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, and is deferred to
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

The Wegscheider conditions — constraints among equilibrium
constants in a directed cycle — become the coboundary condition
for
F_{G}^{T}
at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
: Proposition
3.18
applied to

F_{G}^{T}
in place of
F_{\!H}
.
The full
\mathcal{L}_{2}
condition
\sum_{r\in\gamma}F_{G}^{T}(r)=0
at
every
T>0
decomposes via
F_{G}^{T}=F_{\!H}-T\cdot F_{S}
into two

T
-independent vanishing conditions: the enthalpy cycle condition

\sum_{r\in\gamma}F_{\!H}(r)=0
(the thermochemical
pre-condition of Section
3.6
) and the entropy
cycle condition
\sum_{r\in\gamma}F_{S}(r)=0
(the additional
content of
\mathcal{L}_{2}
).
The
\mathcal{L}_{1}
pre-condition is therefore one of two independent
constraints required by Wegscheider, not a singular limit.

§4.
\mathcal{L}_{2}
: The Equilibrium Level

§4.1. Forcing the extension: what
\mathcal{L}_{1}

cannot express

Section
3.7
identified the gap at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
:
two reactions with equal enthalpy changes but different entropy
changes respond to temperature in completely opposite ways, yet are
indistinguishable by
F_{\!H}
alone.
Before making this precise categorically, we establish the chemical
reality that such pairs are not exotic but
generic
in
complex reaction networks like a biochemical system.

Abstract forcing pair for
\mathcal{L}_{2}

The mathematical content of the gap at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
is a pair of
generating reactions

r_{1},\;r_{2}\;:\;{\bf u}\to{\bf v}

in some Petri net
P
, with the same enthalpy but different
entropies:

F_{\!H}(r_{1})=F_{\!H}(r_{2}),\qquad F_{\!S}(r_{1})\neq F_{\!S}(r_{2}).

The label swap
\sigma:r_{1}\leftrightarrow r_{2}
preserves the

\mathcal{L}_{1}
-decoration (
F_{\!H}\circ\sigma=F_{\!H}
on chemical
generators) but does not preserve any decoration recording entropy,
since
F_{\!S}\circ\sigma\neq F_{\!S}
on
\{r_{1},r_{2}\}
.
By the automorphism sequence of §
2.5
,
\sigma

represents a non-trivial coset in
\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{2}
: the
forgetful operation
U_{2}
(Definition
4.1
) is not
injective on decorated triples — the underlying

\mathcal{L}_{1}
-decoration
(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{\!H})
alone does not determine

F_{\!S}
.

\mathcal{L}_{1}
conflates the two reactions;
\mathcal{L}_{2}
separates them, since
their Gibbs free energies

F_{G}^{T}(r_{i})=F_{\!H}(r_{i})-T\,F_{\!S}(r_{i})
differ at every
T>0
.

The chembox below establishes that such pairs are generic in real
chemistry — a feature of biochemical reaction networks under
coarse-graining, not a mathematical contrivance.

Binding thermodynamics:
\Delta H
and
\Delta S
need not covary

Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) studies of
protein–ligand binding show that the enthalpic and entropic
contributions to binding can vary separately across a ligand series.
This is a structural feature of molecular recognition:

\Delta H
and
\Delta S
report on different physical aspects of binding and
there is no general law forcing them to change together

[
62
]
.

The binding enthalpy
\Delta H
is often associated with the quality of
direct intermolecular interactions, such as hydrogen bonding,
electrostatics, van der Waals contacts, and the enthalpic cost of
desolvating polar groups.
The binding entropy
\Delta S
reflects changes in solvent organisation and
molecular freedom, including favorable release of ordered water and
unfavorable losses of ligand and protein conformational freedom upon
complex formation.
Because these contributions arise from different physical mechanisms,
modifying one does not in general determine the other

[
102
,
182
,
170
]
.

A useful illustration is provided by Biela et al.’s ITC and
crystallographic study of thrombin inhibitors with systematically
varied P3 substituents
[
42
]
.
These ligands probe the same hydrophobic S3/4 pocket and therefore
belong to the same stoichiometric reaction class at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
:
Inhibitor
+
Thrombin
\to
Complex.
Across the series, increasing hydrophobic bulk produced an overall
affinity enhancement of about 40-fold that was attributed mainly to a
more favorable entropy term, consistent with stepwise disruption of
the pocket water network
[
42
]
.
At the same time, the enthalpy changed much less strongly than the
entropy, so the dominant thermodynamic trend in the series was
entropy-driven rather than enthalpy-driven.

For broader context, thermodynamic profiling of marketed HIV-1
protease inhibitors shows a wide spread of binding enthalpies.
In Freire’s analysis, Indinavir is enthalpically unfavourable
(
\Delta H\approx+7.6\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
),
whereas Darunavir is strongly enthalpy-driven
(
\Delta H\approx-53.1\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
).
Across this inhibitor class, the progression from earlier to later,
more potent compounds is accompanied by increasingly favourable
binding enthalpies
[
102
]
.

What minimal additional structure allows the tower to distinguish
the two reactions of the forcing pair?
The same three physical observations that forced
F_{\!H}
in
Section
3.1
apply to entropy:

(a)

Sequential additivity of standard reaction entropy.

\Delta S(r_{2}\circ r_{1})=\Delta S(r_{1})+\Delta S(r_{2})
:
the total entropy change of a sequence of reactions is the sum
of each step’s contribution.

(b)

Parallel additivity.

\Delta S(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})=\Delta S(r_{1})+\Delta S(r_{2})
:
independent reactions contribute independently to the total
entropy change.

(c)

No spurious entropy.

\Delta S(\mathrm{id}_{\bf u})=0
for every complex
{\bf u}
:
the identity process produces no entropy change.

These are the same three constraints that characterised
F_{\!H}
in
Section
3.1
, with enthalpy replaced by entropy.
They uniquely identify a strict symmetric monoidal functor

F_{\!S}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
.
The universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
(Theorem
2.14
)
guarantees existence and uniqueness of
F_{\!S}
given one real number
per generating reaction — the same theorem applied a second time,
with
\Delta S^{\circ}_{r}
in place of
\Delta H^{\circ}_{r}
.
No new categorical machinery is required.

§4.2. Definition of
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)

Definition 4.1

(Equilibrium level
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
)
.

Let
P
be a Petri net with reaction set
\mathcal{R}
.
The
equilibrium level
of
P
is the triple

\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)\;:=\;\bigl(\,\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),\;F_{\!H},\;F_{\!S}\,\bigr)\;=\;\bigl(\,\mathcal{L}_{1}(P),\;F_{\!S}\,\bigr),

where

•

F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
is the thermochemical functor
from
\mathcal{L}_{1}
(Definition
3.1
), and

•

F_{\!S}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
is a strict symmetric monoidal
functor assigning to each generating reaction
r\in\mathcal{R}

its standard molar entropy change
F_{\!S}(r)=\Delta S^{\circ}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}
.

As with
\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)
(Definition
3.1
), the notation

\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
refers to this decorated triple — a structure, not
itself a category.
We write
U_{2}
for the
forgetful operation

U_{2}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{\!H},F_{\!S}\bigr)\;:=\;\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{\!H}\bigr),

which drops
F_{\!S}
and returns the underlying
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-decorated
pair.

The tower so far: same underlying category throughout

The domain of both
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
is
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, the free skeletal
permutative category of Section
2
.
The underlying category does not change at this step:
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

retains the same objects (complexes), morphisms (reaction paths),
and compositional structure.
What changes is the amount of functor data decorating it.
The tower so far is:

\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)}_{\text{free skeletal permutative}}\;\hookrightarrow\;\underbrace{(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),\,F_{\!H})}_{\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)}\;\hookrightarrow\;\underbrace{(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),\,F_{\!H},\,F_{\!S})}_{\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)}.

Each arrow adds one strict SMC functor into
B\mathbb{R}
, uniquely
determined by one real number per generating reaction.
The universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
(Theorem
2.14
) is
invoked once at each step;
B\mathbb{R}
is a one-object category, so
its object monoid is trivially strictly commutative and the
hypothesis of Theorem
2.14
is satisfied for both
applications.

Proposition 4.2

(Existence and uniqueness of
F_{\!S}
)
.

Given any assignment
\Delta S_{0}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R}
, there is a unique
strict symmetric monoidal functor

F_{\!S}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}

satisfying
F_{\!S}(r)=\Delta S_{0}(r)
for every generator
r\in\mathcal{R}
.

Proof.

Identical to Proposition
3.2
:
B\mathbb{R}
is a
one-object category, so its object monoid is trivially strictly
commutative, and Theorem
2.14
provides a unique strict
symmetric monoidal functor extending the generator assignment

\Delta S_{0}
.
∎

Theorem 4.3

(Universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
)
.

Let
P
be a Petri net with reaction set
\mathcal{R}
, and let

\Delta H_{0},\Delta S_{0}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R}
be any two assignments
of real numbers to generators.
There exists a unique
\mathcal{L}_{2}
-structure on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, namely the
unique pair of strict SMC functors
(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
satisfying

F_{\!H}(r)=\Delta H_{0}(r)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F_{\!S}(r)=\Delta S_{0}(r)\qquad\text{for every }r\in\mathcal{R}.

Equivalently,
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
is the universal
\mathbb{R}^{2}
-decorated strict
SMC over
P
: any pair of strict SMC functors

(\Phi,\Psi):\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
is uniquely and freely
determined by its values on the generating reactions.

Proof.

Apply Theorem
2.14
twice independently: once with the
generator assignment
\Delta H_{0}
to produce
F_{\!H}
(this is
Proposition
3.2
), and once with
\Delta S_{0}
to
produce
F_{\!S}
(this is Proposition
4.2
).
Each application produces a unique extension; the two applications
do not interact, since the generator data
\Delta H_{0}
and

\Delta S_{0}
are independent real-valued assignments to the same
set
\mathcal{R}
.
∎

Remark 4.4

(Relation to the
\dagger
-SMC literature)
.

The tower table in Section
1
compresses
\mathcal{L}_{2}
as
a
\dagger
-symmetric monoidal category
(
\dagger
-SMC),
with
r^{\dagger}
the reverse reaction and equilibrium locus

\ker F_{G}^{T}
.
Definition
4.1
is the precise version of that shorthand:

\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)=(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
is the free skeletal permutative
category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
equipped with two real-valued decorating functors.
No additional categorical structure is assumed
[
269
,
268
,
2
]
.

The
\dagger
-SMC structure is available as
supplementary

data, on
\mathcal{L}_{2}(\bar{P})
(the equilibrium level of the reversible
closure
\bar{P}
, constructed in Definition
4.5
), but it is not constitutive
of
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
for a general Petri net.
The anti-symmetry axioms of Definition
4.6
encode
the
\dagger
-structure as linear constraints on the functor pair

(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
, without modifying the underlying category.
In particular: detailed balance (Proposition
4.16
)
and the Wegscheider conditions
(Proposition
4.31
) are theorems about

\mathcal{L}_{2}(\bar{P})
, conditional on reversibility — not theorems
about
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
in general.

4.2.1. Reversible Petri nets and the dagger

Physical chemical reactions are, in principle, reversible:
thermodynamics does not forbid the transformation in either direction.
For ordinary chemical systems governed by classical or
non-relativistic quantum dynamics, the principle of microscopic
reversibility is a consequence of the time-reversal symmetry of the
underlying equations, so each elementary reaction step has a
corresponding reverse step
[
30
,
177
,
285
]
.
The thermodynamic data
(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})

therefore determines not whether the reverse process exists, but how
the equilibrium is biased toward reactants or products

[
234
,
23
]
.
This has a direct modelling consequence: a faithful Petri net for a
system at or near equilibrium should contain both
r
and
r^{\dagger}

for every reaction
r
it models.

The following definition formalises this and introduces the

reversible closure
— the smallest reversible Petri net
containing a given one.
The term
closure
is used in its standard algebraic sense: just
as the algebraic closure of a field adjoins all missing roots and
nothing more, the reversible closure of a Petri net freely adjoins,
for each generator
r
, the reverse generator
r^{\dagger}
that is
missing, and nothing more.
The result is characterised by a universal property: it is the initial
reversible Petri net equipped with an embedding of
P
.
Petri nets as freely generated categorical / monoidal structures go
back to Meseguer–Montanari
[
221
]
, while open
Petri nets and reaction networks are treated categorically by
Baez–Pollard and Baez–Master

[
28
,
27
]
. Reversibility via adjoining
reverse transitions is also standard in the reversible-Petri-net
literature
[
32
,
219
]
.
In the present paper, we call the resulting initial reversible
completion of
P
its reversible closure.

Definition 4.5

(Reversible Petri net and reversible closure)
.

A Petri net
P
is
reversible
if for every generator

r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
in
\mathcal{R}
, its reverse

r^{\dagger}:{\bf v}\to{\bf u}
is also a generator in
\mathcal{R}
,
with
(r^{\dagger})^{\dagger}=r
.
The
reversible closure

\bar{P}
of any Petri net
P
is the
reversible Petri net obtained by freely adjoining, for each

r\in\mathcal{R}
, a new generator
r^{\dagger}:{\bf v}\to{\bf u}

subject to
(r^{\dagger})^{\dagger}=r
.
It is the initial reversible Petri net equipped with a Petri net
embedding
\iota:P\hookrightarrow\bar{P}
.

Dagger structures and opposite categories

For any category
\mathcal{C}
, the
opposite category

\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}
has the same objects as
\mathcal{C}

but every morphism
f:X\to Y
in
\mathcal{C}
becomes a
morphism
f^{\mathrm{op}}:Y\to X
in
\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}
,
with composition reversed:

g^{\mathrm{op}}\circ f^{\mathrm{op}}=(f\circ g)^{\mathrm{op}}

[
25
,
196
]
.
This is a purely formal construction; it does not equip

\mathcal{C}
with any extra structure, only relates
\mathcal{C}

to a “mirror” category with the same objects.

A
dagger structure
on
\mathcal{C}
is something stronger:
an identity-on-objects contravariant involution

(-)^{\dagger}\;:\;\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathcal{C},\qquad(f:X\to Y)\;\longmapsto\;(f^{\dagger}:Y\to X),

satisfying

(f^{\dagger})^{\dagger}=f,\qquad\mathrm{id}^{\dagger}_{X}=\mathrm{id}_{X},\qquad(g\circ f)^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger}\circ g^{\dagger}.

For a reversible Petri net (Definition
4.5
),
the operation
r\mapsto r^{\dagger}
is first defined on chemical
generators and then extended contravariantly to composite
morphisms, giving
\mathcal{L}_{0}(\bar{P})
the structure of a
dagger-symmetric-monoidal category
[
269
]
.
The opposite category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(\bar{P})^{\mathrm{op}}
exists as a
formal mirror for any
\bar{P}
; what makes
\mathcal{L}_{0}(\bar{P})
a

dagger
-SMC is the additional datum that the dagger operation
is identity on objects — i.e., a canonical identification of
source and target of each reversed morphism with the original
target and source.

Definition 4.6

(Anti-symmetry axioms)
.

For a reversible Petri net, the functor pair
(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
is
required to satisfy, for every generator
r\in\mathcal{R}
:

F_{\!H}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{\!H}(r),\qquad F_{\!S}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{\!S}(r).

Remark 4.7

(Anti-symmetry is automatic under Layer 2)
.

Definition
4.6
is stated as a Layer 1 axiom — an
additional constraint on the functor pair
(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
beyond the
SMC functor axioms.
Under Layer 2 for both functors
(Definition
3.6
for
F_{\!H}
, Definition
4.18

below for
F_{\!S}
), anti-symmetry is not an additional constraint but a

theorem
: if
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h_{f}
and
F_{\!S}=\delta^{0}h_{S}
on
the reversible closure
\bar{P}
, then for every generator

r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
,

F_{\!H}(r^{\dagger})=h_{f}({\bf u})-h_{f}({\bf v})=-F_{\!H}(r),\qquad F_{\!S}(r^{\dagger})=h_{S}({\bf u})-h_{S}({\bf v})=-F_{\!S}(r),

by applying Proposition
3.7
separately to each functor.
Anti-symmetry is thus a Layer 1 axiom — required to state detailed
balance without invoking Layer 2 structure — that becomes a Layer 2
theorem.

Anti-symmetry: state functions force sign flips

Both conditions are direct consequences of the state-function character
of enthalpy and entropy — among the most firmly established facts in
chemical thermodynamics

[
23
,
175
]
.

Enthalpy anti-symmetry.

Since enthalpy
H
is a state function, its change along any path
from complex
{\bf u}
to complex
{\bf v}
depends only on the
endpoints:
F_{\!H}(r)=H({\bf v})-H({\bf u})
for

r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
(Layer 2/coboundary form,
Proposition
3.11
).
Reversing the reaction gives

F_{\!H}(r^{\dagger})=H({\bf u})-H({\bf v})=-F_{\!H}(r).

This is Hess’s Law applied to a single step: if the forward
reaction releases
\Delta H
kJ/mol, the reverse absorbs exactly

|\Delta H|
kJ/mol, and vice versa
[
139
,
23
]
.

Entropy anti-symmetry.

Entropy
S
is likewise a state function (a consequence of the
second and third laws
[
23
]
).
By the same coboundary argument:

F_{\!S}(r^{\dagger})=S({\bf u})-S({\bf v})=-F_{\!S}(r)
.
At the molecular level this reflects
microscopic
reversibility

[
234
]
: at equilibrium, the forward and
reverse fluxes through every elementary step are equal, so any
state-function difference associated with the step must reverse
sign upon reversal of the step.
A process that increases the system’s entropy by
|F_{\!S}(r)|
in the
forward direction decreases it by the same amount in the reverse.

What this is, and what it is not.

The sign-flip refers to the
reaction entropy change

\Delta S^{\circ}_{r}
— a state-function difference that is
positive, negative, or zero depending on the reaction.
It must not be confused with the
entropy production rate

\sigma\geq 0
, a non-negative quantity in nonequilibrium
thermodynamics that quantifies irreversibility and belongs to the
kinetic/open-system level
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, not to the standard-state

\mathcal{L}_{2}
decoration.
Reaction entropy changes flip sign upon reversal; entropy
production does not.

Both axioms are imposed as constraints on the functor pair

(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
, not on the category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
itself.
The underlying category remains the free skeletal permutative
category.

Remark 4.8

(Anti-symmetry halves the parameter count, matching thermochemical tables)
.

For a reversible Petri net with
|\mathcal{R}|=2m
generators
(forward/reverse pairs), anti-symmetry reduces the free parameter
space of
(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
from
4m
to
2m
real numbers:
m
values
of
\Delta H^{\circ}
and
m
values of
\Delta S^{\circ}
, one per forward
reaction — precisely the entries of a standard thermochemical
table
[
203
,
23
]
.

This matters for two distinct reasons.

First, it is
canonical
: the reduced parameter count matches
exactly the format in which experimental thermochemical data is
tabulated and used.
Standard references
[
203
]
list one
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}
and
one
S^{\circ}
per species, not separate entries for forward and
reverse reactions.
The anti-symmetry axiom is not an extra mathematical assumption but
the categorical encoding of an empirical convention that is itself
forced by energy conservation and the state-function property.

Second, it is
consistency-enforcing
: without anti-symmetry,
assigning independent values to
r
and
r^{\dagger}
would permit

F_{\!H}(r)+F_{\!H}(r^{\dagger})\neq 0
, violating energy conservation and
making the thermodynamic model internally inconsistent.
Anti-symmetry is therefore the minimal algebraic condition that
keeps the decorating functors in agreement with the physical content
they are supposed to represent.

§4.3. The Gibbs functor and the equilibrium locus

With both
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
available on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, the Gibbs free
energy functor is an immediate derived object: no new axiom, no new
structure, only a linear combination of the two functors already in
hand.

Why
\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S
is the equilibrium criterion

At constant temperature and constant pressure, the second law of
thermodynamics requires that any spontaneous process decreases the
Gibbs free energy of the system:
dG\leq 0
, with equality at
equilibrium
[
23
,
175
]
.
For a reaction
r
proceeding by an infinitesimal extent
d\xi
:

dG=\Delta G_{r}\,d\xi,\qquad\Delta G_{r}=\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}+RT\ln Q,

where
Q
is the reaction quotient.
At standard conditions (
Q=1
) this reduces to
\Delta G_{r}=\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}
.
The conditions become:

•

\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}<0
: forward reaction spontaneous at standard
conditions (product-favoured);

•

\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}>0
: reverse reaction spontaneous (reactant-favoured);

•

\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}=0
: standard equilibrium,
K_{\mathrm{eq}}=1
.

The general equilibrium condition
\Delta G_{r}=0
gives

\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}=-RT\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}
, connecting the functor
value
F_{G}^{T}(r)=\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}
directly to the equilibrium
constant via exponentiation.

From statistical mechanics,
\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}=-k_{B}T\ln(Z_{\mathrm{prod}}/Z_{\mathrm{react}})
,
the logarithmic ratio of partition functions of products and reactants

[
23
]
.
The functor
F_{G}^{T}
therefore encodes, in a single real number per
generating reaction, the entire statistical mechanical content of the
reaction’s thermodynamic favourability at temperature
T
.

Remark 4.9

(Precedents for the Gibbs functor)
.

To the author’s knowledge, the treatment of
\Delta G^{\circ}
as a strict SMC
functor
F_{G}^{T}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
is new to this manuscript.
The closest precursor is Baez–Pollard
[
28
]
, who
use functor-language for entropy production and the composition of
open reaction networks, but do not single out the Gibbs functor as a
primary categorical object.
The axiomatic treatment of thermodynamic state functions as
homomorphisms (a structure close to our functor language) appears in
Lieb–Yngvason
[
200
]
.
The compositional property
F_{G}^{T}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})=F_{G}^{T}(r_{2})+F_{G}^{T}(r_{1})
— proved as Proposition
4.12
below —
is precisely Hess’s Law for Gibbs free energy, here elevated from an
empirical observation to a structural consequence of the functor axioms.

Definition 4.10

(Gibbs functor)
.

For each temperature
T>0
, the
Gibbs functor at
temperature
T
is the strict symmetric monoidal functor

F_{G}^{T}\;:=\;F_{\!H}\;-\;T\cdot F_{\!S}\;:\;\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\;\longrightarrow\;B\mathbb{R}.

The
Gibbs family
is the map

(0,\infty)\to\{\text{strict SMC functors }\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}\}
,

T\mapsto F_{G}^{T}
.
We write
F_{G}^{T}
uniformly throughout;
F_{G}
alone is reserved
only for fixed-
T
contexts where the temperature has been
specified explicitly.

Remark 4.11

(Equivalent characterisations of
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
: the role of the Gibbs functor)
.

Whether
F_{G}^{T}
alone suffices to characterise
\mathcal{L}_{2}
depends on

how many
temperatures are used; the answer is precise.

A single Gibbs functor is insufficient from
\mathcal{L}_{0}
.

Given only
F_{G}^{T_{0}}=F_{\!H}-T_{0}\cdot F_{\!S}
for one temperature

T_{0}
, one recovers only the single linear combination

F_{\!H}(r)-T_{0}\,F_{\!S}(r)
per generator
r
: the individual values

F_{\!H}(r)
and
F_{\!S}(r)
cannot be separated.
A single Gibbs functor thus gives a strictly weaker structure than

(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
.

The Gibbs family is equivalent to
(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
.

The Gibbs family
\{F_{G}^{T}\}_{T>0}
assigns to each generator
r

the affine function of temperature

T\;\mapsto\;F_{G}^{T}(r)\;=\;\underbrace{F_{\!H}(r)}_{\text{intercept at }T=0}\;-\;T\cdot\underbrace{F_{\!S}(r)}_{\text{negative slope}}.

Since an affine function is uniquely determined by its intercept and
slope, the values

F_{\!H}(r)=\lim_{T\to 0^{+}}F_{G}^{T}(r),\qquad F_{\!S}(r)=-\frac{d}{dT}F_{G}^{T}(r)

are recovered at every generator
r\in\mathcal{R}
.
By Theorem
2.14
these pointwise assignments extend
uniquely to strict SMC functors
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
;
the Gibbs family and the pair
(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
therefore encode

identical
information.

\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
may equivalently be defined as
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
equipped with
the Gibbs family
T\mapsto F_{G}^{T}
.

The recovery formulas above are an algebraic statement about the
chosen affine approximation, not a physical assertion about the

T\to 0
limit of standard Gibbs free energies.
Treating
F_{\!H},F_{\!S}
as temperature-independent makes

T\mapsto F_{G}^{T}(r)
literally affine; a physically faithful
extrapolation to
T=0
would also need heat-capacity data

C_{p}(S,T)
and any phase transitions in the relevant interval —
content beyond the present
\mathcal{L}_{2}
decoration (cf. the integrated
van ’t Hoff form in §
4.5
).

From
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, one extra temperature suffices.

If
F_{\!H}
is already known (from
\mathcal{L}_{1}
), then a single

F_{G}^{T_{0}}
at any
T_{0}>0
determines

F_{\!S}(r)=(F_{\!H}(r)-F_{G}^{T_{0}}(r))/T_{0}
for every generator.
The extension
\mathcal{L}_{1}\to\mathcal{L}_{2}
therefore requires exactly one
additional real number per generator — the value of
\Delta G^{\circ}
at
one reference temperature — which is precisely the format of a
standard thermochemical table entry.

Proposition 4.12

(
F_{G}^{T}
is a strict SMC functor for each
T>0
)
.

For every
T>0
, the map
F_{G}^{T}=F_{\!H}-T\cdot F_{\!S}
is a strict
symmetric monoidal functor
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
.

Proof.

Let
r_{1}:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
and
r_{2}:{\bf v}\to{\bf w}
.

Composition:

\displaystyle F_{G}^{T}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})

\displaystyle=F_{\!H}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})-T\,F_{\!S}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})

\displaystyle=\bigl[F_{\!H}(r_{2})+F_{\!H}(r_{1})\bigr]-T\bigl[F_{\!S}(r_{2})+F_{\!S}(r_{1})\bigr]

\displaystyle=F_{G}^{T}(r_{2})+F_{G}^{T}(r_{1}).

Monoidality:

\displaystyle F_{G}^{T}(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})

\displaystyle=F_{\!H}(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})-T\,F_{\!S}(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})

\displaystyle=\bigl[F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2})\bigr]-T\bigl[F_{\!S}(r_{1})+F_{\!S}(r_{2})\bigr]

\displaystyle=F_{G}^{T}(r_{1})+F_{G}^{T}(r_{2}).

Unitality:

F_{G}^{T}(\mathrm{id}_{\bf u})=F_{\!H}(\mathrm{id}_{\bf u})-T\,F_{\!S}(\mathrm{id}_{\bf u})=0-T\cdot 0=0
.
∎

A linear combination of functors is a functor

The morphism-sets
\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),B\mathbb{R}):=\{\text{strict SMC functors }\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}\}
form a real vector space under pointwise
addition and scalar multiplication (since
B\mathbb{R}
is an abelian group
object in strict SMC categories).
The Gibbs family
T\mapsto F_{\!H}-T\cdot F_{\!S}
is a
straight line

in this space, parametrized by temperature.
The functor axioms are inherited by every element of the family.

Definition 4.13

(Standard Gibbs-zero locus)
.

The
standard Gibbs-zero locus at temperature
T
(or

K=1
locus
) is

Z_{G}(T)\;:=\;\ker\!\bigl(F_{G}^{T}\bigr)\;:=\;\bigl\{\,r\in\mathrm{Mor}\!\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\bigr)\;\big|\;F_{G}^{T}(r)=0\,\bigr\}.

A generating reaction
r\in\mathcal{R}
lies in
Z_{G}(T)
iff

F_{\!H}(r)=T\,F_{\!S}(r)
, equivalently iff its standard equilibrium
constant satisfies
K_{r}(T)=1
.
This is the locus where the standard Gibbs free energy change
vanishes; it is
not
the same as the system being at
equilibrium at a given concentration vector
x
, which requires

\Delta G_{r}(x,T)=\Delta G_{r}^{\circ}(T)+RT\ln Q_{r}(x)=0
.

Observation 4.14

(Temperature dependence of the Gibbs-zero locus)
.

For a generating reaction
r
with
F_{\!S}(r)\neq 0
, define the

crossover temperature

T^{*}(r)\;:=\;\frac{F_{\!H}(r)}{F_{\!S}(r)}.

The behaviour of
F_{G}^{T}(r)
as a function of
T>0
splits into
cases by the signs of
F_{\!H}(r)
and
F_{\!S}(r)
:

•

Same signs (
T^{*}(r)>0
):

r
enters the
Gibbs-zero locus
Z_{G}(T^{*}(r))
.
For
T<T^{*}(r)
,
F_{G}^{T}(r)
has the same sign as
F_{\!H}(r)

(enthalpy-controlled regime);
for
T>T^{*}(r)
, it has the opposite sign
(entropy-controlled regime).

•

Opposite signs (
T^{*}(r)\leq 0
):
the crossover
temperature is unphysical.

F_{G}^{T}(r)
has constant sign for all
T>0
: if

F_{\!H}(r)<0
and
F_{\!S}(r)>0
, the reaction is
product-favoured under standard conditions at every
temperature; if
F_{\!H}(r)>0
and
F_{\!S}(r)<0
, it is
reactant-favoured under standard conditions at every
temperature.

If
F_{\!S}(r)=0
then
F_{G}^{T}(r)=F_{\!H}(r)
for all
T
:
r
never
enters the Gibbs-zero locus, and the sign of
F_{G}^{T}(r)
is fixed
by
F_{\!H}
alone.

What
\mathcal{L}_{2}
adds over
\mathcal{L}_{1}

At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, reactions are labelled by enthalpy alone:
exothermic, endothermic, or thermoneutral.
At
\mathcal{L}_{2}
they are additionally classified at each temperature by
the sign of
F_{G}^{T}
: product-favoured under standard conditions
(
F_{G}^{T}<0
,
K_{r}(T)>1
), reactant-favoured under standard
conditions (
F_{G}^{T}>0
,
K_{r}(T)<1
), or in the standard
Gibbs-zero locus (
F_{G}^{T}=0
,
K_{r}(T)=1
).
The single most important quantity in chemical thermodynamics —
the equilibrium constant
K_{\mathrm{eq}}(T)
— lives precisely
here, via
K_{r}(T)=\exp(-F_{G}^{T}(r)/RT)
.

“Reactant-favoured under standard conditions” is not the same as
“forbidden”: a reaction with
F_{G}^{T}(r)>0
may proceed forward
under non-standard concentrations (when
RT\ln Q_{r}<-\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}
), by coupling to driven processes, or kinetically.
The classification above is a
\mathcal{L}_{2}
standard-state statement, not
a universal verdict on the reaction.

Remark 4.15

(Notes on the term locus and the Gibbs-zero condition)
.

The term
locus
(Latin:
place
; plural
loci
) is
standard mathematical vocabulary for the set of all objects
satisfying a given condition: the zero locus of a function
f
is

\{x:f(x)=0\}
.
It is the same concept as
zero set
,
vanishing locus
,
or
level set at zero
, and appears throughout algebra and
geometry
[
132
]
.

In the CRNT literature, the analogous object is the

positive steady-state variety
or
equilibrium ideal
:
the algebraic set of concentration vectors
x\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}
at
which the ODE
dx/dt=0

[
69
,
4
,
166
]
.
Connections between this variety and algebraic geometry underlie
the study of multistationarity and toric geometry in reaction
networks.

The standard Gibbs-zero locus
Z_{G}(T)=\ker(F_{G}^{T})
is a different
but related object: it lives in
morphism space
(reaction
space), not concentration space.
It is the set of generating reactions
r
for which the standard
Gibbs free energy change vanishes at temperature
T
, equivalently
the set of reactions with
K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,T)=1
.
This is the
thermodynamic
layer of the equilibrium
structure — a standard-state statement about reaction labels,
not about concentrations.
The kinetic layer — which concentration vectors are actually
reached, and at what rates — belongs to
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.
The algebraic geometry of
Z_{G}(T)
as a function of
T
is
precisely the content of Observation
4.14
and the
van ’t Hoff equation (Proposition
4.26
).

4.3.1. Reversal symmetry of the standard Gibbs-zero locus

Detailed balance
is a central principle of chemical kinetics
and non-equilibrium thermodynamics.
Chemically, it states that at thermodynamic equilibrium, every
elementary reaction step is individually balanced by its reverse:
the forward and reverse
fluxes
through each step are equal,
not merely the net flux around each cycle

[
234
,
94
]
.
For a single reversible step
r:A\rightleftharpoons B
with
forward rate constant
k_{+}
and reverse rate constant
k_{-}
,
detailed balance at an equilibrium concentration vector requires

k_{+}[A]_{\mathrm{eq}}\;=\;k_{-}[B]_{\mathrm{eq}},

which gives
K_{\mathrm{eq}}=k_{+}/k_{-}
.
This is a kinetic flux equality, requiring rate constants and
equilibrium concentrations — data that lives at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, not

\mathcal{L}_{2}
.

What
\mathcal{L}_{2}
supplies, and the proposition below makes precise, is
the
thermodynamic precondition
for detailed balance: when a
reaction lies in the standard Gibbs-zero locus

Z_{G}(T)=\ker F_{G}^{T}
, so does its reverse, and the standard
equilibrium constants of the two satisfy

K_{r^{\dagger}}(T)=1/K_{r}(T)
.
In networks this thermodynamic precondition extends to a cycle
condition — the
Wegscheider conditions

[
296
]
, that the product of standard equilibrium
constants around every directed cycle equals one
(Proposition
4.31
).
The full kinetic content of detailed balance — equality of
forward and reverse fluxes at given concentrations — is deferred
to
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, where it appears as a consistency condition between
the rate constants and the
\mathcal{L}_{2}
equilibrium constants.

Proposition 4.16

(Reversal symmetry of the standard Gibbs-zero locus)
.

Let
P
be a reversible Petri net satisfying
Definition
4.6
.
For any generator
r\in\mathcal{R}
and temperature
T>0
:

F_{G}^{T}(r)=0\;\iff\;F_{G}^{T}(r^{\dagger})=0.

Equivalently, the standard Gibbs-zero locus
Z_{G}(T)
is closed
under the dagger involution:
r\in Z_{G}(T)
iff

r^{\dagger}\in Z_{G}(T)
.

Proof.

The anti-symmetry axioms give

F_{G}^{T}(r^{\dagger})=F_{\!H}(r^{\dagger})-T\,F_{\!S}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{\!H}(r)-T(-F_{\!S}(r))=-F_{G}^{T}(r)
.
So
F_{G}^{T}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{G}^{T}(r)
, and the claim is immediate.
∎

Remark 4.17

(Scope and categorical status of reversal symmetry)
.

Proposition
4.16
holds for reversible Petri
nets
P
satisfying the anti-symmetry axioms
(Definition
4.6
); equivalently, it is a theorem
about
\mathcal{L}_{2}(\bar{P})
, the equilibrium level of the reversible
closure of
P
.
For a general Petri net without the dagger structure, the
anti-symmetry axioms do not apply and the proposition is silent
(see Remark
4.4
).

Within this scope, reversal symmetry of the Gibbs-zero locus is a

theorem
— a consequence of anti-symmetry alone — not
an additional postulate on the kinetics or the rate constants.
The familiar relation

K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r^{\dagger},\,T)\;=\;\frac{1}{K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,\,T)}

follows immediately by exponentiating

F_{G}^{T}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{G}^{T}(r)
.
This is the thermodynamic content recovered at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
.
The full kinetic detailed-balance condition —
K_{\mathrm{eq}}=k_{+}/k_{-}
for mass-action kinetics, with equality of forward
and reverse fluxes at equilibrium concentrations — belongs to

\mathcal{L}_{3}
and is established there as a consistency condition
between the levels.

§4.4. Layer 1 and Layer 2 for
F_{\!S}
,
the third law, and standard chemical potential

The Layer 1/Layer 2 split introduced for
F_{\!H}
in
Sections
3.3
and
3.4
applies to

F_{\!S}
with the same categorical structure but one physically
decisive difference at Layer 2.

At
Layer 1
, the structure is identical for both functors:

F_{\!S}
is any strict SMC functor
F_{\!S}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
,
with no constraint beyond the functor axioms (and anti-symmetry

F_{\!S}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{\!S}(r)
for reversible nets,
Definition
4.6
).
The Layer 1 parameter space for
F_{\!S}
has
|\mathcal{R}|
free real numbers,
reduced to
|\mathcal{R}|/2
by anti-symmetry for reversible Petri nets.
This is entirely parallel to
F_{\!H}
: one real number per generating
reaction, freely chosen, with no further constraint.

At
Layer 2
, both
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
are required to satisfy a
state-function condition: each must arise as the coboundary

\delta^{0}h
of a species-level potential
h
.
The categorical machinery is identical in both cases: the
species-level potential is determined by the reaction data

F=\delta^{0}h
only up to the gauge
\ker(N^{\top})\subset\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
(Remark
3.12
), the space of conservation
laws viewed as species potentials.
What differs between
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
is the physical convention
used to fix a distinguished representative within this gauge
equivalence class: for
F_{\!H}
, a chosen convention (IUPAC:

\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(E)=0
for elemental references); for
F_{\!S}
, an
external physical principle (the third law:
S(X,0\,\mathrm{K})=0
for perfect crystalline ground states).
This asymmetry — between conventional and principled gauge
fixing — is the subject of Section
4.4.2
below.

4.4.1. Layer 2 for
F_{\!S}
: the entropy
state-function condition

Layer 2 requires
F_{\!S}
to satisfy the entropy state-function
condition: the entropy change of a reaction must be expressible as
the difference of species-level entropy values, exactly as the
enthalpy change at Layer 2 for
F_{\!H}
is the difference of formation
enthalpies.

Definition 4.18

(Layer 2 for
F_{\!S}
: entropy state-function condition)
.

F_{\!S}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}
satisfies
Layer 2
if there
exists a monoid homomorphism

h_{S}:(\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}],+,\mathbf{0})\to(\mathbb{R},+,0)

such that, for every generator
r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
:

F_{\!S}(r)\;=\;\delta^{0}h_{S}(r)\;:=\;h_{S}({\bf v})-h_{S}({\bf u}).

Since
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]=\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
is the free commutative monoid,
h_{S}
is
uniquely determined by its values on species:

h_{S}\!\bigl(\sum_{S}n_{S}S\bigr)=\sum_{S}n_{S}h_{S}(S)
.

Proposition 4.19

(Standard entropies give the canonical potential
for
F_{\!S}
)
.

Define
h_{S}(S):=S^{\circ}(S)
, the standard molar entropy of
species
S
, and extend by linearity.
Then
h_{S}
is a monoid homomorphism and, for every generator

r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
:

F_{\!S}(r)\;=\;h_{S}({\bf v})-h_{S}({\bf u})\;=\;\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}N_{S,r}\,S^{\circ}(S).

Proof.

Identical to Proposition
3.11
with
h_{f}

replaced by
h_{S}
and
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}
replaced by
S^{\circ}
.
The universal property of
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
supplies uniqueness.
∎

4.4.2. The third law: an absolute reference for
h_{S}

This is the sole asymmetry between
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
at Layer 2, and
it has no categorical source: it is a fact about the physical world.
The discussion below is needed because the asymmetry has practical
consequences for what thermochemical data can and cannot be compared
across systems, and because it determines the structure of the
Layer 2 parameter space for
F_{\!S}
.

Gauge fixing for
h_{f}
vs
h_{S}
: convention vs universal principle

The Layer 2 coboundary condition
F=\delta^{0}h
does not fix

h
uniquely: categorically,
h
is determined by
F=\delta^{0}h

only up to the gauge
\ker(N^{\top})\subset\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}

(Remark
3.12
), the space of conservation laws viewed as
species potentials.
This gauge applies equally to
h_{f}
and
h_{S}
— the categorical
machinery does not distinguish them.
What differs is the physical convention used to fix a distinguished
representative.

Gauge fixing for
h_{f}
: a chosen convention.

The potential
h_{f}(S)=\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)
is the standard enthalpy of
formation of
S
from its constituent elements in their standard
states.
The choice of elemental reference set
\mathcal{E}
together with
the convention
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(E)=0
for
E\in\mathcal{E}
selects
one representative within the
\ker(N^{\top})
equivalence class

[
249
]
.
A different choice of references (or different convention values
for the elementals) would shift
h_{f}
by a conservation-law
potential
g\in\ker(N^{\top})
, leaving

F_{\!H}(r)=\delta^{0}h_{f}(r)
invariant.
There is no physical law that selects a canonical
\mathcal{E}
:
“absolute enthalpies do not exist”
[
23
]
, only
enthalpy differences.
In practice, formation enthalpies from tables using different
elemental reference conventions cannot be compared without
conversion, whereas reaction enthalpies are gauge-invariant.

Gauge fixing for
h_{S}
: a universal physical principle.

The third law of thermodynamics — formulated by Nernst and given
its modern form by Planck
[
229
,
242
]
— states
that the entropy of every perfect crystalline substance vanishes at
absolute zero:

S(X,\;0\,\mathrm{K})=0\qquad\text{for all pure substances }X,

under the assumption of a unique, perfectly ordered ground state.
Species with residual entropy (such as CO, ice
\mathrm{I_{h}}
, and
amorphous glasses frozen into multiple equivalent configurations)
are the standard practical caveat
[
23
]
, but this
does not affect the structural argument: for every species in a
standard thermochemical compilation, a canonical basepoint is
fixed.
The standard molar entropy at any reference temperature

T_{\mathrm{ref}}>0
is then computed by integrating the heat
capacity from absolute zero:

S^{\circ}(X,\;T_{\mathrm{ref}})\;=\;\int_{0}^{T_{\mathrm{ref}}}\frac{C_{p}(X,\,T^{\prime})}{T^{\prime}}\,dT^{\prime},

with additive corrections for any phase transitions

[
23
]
.
The third law thus selects the canonical species representative

h_{S}(S)=S^{\circ}(S,T_{\mathrm{ref}})
within the
\ker(N^{\top})

gauge equivalence class — not by suppressing the categorical
gauge, but by importing an external physical principle that
specifies absolute species entropies.

The asymmetry, precisely stated.

Categorically, both
h_{f}
and
h_{S}
live in

C^{0}=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Mon}}(\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}],\mathbb{R})
with gauge
\ker(N^{\top})
:
only the coboundaries
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h_{f}
and

F_{\!S}=\delta^{0}h_{S}
are physically meaningful.
The asymmetry is in the
kind
of physical input that fixes a
representative:
h_{f}
is fixed by a chosen convention (IUPAC
elemental references), while
h_{S}
is fixed by a universal physical
principle (the third law).
The third law is external input to the
\mathcal{L}_{2}
categorical
structure — a physical datum that has no categorical source.

Observation 4.20

(The third law as canonical normalisation of
h_{S}
)
.

Categorically, the species-level potential
h_{S}
is determined by

F_{\!S}=\delta^{0}h_{S}
only up to the
\ker(N^{\top})
gauge, exactly
as for
h_{f}
.
The third law of thermodynamics fixes a canonical representative
within this gauge equivalence class: for any reference temperature

T_{\mathrm{ref}}>0
,

h_{S}(S)\;=\;S^{\circ}(S,\;T_{\mathrm{ref}})\;=\;\int_{0}^{T_{\mathrm{ref}}}\frac{C_{p}(S,\,T^{\prime})}{T^{\prime}}\,dT^{\prime}\;>\;0\qquad\text{for all }S.

This is the unique representative consistent with the third-law
normalisation
S(X,0\,\mathrm{K})=0
for perfect crystalline
ground states.
For
h_{f}
, the analogous fixing comes from a chosen convention
(IUPAC:
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(E)=0
for elemental references), not from
a universal physical principle.
The asymmetry between
h_{f}
and
h_{S}
is therefore at the level
of
physical conventions used to fix the gauge
, not at the
level of categorical structure: it is a physical datum (the third
law) external to the
\mathcal{L}_{2}
functor structure.

4.4.3. Standard chemical potential as a derived object

With Layer 2 satisfied for both
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
, the standard
chemical potential emerges as a canonical derived object that
combines both species-level potentials into a single
temperature-dependent quantity.
It is the height function of the Gibbs functor
F_{\!G}^{T}
, playing the
same organisational role that
h_{f}
plays for
F_{\!H}
and
h_{S}
plays
for
F_{\!S}
.

The standard chemical potential: for chemists and
mathematicians

The
standard chemical potential

\mu^{\circ}(S,T)
of species

S
at temperature
T
is the molar Gibbs free energy of
S
under
standard conditions.
It was introduced by Gibbs
[
119
]
as the fundamental
thermodynamic quantity governing the direction of chemical change
and the position of equilibrium.

For mathematicians.

\mu^{\circ}(S,T)
is simply the pointwise combination

h_{f}(S)-Th_{S}(S)
of the two Layer 2 potentials at a common
species
S
.
It is the height function whose coboundary gives
F_{\!G}^{T}
: just as

h_{f}
encodes the “enthalpy height” of each species and
h_{S}

encodes the “entropy height”,
\mu^{\circ}
encodes the “free
energy height” at temperature
T
.
The drop
h_{\mu^{\circ}}({\bf v},T)-h_{\mu^{\circ}}({\bf u},T)

from reactants to products is exactly
F_{\!G}^{T}(r)
: the Gibbs free
energy of the reaction.

For chemists.

The
Gibbs fundamental relation
at constant
T
and
P

[
23
,
175
]
states

dG\;=\;\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\mu_{S}\,dn_{S},\qquad\mu_{S}\;=\;\Bigl(\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_{S}}\Bigr)_{T,P,n_{j\neq S}},

so the chemical potential
\mu_{S}
is the partial molar Gibbs free
energy of
S
.
At standard conditions,
\mu_{S}=\mu^{\circ}(S,T)
, and the standard
Gibbs free energy of a reaction is the signed sum of chemical
potentials over all species.

Definition 4.21

(Standard chemical potential)
.

For species
S\in\mathcal{S}
and temperature
T>0
, the

standard chemical potential
is

\mu^{\circ}(S,\,T)\;:=\;h_{f}(S)-T\,h_{S}(S)\;=\;\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)-T\,S^{\circ}(S).

Extend to complexes by linearity:

h_{\mu^{\circ}}({\bf u},\,T):=\sum_{S}\nu_{S}^{({\bf u})}\,\mu^{\circ}(S,\,T)
.

The species-level value
\mu^{\circ}(S,T)=h_{f}(S)-T\,h_{S}(S)

inherits the
\ker(N^{\top})
gauge from
h_{f}
: the third-law
contribution
T\,h_{S}(S)
is canonically fixed (Edit 2 chembox), but
the formation contribution
h_{f}(S)
is not.
Only the coboundary
F_{G}^{T}=\delta^{0}h_{\mu^{\circ}}
is
gauge-invariant, and on balanced reactions (the only kind a
chemically valid Petri net contains) it agrees with the textbook
standard reaction Gibbs free energy

\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}=\sum_{S}N_{S,r}\,\mu^{\circ}_{\mathrm{textbook}}(S,T)
.
On non-balanced reactions, the chapter’s
\mu^{\circ}
would differ
from the textbook standard chemical potential by a gauge term
involving elemental reference entropies; on balanced reactions
this difference vanishes.

The significance of this definition is that it reduces the
thermochemical data of the entire network to species-level data.
At Layer 1,
F_{G}^{T}
requires one real number per reaction; at
Layer 2, one number per species — the value
\mu^{\circ}(S,T)

— suffices to compute
F_{G}^{T}(r)
for every reaction
simultaneously.
Proposition
4.22
makes this precise.

Proposition 4.22

(Gibbs functor via standard chemical potential)
.

Under Layer 2 for both
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
, the Gibbs functor is
the coboundary of
h_{\mu^{\circ}}
:
for every generator
r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
,

F_{\!G}^{T}(r)\;=\;h_{\mu^{\circ}}({\bf v},\,T)-h_{\mu^{\circ}}({\bf u},\,T)\;=\;\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}N_{S,r}\,\mu^{\circ}(S,\,T).

Proof.

\displaystyle F_{\!G}^{T}(r)

\displaystyle=F_{\!H}(r)-T\,F_{\!S}(r)

\displaystyle=\bigl[h_{f}({\bf v})-h_{f}({\bf u})\bigr]-T\bigl[h_{S}({\bf v})-h_{S}({\bf u})\bigr]

\displaystyle=\bigl[h_{f}({\bf v})-T\,h_{S}({\bf v})\bigr]-\bigl[h_{f}({\bf u})-T\,h_{S}({\bf u})\bigr]

\displaystyle=h_{\mu^{\circ}}({\bf v},\,T)-h_{\mu^{\circ}}({\bf u},\,T).\qed

The chemical potential as the height function
of
\mathcal{L}_{2}

Proposition
4.22
states that, under Layer 2 for both
decorating functors, the Gibbs functor
F_{\!G}^{T}
is itself a coboundary:

F_{\!G}^{T}=\delta^{0}h_{\mu^{\circ}}
.
The standard chemical potential
\mu^{\circ}(S,T)
is the height
function at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, playing the same role that
h_{f}
plays for

F_{\!H}
and
h_{S}
plays for
F_{\!S}
.

This is the precise categorical content of the chemist’s formula

[
119
,
23
]
:

\Delta G^{\circ}_{\mathrm{rxn}}\;=\;\sum_{\mathrm{products}}\nu_{i}\,\mu^{\circ}_{i}\;-\;\sum_{\mathrm{reactants}}\nu_{j}\,\mu^{\circ}_{j}.

The coboundary structure
F_{\!G}^{T}=\delta^{0}h_{\mu^{\circ}}
is not an
approximation: it is the exact content of Layer 2, holding for every
reaction in the network simultaneously.
At Layer 1, one real number per reaction is needed to specify
F_{\!G}^{T}
;
at Layer 2, one number per species (
\mu^{\circ}(S,T)
) suffices for
the entire network.
This is the maximal compression of thermochemical information
available at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
.

§4.5. Thermodynamic theorems at
\mathcal{L}_{2}

The Gibbs family
T\mapsto F_{\!G}^{T}=F_{\!H}-T\cdot F_{\!S}
suffices to
derive, within the categorical framework of
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, four classical
results of chemical thermodynamics as theorems for reaction networks:
the second law criterion for chemical spontaneity (Proposition
4.24
), the van ’t Hoff
equation for the temperature dependence of equilibrium constants, the
Gibbs–Helmholtz equation recovering the reaction enthalpy from
free-energy measurements, and Le Chatelier’s principle for temperature
perturbations.
Each is a statement about morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
labelled by the
Gibbs family; none requires data beyond what is already in
\mathcal{L}_{2}
.

4.5.1. The equilibrium constant

What is the equilibrium constant and why does it
matter?

The equilibrium constant
K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,T)
is the central
quantitative tool of chemical thermodynamics
[
23
,
175
]
.
It encodes the position of equilibrium for a reaction
r
at
temperature
T
: the ratio of product to reactant concentrations (or
activities) when the system has reached thermodynamic equilibrium.

For a reaction
r:\sum_{j}\nu_{j}^{-}S_{j}\to\sum_{i}\nu_{i}^{+}S_{i}
under
the law of mass action:

K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,T)\;=\;\frac{\prod_{i}a_{i}^{\nu_{i}^{+}}}{\prod_{j}a_{j}^{\nu_{j}^{-}}}\Bigg|_{\text{equilibrium}},

where
a_{S}
is the thermodynamic activity of species
S
.
A large
K_{\mathrm{eq}}\gg 1
means the reaction is
product-favoured;
K_{\mathrm{eq}}\ll 1
means reactant-favoured;

K_{\mathrm{eq}}=1
means the system is at standard equilibrium,
i.e., the reaction lies in the equilibrium locus

\ker(F_{G}^{T})
(Definition
4.13
).

The connection to the Gibbs functor is the fundamental relation

[
119
,
23
]
:

\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}\;=\;-RT\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}},

or equivalently
K_{\mathrm{eq}}=\exp(-\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}/RT)
.
In our framework,
\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}=F_{G}^{T}(r)
, so the equilibrium
constant is the exponential of the (negative, rescaled) Gibbs functor
value.
The functor
F_{G}^{T}
thus encodes all equilibrium position information
in a single real number per generating reaction, from which

K_{\mathrm{eq}}
is recovered by exponentiation.

Definition 4.23

(Equilibrium constant)
.

For a generating reaction
r\in\mathcal{R}
and temperature
T>0
,
the
standard equilibrium constant
is

K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,\,T)\;:=\;\exp\!\left(\frac{-F_{G}^{T}(r)}{RT}\right),

where
R=8.314\;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}
is the gas constant.

4.5.2. The second law for chemical reactions

The second law of thermodynamics, at constant temperature and
pressure, takes the following form for individual reaction steps.

Proposition 4.24

(Sign of
F_{G}^{T}
at standard conditions)
.

Let
r\in\mathcal{R}
be a generating reaction and
T>0
.

(i)

F_{G}^{T}(r)<0
:
r
is product-favoured under standard
conditions,
K_{r}(T)>1
.

(ii)

F_{G}^{T}(r)>0
:
r
is reactant-favoured under standard
conditions,
K_{r}(T)<1
; the reverse
r^{\dagger}
is
product-favoured.
The forward direction can still proceed at non-standard
concentrations (when
RT\ln Q_{r}<-F_{G}^{T}(r)
), by coupling
to driven processes, or kinetically.

(iii)

F_{G}^{T}(r)=0
:
r
lies in the standard Gibbs-zero locus

Z_{G}(T)=\ker(F_{G}^{T})
, equivalently
K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,T)=1
.

The Gibbs-zero locus
Z_{G}(T)
partitions the generating reactions
at temperature
T
into these three classes by the sign of

F_{G}^{T}
.

Proof.

At constant temperature and constant pressure, the second law
requires
dG\leq 0
for any spontaneous process

[
23
,
175
]
.
For a reaction proceeding by extent
d\xi>0
,

dG=\Delta G_{r}(x,T)\,d\xi
, where

\Delta G_{r}(x,T)=F_{G}^{T}(r)+RT\ln Q_{r}(x)
depends on
concentrations through the reaction quotient
Q_{r}
.
At standard conditions (
Q_{r}=1
),
\Delta G_{r}
reduces to

F_{G}^{T}(r)
, and the three cases follow from

K_{\mathrm{eq}}=\exp(-F_{G}^{T}(r)/RT)
:
F_{G}^{T}<0
gives

K_{\mathrm{eq}}>1
(product-favoured under standard conditions);

F_{G}^{T}>0
gives
K_{\mathrm{eq}}<1
(reactant-favoured under
standard conditions);
F_{G}^{T}=0
gives
K_{\mathrm{eq}}=1
(
r

in the Gibbs-zero locus).
∎

Remark 4.25

(The second law as a level-stratified statement)
.

At
\mathcal{L}_{0}
: no thermodynamic quantity is defined; spontaneity
cannot be formulated.
At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
with
F_{\!H}
only: exothermic reactions (
F_{\!H}<0
) might
seem spontaneous, but this is only true when
TF_{\!S}(r)\ll F_{\!H}(r)
;
the general criterion requires
F_{\!S}
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{2}
: Proposition
4.24
is a theorem, and the
enthalpy-only intuition is recovered as the low-temperature limit
of the exact criterion
F_{G}^{T}(r)=F_{\!H}(r)-TF_{\!S}(r)<0
.

4.5.3. The van ’t Hoff equation

The van ’t Hoff equation: history and use

The van ’t Hoff equation describes how the equilibrium constant of a
reaction changes with temperature.
It was derived by Jacobus Henricus van ’t Hoff in 1884 from the
Clausius–Clapeyron equation and Hess’s Law

[
291
,
23
]
, and is one of the most
practically important equations in chemical thermodynamics.

Its primary use is measurement: plotting
\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}
against

1/T
(the
van ’t Hoff plot
) gives a straight line with slope

-F_{\!H}(r)/R
and intercept
F_{\!S}(r)/R
when
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
are
temperature-independent.
This allows
F_{\!H}(r)
and
F_{\!S}(r)
to be extracted from
equilibrium constant measurements at multiple temperatures, without
calorimetry.
The van ’t Hoff plot is the experimental foundation for the Layer 1
parameter space: it is the direct measurement procedure that assigns
one real number (
F_{G}^{T}
, at any chosen reference temperature) to each reaction.

In our framework, the equation is not a separate physical input but
a two-line consequence of differentiating the affine function

T\mapsto\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,T)=-F_{G}^{T}(r)/RT
with respect
to
T
.
The approximation that
F_{\!H}(r)
and
F_{\!S}(r)
are
temperature-independent corresponds to a
T
-independent reading of
the Layer 2 potentials — i.e., using fixed
h_{f}(S,T_{\mathrm{ref}})

and
h_{S}(S,T_{\mathrm{ref}})
at a reference temperature and ignoring
heat-capacity corrections.
Fully temperature-dependent Layer 2 data — available for both

h_{f}(S,T)
and
h_{S}(S,T)
in the references like JANAF tables
[
60
]
—
gives the integrated form of the van ’t Hoff equation accounting
for
C_{p}(T)
.

Proposition 4.26

(Van ’t Hoff equation)
.

Treating
F_{\!H}(r)
and
F_{\!S}(r)
as temperature-independent
(the standard approximation for
\Delta H^{\circ}
and
\Delta S^{\circ}

[
23
]
):

\frac{d\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,\,T)}{dT}\;=\;\frac{F_{\!H}(r)}{RT^{2}}.

Proof.

Expand
\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}
using Definition
4.23
and the
Gibbs functor:

\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,\,T)=\frac{-F_{G}^{T}(r)}{RT}=\frac{-F_{\!H}(r)+T\,F_{\!S}(r)}{RT}=\frac{-F_{\!H}(r)}{RT}+\frac{F_{\!S}(r)}{R}.

Differentiating with respect to
T
(both
F_{\!H}(r)
and
F_{\!S}(r)

constant by assumption):

\frac{d\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}}{dT}=\frac{F_{\!H}(r)}{RT^{2}}+0=\frac{F_{\!H}(r)}{RT^{2}}.\qed

Remark 4.27

(The van ’t Hoff equation as a level-stratified
statement)
.

At
\mathcal{L}_{0}
: neither
K_{\mathrm{eq}}
nor
T
is part of the structure; the
equation cannot be formulated.
At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
with
F_{\!H}
only:
K_{\mathrm{eq}}
could be defined via a partially
specified
F_{G}^{T}
, but its
T
-derivative would require
F_{\!S}
, which
is absent.
At
\mathcal{L}_{2}
: the equation is a two-line computation from

F_{G}^{T}=F_{\!H}-T\cdot F_{\!S}
.
It is the statement
