\partial(-F_{G}^{T}/RT)/\partial T=F_{\!H}/RT^{2}
,
an identity in the definition of the Gibbs family.
The van ’t Hoff plot (slope
=-F_{\!H}/R
, intercept
=F_{\!S}/R
) is the
geometric picture of the Gibbs family as a straight line in the
space of strict SMC functors
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathbb{R}

(Mathbox, Section
4.3
).

4.5.4. The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation

The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation: physical meaning and
practical use

The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation
[
119
,
137
,
23
]
is the relation between the temperature dependence of
the Gibbs free energy and the enthalpy of a process.
Physically, it answers the following question: if one measures

\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}=F_{G}^{T}(r)
at two temperatures
T_{1}
and
T_{2}

without calorimetry, can one recover
F_{\!H}(r)
?

The answer is yes:
F_{\!H}(r)
is the
slope
of the function

F_{G}^{T}(r)/T
plotted against
1/T
.
Under the constant-
F_{\!H},F_{\!S}
approximation,

F_{G}^{T}(r)/T=F_{\!H}(r)\cdot(1/T)-F_{\!S}(r)
, so the plot is a straight
line with slope
F_{\!H}(r)
and intercept
-F_{\!S}(r)
— a second route
to the Layer 1 parameter
F_{\!H}(r)
that does not require measuring
heat directly.
This is important in practice whenever calorimetry is difficult (e.g.,
for reactions in solution or in biological systems), where
\Delta G

can be measured via
K_{\mathrm{eq}}
but
\Delta H
is harder to
access
[
23
,
102
]
.

Proposition 4.28

(Gibbs–Helmholtz equation)
.

For any generator
r
and temperature
T>0
:

F_{\!H}(r)\;=\;-T^{2}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\!\left[\frac{F_{G}^{T}(r)}{T}\right].

Proof.

\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\!\left[\frac{F_{G}^{T}(r)}{T}\right]=\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\!\left[\frac{F_{\!H}(r)}{T}-F_{\!S}(r)\right]=\frac{-F_{\!H}(r)}{T^{2}}.

Multiplying by
-T^{2}
gives the result.
∎

Gibbs–Helmholtz in practice and in the tower

The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation extracts
F_{\!H}(r)
from measurements
of
F_{G}^{T}(r)
at two temperatures, without direct calorimetry

[
23
]
.
Categorically,
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
are the “intercept” and
“negative slope” of the affine function

T\mapsto F_{G}^{T}(r)=F_{\!H}(r)-T\,F_{\!S}(r)
.
The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation recovers
F_{\!H}(r)
from a single
derivative,

F_{\!H}(r)=-T^{2}\,\partial(F_{G}^{T}/T)/\partial T
, and this is also
connected to Remark
4.11
: the affine structure of

T\mapsto F_{G}^{T}(r)
means that two temperature measurements
suffice to determine both
F_{\!H}(r)
and
F_{\!S}(r)
individually,
providing a complete
\mathcal{L}_{2}
characterisation from
\mathcal{L}_{1}
data at
two temperatures.

4.5.5. Le Chatelier’s principle

Observation 4.29

(Le Chatelier’s principle, under the constant-
F_{\!H}
approximation)
.

Under the temperature-independent-enthalpy approximation
inherited from Proposition
4.26
, for any generator

r
:

•

F_{\!H}(r)>0
(endothermic):
d\ln K/dT>0
, so
K

increases with
T
.
Heating shifts equilibrium toward products.

•

F_{\!H}(r)<0
(exothermic):
d\ln K/dT<0
, so
K

decreases with
T
.
Heating shifts equilibrium toward reactants.

•

F_{\!H}(r)=0
(thermoneutral):
K
is independent of
T
.

This is Le Chatelier’s principle
[
194
]
for
temperature perturbations: a system at equilibrium responds to
heating by shifting in the endothermic direction.
At
\mathcal{L}_{2}
it is a theorem in the same approximation that supports
the van ’t Hoff equation; if heat-capacity effects change the sign
of
\Delta H^{\circ}
over the temperature interval considered, the
directional statement must be re-evaluated using the integrated
van ’t Hoff form.

§4.6. Wegscheider conditions at
\mathcal{L}_{2}

Wegscheider conditions in the CRNT literature

The Wegscheider conditions were introduced by Rudolf Wegscheider in
1901
[
296
]
as necessary constraints on the
equilibrium constants of a reversible reaction network with cycles.
For a directed cycle
r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}
in the reaction graph, the
conditions state:

\prod_{i=1}^{k}K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r_{i},\,T)\;=\;1,\qquad\text{equivalently,}\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{k}\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r_{i},\,T)\;=\;0.

Their physical content is that thermodynamics forbids perpetual
motion: no network of reactions can have a cycle in which every step
is spontaneous, since that would allow work to be extracted from a
system at uniform temperature and pressure.

In the CRNT literature, the Wegscheider conditions appear as linear
constraints on the vector of
\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}
values.
Horn and Jackson
[
146
]
showed that they are
equivalent to the existence of a thermodynamic potential (a species-
level free energy function) whose coboundary gives the reaction free
energies — precisely the Layer 2 condition
F_{\!G}^{T}=\delta^{0}h_{\mu^{\circ}}
of Proposition
4.22
.
Feinberg
[
94
]
used the conditions as a necessary
criterion for detailed balance in mass-action systems.
Müller and Regensburger
[
227
]
gave
a systematic treatment of the conditions in the context of
generalised mass-action kinetics.

What is new in Proposition
4.31
below is not the
conditions themselves but their derivation: they follow directly and
necessarily from Layer 2 applied independently to
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
,
without invoking kinetics or rate constants.
In the standard CRNT treatment, the conditions on
\Delta H^{\circ}
and

\Delta S^{\circ}
are stated separately from the multiplicative condition
on
K_{\mathrm{eq}}
values.
The proof below shows they are the same condition at different levels
of the tower.

Before stating the proposition, we fix notation for the reaction
graph.

Definition 4.30

(Reaction graph
G(\mathcal{R})
and directed cycle)
.

The
reaction graph

G(\mathcal{R})
of a Petri net
P
is the
directed graph whose vertices are the complexes

{\bf u}\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
and whose directed edges are the generating
reactions
r:{\bf u}\to{\bf v}
in
\mathcal{R}
.
A
directed cycle
in
G(\mathcal{R})
of length
k
is a sequence
of generators
r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}\in\mathcal{R}
such that the target of
each
r_{i}
equals the source of
r_{i+1}
(indices modulo
k
):

r_{1}:{\bf u}_{1}\to{\bf u}_{2},\quad r_{2}:{\bf u}_{2}\to{\bf u}_{3},\quad\ldots,\quad r_{k}:{\bf u}_{k}\to{\bf u}_{1}.

Such a cycle determines a composite morphism

r_{k}\circ\cdots\circ r_{1}:{\bf u}_{1}\to{\bf u}_{1}
in

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
whose source and target coincide.
This composite need not equal
\mathrm{id}_{{\bf u}_{1}}
— in the free
skeletal permutative category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, distinct sequences of
chemical generators can yield distinct morphisms with the same source and target.
The cycle conditions that follow are the statement that this
composite maps to
0
under
F_{\!H}
,
F_{\!S}
, and
F_{\!G}
, despite not
being the identity morphism.

For a Petri net satisfying Layer 2 for
F_{\!H}
(equivalently, for any
coboundary functor), the cycle condition
\sum_{i}F_{\!H}(r_{i})=0
is
an immediate consequence of the coboundary property

F_{\!H}(r)=h_{f}({\bf v})-h_{f}({\bf u})
: the sum telescopes around
the cycle.
This is Kirchhoff’s cycle law, or equivalently Hess’s Law for
networks
[
139
]
.
The same argument applies to
F_{\!S}
under Layer 2 for
F_{\!S}
.
Proposition
4.31
combines both.

Proposition 4.31

(Wegscheider conditions)
.

Let
(P,\,h_{f},\,h_{S})
be a thermochemical network at
\mathcal{L}_{2}

with Layer 2 satisfied for both
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
.
Let
r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}
form a directed cycle in
G(\mathcal{R})
.
Then for every
T>0
:

\sum_{i=1}^{k}F_{G}^{T}(r_{i})\;=\;0,\qquad\text{equivalently,}\qquad\prod_{i=1}^{k}K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r_{i},\,T)\;=\;1.

(5)

Proof.

Additive form.

By Proposition
3.18
(Kirchhoff’s cycle condition applied
to
F_{\!H}
at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, a consequence of
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h_{f}
):

\sum_{i=1}^{k}F_{\!H}(r_{i})=0
.
The same proposition applied to
F_{\!S}
(since Definition
4.18

imposes the same coboundary condition
F_{\!S}=\delta^{0}h_{S}
):

\sum_{i=1}^{k}F_{\!S}(r_{i})=0
.
Therefore, for all
T>0
:

\sum_{i=1}^{k}F_{G}^{T}(r_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\bigl[F_{\!H}(r_{i})-T\,F_{\!S}(r_{i})\bigr]=0-T\cdot 0\;=\;0.

Multiplicative form.

\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{k}K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r_{i},\,T)=\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{RT}\sum_{i}F_{G}^{T}(r_{i})\Bigr)=\exp(0)=1
.
∎

Why universality in
T
forces two independent
conditions

The Wegscheider conditions in the CRNT literature are sometimes
stated only at a single reference temperature.
The categorical structure at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
shows why this is insufficient
for full thermodynamic consistency.

Suppose the Layer 2 cycle condition were imposed on
F_{G}^{T_{0}}
only at a single temperature
T_{0}
.
The condition
\sum_{i}F_{G}^{T_{0}}(r_{i})=0
would hold at
T_{0}
but
fail at other temperatures: a model satisfying it would be
thermodynamically inconsistent outside a narrow temperature range.
Requiring the cycle condition for
all

T>0
:

\sum_{i}F_{\!H}(r_{i})-T\sum_{i}F_{\!S}(r_{i})=0\quad\forall\,T>0.

Since this is an affine function of
T
that vanishes identically,
both coefficients must vanish independently:

\sum_{i}F_{\!H}(r_{i})=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{i}F_{\!S}(r_{i})=0.

These are the independent coboundary conditions for
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
.
The Wegscheider conditions are exactly their joint content, and
full temperature-universality requires both.
This is also the content of Remark
4.11
: the
Gibbs family encodes
(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
independently, and consistency
at all temperatures forces both to satisfy the cycle condition
separately.

Observation 4.32

(Degrees of freedom at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
and the deficiency hierarchy)
.

The Layer 2 cycle conditions inherit the three-tier hierarchy of
Observation
3.19
, applied independently to
F_{\!H}
,

F_{\!S}
, and the Gibbs family:

\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|}\;\supseteq\;\mathrm{im}(I_{a}^{\top})\;\supseteq\;\mathrm{im}(N^{\top}),\qquad|\mathcal{R}|\;\geq\;n-\ell\;\geq\;\rho.

Imposing graph-cycle conditions on the reaction graph alone
reduces
\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|}
to
\mathrm{im}(I_{a}^{\top})
of dimension
n-\ell

(arbitrary complex potentials, not necessarily species-additive);
imposing the further species-additive structure of Layer 2
reduces this to
\mathrm{im}(N^{\top})
of dimension
\rho
.
The gap
\delta:=(n-\ell)-\rho\geq 0
is the deficiency
of the network; for deficiency-zero networks
\rho=n-\ell
.
The
intrinsic
reaction-level parameter count of
\mathcal{L}_{2}

thermodynamics is therefore
2\rho
:
\rho
each for
F_{\!H}
and

F_{\!S}
via
\mathrm{im}(N^{\top})=\mathrm{im}(\delta^{0})
.

In the species-table representation used in standard
thermochemistry, this content is encoded by:

•

|\mathcal{S}|
formation enthalpies
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(S)
,
determined up to the
\ker(N^{\top})
gauge — the IUPAC
convention
\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(E)=0
for elemental references
provides the standard fixing.

•

|\mathcal{S}|
standard entropies
S^{\circ}(S)
, also with the

\ker(N^{\top})
gauge categorically — the third law fixes
the canonical representative
(Section
4.4.2
).

These
2|\mathcal{S}|
entries determine all reaction enthalpies,
entropies, Gibbs free energies, and equilibrium constants at
every temperature; the Wegscheider conditions are then
automatically satisfied.
The species-table representation has
2(|\mathcal{S}|-\rho)
gauge
degrees of freedom relative to the intrinsic
2\rho

reaction-level parameters.

§4.7. Worked examples at
\mathcal{L}_{2}

All thermochemical data in this section are taken from the
NIST Chemistry WebBook
[
203
]
and the NIST-JANAF
Thermochemical Tables
[
60
]
at the standard reference
temperature
T_{\mathrm{ref}}=298.15\,\mathrm{K}
and pressure

p^{\circ}=1\,\mathrm{bar}
, unless otherwise noted.

4.7.1. Thermal dissociation of dinitrogen tetroxide

Example 4.33

(
\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}(g)\rightleftharpoons 2\,\mathrm{NO_{2}}(g)
)
.

Species:
\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g)},\,\mathrm{NO_{2}(g)}\}
.
Reversible Petri net
\bar{P}
with generators:

r_{1}:\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g)}\to 2\,\mathrm{NO_{2}(g)},\qquad r_{1}^{\dagger}:2\,\mathrm{NO_{2}(g)}\to\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g)}.

\mathcal{L}_{1}
data.

Standard formation enthalpies:

\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NO_{2}})=+33.2\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
,

\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}})=+9.16\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
.

F_{\!H}(r_{1})=2(33.2)-9.16=+57.2\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\quad\text{(endothermic)}.

\mathcal{L}_{2}
data.

Standard molar entropies at 298.15 K:

S^{\circ}(\mathrm{NO_{2}})=240.1\;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}
,

S^{\circ}(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}})=304.4\;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}
.

F_{\!S}(r_{1})=2(240.1)-304.4=+175.8\;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}.

Anti-symmetry check (Definition
4.6
).

F_{\!H}(r_{1}^{\dagger})=-57.2\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
(exothermic),

F_{\!S}(r_{1}^{\dagger})=-175.8\;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}
(entropy decrease).
Both signs flip as expected.

Gibbs functor at selected temperatures.

\displaystyle F_{G}^{298}(r_{1})

\displaystyle=57.2-298\times 0.1758=+4.85\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}>0

\displaystyle\Rightarrow\;

\displaystyle\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\text{ favoured},

\displaystyle F_{G}^{400}(r_{1})

\displaystyle=57.2-400\times 0.1758=-13.1\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}<0

\displaystyle\Rightarrow\;

\displaystyle\mathrm{NO_{2}}\text{ favoured}.

Equilibrium constants (Definition
4.23
):

K(298)=\exp\!\!\left(\frac{-4850}{8.314\times 298}\right)\approx 0.14,\qquad K(400)=\exp\!\!\left(\frac{-(-13100)}{8.314\times 400}\right)\approx 51.

Crossover temperature (Observation
4.14
).

T^{*}(r_{1})=\frac{F_{\!H}(r_{1})}{F_{\!S}(r_{1})}=\frac{57200}{175.8}\approx 325\;\mathrm{K}.

Below 325 K:
\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}
is thermodynamically favoured (
K<1
).
Above 325 K:
\mathrm{NO_{2}}
is favoured (
K>1
).
At exactly 325 K:
K=1
.

Van ’t Hoff (Proposition
4.26
).

\frac{d\ln K}{dT}=\frac{+57200}{8.314\,T^{2}}>0\quad\text{for all }T>0\text{:}

K
is strictly increasing with temperature.
Le Chatelier (Observation
4.29
): heating shifts
equilibrium toward
\mathrm{NO_{2}}
, consistent with the forward
reaction being endothermic.

Layer 2 check.

F_{\!H}(r_{1})=\delta^{0}h_{f}(r_{1})
uses formation enthalpies, and
F_{\!S}(r_{1})=\delta^{0}h_{S}(r_{1})
uses absolute standard entropies (third-law normalised) from the same data used above.

By Proposition
4.22
,
F_{\!G}^{T}(r_{1})=\delta^{0}h_{\mu^{\circ}}(r_{1})
can be obtained immediately.

Reversal symmetry of the Gibbs-zero locus
(Proposition
4.16
).

F_{G}^{T}(r_{1}^{\dagger})=-F_{G}^{T}(r_{1})
, so

r_{1}\in Z_{G}(T)=\ker(F_{G}^{T})
iff
r_{1}^{\dagger}\in Z_{G}(T)
.
At
T=325\;\mathrm{K}
both lie in the Gibbs-zero locus
simultaneously, with

K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r_{1},325)=K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r_{1}^{\dagger},325)=1
.

4.7.2. An
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
reaction
\mathrm{CH_{3}Cl}+\mathrm{OH^{-}}\to\mathrm{CH_{3}OH}+\mathrm{Cl^{-}}
:
dG^{\circ}
and

K_{\mathrm{eq}}
(schematic)

Example 4.34

(
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
— schematic)
.

Consider the reaction:
\mathrm{CH_{3}Cl}+\mathrm{OH^{-}}\to\mathrm{CH_{3}OH}+\mathrm{Cl^{-}}
in aqueous solution.
The data below are presented as a
schematic illustration
of
the
\mathcal{L}_{2}
apparatus on a familiar reaction, using
order-of-magnitude estimates rather than rigorous aqueous
reference-state thermodynamics; aqueous ionic standard-state
conventions are subtle, and the high-temperature extrapolation
appearing later should not be taken literally.

\mathcal{L}_{1}
data.

F_{\!H}(r)=-75.0\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}
(exothermic; from
Section
3.5
, using standard enthalpies of
formation in aqueous solution).

\mathcal{L}_{2}
data
[
23
]
.

Entropy change:

F_{\!S}(r)\approx-90\;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}

(order-of-magnitude estimate consistent with reported ion–molecule

\mathrm{S_{N}2}
reaction entropies in water; the precise value is
solvent- and ionic-strength-dependent
[
1
]
).
Two solvated ions react to give one neutral molecule and one ion;
the net ordering of the solvation shell around the charged species
and the reduction in the number of solute particles decrease the
solution entropy, an effect well-documented for ionic substitution
reactions in polar solvents.

Gibbs functor at 298 K.

F_{G}^{298}(r)=-75.0-298(-0.090)=-75.0+26.8=-48.2\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.

The reaction lies outside the Gibbs-zero locus

Z_{G}(298)=\ker(F_{G}^{298})
: it is strongly product-favoured under
standard conditions.

K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,\,298)=\exp\!\!\left(\frac{48200}{8.314\times 298}\right)\approx 2.8\times 10^{8}.

Temperature dependence.

F_{\!S}(r)=-0.090\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}<0
:

\frac{d\ln K}{dT}=\frac{-75000}{RT^{2}}<0.

K
decreases with temperature (Le Chatelier under the constant-
F_{\!H}

approximation, Observation
4.29
: exothermic,
heating disfavours products).
The crossover formula gives

T^{*}(r)=\frac{-75000}{-90}\approx 833\;\mathrm{K},

but this extrapolation lies well outside the regime of the aqueous
standard-state thermodynamics from which
\Delta H^{\circ}
and
\Delta S^{\circ}

were taken: water’s normal boiling point is
373\;\mathrm{K}
, and
above the critical point (
\approx 647\;\mathrm{K}
) liquid-water
reference states are not defined.
The
T^{*}
value should therefore be read as the formal
extrapolation of constant-
\Delta H^{\circ},\Delta S^{\circ}
data, not as a
physical prediction.
Within the validity range of the aqueous standard state, the model
predicts that the reaction becomes reactant-favoured under standard
conditions at sufficiently high
T
; nothing more.

What
\mathcal{L}_{1}
gives vs. what
\mathcal{L}_{2}
adds.

Level

Data

Conclusion (at 298 K, aqueous)

\mathcal{L}_{1}

F_{\!H}=-75.0\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

Reaction is exothermic.

\mathcal{L}_{2}

F_{\!S}=-90\;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}

K_{\mathrm{eq}}(298)\approx 2.8\times 10^{8}
;
strongly product-favoured under standard conditions.

d\ln K/dT<0
: equilibrium shifts toward reactants
with heating, within the validity range of the aqueous
standard state.

What
\mathcal{L}_{2}
cannot express.

Both
K_{\mathrm{eq}}
and
F_{\!G}^{T}
say nothing about how fast
equilibrium is reached.
The rate constant

k\approx 4\times 10^{-3}\;\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}
at 298 K

[
233
]
is invisible at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
: it enters at

\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

§4.8. What
\mathcal{L}_{2}
cannot express: forcing of
\mathcal{L}_{3}

Forcing pair for
\mathcal{L}_{3}
: same
\Delta G^{\circ}
, different rates

Consider a coarse-grained reversible Petri net
P
with species

\mathcal{S}=\{\mathrm{CO_{2}(aq)},\,\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)},\,\mathrm{H_{2}CO_{3}(aq)}\}

— the catalyst (carbonic anhydrase II) is
not
represented
as a net species — and
two parallel generating reactions

for
\mathrm{CO_{2}}
hydration:

r_{A},\;r_{B}\;:\;\mathrm{CO_{2}(aq)}+\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{H_{2}CO_{3}(aq)},

the uncatalysed pathway and the enzyme-catalysed pathway.
Both pathways coexist in biological systems (cells express
carbonic anhydrase wherever fast
\mathrm{CO_{2}}
/bicarbonate
interconversion is needed); at this coarse-grained level they have
the same source and target complex and are genuinely distinct
elementary reactions in the Petri net, distinguished by their
transition states.
At a finer-grained level where the enzyme is tracked as a species,

r_{B}
would expand into a sequence of enzyme-binding, turnover, and
product-release steps; the two-pathway forcing pair above is
meaningful precisely because we have chosen the coarse-grained
framing in which the catalyst is not a net species.

Thermochemical data coincide.

Both reactions have the same stoichiometry and therefore identical

\mathcal{L}_{2}
data
[
203
,
60
]
:

\displaystyle F_{\!H}(r_{A})=F_{\!H}(r_{B})

\displaystyle=-2.9\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},

\displaystyle F_{\!S}(r_{A})=F_{\!S}(r_{B})

\displaystyle=-98\;\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}},

giving

F_{G}^{298}(r_{A})\;=\;F_{G}^{298}(r_{B})\;=\;-2900-298\times(-98)\;\approx\;+26.3\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},

and
K_{\mathrm{eq}}(298)\approx 2.4\times 10^{-5}
identically.
Their
\Delta H^{\circ}
,
\Delta S^{\circ}
,
\Delta G^{\circ}(T)
, and

K_{\mathrm{eq}}(T)
agree for every
T>0
: as parallel morphisms
in
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
they are
indistinguishable
.

Rates differ by seven orders of magnitude.

The pathways have vastly different kinetic behaviour

[
168
,
272
]
:

\displaystyle r_{A}

\displaystyle:\;\text{uncatalysed},\quad k_{A}\approx 3.7\times 10^{-2}\;\mathrm{s^{-1}}\quad\text{(half-life $\approx 19$~s at 298~K)},

\displaystyle r_{B}

\displaystyle:\;\text{catalysed by carbonic anhydrase II},\quad k_{B}\approx 10^{6}\;\mathrm{s^{-1}}\quad\text{(half-life $\approx 0.7\;\mu$s)}.

The ratio
k_{B}/k_{A}\approx 2.7\times 10^{7}
: carbonic anhydrase II
is among the most efficient enzymes known, accelerating the
hydration of
\mathrm{CO_{2}}
by over seven orders of magnitude

[
202
]
.
Equilibrium position is the same in both cases; the time to reach
it differs enormously.

The swap is an
\mathcal{L}_{2}
-automorphism not lifting to
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

The swap
\sigma:r_{A}\leftrightarrow r_{B}
preserves the source
complex, the target complex, and both decorating functor values:

F_{\!H}\circ\sigma=F_{\!H},\qquad F_{\!S}\circ\sigma=F_{\!S}.

It is therefore a well-defined automorphism of
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
, i.e.
\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{2}(P))
.
However,
\sigma
does not lift to an automorphism of any
structure assigning rate constants to generators, since

k_{A}\neq k_{B}
:
\sigma\notin\mathrm{im}(\varphi_{3})
, where

\varphi_{3}:\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{2}(P))
is the forgetful
map in the automorphism sequence (§
2.5
).
Equivalently,
\sigma
represents a non-trivial element of

\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{3})
, witnessing that
\mathcal{L}_{2}
conflates two
kinetically distinct reaction pathways of the same stoichiometry.

This forces
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, which must add:

(i)

A
rate decoration
on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
assigning to each
chemical generator
r\in\mathcal{R}
either a deterministic rate
constant
k_{r}>0
(mass-action ODE setting) or a stochastic
propensity function
\lambda_{r}:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}

(chemical-master-equation setting).
The level
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
is then the quadruple

\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),\,F_{\!H},\,F_{\!S},\,\{k_{r}\}_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\bigr)
—
the
\mathcal{L}_{2}
thermodynamic data plus per-generator kinetic data.
The categorical assembly of these rate data into a functor

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\mathbf{Stoch}

[
103
,
61
]

(with stochastic kernels arising as exponentials

P_{t}=e^{t\Omega}
of the per-reaction generator
contributions
Q_{r}
,
\Omega=\sum_{r}Q_{r}
) is part of the

\mathcal{L}_{3}
construction proper, deferred to that chapter.

(ii)

For mass-action kinetics, the per-reaction rate is

v_{r}(c)\;=\;k_{r}\prod_{i\in\mathcal{S}}c_{i}^{s_{i}(r)}\quad\text{(deterministic, on concentrations $c$),}

and the stochastic propensity on copy-number states

x\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
has the falling-factorial form

\lambda_{r}(x)\;=\;\kappa_{r}\prod_{i\in\mathcal{S}}(x_{i})_{s_{i}(r)}\;=\;\kappa_{r}\prod_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{x_{i}!}{(x_{i}-s_{i}(r))!},

where
s_{i}(r)
is the stoichiometric coefficient of species

i
in the source of
r
, and the volume-scaling between
k_{r}

and
\kappa_{r}
follows the standard convention

[
91
,
23
]
.

(iii)

The
chemical master equation

\tfrac{d}{dt}p=\Omega\,p
, with generator

\Omega=\sum_{r}Q_{r}
summing per-reaction contributions; the
probability distribution
p
over copy-number states evolves
under the Markov semigroup
e^{t\Omega}
.
In the deterministic large-copy-number limit, this reduces to
the mass-action ODE system
\dot{c}=N\,v(c)

[
179
]
, where
N
is the stoichiometric matrix of
§
2.6
and
v(c)
is the vector of
per-reaction rates from item (ii).

(iv)

Trajectory-level theorems — most notably the

Deficiency Zero Theorem
of Feinberg–Horn–Jackson

[
91
,
146
]
, which gives global
asymptotic stability of complex-balanced equilibria in weakly
reversible deficiency-zero networks under mass-action kinetics,
and the
Anderson–Craciun–Kurtz
theorem

[
18
]
for the stochastic analogue
(product-form Poisson stationary distribution).
These results require the rate data of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
— the
\mathcal{L}_{0}

deficiency hypothesis
\delta=0
alone is insufficient to
guarantee them — and are stated and proved in the
\mathcal{L}_{3}

chapter; they are mentioned here only to indicate what becomes
accessible once kinetic data is added.

The bridge from
\mathcal{L}_{2}
to
\mathcal{L}_{3}
is the
kinetic
Wegscheider condition

[
296
,
94
,
146
]
, derived as follows.
For each reversible elementary pair
r,\,r^{\dagger}
in a reversible
mass-action network, detailed balance in the kinetic sense
requires that the ratio of forward and reverse rate constants
equal the standard equilibrium constant:

\frac{k_{r}^{+}}{k_{r}^{-}}\;=\;K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,\,T),

with the appropriate standard-state and activity conventions.
Multiplying this elementary relation around a directed cycle

r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}
in the reaction graph gives

\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{k_{r_{i}}^{+}}{k_{r_{i}}^{-}}\;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{k}K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r_{i},\,T)\;=\;1,

where the final equality is the thermodynamic Wegscheider
condition of Proposition
4.31
.
This bridge operates at the interface of
\mathcal{L}_{2}
and
\mathcal{L}_{3}
: the
equilibrium constants on the right are computed from
\mathcal{L}_{2}

thermochemical data (
F_{\!H}
,
F_{\!S}
), while the rate constants on
the left are
\mathcal{L}_{3}
kinetic data.
The
\mathcal{L}_{2}
Wegscheider conditions constrain the
\mathcal{L}_{3}
rate
constants without determining them: knowing
K_{\mathrm{eq}}

fixes the
ratio

k^{+}/k^{-}
per reversible pair but leaves
their absolute magnitudes free, which is precisely the information
added at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.
Conversely, rate constants at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
determine
K_{\mathrm{eq}}(T)

through this ratio condition, independent of the thermochemical
data used to compute
K
at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
— providing a non-trivial
cross-level consistency check between the two levels.

§5.
\mathcal{L}_{3}
: The Kinetic Level

§5.1. Forcing the extension: what
\mathcal{L}_{2}

cannot express

What
\mathcal{L}_{3}
adds: rates, time, and stochastic dynamics

At
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, two physically distinct systems can be indistinguishable:
they share the same enthalpy
F_{\!H}(r)
, entropy
F_{\!S}(r)
,
free-energy change
F_{G}^{T}(r)
, and equilibrium constant

K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,T)
for every
T>0
.
The single new datum at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
is a positive rate constant

k_{r}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
per generating reaction.

What this unlocks.

For the
\mathrm{CO_{2}}
hydration network of
Section
4.8
, both the uncatalysed system
(
k_{A}\approx 3.7\times 10^{-2}\;\mathrm{s^{-1}}
,
half-life
\approx 19
s) and the carbonic anhydrase-catalysed
system (
k_{B}\approx 10^{6}\;\mathrm{s^{-1}}
,
half-life
\approx 0.7\;\mu\mathrm{s}
) are now
distinguishable — their
\mathcal{L}_{2}
data are identical, their

\mathcal{L}_{3}
data differ by over seven orders of magnitude

[
168
,
272
,
202
]
.

Stochastic predictions.

With rate constants in hand,
\mathcal{L}_{3}
supports a full probability
distribution over species-count states.
For a weakly reversible network with deficiency
\delta=0

(an
\mathcal{L}_{0}
invariant, Definition
2.25
)
equipped with mass-action rate constants,
the stationary distribution of the chemical master equation is a
product-of-Poissons
[
18
]
:

\pi(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\frac{1}{Z}\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{(c_{s}^{*})^{x_{s}}}{x_{s}!},

where
\mathbf{c}^{*}
is the unique positive complex-balanced steady
state guaranteed by the Deficiency Zero Theorem

[
147
,
92
]
(Section
5.6
).
This product form — and the very notion of a “time to equilibrium”
— is invisible at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
: it requires the rate functor
\FP
.

Section
4.8
established the forcing gap at

\mathcal{L}_{2}
: the uncatalysed and catalysed
\mathrm{CO_{2}}
hydration
systems define two distinct points in the fibre of the forgetful
operation
U_{3}:\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
over a single
\mathcal{L}_{2}

object — their
F_{\!H}
,
F_{\!S}
, and
F_{G}^{T}
values agree for
every
T>0
, while their rate constants differ by seven orders
of magnitude.
Since both points project to the same
\mathcal{L}_{2}
decoration, the
label swap
r_{A}\leftrightarrow r_{B}
is a well-defined
automorphism of the
\mathcal{L}_{2}
-decoration that does not lift along

\varphi_{3}:\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{2}(P))
:
in the automorphism sequence

1\;\to\;\ker\varphi_{3}\;\to\;\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))\;\xrightarrow{\;\varphi_{3}\;}\;\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{2}(P))\;\to\;\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{3})\;\to\;1,

the swap represents a non-trivial coset in the pointed-set
quotient

\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{3})=\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{2}(P))/\mathrm{im}(\varphi_{3})

(§
2.5
; the cokernel is a pointed-set quotient,
not a group cokernel).
A non-trivial
\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{3})
proves
U_{3}
is not injective
on decorated quadruples and that the extension to
\mathcal{L}_{3}
is

necessary
:
\mathcal{L}_{2}
conflates kinetically distinct systems
that
\mathcal{L}_{3}
separates.

Why the target is not
B\mathbb{R}
.

At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
and
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, the decorating functors targeted
B\mathbb{R}
:
enthalpy and entropy are real numbers, sequential composition is
addition, and parallel composition is also addition.
The additive structure of
\mathbb{R}
matches the additivity of
state-function differences along reaction paths.

For kinetics, the corresponding additive structure lives on

Markov-semigroup generators
, not on rate constants
themselves.
The generator contribution of a reaction
r
is the operator

\FP(r)=M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)
on observables

f:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}

(Definitions
5.8
,
5.5
);
per-reaction generator contributions sum into a single CME
generator
\Omega=\sum_{r}\FP(r)
, and parallel reactions on
disjoint species combine via Kronecker sum

\FP(r_{1})\otimes I+I\otimes\FP(r_{2})

(Propositions
5.10
,
5.11
).
The natural ambient algebra is therefore the cone
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

of Markov-semigroup generators on
\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}
, viewed as a
one-object strict SMC with sequential composition by addition,
monoidal product by Kronecker sum, and unit the zero generator
(Remark
5.3
).
Every complex
\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
maps to the unique object
of this one-object category, interpreted as the global state
space
\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}
.

Markov
kernels
(probability transition functions) live in
the ambient symmetric monoidal category
\Stoch

[
103
,
61
]
, but enter the picture only via
finite-time evolution: a generator
L\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

exponentiates to a one-parameter Markov semigroup

\{e^{tL}\}_{t\geq 0}
of kernels in

\mathrm{End}_{\Stoch}(\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}})
.
This exponentiation
\exp_{t}:L\mapsto e^{tL}
is
not
an
SMC functor (sequential composition fails to commute with
addition off the abelian locus, by Trotter–Kato), and that
failure is the precise categorical content of the

\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
forcing pair
(Section
5.9
).
The shorthand “
\FP:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\Stoch
” that appears in
some places in this chapter abbreviates the composite

\exp_{t}\circ\FP
, with
\FP
landing in
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
at
the categorical level.

The same physical logic that forced
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
at earlier
levels forces
\FP:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
here, with
three axioms whose content is now non-trivial:

(a)

Sequential composition.

For composable reactions

r_{1}:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{v}
,

r_{2}:\mathbf{v}\to\mathbf{w}
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, the
composite
r_{2}\circ r_{1}
maps under
\FP
to the additive
sum

\FP(r_{2}\circ r_{1})\;=\;\FP(r_{2})+\FP(r_{1})\quad\text{in }\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

(Proposition
5.10
).
This is the generator of the CTMC in which both reaction
channels
r_{1}
and
r_{2}
are simultaneously available; it is

not
an effective single-step rate law for the
coarse-grained reaction
\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{w}
obtained
by eliminating
\mathbf{v}
.
Such a coarse-graining requires a quasi-steady-state or
rapid-equilibrium reduction, which lies outside the strict

\mathcal{L}_{3}
functorial assignment and is recovered only as a
derived approximation under additional hypotheses on the
rate constants.

(b)

Parallel composition.

If
r_{1}
and
r_{2}
act on independent subsystems with
disjoint species sets
\mathcal{S}_{1},\mathcal{S}_{2}
, their combined
generator on the joint state space

\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}_{1}|}\times\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}_{2}|}
is the Kronecker sum

\FP(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})\;=\;\FP(r_{1})\otimes I+I\otimes\FP(r_{2})

(Proposition
5.11
), the infinitesimal of
the kernel tensor product in
\Stoch
.

(c)

Identity.

The “do nothing” morphism
\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}}
produces no
state change:

\FP(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}})=0\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

(Definition
5.5
), the zero generator, which
exponentiates to the identity Markov kernel

e^{0}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}}\in\mathrm{End}_{\Stoch}(\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}})
.

These are the three axioms of a strict symmetric monoidal
functor, now targeting
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
rather than
B\mathbb{R}
.
The extension is
forced
by the same physical logic; what
changes is the additive monoid in which the new datum lives —
from
\mathbb{R}
to the cone
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
of Markov-semigroup
generators on
\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}
.

§5.2. Definition of
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)

and the target
\Stoch

5.2.1. The Markov generator algebra and the ambient
\Stoch

The stochastic description of a chemical reaction network is
classical: given the countable state space of species-count
vectors
\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
— or a finite closed
irreducible subset of it, when conservation laws bound the total
copy numbers — the network evolves as a continuous-time Markov
chain (CTMC) whose generator encodes the rates at which each
reaction fires

[
18
,
96
]
.
This description underlies a large body of work in the CRNT
literature — on stationary distributions

[
55
,
141
]
,
on product-form Poisson distributions and their extensions

[
21
]
,
and on stochastic approximation of arbitrary distributions

[
56
]
—
without requiring a categorical language.

Two categorical objects are needed to make the compositional
structure of CTMCs explicit:

•

the symmetric monoidal category
\Stoch
, in which
finite-time Markov
kernels

K(\,\cdot\mid x)

compose by Chapman–Kolmogorov integration — the ambient
setting in which the time-evolved chain lives;

•

the cone
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
of Markov
generators

on
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, viewed as the morphism set of the
one-object strict SMC
B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
, with sequential
composition by addition, monoidal product by Kronecker sum,
and unit the zero generator — the actual functorial target
of the kinetic functor
\FP
.

Generators and kernels are linked by exponentiation

\exp_{t}:L\mapsto e^{tL}
, which sends a generator

L\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
to its one-parameter Markov semigroup

\{e^{tL}\}_{t\geq 0}
in

\mathrm{End}_{\Stoch}(\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|})
.
This section defines both, and shows that
\FP
targets

B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
at the categorical level — with
\Stoch

entering only as the home of finite-time evolution.

Definition 5.1

(
\Stoch
)
.

The category
\Stoch
has:

•

Objects
: measurable spaces
(X,\Sigma_{X})
.

•

Morphisms
: Markov kernels
K:X\to Y
,
i.e. functions
K:X\times\Sigma_{Y}\to[0,1]
such
that (i) for each
x\in X
,
K(x,\cdot)
is a
probability measure on
(Y,\Sigma_{Y})
, and (ii) for
each
A\in\Sigma_{Y}
, the map
K(\cdot,A):X\to[0,1]

is measurable.

•

Composition
: for
K:X\to Y
and
L:Y\to Z
,

(L\circ K)(\cdot\mid x):=\int_{Y}L(\cdot\mid y)\,K(dy\mid x)

(Chapman–Kolmogorov integration).

•

Monoidal product
:
(X,\Sigma_{X})\otimes(Y,\Sigma_{Y}):=(X\times Y,\,\Sigma_{X}\otimes\Sigma_{Y})
,
with
(K_{1}\otimes K_{2})(\cdot\mid x_{1},x_{2}):=K_{1}(\cdot\mid x_{1})\otimes K_{2}(\cdot\mid x_{2})
.

•

Monoidal unit
: the one-point space

I=(\{*\},\{\emptyset,\{*\}\})
.

\Stoch
is a symmetric monoidal category under this structure;
it is moreover a
Markov category
in the sense of Fritz

[
103
]
, with a canonical copy/discard structure that
encodes conditional independence

[
103
,
61
]
.

Definition 5.2

(The generator algebra
B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
)
.

The
Markov-generator algebra

\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
is the
positive cone of generators of Markov semigroups on

\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
: a (possibly unbounded) operator
L
on observables

f:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}
with off-diagonal-non-negative matrix
entries and rows summing to zero, closable to a CTMC under
standard non-explosion conditions
[
19
]
.
The
one-object category

B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
has a single
formal object
\ast
— interpreted as the global state space

\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
, the carrier on which every complex

\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
acts under
\FP
— and morphism set

\mathrm{End}(\ast)=\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
.

B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
is a strict symmetric monoidal category:

•

sequential composition: addition,
L_{1}+L_{2}
;

•

monoidal product: Kronecker sum,

L_{1}\otimes I+I\otimes L_{2}
(the infinitesimal of the
kernel tensor product in
\Stoch
);

•

unit: the zero generator on
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.

All associativity, unit, and symmetry equations hold as
equalities, not merely up to isomorphism.

B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
versus
B\mathbb{R}

At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
and
\mathcal{L}_{2}
the target was
B\mathbb{R}
: one object,
morphisms
\mathbb{R}
, sequential composition and monoidal product
both given by addition.

F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
were essentially monoid homomorphisms

(\mathrm{Mor}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)),\circ,\otimes)\to(\mathbb{R},+,+)
,
labelling each reaction by a single real number.

At
\mathcal{L}_{3}
the target
B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
is structurally
parallel — one object, morphism set additive, with sequential
composition and monoidal product both additive in their
respective senses — but the additive monoid is enriched from

\mathbb{R}
to the cone
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
of Markov-semigroup
generators on
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
This enrichment has three direct probabilistic consequences:

•

Morphisms encode full stochastic transitions.

A generator
L\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
encodes, via
exponentiation
e^{tL}
, the entire family of finite-time
transition probabilities

P(\mathbf{x}(t)\in\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}(0)=\mathbf{x})

of the underlying CTMC
[
18
]
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
and
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, a reaction
r
was labelled by a
single real number; at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
the label

\FP(r)\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
is an unbounded operator on
observables that determines, after exponentiation, every
conditional probability associated with
r
.

•

Sequential composition is operator addition,
extending real addition.

For composable reactions,

\FP(r_{2}\circ r_{1})=\FP(r_{2})+\FP(r_{1})
in

\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

(Proposition
5.10
).
This sum is the generator of the CTMC in which both
reaction channels are simultaneously available; it is

not
an effective single-step rate law for the
coarse-grained reaction
\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{w}

obtained by eliminating the intermediate (which would
require a quasi-steady-state reduction outside the strict

\mathcal{L}_{3}
functorial assignment).
The collapse to scalar addition recovers
\mathcal{L}_{1}
/
\mathcal{L}_{2}

additivity in the degenerate one-state case.

•

Monoidal product is Kronecker sum, extending
real addition.

For reactions on independent subsystems with disjoint
species sets,

\FP(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})=\FP(r_{1})\otimes I+I\otimes\FP(r_{2})
as generator contributions on the joint state
space (Proposition
5.11
).
This is the infinitesimal of the kernel tensor product in

\Stoch
and encodes probabilistic independence

[
103
]
: each subsystem evolves on its own
Poisson clock.
Again, this collapses to real addition in the degenerate
one-state case.

The three axioms of a strict SMC functor

\FP:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
have non-trivial
probabilistic content while preserving the structural role of
“additive functor” that
F_{\!H}
and
F_{\!S}
played at lower
levels.
The Markov-
kernel
interpretation of these data — the
finite-time transition probabilities — lives in
\Stoch
and
is recovered from
\FP(r)
by exponentiation

e^{t\,\FP(r)}
, which intertwines addition with kernel
composition only on the abelian locus of
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

(the Trotter–Kato obstruction; this non-functoriality of

\exp_{t}
is the categorical content of the
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}

forcing pair, Section
5.9
).

Remark 5.3

(Why
\exp_{t}
is not an SMC functor)
.

The functor
\FP:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
takes values
in generators, not in finite-time Markov kernels.
The link to
\Stoch
proper is the exponential

\exp_{t}:L\mapsto e^{tL}
, which sends
L\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

to its one-parameter Markov semigroup of kernels in

\mathrm{End}_{\Stoch}(\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|})
under standard non-explosion
conditions
[
19
]
.
This exponential is
not
a symmetric monoidal functor:
it intertwines addition with kernel composition only on the
abelian locus of
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
(the Trotter–Kato / BCH
obstruction).
On a sequential composite
r_{2}\circ r_{1}
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
,

\FP
records the additive generator

\FP(r_{2})+\FP(r_{1})\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
—
the generator of the CTMC in which both reaction channels are
simultaneously available — whose finite-time kernel

e^{t\,(\FP(r_{2})+\FP(r_{1}))}
differs from

e^{t\,\FP(r_{2})}\circ e^{t\,\FP(r_{1})}
by
Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff commutator terms.
This loss of path-order information at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
is precisely the
categorical content of the
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
forcing pair
(Section
5.9
); recovering bond-level order
information requires the DPO machinery of
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.

5.2.2. The state space is
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data

In classical CRNT, species counts in
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}

is read off directly from the reaction network: the
species set
\mathcal{S}
is part of the network definition, and a
state is simply a non-negative integer count for each species.
No kinetic data — no rate constants, no activation energies
— are needed to write down
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
The stoichiometric change vector
\mathbf{n}_{r}
of a reaction

r
is likewise determined by the network’s stoichiometry alone
(the left- and right-hand side complexes), as discussed in Chapter
2
.
In the tower language, this means
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
and

\mathbf{n}_{r}
are
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data: they are visible at the
stoichiometric level before any rate constants are introduced.

Observation 5.4

(State space from
\mathcal{L}_{0}
)
.

The kinetic state space
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
is determined
entirely by
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data:

•

The species set
\mathcal{S}
is a
\mathcal{L}_{0}
datum.

•

A state is a species-count vector

\mathbf{x}=(x_{s})_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.

•

The stoichiometric change vector of generator

r:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{v}

is
\mathbf{n}_{r}:=\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{v})}-\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{u})}\in\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
,
directly read from the
\mathcal{L}_{0}
morphism
r
.

The single new datum at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
is a positive rate constant

k_{r}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
per generator.
Everything else required to define
\FP(r)
is already present
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

5.2.3. Definition of
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)

In this chapter, the formulation is given in the Heisenberg
picture:
\FP(r)
acts on observables

f:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}
on the maximal domain on which it is
well-defined, with finitely-supported functions as a canonical
core
[
19
]
.

Definition 5.5

(Kinetic level
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
)
.

Let
P
be a Petri net with species set
\mathcal{S}
and reaction set

\mathcal{R}
.
The
kinetic level

\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
is the quadruple

\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)\;:=\;\bigl(\,\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),\;F_{\!H},\;F_{\!S},\;\FP\,\bigr),

where
F_{\!H}
,
F_{\!S}
are the thermochemical and entropy functors
from
\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)
, and

\FP:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\;\longrightarrow\;B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

is a strict symmetric monoidal functor
(Definition
5.2
) satisfying:

•

every complex
\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
maps to the
unique object
\ast
of
B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
, interpreted
as the global state space
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
;

•

every identity morphism
\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}}
maps to the
zero generator,

\FP(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{u}})=0\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
;

•

each chemical generator
r\in\mathcal{R}
maps to the

generator contribution

\FP(r)\;:=\;M_{\lambda_{r}}\,(R_{r}-I),

the standard CME generator contribution of reaction
r
in
the Heisenberg picture, acting on observables

f:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}
, where:

–

R_{r}
is the shift operator

(R_{r}f)(\mathbf{x}):=f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{n}_{r})
;

–

M_{\lambda_{r}}
is multiplication by the
mass-action propensity

\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x})\;:=\;k_{r}\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\binom{x_{s}}{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u}_{r})}}\qquad(k_{r}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0});

–

the binomial coefficient vanishes when

x_{s}<\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u}_{r})}
, so
\FP(r)

automatically vanishes at boundary states with
insufficient reactants.

Explicitly,

\bigl(\FP(r)f\bigr)(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x})\bigl[f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{n}_{r})-f(\mathbf{x})\bigr]\quad\text{\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{AndersonCraciunKurtz2010, AndersonKurtz2015}{}{}]}.}

Propensities are polynomial in
\mathbf{x}
, so
\FP(r)
is
in general unbounded; we take its domain to be functions of
compact support, on which the assembled generator

\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\FP(r)
admits a closure generating a
Markov semigroup under the standard non-explosion conditions

[
19
]
.
The full CME generator

\Omega=\overline{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\FP(r)}

is assembled in Section
5.4
.

The
forgetful operation

U_{3}
acts on decorated
quadruples by

(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{\!H},F_{\!S},\FP)\mapsto(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
,
dropping
\FP
.

In the literature,
k_{r}
is in general non-negative.
The case
k_{r}=0
corresponds to a vanishing generator
contribution,
\FP(r)=0\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
, which
exponentiates to the identity kernel
\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}}\in\Stoch
:
no reaction takes place.

Remark 5.6

(
\FP(r)
versus a Markov kernel)
.

The generator contribution
\FP(r)=M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)

is a Markov generator on
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
: it is not itself a
Markov kernel (which must be a probability measure for each
input state), but rather its infinitesimal version.
The associated Markov kernel is the integrated semigroup

e^{t\,\FP(r)}
, which describes the probability distribution
over states after time
t
if only reaction
r
could fire.
Working at the generator level — standard in the chemical
master equation (CME) literature
[
18
]

— allows one to sum contributions linearly:

\Omega=\sum_{r}\FP(r)
is itself a valid CME generator,
whereas Markov kernels compose by Chapman–Kolmogorov
integration, not addition.

The tower now reads:

\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)}_{\text{free skeletal permutative category}}\;\hookrightarrow\;\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{1}}_{+\,F_{\!H}}\;\hookrightarrow\;\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{2}}_{+\,F_{\!S}}\;\hookrightarrow\;\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{3}}_{+\,\FP}.

The first two extensions add functors into
B\mathbb{R}
(real numbers
under addition), reflecting the additive nature of standard
reaction enthalpies and entropies.
The third adds a functor into
B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
, whose
additive structure (sequential = addition, monoidal product =
Kronecker sum) extends the additivity of
\mathbb{R}
to the genuinely
probabilistic setting of kinetics: this enrichment of the
target’s additive monoid — from
\mathbb{R}
to
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

— is the categorical signature of the passage from
thermodynamics to dynamics.
The underlying free skeletal permutative category
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

remains unchanged throughout.

Proposition 5.7

(Existence and uniqueness of
\FP
)
.

Given any assignment
k:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}
of positive rate
constants to chemical generators, there is a unique strict
SMC functor

\FP:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

extending
k
via
r\mapsto M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)
.

Proof.

By Theorem
2.14
,
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is the free skeletal
permutative category generated by
P
: given any strict SMC

\mathcal{C}
with strictly commutative object monoid, an
assignment of (i) species in
\mathcal{S}
to objects of
\mathcal{C}

and (ii) chemical generators
r\in\mathcal{R}
to morphisms in

\mathcal{C}
with matching sources and targets extends
uniquely to a strict SMC functor
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to\mathcal{C}
.
The target
\mathcal{C}=B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

(Definition
5.2
) is one-object, so its object
monoid is the singleton — trivially strictly commutative —
and the species assignment (i) is forced to map every species
to the unique object
\ast
; only the morphism assignment (ii)
carries information.

The proposed assignment

r\mapsto M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
is
well-typed:
\lambda_{r}\geq 0
pointwise, the matrix entries of

M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)
are off-diagonal-non-negative with
zero row sums (the defining structure of a Markov generator),
and the assembled
\sum_{r}\FP(r)
admits a closure generating
a Markov semigroup under standard non-explosion conditions

[
18
,
19
]
.
Applying the universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
to this
assignment yields the unique strict SMC functor

\FP:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
extending
k
;
the value on each generator is determined by
\mathbf{n}_{r}

(from
\mathcal{L}_{0}
, fixing
R_{r}
) and
k_{r}
(the new datum at

\mathcal{L}_{3}
).
∎

Proposition
5.7
has the same logical
structure as the existence-and-uniqueness statements for

F_{\!H}
(Proposition
3.2
) and
F_{\!S}

(Proposition
4.2
): in all three cases, the
universal property of the free skeletal permutative category

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
guarantees that a single real-valued assignment per
chemical generator extends uniquely to a strict SMC functor on
all of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
The only difference is what the real number labels and where it
lands, which is precisely what the insightbox below records.

One positive real per reaction — again

Propositions
3.2
,
4.2
,
and
5.7
are the same theorem applied three
times to three different targets:

Level

Functor

Target

New datum per chemical generator

\mathcal{L}_{1}

F_{\!H}

B\mathbb{R}

\Delta H^{\circ}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}

\mathcal{L}_{2}

F_{\!S}

B\mathbb{R}

\Delta S^{\circ}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}

\mathcal{L}_{3}

\FP

B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

k_{r}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}

The universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is the single engine
driving all three extensions.
At
\mathcal{L}_{3}
the target changes from
B\mathbb{R}
to
B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

— from the additive monoid of real numbers to the richer
additive cone of Markov-semigroup generators on
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}

— but the argument is structurally identical.
The positivity constraint
k_{r}>0
(absent for
\Delta H^{\circ}_{r}

and
\Delta S^{\circ}_{r}
, which can be any real number) reflects the
physical requirement that reaction rates are non-negative:
a non-positive
k_{r}
would yield a generator contribution

M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)
that fails to define a valid Markov
semigroup.

§5.3. Mass-action kinetics: unpacking

\FP

The assignment of a rate constant
k_{r}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
to each
generating reaction
r
is standard practice in stochastic
chemical kinetics: it is the starting point for Gillespie’s
stochastic simulation algorithm
[
121
]
, for the
derivation of the chemical master equation
[
215
,
122
]
, and for the CTMC models of chemical reaction
networks that underlie the CRNT stochastic literature

[
17
,
18
]
.
The role of this section is to make explicit how
k_{r}
enters
the functor
\FP
and how the resulting propensity function

\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x})
relates to the stoichiometric data
already present in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

5.3.1. The propensity and generator contribution

For a generator
r:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{v}
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

with stoichiometric vector

\mathbf{n}_{r}=\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{v})}-\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{u})}\in\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|}

and rate constant
k_{r}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}
, the kinetic functor
assigns the following data.

Definition 5.8

(Mass-action propensity and generator contribution)
.

Fix a system volume
V>0
(in units consistent with the
rate-constant convention below).
The
stochastic mass-action propensity
of reaction

r:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{v}
in state

\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
is

\lambda_{r}^{V}(\mathbf{x})\;:=\;\kappa_{r}\,V^{1-|\mathbf{u}|}\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\binom{x_{s}}{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}}\qquad(\kappa_{r}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}),

where:

•

\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}
is the stoichiometric
coefficient of species
s
in the source complex

\mathbf{u}
;

•

|\mathbf{u}|:=\sum_{s}\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}
is
the molecularity (total reactant count) of
r
;

•

\kappa_{r}
is the
stochastic mass-action rate
constant
, fixed independently of
V
and chosen so that
the deterministic-limit rate

v_{r}(\mathbf{c})=\kappa_{r}\prod_{s}c_{s}^{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}}

has the conventional concentration units (Proposition
5.18
);

•

\binom{x_{s}}{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}}=0
if

x_{s}<\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}
, so
\lambda_{r}^{V}
vanishes
automatically at boundary states with insufficient
reactants.

The volume factor
V^{1-|\mathbf{u}|}
is the standard
classical scaling

[
179
,
19
,
122
]

that makes the propensity behave correctly in the
large-volume limit:
V^{-1}\lambda_{r}^{V}(V\mathbf{c})\to v_{r}(\mathbf{c})

pointwise as
V\to\infty
with
\mathbf{x}=V\mathbf{c}

fixed (proof in Section
5.4
).
Without this scaling, bimolecular and higher reactions have
no finite macroscopic limit.

The
shift operator

R_{r}
acts on observables

f:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}
by

(R_{r}f)(\mathbf{x}):=f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{n}_{r})
.
The
generator contribution
of
r
at volume
V
is the
operator

\FP^{V}(r)\;:=\;M_{\lambda_{r}^{V}}\,(R_{r}-I),

acting on observables
f
in the Heisenberg picture as

\bigl(\FP^{V}(r)\,f\bigr)(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\lambda_{r}^{V}(\mathbf{x})\bigl[f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{n}_{r})-f(\mathbf{x})\bigr],

the standard CME generator contribution

[
18
,
19
]
,
consistent with Definition
5.5
.

\FP^{V}(r)
is in general unbounded (the propensity is
polynomial in
\mathbf{x}
); it is well-defined on
finitely-supported functions, on which

\sum_{r}\FP^{V}(r)
closes to a Markov-semigroup generator
under standard non-explosion conditions

[
19
]
.
We write
\FP(r)
in place of
\FP^{V}(r)
when the volume is
fixed and unambiguous.

Remark 5.9

(Convention: binomial vs. falling-factorial propensities)
.

Two equivalent stochastic propensity conventions appear in the
literature, differing only by where the combinatorial factors

\prod_{s}\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}!
are placed:

•

Binomial form
(used in this chapter,
Definition
5.8
):

\lambda_{r}^{V}(\mathbf{x})=\kappa_{r}\,V^{1-|\mathbf{u}|}\prod_{s}\binom{x_{s}}{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}}
.

•

Falling-factorial form
(Anderson–Kurtz

[
17
]
, Feinberg

[
96
]
):

\lambda_{r}^{V}(\mathbf{x})=\kappa_{r}^{\mathrm{ff}}\,V^{1-|\mathbf{u}|}\prod_{s}(x_{s})_{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}}
,
where
(x_{s})_{n}:=x_{s}(x_{s}-1)\cdots(x_{s}-n+1)
.

The two are related by

\kappa_{r}^{\mathrm{ff}}=\kappa_{r}/\prod_{s}\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}!
,
since
(x_{s})_{\nu}=\nu!\,\binom{x_{s}}{\nu}
.
The deterministic limit
v_{r}(\mathbf{c})=\kappa_{r}\prod_{s}c_{s}^{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}}

(Proposition
5.18
) is the same in both conventions —
the combinatorial factors cancel between numerator and the

1/\nu_{s}!
in
\binom{x_{s}}{\nu_{s}}
when one passes to the
deterministic rate.

A third
macroscopic
convention, customary in
physical-chemistry textbooks

[
23
,
96
]
, absorbs both the volume
scaling and the combinatorial factor into a single
concentration-based rate constant

k_{r}^{\mathrm{macro}}\;:=\;\kappa_{r}\;=\;\kappa_{r}^{\mathrm{ff}}\prod_{s}\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}!,

so that
v_{r}(\mathbf{c})=k_{r}^{\mathrm{macro}}\prod_{s}c_{s}^{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}}
directly.
The kinetic Wegscheider condition takes its familiar macroscopic
form

k_{r}^{\mathrm{macro}}/k_{r^{\dagger}}^{\mathrm{macro}}=K_{\mathrm{eq}}(r,T)

in this convention; the binomial-form analogue
(Definition
5.21
) carries an explicit factorial
factor
\prod_{s}\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}!/\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{v})}!
,
which is a convention artefact, not a thermodynamic correction.
The three conventions agree on every gauge-invariant kinetic
prediction (deterministic rates, equilibrium ratios, mean steady
states); they differ only in where the
\nu!
factors are
bookkept.

What is
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data and what is new

In the propensity
\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x})
:

•

The stoichiometric coefficients

\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u})}
:
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data
(from the source complex
\mathbf{u}
of the morphism
r
).

•

The shift vector
\mathbf{n}_{r}
:
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data
(the stoichiometric change, computed from
r
).

•

The rate constant
k_{r}
: the single new datum at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

The falling factorial

\binom{x_{s}}{\nu}=x_{s}(x_{s}-1)\cdots(x_{s}-\nu+1)/\nu!

is the exact stochastic mass-action term first written down by
McQuarrie
[
215
]
and given its definitive
physical derivation by Gillespie
[
121
]
.
For large copy numbers,
\binom{x_{s}}{\nu}\approx(x_{s}/V)^{\nu}V^{\nu}/\nu!\to c_{s}^{\nu}V^{\nu}/\nu!
as
V\to\infty
with

c_{s}=x_{s}/V
fixed, recovering the deterministic power-law
rate
k_{r}\prod_{s}c_{s}^{\nu_{s}}
after rescaling by
V

(Proposition
5.18
).

5.3.2. Functoriality unpacked

Two reactions
r_{1}
and
r_{2}
can be arranged in sequence in

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
: the target complex of
r_{1}
is the source complex
of
r_{2}
, giving a composite morphism
r_{2}\circ r_{1}
in

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
The functor axiom
\FP(r_{2}\circ r_{1})=\FP(r_{2})\circ\FP(r_{1})

in the target
B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
unpacks — since sequential
composition in
B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
is operator addition
(Definition
5.2
) — as the additivity of generator
contributions:

\FP(r_{2}\circ r_{1})\;=\;\FP(r_{2})+\FP(r_{1})\quad\text{in }\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}.

This is a statement about generator-level assembly: the
right-hand side is the generator of the CTMC in which both
reaction channels
r_{1}
and
r_{2}
are simultaneously available
on the joint state space.
It is
not
an effective single-step rate law for the
coarse-grained reaction
\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{w}
; eliminating
the intermediate complex
\mathbf{v}
requires a quasi-steady-state
or rapid-equilibrium reduction outside the strict
\mathcal{L}_{3}

functorial assignment, recovered only as a derived approximation
under additional hypotheses on the rate constants.
At the level of stoichiometry, the same composition gives net
shift vector

\mathbf{n}_{r_{2}\circ r_{1}}=\mathbf{n}_{r_{1}}+\mathbf{n}_{r_{2}}
,
implicit throughout CRNT wherever net reactions are obtained by
adding elementary steps
[
96
]
.

Proposition 5.10

(Generator additivity along
\mathcal{L}_{0}
composition)
.

For composable chemical generators

r_{1}:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{v}
and

r_{2}:\mathbf{v}\to\mathbf{w}
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, the
generator contributions satisfy

\FP(r_{2}\circ r_{1})\;=\;\FP(r_{2})+\FP(r_{1})\quad\text{in }\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}},

the generator of the CTMC in which both reaction channels are
simultaneously available; and the stoichiometric change of
the composite equals the sum of the individual changes,

\mathbf{n}_{r_{2}\circ r_{1}}=\mathbf{n}_{r_{1}}+\mathbf{n}_{r_{2}}\in\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.

Proof.

The composite
r_{2}\circ r_{1}
is a morphism in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, not
an additional chemical generator: it carries no rate constant of
its own.
The functor axiom is the statement that
\FP
extends correctly
from chemical generators to such composites under the universal
property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
(Proposition
5.7
).
The target
B\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
has sequential composition given
by operator addition (Definition
5.2
; the standard
additivity of CME generator contributions

[
18
]
), so

\FP(r_{2}\circ r_{1})\;=\;\FP(r_{2})+\FP(r_{1})\quad\text{in }\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}.

For the stoichiometric statement, the composite

r_{2}\circ r_{1}:\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{w}
has shift vector

\mathbf{n}_{r_{2}\circ r_{1}}\;=\;\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{w})}-\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{u})}\;=\;\bigl(\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{w})}-\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{v})}\bigr)+\bigl(\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{v})}-\bm{\nu}^{(\mathbf{u})}\bigr)\;=\;\mathbf{n}_{r_{2}}+\mathbf{n}_{r_{1}},

the additivity of shift vectors in
\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.

A note on what this proposition does
not
say.
The shift operators
R_{r}
acting on observables factor
multiplicatively along composition,

R_{r_{2}\circ r_{1}}=R_{r_{2}}\,R_{r_{1}}
, while the generator
contributions
\FP(r_{i})=M_{\lambda_{r_{i}}}(R_{r_{i}}-I)
add.
The two live in different algebras — the shift semigroup of
bounded operators on observables and the additive cone

\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
of Markov generators — and
\FP
uses
each in its proper place: the multiplicative structure of
R_{r}

inside the individual
M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)
, and the additive
structure of
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
when assembling contributions
along a
\mathcal{L}_{0}
composite.
This additive assembly is the generator of the joint CTMC, not
an effective rate law for the coarse-grained one-step reaction

\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{w}
; recovering an effective rate law
requires a separate reduction (quasi-steady state, rapid
equilibrium) that is not part of the strict
\mathcal{L}_{3}
functorial
assignment.
∎

What this proposition means physically, and what it does not

What it says.

Sequential reactions compose correctly at the levels of
stoichiometry and generator-of-joint-CTMC: if
r_{1}
consumes
species
A
and produces
B
, and
r_{2}
consumes
B
and
produces
C
, then the net stoichiometric change of doing both
is the shift from the
A
-count to the
C
-count, and the
generator of the CTMC with both channels available is

\FP(r_{2})+\FP(r_{1})
.
This is the additive content of Hess’s Law applied to
stoichiometry — the overall stoichiometric balance is
independent of how it is decomposed into elementary steps.

What it does not say.

The proposition does
not
claim that the effective rate
at which the coarse-grained reaction
A\to C
proceeds is some
simple function of
\kappa_{r_{1}}
and
\kappa_{r_{2}}
.
The actual time evolution of the joint CTMC depends on both
propensities through the Gillespie waiting times

[
121
]
, and eliminating the intermediate species

B
to obtain an effective one-step rate law requires
quasi-steady-state or rapid-equilibrium reduction — a
chemical-engineering approximation valid only when
B
is
short-lived, and not part of the strict
\mathcal{L}_{3}
assignment.
The proposition captures stoichiometric composition and
joint-CTMC assembly; effective coarse-grained rates are a
separate, approximation-dependent question.

5.3.3. Monoidality unpacked

Two reactions
r_{1}
and
r_{2}
can also be placed in independent
parallel subsystems with disjoint species sets
\mathcal{S}_{1}
and

\mathcal{S}_{2}
.
The monoidal product
r_{1}\otimes r_{2}
is their simultaneous
presence in the joint system, and the functor axiom

\FP(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})=\FP(r_{1})\otimes\FP(r_{2})

demands that the joint generator contribution decomposes
correctly.
This is the categorical expression of the familiar CTMC
independence result: two reactions on disjoint species evolve
independently, and their joint generator is the sum of the
individual generators, a fact used constantly when constructing
modular kinetic models
[
17
]
.

Proposition 5.11

(Monoidality of
\FP
: parallel reactions)
.

For generators
r_{1}
and
r_{2}
in independent subsystems
with disjoint species sets
\mathcal{S}_{1}
,
\mathcal{S}_{2}
,

\FP(r_{1}\otimes r_{2})\;=\;\FP(r_{1})\otimes\FP(r_{2})

as generator contributions on the joint state space

\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}_{1}|}\times\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}_{2}|}
.
At the level of the assembled CME generators
(Definition
5.13
in Section
5.4
),
this corresponds to the Kronecker sum:

\Omega_{12}=\Omega_{1}\otimes I+I\otimes\Omega_{2}.

Proof.

Independent reactions act on independent coordinates of the
joint state
(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2})
.
Reaction
r_{1}
fires at propensity

\lambda_{r_{1}}^{V}(\mathbf{x}_{1})
independently of
\mathbf{x}_{2}
,
and
r_{2}
fires at propensity

\lambda_{r_{2}}^{V}(\mathbf{x}_{2})
independently of
\mathbf{x}_{1}

(volume scaling per Definition
5.8
).
The generator contribution of
r_{1}
on the joint space acts as

M_{\lambda_{r_{1}}^{V}}(R_{r_{1}}-I)\otimes I
, and that of
r_{2}

as
I\otimes M_{\lambda_{r_{2}}^{V}}(R_{r_{2}}-I)
.
The combined reaction
r_{1}\otimes r_{2}
therefore has generator
contribution

\bigl(M_{\lambda_{r_{1}}^{V}}(R_{r_{1}}-I)\otimes I\bigr)+\bigl(I\otimes M_{\lambda_{r_{2}}^{V}}(R_{r_{2}}-I)\bigr)
in the
Kronecker-sum form of the joint
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}_{1}\sqcup\mathcal{S}_{2}}
,
and summing over chemical generators in each subsystem gives

\Omega_{12}=\Omega_{1}\otimes I+I\otimes\Omega_{2}
.
∎

Remark 5.12

(Kronecker sum versus tensor product of generators)
.

The Kronecker sum
\Omega_{12}=\Omega_{1}\otimes I+I\otimes\Omega_{2}
is the generator of
independent

parallel evolution: each subsystem runs on its own Poisson
clock, and the two clocks are independent.
The tensor product
\Omega_{1}\otimes\Omega_{2}
would describe
simultaneous firing of both reactions at every event —
a different (and physically unnatural) process.
This distinction is the categorical precision behind the
everyday CRNT modelling choice to write

\dot{\mathbf{c}}=N_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1}+N_{2}\mathbf{v}_{2}

for a combined network rather than any product structure

[
96
]
.

§5.4. The Chemical Master Equation

The chemical master equation (CME) was introduced by McQuarrie

[
215
]
as the master equation for stochastic
chemical kinetics and was given its definitive probabilistic
foundation by Gillespie
[
121
,
122
]
,
who derived it from first principles of molecular collision
theory.
Within the tower, the CME is not an independent postulate: it
is the object obtained by
assembling
all the generator
contributions
\{\FP(r)\}_{r\in\mathcal{R}}
assigned by the kinetic
functor.
Specifically,
\FP
assigns an operator

\FP(r)=M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)
to each generating reaction

r
via the universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
(Proposition
5.7
).
The CME generator
\Omega
is the sum of all these operators;
it is not a single functor value but a derived object assembled
from the full image of
\FP
.

This assembly step — summing over all reactions — is what
distinguishes
\mathcal{L}_{3}
from
\mathcal{L}_{1}
and
\mathcal{L}_{2}
:
the functors
F_{\!H}(r)\in\mathbb{R}
and
F_{\!S}(r)\in\mathbb{R}
are
direct numerical outputs of the functor on a single morphism,
whereas the CME generator requires summing
\FP(r)
over all
generators in
\mathcal{R}
.
The analogue at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
would be to form

\sum_{r}F_{\!H}(r)
along a closed loop — but that sum vanishes
identically by the additive content of Hess’s Law on cycles
(§
3.3
), so it produces no new object;
here the sum genuinely produces a new mathematical entity, the
infinitesimal generator of a Markov semigroup.

\FP
versus
\Omega
: assignment versus assembly

The functor
\FP
assigns an individual generator contribution

\FP(r)=M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)
to each reaction
r\in\mathcal{R}

via the universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
The CME generator

\Omega\;=\;\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\FP(r)\;=\;\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)

is assembled from the entire image of
\FP
.
It is not a single morphism value of
\FP
, but a global object.

This two-step structure — functor assigns, sum assembles —
has no analogue at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
or
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, where the individual
values
F_{\!H}(r)
and
F_{\!S}(r)
directly gave the thermochemical
invariants without further assembly.
The CME is the characteristic assembled object of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

Definition 5.13

(CME generator and the Chemical Master Equation

[
215
,
122
]
)
.

Fix a system volume
V>0
.
The
CME generator
of
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
at volume
V
is the
operator on observables
f:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}

\Omega^{V}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))\;:=\;\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\FP^{V}(r),

with
\FP^{V}(r)=M_{\lambda_{r}^{V}}(R_{r}-I)
and
\lambda_{r}^{V}

the volume-scaled mass-action propensity of
Definition
5.8
.
The
Chemical Master Equation
of
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
is the
Kolmogorov forward equation of the CTMC with generator

\Omega^{V}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
:

\frac{d}{dt}p(\mathbf{x},t)\;=\;\bigl(\Omega^{V}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))^{\top}\,p\bigr)(\mathbf{x},t)\;=\;\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\Bigl[\lambda_{r}^{V}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{n}_{r})\,p(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{n}_{r},t)\;-\;\lambda_{r}^{V}(\mathbf{x})\,p(\mathbf{x},t)\Bigr],

where
p(\mathbf{x},t)\geq 0
is the probability of being in
state
\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
at time
t\geq 0
.
We write
\Omega(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
in place of
\Omega^{V}
when the
volume is fixed and unambiguous.

Remark 5.14

(Operator form versus gain–loss form)
.

The CME above uses the notation established in
Definition
5.8
:
\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x})
is the
full mass-action propensity (incorporating
\kappa_{r}
and the
volume factor), so the gain–loss form does not carry an extra
factor of
\kappa_{r}
.
The two equivalent forms are related by transposition between
the Heisenberg and Schrödinger pictures.
On observables
f
, the Heisenberg-picture generator acts as

(\Omega f)(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x})\,\bigl[f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{n}_{r})-f(\mathbf{x})\bigr],

which is the operator form
\Omega=\sum_{r}M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)
.
On probabilities
p
, the dual
\Omega^{\top}
acts as

(\Omega^{\top}p)(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\bigl[\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{n}_{r})\,p(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{n}_{r})-\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x})\,p(\mathbf{x})\bigr],

which is the gain–loss form.
The two are interchanged by the duality

\langle\Omega f,p\rangle=\langle f,\Omega^{\top}p\rangle

of summation against
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
; the Kolmogorov forward
equation
\dot{p}=\Omega^{\top}p
uses the second form.

Reading the CME term by term

Each summand in the CME has two contributions, familiar from
any textbook treatment of CTMCs
[
17
]
:

•

Gain term
:

\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{n}_{r})\,p(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{n}_{r},t)
— probability flowing

into
state
\mathbf{x}
from the predecessor state

\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{n}_{r}
via reaction
r
.

•

Loss term
:

\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{x})\,p(\mathbf{x},t)
— probability
flowing
out of
state
\mathbf{x}
via reaction
r
.

The net change in
p(\mathbf{x},t)
is the algebraic sum of all
gains and losses across all reactions.
Probability is conserved at the generator level:

\displaystyle\Omega^{V}\mathbf{1}

\displaystyle\;=\;0\quad\text{(Heisenberg picture, on the constant observable),}

\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\bigl(\Omega^{V\,\top}\,p\bigr)(\mathbf{x},t)

\displaystyle\;=\;0\quad\text{(Schr{\"{o}}dinger picture).}

The two are the same conservation law expressed on observables
and on probability distributions respectively, related by
duality
\langle\Omega^{V}f,p\rangle=\langle f,\Omega^{V\,\top}p\rangle
.
In the tower language, this conservation law is the statement
that
\Omega^{V}
is a valid Markov generator on
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}

(an element of
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
): the row-sum-zero condition
on the matrix entries of
\Omega^{V}
in the Heisenberg picture
is exactly the infinitesimal form of
\sum_{\mathbf{y}}K(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x})=1
for Markov kernels
K

[
103
]
.

The CME generator
\Omega(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
inherits the
species-permutation symmetry of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
This is the first tower-native statement about
\Omega
as
an object in its own right, and it is the equivariance
property that will lift to the Para shadow

\mathcal{L}_{3}^{\mathrm{Para}}
in Chapter
11
: a learned
kinetic model is a valid object of
\mathcal{L}_{3}^{\mathrm{Para}}
only if it satisfies the analogue of Proposition
5.15
below.

Proposition 5.15

(Species-permutation covariance of
\Omega
)
.

Let
\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P))
be an automorphism induced
by a species permutation
\sigma:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S}
, and let

\sigma\cdot\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
denote the kinetic level structure
with species relabelled by
\sigma
and rate constants
transported along the induced bijection

\sigma_{*}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{R}
via

(\sigma\cdot\kappa)_{\sigma_{*}(r)}:=\kappa_{r}.
.
Let
U_{\sigma}
denote the operator on observables induced by
the coordinate permutation
\mathbf{x}\mapsto\sigma\cdot\mathbf{x}
,
i.e.
(U_{\sigma}f)(\mathbf{x})=f(\sigma^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{x})
.
Then

U_{\sigma}\,\Omega(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))\,U_{\sigma}^{-1}\;=\;\Omega(\sigma\cdot\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)).

Proof.

It suffices to prove the identity generator-by-generator,
since
\Omega
is a linear sum over
\mathcal{R}
and conjugation by

U_{\sigma}
distributes over the sum.
Fix
r\in\mathcal{R}
; we compute the action of

U_{\sigma}\,\FP(r)\,U_{\sigma}^{-1}=U_{\sigma}\,M_{\lambda_{r}}(R_{r}-I)\,U_{\sigma}^{-1}

on a test function
f
, using
(U_{\sigma}^{-1}g)(\mathbf{x})=g(\sigma\cdot\mathbf{x})
throughout.

For the shift operator,

(U_{\sigma}R_{r}U_{\sigma}^{-1}f)(\mathbf{x})\;=\;(R_{r}(U_{\sigma}^{-1}f))(\sigma^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{x})\;=\;(U_{\sigma}^{-1}f)(\sigma^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{n}_{r})\;=\;f(\mathbf{x}+\sigma\cdot\mathbf{n}_{r}),

so
U_{\sigma}R_{r}U_{\sigma}^{-1}=R_{\sigma_{*}(r)}
, since

\sigma\cdot\mathbf{n}_{r}=\mathbf{n}_{\sigma_{*}(r)}
by
definition of the induced action
\sigma_{*}
on reactions.

For the multiplication operator,

(U_{\sigma}M_{\lambda_{r}}U_{\sigma}^{-1}f)(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\lambda_{r}(\sigma^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{x})\,f(\mathbf{x}).

Now

\lambda_{r}(\sigma^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{x})=\kappa_{r}\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\binom{x_{\sigma(s)}}{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u}_{r})}}=\kappa_{r}\prod_{t\in\mathcal{S}}\binom{x_{t}}{\nu_{\sigma^{-1}(t)}^{(\mathbf{u}_{r})}}

(reindexing
t=\sigma(s)
).
By definition of the species relabelling, the source complex
of
\sigma_{*}(r)
has stoichiometric coefficients

\nu_{t}^{(\mathbf{u}_{\sigma_{*}(r)})}=\nu_{\sigma^{-1}(t)}^{(\mathbf{u}_{r})}
,
and the rate constant is

(\sigma\cdot\kappa)_{\sigma_{*}(r)}=\kappa_{r}
, so

\lambda_{r}(\sigma^{-1}\cdot\mathbf{x})=\lambda_{\sigma_{*}(r)}(\mathbf{x})
in the relabelled
network.
Hence
U_{\sigma}M_{\lambda_{r}}U_{\sigma}^{-1}=M_{\lambda_{\sigma_{*}(r)}}
.

Combining the two,

U_{\sigma}\,\FP(r)\,U_{\sigma}^{-1}\;=\;M_{\lambda_{\sigma_{*}(r)}}(R_{\sigma_{*}(r)}-I)\;=\;(\sigma\cdot\FP)(\sigma_{*}(r)).

Summing over
r\in\mathcal{R}
and reindexing by the bijection

\sigma_{*}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{R}
gives

U_{\sigma}\Omega(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))U_{\sigma}^{-1}=\Omega(\sigma\cdot\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
as claimed.
∎

Remark 5.16

(Two levels of invariance and why it matters)
.

Proposition
5.15
is a

covariance
statement, not an invariance statement:

\Omega
changes under
\sigma
, but changes in exactly the
way the relabelled
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
prescribes.
Two special cases are worth naming.

•

Stabilisers of
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
.

If
\sigma
fixes the tuple
(\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),\{k_{r}\})
—
i.e.
\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
—
then
\sigma\cdot\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)=\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
and the
proposition reduces to

U_{\sigma}\Omega U_{\sigma}^{-1}=\Omega
:
the CME generator commutes with the stabiliser action.
This is the statement that symmetry-related states
evolve identically under the CTMC.

•

Forcing-pair diagnostic.

If
\sigma
lies in
\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{2}(P))\setminus\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
— the rate-constant-swapping
automorphisms of Section
5.1
, which
witness
\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{3})\neq 1
—
then
\sigma\cdot\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)\neq\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
and

U_{\sigma}\Omega U_{\sigma}^{-1}\neq\Omega
.
The proposition detects the forcing pair: the CME
generator itself distinguishes what
\mathcal{L}_{2}
cannot.

Viewed as an equivariance condition, the proposition says:
the assignment
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)\mapsto\Omega(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
is a
permutation-equivariant map, where the permutations acts on

\mathcal{L}_{3}
-structures by species relabelling and on the space
of generators by conjugation.
A parametric kinetic model

(\Theta,f_{\theta}):\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)\to\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}

is a morphism in
\mathcal{L}_{3}^{\mathrm{Para}}
only if it is equivariant
in this sense: the species-permutation symmetry is not an
architectural choice but a
defining
property of the
level, exactly as Gavranović et al.

[
112
]
identifies equivariance with the

\mathrm{Lax}
-algebra homomorphism condition.

5.4.1. The deterministic limit as a forgetful functor

The reaction rate equation (RRE) is relevant here for the following reason: it shows that
\mathcal{L}_{3}
strictly contains
\mathcal{L}_{0}
as a limiting case.
Concretely, the stoichiometric matrix
N
of
\mathcal{L}_{0}
and the rate functor
\FP
of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
together determine the RRE via a
large-volume forgetful functor

\Phi_{\infty}
; the RRE is not a separate postulate but a derived image of
\FP
.
Rewriting Kurtz’s theorem
[
178
,
179
]
in tower language makes this factorisation explicit.

Definition 5.17

(Large-volume scaling limit)
.

For each volume
V>0
, define the
scaling map

\phi_{V}:\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{|\mathcal{S}|},\qquad\phi_{V}(\mathbf{x})\;:=\;\mathbf{x}/V.

Let
\{A^{V}\}_{V>0}
be a volume-indexed family of operators
on observables, with
A^{V}\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
for each
V
;
the family is said to be
classically scaled
if the
limit

(\Phi_{\infty}\{A^{V}\})(\mathbf{c})\;:=\;\lim_{V\to\infty}V\cdot\bigl((\phi_{V})_{*}A^{V}\bigr)\!\bigl[\mathbf{c}\bigr]\;\in\;T_{\mathbf{c}}\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{|\mathcal{S}|}

exists for every
\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
in the
sense of pointwise convergence on smooth compactly-supported
test functions, where
(\phi_{V})_{*}
denotes the pushforward of

A^{V}
along
\phi_{V}
.
The
large-volume scaling limit

\Phi_{\infty}
assigns
to each classically-scaled family the resulting smooth vector
field on
\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.

\Phi_{\infty}
is not a functor on arbitrary generators: it is
defined only on volume-indexed families satisfying the
classical density-dependent scaling

[
179
,
17
]
.
Mass-action families

A^{V}=\Omega^{V}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))=\sum_{r}\FP^{V}(r)

built from the volume-scaled propensities of
Definition
5.8
are classically scaled by
construction; this is the content of
Proposition
5.18
below.

Proposition 5.18

(The RRE as the scaling limit of the mass-action CME family

[
178
,
179
,
17
]
)
.

The volume-indexed family of CME generators

\{\Omega^{V}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))\}_{V>0}
, with

\Omega^{V}=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\FP^{V}(r)
assembled from the
volume-scaled mass-action propensities of
Definition
5.8
, is classically scaled, and
its large-volume scaling limit (Definition
5.17
)
is the reaction-rate vector field:

\Phi_{\infty}\!\bigl(\{\Omega^{V}\}\bigr)\;=\;N\circ\mathbf{v},

where:

•

N\in\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|\times|\mathcal{R}|}
is the stoichiometric
matrix, an
\mathcal{L}_{0}
datum.

•

\mathbf{v}:\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{|\mathcal{R}|}
,

v_{r}(\mathbf{c})=\kappa_{r}\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S}}c_{s}^{\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u}_{r})}}
,
is the mass-action rate function, with
\kappa_{r}
from

\FP
(the stochastic mass-action rate constant of
Definition
5.8
) and exponents

\nu_{s}^{(\mathbf{u}_{r})}
