The mass-action functional form of
\FP
is fixed by the
stoichiometry, hence agrees automatically.
The remaining datum is the rate constant: this agrees when
the rate-limiting step in either mechanism couples the same
molecules in the same orders — in particular, under
steady-state on a buried intermediate with matching
effective rate constants

[
222
,
191
]
.
The forcing pair below is an idealisation in which all four

\mathcal{L}_{3}
decorations agree exactly; this is the regime in
which bulk kinetic measurements cannot distinguish the
mechanisms, and is the regime in which the categorical
indistinguishability witnessed by an element of

\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
holds.

The principled content separating
r_{1}
from
r_{2}
is the

mechanism
: which bonds break and form, whether the
reaction proceeds through a single transition state or
through a discrete intermediate, and what that intermediate
is.
Encoding this requires replacing
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
with a category
in which morphisms carry bond-level data and intermediates
are themselves species — a
structural
extension,
not a decoration.

The forcing pair for
\mathcal{L}_{4}

For the methoxyl exchange at methyl ethylphenylphosphinate

[
222
]
,

r:\;{}^{18}\mathrm{OMe^{-}}+\mathrm{Et(Ph)P(=O)OMe}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{Et(Ph)P(=O){}^{18}OMe}+\mathrm{OMe^{-}},

two distinct generators
r_{\text{concerted}},r_{\text{stepwise}}\in\mathcal{R}
realise the same source-target
transformation:

•

r_{\text{concerted}}
: a single trigonal-bipyramidal
transition state, simultaneous P–
\mathrm{OMe}

cleavage and P–
{}^{18}\mathrm{OMe}
formation.
No intermediate.

•

r_{\text{stepwise}}
: a discrete pentacoordinate
intermediate
\mathrm{TBI}
, bracketed by addition and
elimination transition states.

Source and target are identical at the
\mathcal{L}_{0}
species level
(isotopes are below the species resolution), so
F_{\!H}
and

F_{\!S}
agree by Hess’s law and Layer 2 is automatic
(
K_{\mathrm{eq}}=1
).
Under steady-state on
\mathrm{TBI}
, both mechanisms have
rate law

\lambda=k\,x_{\mathrm{MeO^{-}}}\,x_{\mathrm{substrate}}
, and
within experimental resolution the effective rate constants
agree, so
\FP
takes the same value on the two generators

[
222
]
.
The full
\mathcal{L}_{3}
tuple

(\mathcal{L}_{0},F_{\!H},F_{\!S},F_{G}^{T},\FP)
therefore takes the same
value on
r_{\text{concerted}}
and
r_{\text{stepwise}}
, and
the swap
r_{\text{concerted}}\leftrightarrow r_{\text{stepwise}}

extends to a category automorphism of
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
preserving
all four decorations — an element of
\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
.

At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
the swap does not lift.
The asymmetry is structural:
r_{\text{concerted}}
is the

U_{4}
-image of a single double pushout (DPO) rule
p_{\text{concerted}}
in

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, whereas the stepwise mechanism is realised at

\mathcal{L}_{4}

only
as the two-step composite

p_{\text{elim}}\circ p_{\text{add}}
through the intermediate
molecular graph
\mathrm{TBI}
; there is no single DPO rule

p_{\text{stepwise}}
at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.
A lift
\widetilde{\sigma}\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))
of the swap

\sigma
would have to send the generator
p_{\text{concerted}}

to a generator of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
whose
U_{4}
-image is

r_{\text{stepwise}}
; no such generator exists.
Hence
\sigma\notin\mathrm{im}(\varphi_{4})
, where
\varphi_{4}:\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))
is the forgetful
homomorphism.
Equivalently,
\sigma
represents a non-trivial coset in the
quotient
\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))/\mathrm{im}(\varphi_{4})
, which we
call
\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4})
:

\ker\varphi_{4}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))\;\xrightarrow{\;\varphi_{4}\;}\;\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))\twoheadrightarrow\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4}),

exact as a sequence of pointed sets (the rightmost map is the
quotient by
\mathrm{im}(\varphi_{4})
, taken as a coset space;
when
\mathrm{im}(\varphi_{4})
is normal the cokernel is a
group).
The same pattern recurs across nucleophilic substitution at
heteroatoms, biological phosphoryl transfer, and a wide
class of identity reactions

[
222
,
191
]
;
the explicit verification appears in
Proposition
6.40
.

Structural rather than decorating
extension.

Earlier transitions added a functor while keeping

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
fixed — decorator extensions.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
the underlying category itself changes.
The tower is not forked: the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
–
\mathcal{L}_{3}
decorations
are retained at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
by pullback along a forgetful
functor
U_{4}:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

(Section
6.6
), with

F_{H}^{(4)}:=F_{\!H}\circ U_{4},\quad F_{S}^{(4)}:=F_{\!S}\circ U_{4},\quad F_{P}^{(4)}:=\FP\circ U_{4}

(Proposition
6.32
).
What is new is not an additional decoration but a refinement
of the morphisms: the DPO structure is intrinsic, not a
functor on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

What minimal structure resolves
the ambiguity.

(i)

Molecular graphs as objects.

Each species becomes a labelled hypergraph: vertices
carry atom type, isotope, charge, lone-pair count, and
radical count; edges carry bond order

[
15
,
83
]
.
Reaction intermediates such as
\mathrm{TBI}
become
first-class species.

(ii)

DPO derivations as morphisms.

A reaction mechanism is a span

L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R
in
\mathbf{LGraph}
,
specifying which bonds break and form

[
82
,
181
]
;
a multi-step mechanism is a sequential composite
through intermediate molecular graphs.

Together these define
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, the free SMC on DPO
spans in
\mathbf{LGraph}
(Section
6.4
).

r_{\text{concerted}}
is the
U_{4}
-image of a single DPO
generator
p_{\text{concerted}}
; the stepwise mechanism is
realised as the composite
p_{\text{elim}}\circ p_{\text{add}}

through
\mathrm{TBI}
, with no single DPO generator

p_{\text{stepwise}}
at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.
This asymmetry between
\mathcal{L}_{0}
(where
r_{\text{stepwise}}
is
postulated as a parallel generator) and
\mathcal{L}_{4}
(where it is
not realised by any single generator) is what obstructs the
lift of the swap to
\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))

(Proposition
6.40
).

Remark 6.1

(Examples beyond the forcing pair)
.

For a haloalkane
\mathrm{RX}
with nucleophile/base

\mathrm{Nu^{-}}/\mathrm{B^{-}}
, four classical mechanisms
are possible
[
210
,
23
]
:

Mech.

Rate law

Steps

Favoured by

\mathrm{S_{N}2}

k[\mathrm{RX}][\mathrm{Nu}]

One (concerted)

1
∘
substrate; strong small nucleophile;
polar aprotic solvent; low
T

\mathrm{S_{N}1}

k[\mathrm{RX}]

Two (carbocation)

3
∘
substrate; polar protic solvent;
weak nucleophile; good leaving group

\mathrm{E2}

k[\mathrm{RX}][\mathrm{B}]

One (concerted)

Any degree; strong bulky base; high
T

\mathrm{E1}

k[\mathrm{RX}]

Two (carbocation)

3
∘
substrate; polar protic solvent;
weak base; high
T

The substitution/elimination split is resolved already at

\mathcal{L}_{0}
(different products).
The bimolecular/unimolecular split within each class
(
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
vs.
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
,
\mathrm{E2}
vs.
\mathrm{E1}
) corresponds to different rate-law forms,
so it is resolved already at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
— not a

\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4})
pair, but a useful illustration of
how
\mathcal{L}_{4}
realises the distinction structurally
(carbocation as intermediate species, two DPO spans
versus one).

§6.2. Labelled molecular graphs:
the ambient adhesive category

Section
6.1
identified two generators

r_{\text{concerted}},r_{\text{stepwise}}\in\mathcal{R}
with
identical
\mathcal{L}_{3}
data, distinguished only by their identity
tags in the Petri net.
The tower up to
\mathcal{L}_{3}
accepts them as distinct only by
fiat: no categorical structure on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)=\mathbf{FreeSMC}(P)
supplies a principled reason why they
are different morphisms.
The resolution requires a new underlying category whose
morphisms carry bond-level information — atoms, bonds,
formal charges, electron counts — so that two generators
projecting to the same stoichiometric transition can
nonetheless be distinct morphisms by virtue of their
internal structure.
This section constructs that category in three steps: the
label algebra that replaces species names with molecular
graphs (§
6.2.1
), the category
\mathbf{LGraph}
of
such graphs with its monoidal and adhesive structure
(§
6.2.2
–§
6.2.3
), and
the grounded variant
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
that connects molecular
graphs back to the species set
\mathcal{S}
of the Petri net
P

(§
6.2.4
).

6.2.1. Label algebra and chemical validity

At
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
through
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
, an object is an element of

\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
: a formal sum of species names
S_{i}
, recording

how many
molecules of each type are present but
recording nothing about their internal structure.
To distinguish mechanisms with the same source and target
complexes — whether already separated at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
or not
— we need objects that encode atoms, bonds, formal
charges, and electron pairs.
The following label algebra does precisely this.

The label set below is not original: it is a categorical
reformulation of the data encoded in the
bond-electron

(BE) matrix of Dugundji and Ugi
[
81
]
,
the standard matrix representation of molecular structure in
cheminformatics and computer-aided synthesis planning since
its introduction in 1973, in continuous
use
[
14
,
78
]
, and the basis of some modern
machine-learning approaches to reaction prediction that
enforce electron conservation
[
156
]
.
What is new here is the organisation of that data into a
quintuple

(\mathrm{el},\mathrm{iso},q,\rho,\ell)
that serves as a
vertex label in a typed graph, making the connection to the
DPO rewriting framework canonical.
Chemical graph transformation with typed molecular graphs is
developed in detail in Andersen et al.
[
14
,
15
]
;
our formulation is tailored to make the validity condition
explicit and to sit naturally inside the adhesive category
framework of Section
6.2.3
.

Definition 6.2

(Atom label and bond label)
.

Let
\Lambda_{V}
denote the set of all
atom labels
,
where each atom label is a quintuple

\lambda_{v}=(\mathrm{el},\mathrm{iso},q,\rho,\ell)

consisting of:

•

\mathrm{el}\in\{\mathrm{H,C,N,O,F,P,S,Cl,Br,I,\ldots}\}
: element type;

•

\mathrm{iso}\in\mathrm{Iso}(\mathrm{el})\cup\{\ast\}
: nuclear-mass label
(e.g.
{}^{16}\mathrm{O}
,
{}^{18}\mathrm{O}
) or
the wildcard
\ast
for natural abundance / unspecified;

•

q\in\mathbb{Z}
: formal charge;

•

\rho\in\{0,1,2\}
: radical electron count
(
0
closed-shell,
1
monoradical,
2
diradical);

•

\ell\in\mathbb{N}
: lone-pair (nonbonding electron-pair)
count.

A
bond label
is an integer
b\in\{1,2,3\}

encoding bond order (single, double, triple).
Absent bonds carry the implicit value
b=0
.

Remark 6.3

(Isotope labels at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
as classical tracers)
.

The component
\mathrm{iso}
records nuclear identity

classically
: it tracks
{}^{16}\mathrm{O}
vs.
{}^{18}\mathrm{O}
,
{}^{12}\mathrm{C}
vs.
{}^{13}\mathrm{C}
, etc., as label data attached to vertices.
This is what is needed to formulate identity-substitution
forcing pairs (Section
6.1
, where the
incoming methoxide is tagged
{}^{18}\mathrm{O}
).
What is postponed to
\mathcal{L}_{7}
is not isotope bookkeeping but

isotope-dependent quantum phenomena
: nuclear quantum
statistics, tunnelling, vibrational zero-point kinetic
isotope effects.
The wildcard
\ast
is the default for atoms whose chemistry
is isotope-independent.

The lone-pair count
\ell
is part of the atom label, not a
derived quantity computed from the other components.
A universal formula

\ell=\tfrac{1}{2}(v_{\mathrm{el}}-q-\rho-\sum b)

breaks for hypervalent main-group atoms: in the central
forcing example of Section
6.1
, the
pentacoordinate phosphorus intermediate (TBI) carries an
incident bond-order sum of six, and the naive formula assigns
it
\ell=-\tfrac{1}{2}
.
Carrying
\ell
as part of the label, with chemical validity
imposed as a per-element
predicate
, accommodates
ordinary octet atoms, hypervalent main-group atoms (P, S, I),
and transition-metal centres alike.

Definition 6.4

(Chemical validity)
.

Fix a per-element
allowed-valence specification

\mathcal{V}
: a function assigning to each element type

\mathrm{el}
a set
\mathcal{V}(\mathrm{el})
of allowed
tuples
(q,\rho,\ell,\beta)
with
\beta\in\mathbb{N}
an
admissible incident bond-order sum.
For ordinary octet atoms,
\mathcal{V}(\mathrm{el})
is the
set of tuples satisfying the row-sum law

2\ell+\rho+\beta\;=\;v_{\mathrm{el}}-q,

(6)

with
v_{\mathrm{el}}
the valence-electron count of

\mathrm{el}
(
v_{\mathrm{el}}=4
for C,
5
for N,

6
for O, etc.).
For hypervalent main-group atoms (pentacoordinate or
hexacoordinate P, hypervalent S, hypervalent I),

\mathcal{V}(\mathrm{el})
extends the octet specification
to admit higher coordination numbers consistent with
three-centre four-electron bonding.
For transition-metal centres,
\mathcal{V}(\mathrm{el})

admits the coordination geometries of
d
-orbital chemistry.

An atom
v
in a typed graph is
chemically valid

if its label

(\mathrm{el},\mathrm{iso},q,\rho,\ell)
together with

\beta(v):=\sum_{e\ni v}b(e)
satisfies

(q,\rho,\ell,\beta(v))\in\mathcal{V}(\mathrm{el})
.
A typed graph is
chemically valid
if every atom is.

Remark 6.5

(Octet recovery and DPO bookkeeping)
.

For ordinary octet atoms,
\mathcal{V}(\mathrm{el})
is the
solution set of (
6
), so any of
q,\rho,\ell,\beta
is determined by the other three.
Elementary DPO generators acting on octet atoms can therefore
be specified by changes in
(q,\rho,\beta)
alone, with

\ell
updating automatically by (
6
); the
elementary generators
g_{1}
–
g_{6}
of
Section
6.3
use this convention.
At hypervalent vertices the row-sum law no longer determines

\ell
uniquely and the explicit attribute is essential.

The diagonal entry of the Dugundji–Ugi bond-electron (BE)
matrix coincides with
2\ell+\rho
at each atom, and the
row-sum law of (
6
) is precisely the BE-matrix
row-sum.
The following mathbox records the BE-matrix as the

matrix shadow
of a labelled graph, and notes what
this shadow captures and what it does not.

The BE-matrix shadow of a labelled graph

The BE-matrix.

For a molecule with
n
atoms, the
bond-electron (BE)
matrix

B\in\mathbb{N}^{n\times n}
introduced by Dugundji and
Ugi
[
81
]
is the symmetric matrix with entries:

B_{ij}\;:=\;\begin{cases}b(e_{ij})&i\neq j,\\
2\ell(i)+\rho(i)&i=j,\end{cases}

where
e_{ij}
denotes the bond between atoms
i
and
j

(
b(e_{ij})=0
if no bond exists).
The diagonal
B_{ii}
counts twice the lone-pair count plus
the radical count at atom
i
; the row-sum law

\sum_{j}B_{ij}=v_{\mathrm{el}}(i)-q(i)
for every atom

i
is the chemical validity condition of
Definition
6.4
restricted to octet atoms.

Shadow, not equivalence.

The atom label

(\mathrm{el},\mathrm{iso},q,\rho,\ell)
together with
the bond orders determines
B
unambiguously, so
B
is a
faithful matrix representation of the bond and electron-count
data of any single labelled graph.
But
B
does not record:
isotope labels (
{}^{16}\mathrm{O}
vs.
{}^{18}\mathrm{O}

have the same
B
);
atom-tracking under composition (a sequence of reactions
composes by adding successive reaction matrices, where each
reaction matrix is itself a difference
R_{\mathrm{BE}}=B^{\prime}-B
, but this addition does not record which atom in
one matrix corresponds to which atom in the next — the
correspondence is supplied categorically by the interface

K
and the match
m
);
and the categorical match data of a DPO derivation.
We therefore call
B
the
BE-matrix shadow
of the
labelled graph: a useful local matrix representation, but
strictly less than the full DPO content.

What the label set distinguishes.

Each mechanistic distinction below is expressed as a condition
on
(\mathrm{el},\mathrm{iso},q,\rho,\ell)
or on the
graph topology:

•

Concerted vs. stepwise at heteroatom centres

(the
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
forcing pair,
Section
6.1
): the stepwise derivation
passes through a discrete intermediate graph whose central
vertex carries a coordination number not realised in any
concerted derivation projecting to the same
\mathcal{L}_{3}

observables (
e.g.
the pentacoordinate TBI in
identity substitution at phosphorus).
Visible via the vertex degree in the intermediate graph.

•

Charged intermediates
(already distinguished at

\mathcal{L}_{3}
for
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
/
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
and

\mathrm{E1}
/
\mathrm{E2}
, see
Remark
6.1
): the stepwise derivation
passes through a graph with a carbocation vertex
(
q=+1
,
\ell(v)=0
); the concerted derivation has

q=0
throughout. Visible via the
q
label.

•

Radical vs. ionic mechanisms
: a radical
intermediate carries
\rho(v)\geq 1
on at least one
atom (monoradicals at one site, diradicals at one site or
distributed across two sites); an ionic intermediate has

\rho(v)=0
everywhere.
Visible via the
\rho
label.

•

Pericyclic vs. ionic reactions
: a pericyclic
DPO rule has a reaction centre with cyclic graph topology
(the atoms forming and breaking bonds lie on a cycle in

L
); an ionic reaction has acyclic reaction-centre
topology. Visible via the topology of
L
.

6.2.2. The category
\mathbf{LGraph}

The label algebra of the preceding section gives data for
individual atoms and bonds.
To speak categorically about reactions, we need molecular graphs
to be
objects
and structure-preserving maps between them
to be
morphisms
.
The following definition assembles these ingredients into a
symmetric monoidal category
\mathbf{LGraph}
, which will serve as the
ambient category for the DPO rules that generate
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.

Originality and comparison to existing work.

The use of typed molecular graphs in chemical graph transformation
goes back to Ehrig et al.
[
83
]

and Andersen et al.
[
15
]
.
Those works use a general typing morphism to a type graph,
without committing to a specific label algebra; our specialisation
to the quintuple
(\mathrm{el},\mathrm{iso},q,\rho,\ell)

of Definition
6.2
is what makes
\mathbf{LGraph}
a
suitable ambient category for mechanistic organic chemistry.
The architectural choice that distinguishes our development
is to keep
\mathbf{LGraph}
as the
ambient
typed-graph
category (adhesive in the sense of
Lack–Sobociński
[
181
]
,
Proposition
6.10
), with chemical
validity (Definition
6.4
) imposed as a

predicate
on objects rather than as a defining feature
of category membership.
This separation matters because pushouts of chemically valid
graphs in
\mathbf{LGraph}
may produce chemically invalid graphs:
adhesivity holds for the ambient typed-graph category, while
validity is enforced as an admissibility condition on rule
patterns and their products
(Remark
6.11
below).

Definition 6.6

(Labelled typed graph)
.

A
labelled typed graph
is a tuple

G=(V,E,\lambda_{V},\lambda_{E})
where:

•

V
is a finite set of
vertices
(atoms).

•

E\subseteq\bigl\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V,\,u\neq v\bigr\}

is a set of
edges
(bonds), i.e. a set of
unordered pairs of distinct vertices.

•

\lambda_{V}:V\to\Lambda_{V}
is the
atom-label
function
, assigning to each vertex an atom label

(\mathrm{el},\mathrm{iso},q,\rho,\ell)\in\Lambda_{V}

in the sense of Definition
6.2
.

•

\lambda_{E}:E\to\{1,2,3\}
is the

bond-order function
.

No chemical-validity constraint is imposed on
G
at the
level of object membership; chemical validity
(Definition
6.4
) is a predicate on objects
of
\mathbf{LGraph}
used as an admissibility condition on rule
patterns (Remark
6.11
).

A chemically valid graph (Definition
6.4
)
determines a BE-matrix unambiguously.
The reverse direction is partial: a BE-matrix together with
element types and isotope labels at each vertex, plus either
closed-shell assumption (
\rho\equiv 0
) or independent
specification of
\rho
at each vertex, recovers the labelled
graph; without that supplementary data, the diagonal entries

B_{ii}=2\ell+\rho
do not uniquely split into

(\ell,\rho)
(for example
B_{ii}=2
admits both

(\ell,\rho)=(1,0)
and
(0,2)
).
In general
\mathbf{LGraph}
admits non-valid labelled graphs as well,
which arise when one considers pushouts of valid graphs.
To make reactions into morphisms, we now equip the labelled
graphs with the structure of a category.

Definition 6.7

(The category
\mathbf{LGraph}
)
.

The category
\mathbf{LGraph}
has:

•

Objects
: labelled typed graphs
(Definition
6.6
);

•

Morphisms
: label-preserving graph

monomorphisms
: injective maps

f:V_{G}\hookrightarrow V_{H}

such that
\lambda_{V}^{H}(f(v))=\lambda_{V}^{G}(v)

for all
v\in V_{G}
, and

\lambda_{E}^{H}(\{f(u),f(v)\})=\lambda_{E}^{G}(\{u,v\})

for all edges
\{u,v\}\in E_{G}
;

•

Composition
: composition of injections;

•

Identity
: the identity injection
\mathrm{id}_{G}
.

The
monoidal product
is the disjoint union

G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}
(disjoint vertex and edge sets, labels
inherited), with unit the empty graph
\emptyset
.
We work in a strictified skeleton in which disjoint copies
are fixed by a chosen tagging convention, so that

\sqcup
is strictly associative and unital.

Proposition 6.8

(
\mathbf{LGraph}
is a well-defined strict symmetric
monoidal category)
.

\mathbf{LGraph}
with the structure of Definition
6.7

is a strict symmetric monoidal category.

Proof.

Category.

Composition of label-preserving monomorphisms is again a
label-preserving monomorphism (injectivity and label preservation
are both stable under composition).
The identity injection
\mathrm{id}_{G}
is label-preserving by definition,
and serves as the two-sided identity.
Associativity of composition is inherited from function composition.

Strict monoidal.

By the strictification convention adopted in
Definition
6.7
, disjoint copies are fixed by a
chosen tagging, so
\sqcup
is strictly associative
(
(G_{1}\sqcup G_{2})\sqcup G_{3}=G_{1}\sqcup(G_{2}\sqcup G_{3})

as objects) and strictly unital (
G\sqcup\emptyset=G
).
The symmetry isomorphism

G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}\cong G_{2}\sqcup G_{1}
is the swap of tagged
copies, natural in
G_{1}
and
G_{2}
.
∎

Remark 6.9

(Restriction to monomorphisms)
.

Working with label-preserving monomorphisms rather than arbitrary
label-preserving graph homomorphisms is standard in chemical graph
transformation
[
15
]
: it ensures
that atoms are not identified and bond structures are faithfully
embedded.
Concretely, a non-injective map could collapse two distinct atoms
of the same element type into one, destroying structural
information.
All results cited from the DPO literature hold for injective
matches
[
83
]
.

6.2.3. Adhesivity of
\mathbf{LGraph}

The category
\mathbf{LGraph}
carries more than just a monoidal
structure: it is
adhesive
in the sense of Lack and
Sobociński
[
181
]
, a property that
makes DPO rewriting internally consistent.

Adhesive categories.

A category
\mathcal{C}
is
adhesive

[
181
]
if:
(i) it has pushouts along monomorphisms;
(ii) monomorphisms are stable under pushout (the pushout of a
monomorphism is again a monomorphism); and
(iii) pushout squares along monomorphisms satisfy the

van Kampen condition
: they are also pullbacks in a
suitable double-categorical sense.
Condition (iii), the van Kampen condition, is what makes DPO
rewriting well-behaved: combined with conditions (i) and (ii),
it guarantees that pushout complements are unique up to
isomorphism (so the gluing context
D
in a DPO step is
well-defined; see Remark
6.12
on
why
D
is not a chemical intermediate) and that independent
rewriting steps can be applied in either order with the same
result (Local Church–Rosser).
Without adhesivity, neither of these properties is guaranteed
and DPO rewriting in
\mathbf{LGraph}
would be ill-defined.

Proposition 6.10

(
\mathbf{LGraph}
is adhesive)
.

The category
\mathbf{LGraph}
with label-preserving monomorphisms
is adhesive in the sense of
Lack and Sobociński.

Proof.

The category
\mathbf{Graph}
of (directed or undirected)
graphs can be presented as a presheaf topos: it is the
functor category
[\mathbf{G},\mathbf{Set}]
where

\mathbf{G}
is the graph schema
s,t:E\rightrightarrows V

(two objects and two parallel morphisms, encoding source and
target of edges).
Every presheaf topos is adhesive

[
181
, Corollary 3.6]
, so
\mathbf{Graph}

is adhesive.

Now identify
\mathbf{LGraph}
with the slice category

\mathbf{Graph}/TG_{\Lambda}
, where
TG_{\Lambda}
is the

type graph
: the graph whose vertices are the atom labels

\Lambda_{V}
and whose edges carry all possible bond labels

\{1,2,3\}
between every pair of label vertices.
A labelled typed graph
G
in the sense of
Definition
6.6
is precisely a graph homomorphism

G\to TG_{\Lambda}
(the typing morphism assigns each atom its
label and each bond its order);
\mathbf{LGraph}\cong\mathbf{Graph}/TG_{\Lambda}
as categories.
This identification is standard in typed graph transformation;
see Ehrig et al.
[
83
, Chapter 2]
.

By Lack–Sobociński
[
181
, Proposition 3.5(ii)]
,
if
\mathcal{C}
is adhesive then so is
\mathcal{C}/X
for
every object
X
.
Since
\mathbf{Graph}
is adhesive and

\mathbf{LGraph}\cong\mathbf{Graph}/TG_{\Lambda}
,
it follows that
\mathbf{LGraph}
is adhesive.
∎

The three consequences of adhesivity for mechanism-level
rewriting deserve explicit statement.
Adhesivity is what makes DPO derivations well-defined: without
unique pushout complements, the gluing context in a DPO step
would not be well-defined; without Local Church–Rosser, the
order of independent steps would matter and sequential
composition would be ambiguous.
These are not abstract concerns — they correspond to
concrete questions about mechanism: “Is the carbocation
produced by ionisation in
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
uniquely determined
by the rule and the substrate?” (yes, by uniqueness of
gluing contexts and by the fact that the carbocation is a
distinct molecular graph between two derivations); “Does
it matter whether we first abstract the proton or first
ionise the leaving group in an E1 mechanism?”
(Local Church–Rosser says no, when the steps are
independent).

What adhesivity gives for chemistry

Proposition
6.10
guarantees
three essential properties for DPO rewriting of labelled
typed graphs:

(i)

Unique gluing contexts
: if a DPO rule
applies to a labelled graph, the gluing context
D

(the host with the reaction-centre bonds removed, prior
to gluing of
R
) is unique up to isomorphism
(Lemma 4.5 of
[
181
]
).

D
is a categorical artefact of a single rule
application, not, in general, a chemically isolable
intermediate (Remark
6.12
).

(ii)

Local Church–Rosser
: two
independent

reaction steps (steps whose reaction centres share no atoms)
applied to the same molecule can be sequenced in either
order, reaching the same product
(Theorem 7.7 of
[
181
]
).
This is the mechanism-level analogue of the fact that
parallel reactions in distinct parts of a molecule do not
interfere.

(iii)

Concurrency
: a sequence of independent DPO
steps can be represented by a single composite rule
(Theorem 7.11 of
[
181
]
).
This is a semantic statement about independent steps,
not the basis of the free SMC structure of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
,
which is by construction (Section
6.4
).

Together, these guarantee that mechanism-level rewriting in

\mathbf{LGraph}
is well-defined and compositional — exactly what
is needed for
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
to be a category.

Remark 6.11

(Chemical validity is admissibility, not membership)
.

Pushouts of chemically valid graphs in
\mathbf{LGraph}
may produce
chemically invalid graphs: a pushout that introduces a bond
at an atom already saturated produces a graph whose row-sum
law fails at that atom.
The full subcollection

\mathbf{LGraph}^{\mathrm{ch}}\subset\mathbf{LGraph}
of chemically valid
graphs (Definition
6.4
) is therefore not closed
under pushouts in
\mathbf{LGraph}
and is not adhesive in its own
right.
The architectural choice taken in this chapter is to perform
all DPO constructions in the ambient adhesive category

\mathbf{LGraph}
and to require chemical validity as a separate

admissibility
condition: a chemical DPO rule
(Section
6.3
) is a span
L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R
in
\mathbf{LGraph}
with
L
and
R
chemically valid,
and a chemically admissible match
m:L\hookrightarrow G

into a valid host
G
requires the resulting product graph
H

to be chemically valid.
The validity check is local — the row-sum law (or its
hypervalent extension) at every atom of the product — and is
the content of Layer 2 at
\mathcal{L}_{4}

(Section
6.7
).

Remark 6.12

(The gluing context
D
is not a chemical
intermediate)
.

The pushout complement
D
supplied by adhesivity is the host
graph
G
with the reaction-centre bonds of
L\setminus l(K)

deleted, prior to gluing of
R
.

D
is a categorical construction internal to a single DPO
step and is in general
not
a chemically isolable
intermediate.
A chemical intermediate, when present, is a complete
molecular graph appearing as the
target
of one DPO
derivation and the
source
of the next: the
carbocation in
\mathrm{S_{N}1}

(Section
6.9
), the trigonal-bipyramidal
phosphorus intermediate in stepwise identity substitution
(Section
6.8
).
The categorical role of
D
is to mediate the two pushouts
of a single rule application; its chemical interpretation,
when it has one, is a transient gluing context, not a
species of the network.

6.2.4. The grounded category

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}

The category
\mathbf{LGraph}
treats labelled typed graphs as abstract
combinatorial objects with no reference to the Petri net
P
.
But
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
must sit in the tower above
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
: its
host objects must be compatible with the stoichiometric
generator set of
P
, so that the forgetful functor

U_{4}:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
(Section
6.6
) is
well-defined.
The grounded category
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
enforces this compatibility:
it equips every host graph with an assignment of its
connected components to species names in
\mathcal{S}
, binding the
abstract graph structure to the chemical species of the
network.

Definition 6.13

(Grounded labelled graph category
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
)
.

Given a Petri net
P
with species set
\mathcal{S}
, the

grounded
category
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
has:

•

Objects
: pairs
(G,\spec)
where

G\in\mathbf{LGraph}
and

\spec:\pi_{0}(G)\to\mathcal{S}
assigns each connected component
of
G
to a species in
\mathcal{S}
.

•

Morphisms
: label-preserving monomorphisms

f:G\hookrightarrow H
compatible with

\spec
(each component of
G
maps into the
component of
H
bearing the same species label).

The monoidal product is grounded disjoint union;
the unit is the empty graph with vacuous
\spec
.
The category
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
is adhesive; the proof reduces to
adhesivity of
\mathbf{LGraph}
via a comma-category argument analogous
to the slice argument for
\mathbf{LGraph}
itself (Ehrig et
al.
[
83
]
).

The BE-matrix shadow of a DPO rule

A DPO rule
(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)
in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}

admits a
BE-matrix shadow
: a pair
(B,B^{\prime})
of
BE-matrices
[
81
]
related by the reaction
matrix
R_{\mathrm{BE}}=B^{\prime}-B

[
14
,
16
]
.
The reactant graph
L
supplies
B
(off-diagonal entries =
bond orders, diagonal entries =
2\ell(v)+\rho(v)
); the
product graph
R
supplies
B^{\prime}
; the context
K
identifies
the rows and columns on which
R_{\mathrm{BE}}
vanishes.

The shadow is faithful for net electron rearrangement but
strictly weaker than the DPO rule.
What it does not record:
isotope labels (
{}^{16}\mathrm{O}
and
{}^{18}\mathrm{O}

share the same matrix);
atom-tracking under composition (BE matrices add, but the
addition does not say which atom in one matrix corresponds to
which atom in the next — supplied categorically by
K
and
the match
m
);
the species-grounding
\spec
;
and the categorical match data of a derivation.
The DPO framework on
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
is therefore strictly richer
than the matrix shadow.

With
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
in hand, the three ingredients needed for

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
are in place: host graphs are
\mathcal{S}
-typed
labelled graphs in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, the generating morphisms are

admissible chemical DPO rules

(chemically valid spans, Section
6.3
), and the
ambient adhesive structure of
\mathbf{LGraph}
guarantees that DPO
derivations are well-defined.
The free strict SMC structure of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is supplied by
the universal property of the free SMC on the directed
signature of admissible DPO derivations
(Section
6.4
).

§6.3. DPO rules and derivations in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}

Section
6.2
built the ambient category
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
:
a strict symmetric monoidal adhesive category whose objects are

\mathcal{S}
-typed labelled graphs and whose morphisms are
label-preserving monomorphisms.
Chemical validity (Definition
6.4
) is enforced
as an admissibility condition on rule patterns and matches,
not as a defining feature of object membership
(Remark
6.11
).
The morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
will be sequences of
DPO
derivations
in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
— the precise way of saying
“bonds break and form according to a specified rule.”
A DPO (
double pushout
) derivation specifies a reaction
by two pushout squares in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, encoding the following
chemical information:

•

L
(left graph) — the
reactant pattern
: the
subgraph that must be present in the host molecule for the
rule to fire; contains the reaction-centre atoms with their
pre-reaction labels and the bonds to be broken.

•

K
(context graph) — the
unchanged frame
:
atoms and bonds that persist through the reaction, embedded
in both
L
and
R
by label-preserving monomorphisms.

•

R
(right graph) — the
product pattern
: the
subgraph produced by the reaction; contains the reaction-centre
atoms with their post-reaction labels and the bonds formed.

•

G
(host graph) — the
substrate molecule
: the
full molecular graph to which the rule is applied.

•

D
(derived context) — the
gluing context
:

G
with the atoms and bonds of
m(L\setminus l(K))

removed; the unique pushout complement guaranteed by the
adhesivity of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
.

D
is a categorical artefact of a single rule application
and is not, in general, a chemically isolable intermediate
(Remark
6.12
).

•

H
(host graph after reaction) — the
product
molecule
: obtained by gluing
R
onto
D
via the second
pushout.

Together the two pushouts implement the chemical intuition that
a reaction (i) removes the bonds and relabels the atoms of the
reaction centre, and (ii) installs the new bonds and relabelled
atoms, leaving everything outside the reaction centre unchanged.
This is the categorical replacement for the stoichiometric
transition used as a morphism at
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
: instead of merely
recording which species disappear and appear, a DPO derivation
records
exactly which bonds break and form, in what
sequence, and on which atoms
.
The free SMC on such derivations is
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
,
constructed in Section
6.4
.

6.3.1. DPO rules

Definition 6.14

(Chemical DPO rule)
.

A
chemical DPO rule
for
P
-species is a pair

p=(s,\gamma)
consisting of:

•

a
span

s=(L\xleftarrow{\;l\;}K\xrightarrow{\;r\;}R)

in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, where both
l:K\hookrightarrow L
and

r:K\hookrightarrow R
are label-preserving monomorphisms;

•

a
generator label

\gamma(p)\in P
identifying which Petri-net reaction
of
P
this rule realises at the stoichiometric level.

The span graphs carry their usual interpretation:

•

K
: the
context
— atoms and bonds
unchanged by the reaction.

•

L\setminus l(K)
: atoms or bonds
consumed

(broken or label-changed at the reaction centre).

•

R\setminus r(K)
: atoms or bonds
produced

(formed or label-changed at the reaction centre).

A rule is
valence-conserving
if every atom in
K

satisfies the same valence constraint in
L
and in
R
,
and
stoichiometrically consistent
if for every
species
S\in\mathcal{S}
, the number of connected components of

R
labelled
S
minus that of
L
labelled
S
equals the
stoichiometric change
\nu(\mathbf{v})_{S}-\nu(\mathbf{u})_{S}

of the Petri-net generator
\gamma(p):\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{v}
.
We restrict to valence-conserving, stoichiometrically
consistent rules throughout.

Two distinct rules may share the same span but carry
different generator labels (when
P
has parallel generators
with identical stoichiometry); two distinct rules may also
share the same generator label but carry different spans
(when a single Petri-net reaction admits multiple
mechanistic realisations).
The Petri net
P
is assumed rich enough to contain a
generator for every named chemical transformation in the
reaction network under study, whether or not that
transformation is mechanistically elementary.

Remark 6.15

(Atoms with changing labels in the DPO span)
.

In our label set

\Lambda_{V}=\{(\mathrm{el},\mathrm{iso},q,\rho,\ell)\}

(Definition
6.2
), a reaction that changes any
component of an atom’s label cannot place that atom in
K
:
the monomorphisms
l
and
r
are label-preserving, so

K
can only contain atoms whose labels are identical in

L
and in
R
.
An atom
v
with label
\lambda_{v}^{L}\neq\lambda_{v}^{R}
must
therefore appear in
L\setminus l(K)
(as a “consumed”
vertex with its pre-reaction label) and separately in

R\setminus r(K)
(as a “produced” vertex with its
post-reaction label).
Chemically, this means the atom is formally deleted and
recreated; its physical identity is preserved by the
match morphism
m:L\hookrightarrow G
, which tracks
which vertex in the host graph
G
corresponds to which
vertex in
L
.
This non-attributed encoding is equivalent to attributed
DPO rewriting
[
83
]
, where
vertex attributes (
q
,
\rho
,
\ell
) may change on
persistent vertices via attribute equations on
K
; the
non-attributed formulation chosen here keeps
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}

as a standard adhesive category without additional
attribute-algebra structure.
In particular, isotope labels rarely change (they enter
the formalism as classical tracers,
Remark
6.3
), and for octet atoms
\ell

is determined by
(q,\rho,\beta)
via the row-sum law
(
6
), so a generator that specifies changes
in
(q,\rho,\beta)
also fixes the change in
\ell
.

6.3.2. DPO derivations and the dangling condition

A DPO
rule
is an abstract pattern.
A DPO
derivation
is the application of a rule to a
specific host molecule
G
: it specifies where the rule fires
(the
match
) and produces the concrete product molecule

H
.
This is the level at which a mechanism becomes an actual
chemical transformation on a named substrate.

Definition 6.16

(DPO derivation)
.

Let
p=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)
be a DPO rule and

G\in\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
a host graph.
A
match
is a monomorphism
m:L\hookrightarrow G

identifying where the reactant pattern occurs in
G
.

A
DPO derivation

G\Rightarrow_{p,m}H
consists of
a commutative diagram

where both squares are pushouts in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
.
The left pushout computes
D
(the pushout complement):

G
with the atoms and bonds of
m(L\setminus l(K))

deleted.
The right pushout computes
H
:
D
with the product
pattern
R
glued in via the shared context
K
.

For a DPO derivation to exist, the gluing context
D

must be well-defined.
By the adhesive structure of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}

(Proposition
6.10
), the pushout
complement exists and is unique precisely when no atoms
outside the reaction centre are left with “half-broken” bonds
— the
dangling condition
.
This is not a restriction on chemistry but a consistency
requirement: any correctly specified mechanism must close off
all bond changes at the reaction centre before the rule fires.

Proposition 6.17

(Gluing / dangling condition)
.

Let
p=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)
be a DPO rule
and
m:L\hookrightarrow G
a match.
The pushout complement
D
in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
exists and is unique
if and only if the
dangling condition
holds:
no atom in
G\setminus m(L)
is bonded to an atom in

m(L\setminus l(K))
.

Proof.

For injective matches in adhesive categories, the pushout
complement
D
exists if and only if the dangling condition
holds (the gluing condition of
[
181
, Def. 7.2]
,
which in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
unpacks to the dangling condition

[
83
]
); when it exists, it is
unique up to isomorphism by

[
181
, Lem. 4.5]
.
∎

The dangling condition in chemistry

The dangling condition says: a reaction-centre atom or bond
cannot be deleted if an atom
outside
the reaction
centre is still attached to it.
Concretely, consider an SN2 rule for the substitution

\mathrm{CH_{3}Br}+\mathrm{OH^{-}}\to\mathrm{CH_{3}OH}+\mathrm{Br^{-}}
: the rule deletes the C–Br bond, repurposes
a lone pair on OH
-
as the new bonding pair, and creates
the C–O bond.
The rule’s
L
must include every atom that, in the host

G
, is bonded to a reaction-centre atom; for instance, the
three hydrogens on C must be present in
L
(and hence in

K
, as unchanged context), since otherwise the carbon’s
relabelling between
L
and
R
would leave them with bonds
into a deleted vertex.
In practice, reaction mechanisms are formulated so that the
reaction centre
L
is self-contained: all atoms incident to
the reaction-centre atoms are included in
L
, making the
dangling condition automatically satisfied for any well-posed
rule.

6.3.3. Elementary generators

A DPO rule in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
can describe any bond rearrangement,
however complex.
For the free SMC structure of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)

(Definition
6.22
), we need a
generating set
: a
minimal collection of rules from which every organic reaction
mechanism can be built by sequential composition
(Definition
6.16
) and monoidal product
(parallel juxtaposition on disjoint molecular graphs).

The decomposition of any reaction mechanism into elementary
electron-pair or radical movements is the foundation of the
mechanistic approach to organic chemistry and has been
formalised independently by Herges
[
138
]

(topological classification), Dugundji and Ugi
[
81
]

(BE-matrix reaction types), and Andersen et
al.
[
14
]
(algorithmic rule
composition).
The six generators below are the categorical counterpart of
this decomposition, expressed as explicit DPO spans in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
.
In the tower, they are the
generators of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
in
the sense of Proposition
6.25
: any assignment
of these six spans to morphisms of a strict SMC
\mathcal{C}

extends uniquely to a functor
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{C}
.

Definition 6.18

(Elementary DPO generators for organic chemistry)
.

For brevity we write atom labels in the abbreviated form

\lambda_{v}=(\mathrm{el}_{v},q_{v},\rho_{v})
throughout the
generators below.
This stands for the full quintuple

(\mathrm{el}_{v},\ast,q_{v},\rho_{v},\ell_{v})
of
Definition
6.2
with isotope
\mathrm{iso}=\ast

(natural abundance) suppressed and lone-pair count
\ell_{v}

fixed by the octet row-sum law (
6
) from

(q_{v},\rho_{v},\beta_{v})
at every reaction-centre atom.
Isotope labels appear explicitly only in identity-tracer
mechanisms (Section
6.1
); hypervalent
atoms (where
\ell
is not octet-determined) appear only in
the stepwise mechanisms of
Section
6.8
.
In each span below,
K
contains the atoms and bonds whose
labels are
unchanged
by the reaction; atoms with
changing labels appear in
L\setminus l(K)
and

R\setminus r(K)
per Remark
6.15
.

g_{1}
:

Heterolytic bond formation
(lone pair

\to
bond).
A nucleophilic atom
\mathrm{Nu}
donates a lone pair
to form a new single bond to an electrophilic atom

\mathrm{E}
.
Since both atoms change formal charge, neither can sit
in
K
(Remark
6.15
); the physical
identity of each atom across the rule is supplied by
the match
m
.

•

K
: remaining molecular context (atoms and
bonds outside the reaction centre).

•

L\setminus l(K)
: two isolated vertices

\{\mathrm{Nu}:(\mathrm{el}_{\mathrm{Nu}},q,0),\;\mathrm{E}:(\mathrm{el}_{\mathrm{E}},q^{\prime},0)\}
,
no edge between them.

•

R\setminus r(K)
: two vertices

\{\mathrm{Nu}:(\mathrm{el}_{\mathrm{Nu}},q+1,0),\;\mathrm{E}:(\mathrm{el}_{\mathrm{E}},q^{\prime}-1,0)\}

connected by a new edge
b=1
.

Effect:
q(\mathrm{Nu})
increases by 1 (Nu loses
negative charge),
q(\mathrm{E})
decreases by 1
(E gains electron density); the derived lone-pair
counts update via Definition
6.4
,
giving
\Delta\ell(\mathrm{Nu})=-1

(one lone pair used to form the bond) and

\Delta\ell(\mathrm{E})=0
.

g_{2}
:

Heterolytic bond cleavage
(bond
\to
lone
pair).
A bond breaks heterolytically; both electrons go to the
more electronegative atom
\mathrm{X}
.

•

K
: remaining context.

•

L\setminus l(K)
: two vertices

\{C:(\mathrm{el}_{C},q,0),\;X:(\mathrm{el}_{X},q^{\prime},0)\}

connected by edge
b=1
.

•

R\setminus r(K)
: two isolated vertices

\{C:(\mathrm{el}_{C},q+1,0),\;X:(\mathrm{el}_{X},q^{\prime}-1,0)\}
,
no edge.

Effect:
q(C)
increases by 1 (C becomes more positive),

q(X)
decreases by 1 (X gains lone pair),
\ell(X)

increases by 1.
This is the formal inverse of
g_{1}
at the bond-rearrangement
level: applying
g_{1}
then
g_{2}
to the same atom pair returns
the molecular graph to its initial state, although the
composite
g_{2}\circ g_{1}
is a non-identity morphism in

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
that records the round-trip mechanism.

g_{3}
:

Concerted electron-pair shift through a
3-atom subgraph
(charge or radical migration).
A coupled bond-order and label shift in a 3-atom

A\!=\!B\!-\!C
subgraph: one bond order decreases, the
other increases, and the (q,
\rho
) labels of the
terminal atoms
A
and
C
change so that valence is
preserved at each.
The canonical chemistry is carbocation migration
(
\Delta q_{A}=+1
,
\Delta q_{C}=-1
, the cation
moving
C\to A
through the
\pi
-system); analogous
rules cover anion migration and radical migration.
Precondition:
b(AB)\in\{2,3\}
and

b(BC)\in\{1,2\}
in
L
, so post-shift bond orders
remain in
\{1,2,3\}
.

•

K
: remaining context, with atom
B
in
K

(unchanged label).

•

L\setminus l(K)
: atoms

\{A:(\mathrm{el}_{A},q_{A},0),\;C:(\mathrm{el}_{C},q_{A}+1,0)\}

(cation on
C
); edges
\{A\!=\!B,\,B\!-\!C\}

(bond orders
b_{1}\in\{2,3\}
on
AB
and

b_{2}\in\{1,2\}
on
BC
).

•

R\setminus r(K)
: atoms

\{A:(\mathrm{el}_{A},q_{A}+1,0),\;C:(\mathrm{el}_{C},q_{A},0)\}

(cation on
A
); edges
\{A\!-\!B,\,B\!=\!C\}

(bond orders
b_{1}-1
on
AB
and
b_{2}+1
on
BC
).

Effect: the cation migrates from
C
to
A
along the
conjugated
\pi
-system; the row-sum law
(
6
) balances the bond-order change against
the charge change at each terminal.
Atoms
A
and
C
are in
L\setminus l(K)
/

R\setminus r(K)
because their labels change; only

B
resides in
K
.

g_{4}
:

Homolytic bond formation
(two radicals
\to

bond).
Two radical atoms combine to form a new single bond.

•

K
: remaining context.

•

L\setminus l(K)
: two isolated vertices

\{A:(\mathrm{el}_{A},q_{A},1),\;B:(\mathrm{el}_{B},q_{B},1)\}

(each monoradical,
\rho=1
), no edge.

•

R\setminus r(K)
: two vertices

\{A:(\mathrm{el}_{A},q_{A},0),\;B:(\mathrm{el}_{B},q_{B},0)\}

connected by edge
b=1
.

Effect:
\rho
decreases from 1 to 0 on both atoms
(radical electrons pair into the new bond),

\ell
is unchanged on each.
This is the radical counterpart of
g_{1}
.

g_{5}
:

Homolytic bond cleavage
(bond
\to
two radicals).
A bond breaks homolytically; each fragment retains one electron.

•

K
: remaining context.

•

L\setminus l(K)
: two vertices

\{A:(\mathrm{el}_{A},q_{A},0),\;B:(\mathrm{el}_{B},q_{B},0)\}

connected by edge
b=1
.

•

R\setminus r(K)
: two isolated vertices

\{A:(\mathrm{el}_{A},q_{A},1),\;B:(\mathrm{el}_{B},q_{B},1)\}
, no edge.

Effect:
\rho
increases from 0 to 1 on both atoms; the
shared bonding pair becomes two unpaired electrons, one on each fragment.

g_{5}
reverses the bond-rearrangement of
g_{4}
:
applying
g_{4}
then
g_{5}
to the same atom pair returns the
molecular graph to its initial state, although the composite
is a non-identity morphism in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.

g_{6}
:

Single-electron transfer
(SET).
One electron moves from donor
\mathrm{Dn}
to acceptor

\mathrm{An}
without bond formation or cleavage.

•

K
: remaining context; no bond
\mathrm{Dn}
–
\mathrm{An}

in
L
or
R
.

•

L\setminus l(K)
: two isolated vertices

\{\mathrm{Dn}:(\mathrm{el}_{\mathrm{Dn}},q_{\mathrm{Dn}},1),\;\mathrm{An}:(\mathrm{el}_{\mathrm{An}},q_{\mathrm{An}},0)\}

(
\mathrm{Dn}
is a monoradical,
\mathrm{An}
is
closed-shell).

•

R\setminus r(K)
: two isolated vertices

\{\mathrm{Dn}:(\mathrm{el}_{\mathrm{Dn}},q_{\mathrm{Dn}}+1,0),\;\mathrm{An}:(\mathrm{el}_{\mathrm{An}},q_{\mathrm{An}}-1,1)\}

(
\mathrm{Dn}
loses the radical electron and gains a
positive charge;
\mathrm{An}
becomes a radical anion).

Effect: charge and radical count transfer simultaneously.
No new bond is formed;
g_{6}
differs from
g_{1}
in that

g_{1}
moves two electrons (a lone pair) while
g_{6}

moves one (a radical).

Remark 6.19

(Status of the generating set)
.

Definition
6.18
proposes six generators as a

working basis
for all organic reaction mechanisms.
The claim that these six generators suffice to generate every
organic reaction mechanism by sequential composition and
monoidal product is supported by the following evidence:

•

Herges
[
138
]
partitions all concerted
organic reactions into three topological types
(linear, pericyclic, coarctate); the linear type aligns
with the topological shape of patterns built from

g_{1}
–
g_{3}
, while pericyclic and coarctate types
require additional primitive generators
(§
6.3.4
).

•

Dugundji and Ugi
[
81
]
identify

\sim
30 reaction-matrix types;
\sim
10 types cover

\sim
93% of all single-step transformations,
consistent with a small generating set.

•

Andersen et al.
[
14
]

develop the algorithmic machinery for rule composition in
typed-graph DPO and apply it to ionic organic chemistry,
where rules of the
g_{1}
–
g_{3}
shape suffice.
The radical and SET generators
g_{4}
–
g_{6}
are added here
to cover homolytic and single-electron-transfer chemistry,
which are needed for the radical sub-network of the
Briggs–Rauscher reaction (Section
6.9
)
and for organic photochemistry more broadly.

A formal proof that Definition
6.18
is both
minimal and complete is not available in the published
literature.
The tower provides a framework for investigating this question:
completeness would follow from showing that the automorphism
exact sequence
1\to\ker\varphi_{4}\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))\xrightarrow{\varphi_{4}}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3}(P))\to\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4})\to 1
is exhausted by the bond-change patterns generated by

g_{1}
–
g_{6}
— i.e., that every element of
\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4})

is the image of a composition of these generators.
Minimality would require showing that no proper subset of

\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{6}\}
generates
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
as a free SMC.
Both statements are conjectured and constitute an original
research direction opened by the categorical framework of
this chapter.
We proceed with the six generators as a well-motivated and
empirically supported working basis.

6.3.4. Pericyclic rules: cyclic reaction-centre topology

The six generators of Definition
6.18
cover

stepwise
bond rearrangements: each generator acts on
two atoms (or three, in the case of
g_{3}
), and larger
mechanisms are built by sequential composition and monoidal
product.
But a significant class of organic reactions is

concerted
across a closed ring of atoms — pericyclic
reactions — and cannot be decomposed into a sequential
chain of two-atom steps without introducing intermediate
molecular graphs that the mechanism provably lacks.
These reactions require DPO rules of a different shape.

Definition 6.20

(Pericyclic DPO rule)
.

A
pericyclic DPO rule
is a chemical DPO rule

p=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)

in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
for which the reaction centre

L\setminus l(K)
(together with its incident atoms in

K
) forms a cycle in the underlying graph of
L
,
with the corresponding cycle in
R
obtained by a
simultaneous reassignment of bond orders around the ring.
No vertex labels change; all bond-order changes occur
within the cycle and are applied concurrently as a single
rule.

Remark 6.21

(Pericyclic rules are primitives)
.

A pericyclic rule is
not
a composite of

g_{1}
–
g_{6}
.
Attempting to decompose, say, a Diels–Alder step into
sequential applications of
g_{1}
and
g_{3}
would force
the derivation to pass through intermediate molecular
graphs (the host after one
g_{1}
, before the next
g_{3}
,
etc.) that carry formal charges or unpaired electrons not
present in either the reactant or the product, and that the
concerted mechanism does not produce.
A single pericyclic DPO step has the entire ring of bond-order
changes occurring in one rule application, with no
intervening discrete molecular graphs at all.
The correct treatment within our framework is to admit
pericyclic rules as
additional primitive generators
,
one for each pattern of cyclic bond-order reassignment.
These primitives are characterised by Herges’ topological
classification
[
138
]
:
linear
(no cycle
in the reaction centre),
pericyclic
(a single
cycle), or
coarctate
(two cycles sharing an atom).
The generator basis for
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is therefore

\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{6}\}\cup\{\text{pericyclic primitives}\}
,
with the pericyclic primitives indexed by cycle length and
Herges type.
A complete classification of pericyclic primitives — and
the question of whether they can be further reduced to a
finite subset — is an open problem left to future work.

Pericyclic reactions in the DPO framework

The three canonical pericyclic reaction types all have
cyclic reaction-centre topology:

•

Diels–Alder cycloaddition

[
76
]
: a diene and a dienophile combine
through a six-membered cyclic concerted step;
three
\pi
-bonds break and one
\pi
-bond plus two
new
\sigma
-bonds form, all within a single ring of six
atoms.

•

Electrocyclic ring closure

[
307
]
: a terminal
\pi
-bond
becomes a
\sigma
-bond closing a ring; the reaction
centre is the newly formed ring itself.

•

[1,j]
sigmatropic shift

[
64
]
:
a
\sigma
-bond migrates across a
\pi
system; the
reaction centre is the cycle traced by the migrating
group and the atoms it visits.

At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, all three are handled by pericyclic primitives
of Definition
6.20
with the appropriate
cycle length and Herges topology.
What
\mathcal{L}_{4}

cannot
do is predict whether a given
pericyclic rule is thermally or photochemically allowed —
that is the content of the Woodward–Hoffmann rules, which
depend on orbital symmetry along the reaction coordinate
and are treated at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
in the stereochemistry
chapter.

§6.4. Definition of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)

Definition 6.22

(Mechanistic level
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
)
.

Let
P
be a Petri net with species set
\mathcal{S}
.
The
mechanistic level

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is the strict symmetric
monoidal category defined as follows.

•

Objects
: finite disjoint unions of

\mathcal{S}
-typed molecular graphs in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
.

•

Generating morphisms
:
valence-conserving chemical DPO rules
(Definition
6.14
) for
P
-species.

•

Morphisms
: composable sequences of DPO
derivations in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, taken up to the congruence
relations of a strict symmetric monoidal category
(associativity and unitality of composition, monoidal
axioms, naturality of the symmetry).

•

Monoidal product
: disjoint union

G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}
of molecular graphs on objects;
parallel juxtaposition of DPO derivations on morphisms.

•

Monoidal unit
: the empty graph
\emptyset
.

That
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
as defined is the
free
strict SMC on
the generating DPO rules requires verification on two fronts:
that the concrete construction is well-defined as a strict
SMC (not just a category, since SMC structure includes
symmetry and tensor coherence), and that it satisfies the
universal property of the free SMC on the chemical DPO
signature.
The three properties of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
established in
Section
6.2.3
are what make the SMC
structure hold concretely; the universal property then
follows from the standard construction of free SMCs on a
directed signature.

Proposition 6.23

(
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is the free strict SMC on its
generating DPO rules)
.

The category
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
of Definition
6.22
is a free
strict symmetric monoidal category over the signature of
valence-conserving DPO rules for
P
-species in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
.

Proof.

The construction in Definition
6.22
presents

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
concretely: morphisms are equivalence classes of
DPO derivation sequences in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
modulo the SMC
congruence (associativity, unitality, monoidal axioms,
naturality of the symmetry).
We verify that this construction is the free strict SMC on
the directed signature
\Sigma
of valence-conserving DPO
rules for
P
-species, in two parts:
(a) the construction is a well-defined strict SMC, and
(b) it satisfies the universal property of the free SMC on

\Sigma
.

For (a), the three properties of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
from
§
6.2.3
establish that the SMC structure
holds concretely for derivation classes.

(i) Adhesivity makes derivations well-defined.

Each generating rule
p=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)

applied at a match
m:L\hookrightarrow G
has a unique
gluing context
D
when the dangling condition holds
(Proposition
6.17
); for well-posed chemical
rules whose reaction centre is enclosed by
L
, the dangling
condition is automatic (Section
6.3
).
The product
H
is therefore unique up to isomorphism, and
sequential composition of derivations is well-defined and
associative on derivation classes.

(ii) Local Church–Rosser realises commutativity of
independent steps concretely.

The SMC’s interchange law and the naturality of the symmetry

\tau
together imply that two independent generators applied
to disjoint parts of an object commute up to SMC congruence.
What requires concrete verification is that this abstract
commutativity is faithfully realised on derivation classes.
The Local Church–Rosser property
(Theorem 7.7 of
[
181
]
) supplies it:
two derivations
d_{1},d_{2}
at disjoint reaction centres in
the same host produce isomorphic products whether applied in
either order.

(iii) Concurrency realises composition concretely.

The Concurrency theorem
(Theorem 7.11 of
[
181
]
) supplies a
single composite rule whose application produces the same end
product as the sequence.
The composition of derivation classes is therefore
representable as a single-rule derivation, consistent with
the abstract SMC composition.

For (b), freeness on
\Sigma
follows from the standard
universal-property construction of the free strict SMC on a
directed signature
[
187
, §XI.2]
,

[
157
, §1]
: the morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
are
finite formal composites of generators under sequential and
monoidal composition, modulo the SMC congruence, with two
composites identified iff forced equal by the SMC axioms.
The DPO interpretation in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, validated by (i)–(iii),
contributes that each generator can be applied at any chosen
match in any host satisfying the gluing condition, witnessing
the formal morphism without introducing any non-SMC-congruent
identifications.
∎

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
as the free SMC: a tower-language
derivation

The free SMC structure of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is automatic from the
universal-property construction of free SMCs on a directed
signature
[
187
, §XI.2]
: given the signature

\Sigma
of valence-conserving DPO rules, the free SMC has
morphisms = equivalence classes of formal composites under
the SMC congruence (associativity, unitality, monoidal
axioms, naturality of the symmetry).
What the three properties of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
from
Section
6.2.3
contribute is the

faithfulness
of the semantic interpretation of these
formal morphisms as concrete DPO derivations.

Adhesivity
\Rightarrow
semantic
well-definedness.

At
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
–
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
, a morphism from complex
\mathbf{u}

to complex
\mathbf{v}
is a stoichiometric transition: a pair

(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})
with no internal structure.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, a morphism is a DPO derivation

G\Rightarrow_{p,m}H
: the unique gluing context
D

(guaranteed by adhesivity of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
) is the categorical
bridge between
L
and
R
, not in general a chemical
intermediate (Remark
6.12
).
A chemical intermediate, when present (e.g., the
trigonal-bipyramidal phosphorus intermediate in stepwise
identity substitution, Section
6.1
), is
the molecular graph
H
output by one derivation and serving
as input to the next, distinct from any single rule’s gluing
context
D
.

Local Church–Rosser
\Rightarrow
semantic
commutation of independent steps.

The free-SMC symmetry

\tau_{G_{1},G_{2}}:G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}\to G_{2}\sqcup G_{1}
is
automatic by construction.
What LCR provides is its semantic realisation: two
derivations at disjoint reaction centres commute as DPO
operations, instantiating the abstract symmetry concretely.
Without LCR, the abstract symmetry would still hold formally
in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, but the order of derivations could matter
in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, leaving the abstract SMC symmetry without a
faithful
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
-realisation.

Concurrency
\Rightarrow
semantic
single-rule composites.

The free-SMC composition is automatic by construction.
What the Concurrency theorem provides is a representation
result: any composite of independent derivations can be
realised as a single composite DPO rule whose pushout produces
the same end product
(Theorem 7.11 of
[
181
]
).
The abstract composite morphism in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
thus has a
concrete single-rule realisation in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
.

Summary.

Free SMC structure: by construction.
Semantic interpretation in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
: well-defined
derivations (adhesivity), independent commutation (Local
Church–Rosser), single-rule composites (Concurrency).
The freeness comes from category theory; the chemistry
comes from the semantic faithfulness via
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
.
The generating data are the chemical DPO rules of
Definition
6.14
; the elementary basis

\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{6}\}
together with pericyclic primitives
(Sections
6.3
,
6.3.4
) is a
conjectured minimal subset
(Remark
6.19
).

Having established that
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is a free strict SMC,
one can now state precisely how it sits in the tower.
The forgetful functor
U_{4}:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

(constructed in Section
6.6
) provides the
downward connection: it sends each molecular graph to its
species-count vector and each DPO derivation to the
corresponding stoichiometric transition.
The decorating functors
F_{\!H}
,
F_{\!S}
,
\FP
of the lower
levels lift to
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
via
U_{4}
(Proposition
6.32
):
no new
primitive
numerical functor enters at
\mathcal{L}_{4}

beyond those lifted from
\mathcal{L}_{3}
via
U_{4}
, but the free SMC
that carries them is genuinely new.
The universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)

(Proposition
6.25
below) is what makes
this connection canonical: any interpretation of the
DPO generators in a target SMC — whether a chemical
database, a retrosynthesis planner, or a Para-level ML
model — extends uniquely to a functor from
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.

Remark 6.24

(The structural break stated precisely)
.

At every previous level
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
through
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
,
the underlying free SMC was
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)=\mathbf{FreeSMC}(P)
,
with objects in
\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}
and morphisms as stoichiometric
transitions.
New levels added functors
F_{\!H},F_{\!S},\FP
on top of the

same
underlying category.

At
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, the underlying category is genuinely new:
objects are molecular graphs, not species-count vectors;
morphisms are DPO derivations, not abstract stoichiometric
transitions.

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is
not
the free SMC of
P
with
additional decoration.
It is a different free SMC, generated by richer data,
connected to the previous levels only via the forgetful
functor
U_{4}
of Section
6.6
.

Proposition 6.25

(Universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be any strict SMC.
An assignment of the valence-conserving DPO rules of

P
-species to morphisms of
\mathcal{C}
, compatible with
source and target molecular graphs, extends uniquely to a
strict SMC functor
F:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{C}
.

Proof.

By Proposition
6.23
,
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is the free
strict SMC on the generating DPO rules.
The universal property of a free SMC states precisely that
any assignment of generators to morphisms of any strict SMC

\mathcal{C}
extends to a unique strict SMC functor.
Existence: define
F
on generators by the given assignment
and extend to composites and monoidal products by the SMC
axioms; the SMC congruence in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
ensures
F
is
well-defined.
Uniqueness: every morphism of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is, by freeness,
a unique composite of generators up to SMC congruence, so
the value of
F
on generators determines
F
on all morphisms.
∎

The tower updated: two qualitatively different
extension types

The tower
\mathcal{L}_{0}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{1}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{2}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{3}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{4}
now contains
two qualitatively different types of extension:

•

Decorator extensions

(
\mathcal{L}_{0}\to\mathcal{L}_{1}
,
\mathcal{L}_{1}\to\mathcal{L}_{2}
,
\mathcal{L}_{2}\to\mathcal{L}_{3}
):
the same underlying free SMC
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is retained;
each new level adds exactly one new functor into
B\mathbb{R}

or
\Stoch
(or more precisely,
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
).
The universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
does all the work.

•

Structural extension
(
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
):
the underlying free SMC is replaced by a new one,

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, generated by DPO rules rather than
stoichiometric transitions.
Previous decorations lift via
U_{4}
.
No new
primitive
numerical functor is added beyond
those inherited from
\mathcal{L}_{3}
via pullback along
U_{4}
;
the new content is in the morphisms themselves
(DPO derivations rather than stoichiometric transitions).
The structural break is forced by the
\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4})

obstruction of Section
6.1
and cannot
be resolved by any decorator extension.

§6.5. Automorphism exact sequences across the tower

The necessity of each tower extension is witnessed by a non-trivial
cokernel in the automorphism exact sequence at that level.
Now that
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is in hand, the complete tower from

\mathcal{L}_{0}
to
\mathcal{L}_{4}
assembles, with each forcing pair
explicit.

Proposition 6.26

(Automorphism tower
\mathcal{L}_{0}
–
\mathcal{L}_{4}
)
.

For
k=1,2,3,4
, let

\varphi_{k}:\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{k}(P))\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{k-1}(P))

be the restriction map induced by the forgetful functor at
level
k
.
The following four exact sequences hold, and all four
cokernels are non-trivial:

\displaystyle 1\to\ker\varphi_{1}\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{1})\xrightarrow{\varphi_{1}}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{0})\to\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}\to 1,

\displaystyle 1\to\ker\varphi_{2}\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{2})\xrightarrow{\varphi_{2}}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{1})\to\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{2}\to 1,

\displaystyle 1\to\ker\varphi_{3}\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3})\xrightarrow{\varphi_{3}}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{2})\to\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{3}\to 1,

\displaystyle 1\to\ker\varphi_{4}\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4})\xrightarrow{\varphi_{4}}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{3})\to\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{4}\to 1.

Proof.

Each exact sequence is the standard kernel-cokernel sequence of
the group homomorphism
\varphi_{k}
.
Non-triviality of each cokernel is witnessed by an explicit
reaction pair that the lower level conflates.

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{1}
contains the swap of reactions with the same
stoichiometry but different
F_{\!H}
(Hess’s Law is invisible at

\mathcal{L}_{0}
).

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{2}
contains the swap of reactions with the same

F_{\!H}
but different
F_{\!S}
(entropy data are invisible at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
).

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{3}
contains the swap of reactions with the same

F_{\!G}^{T}
but different propensity
\FP
(kinetic data are
invisible at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
).

\mathrm{coker}\varphi_{4}
contains the swap

r_{\text{concerted}}\leftrightarrow r_{\text{stepwise}}
for
identity nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus
(Section
6.1
, Forcingbox): two generators
with identical source and target complexes in
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
,
identical functorial images under
F_{\!H}
,
F_{\!S}
,
F_{\!G}^{T}
,
\FP

at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, but distinct DPO-derivation structure at
\mathcal{L}_{4}

(Proposition
6.45
).
∎

The following portrait diagram displays the full tower together
with its automorphism groups.
The left column shows the tower levels with forgetful functors;
the right column shows the automorphism groups with the
restriction maps
\varphi_{k}
connecting them; the horizontal
dashed arrows indicate the natural action
\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{k})\curvearrowright\mathcal{L}_{k}

of each automorphism group on its level.

Reading the diagram top-down along the right column traces the
progressive loss of mechanistic information as one descends the

\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4})
distinguishes every bond-change sequence;

\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{0})
sees only species-name permutations.
Reading bottom-up recovers the
forcing
structure: each
non-trivial cokernel names a pair of physically distinct reactions
that the previous level conflates, compelling the next level’s

The chapter terminates at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
because the next distinction
— between enantiomers, which share the same DPO rule but differ

, developed
