).

§6.6. The forgetful functor

U_{4}:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

The free SMC
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
sits above the rest of the tower
via a forgetful functor
U_{4}
that strips away all
bond-level information and returns the plain stoichiometric
data of
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
This functor is the categorical bridge that embeds the new
mechanistic level into the existing tower: the previous
decorations
F_{\!H}
,
F_{\!S}
,
\FP
lift to
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
by
precomposing with
U_{4}
, and the tower structure from

\mathcal{L}_{0}
through
\mathcal{L}_{3}
is recovered by factoring through
U_{4}
.

6.6.1. Definition and well-definedness

Definition 6.27

(Forgetful functor
U_{4}
)
.

Recall from Definition
6.13
that every object
of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
is a pair
(G,\spec)
where
G
is a labelled
molecular graph and
\spec:\pi_{0}(G)\to\mathcal{S}
assigns each
connected component of
G
(each individual molecule) to a
species name in
\mathcal{S}
.

The
forgetful functor

U_{4}:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

is defined as follows.

•

On objects
: for
(G,\spec)\in\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
,

U_{4}(G)\;:=\;\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\Bigl|\bigl\{C\in\pi_{0}(G)\;\big|\;\spec(C)=S\bigr\}\Bigr|\cdot S\;\;\in\;\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}.

That is,
U_{4}(G)
counts how many connected components of

G
are assigned to each species by
\spec
, producing the
corresponding complex in the free commutative monoid
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.

•

On morphisms
: for a DPO derivation

d:G\Rightarrow H
implementing a chemical DPO rule

p=(s,\gamma(p))
(Definition
6.14
),
define

U_{4}(d)\;:=\;\gamma(p)\;\in\;\mathcal{L}_{0}(P),

the Petri-net generator carried as label data by the
rule
p
, regarded as a morphism in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)=\mathbf{FreeSMC}(P)
.
For a composite derivation
d_{2}\circ d_{1}
, set

U_{4}(d_{2}\circ d_{1}):=U_{4}(d_{2})\circ U_{4}(d_{1})
using
composition in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

Remark 6.28

(On the generator label)
.

The generator label
\gamma(p)
is essential to making
U_{4}

well-defined on morphisms.
Since
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)=\mathbf{FreeSMC}(P)
is
not
a thin
category (Petri nets may contain distinct generators

r_{1},r_{2}\in\mathcal{R}
with identical source and target complexes),

U_{4}(d)
cannot be defined as “the unique morphism from

U_{4}(G)
to
U_{4}(H)
”; there may be several candidates.
The explicit label
\gamma(p)
in the DPO rule data
(Definition
6.14
) resolves the ambiguity:

U_{4}(d)
is the specific generator
\gamma(p)
, not merely
any morphism with matching source and target.
This matters precisely for the forcing pair of
Section
6.1
: when the Petri net
P

contains two distinct generators

r_{\text{concerted}},r_{\text{stepwise}}\in\mathcal{R}
that
realise the same identity substitution at phosphorus
through mechanistically distinct routes, the corresponding
DPO rules
p_{\text{concerted}}
and
p_{\text{stepwise}}

carry distinct labels

\gamma(p_{\text{concerted}})=r_{\text{concerted}}
and

\gamma(p_{\text{stepwise}})=r_{\text{stepwise}}
.

U_{4}
projects them to these two parallel generators in

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
— distinct morphisms with identical source and
target complexes — rather than collapsing them to a single
morphism.
When
P
has only one generator per stoichiometry (the
generic case), the label is redundant and can be inferred
from
(U_{4}(L),U_{4}(R))
.

Proposition 6.29

(
U_{4}
is a strict SMC functor)
.

U_{4}:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is a well-defined strict
symmetric monoidal functor.

Proof.

Well-definedness on objects.

U_{4}(G)\in\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
by construction: the sum counts
components by their species assignment
\spec
.

Well-definedness on morphisms.

For each DPO derivation
d
, the generator label

\gamma(p)
is a fixed datum of the rule
p
(part of the
grounding structure of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
).
Thus
U_{4}(d)=\gamma(p)
is a specific, uniquely
determined morphism in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, independent of which
host graph
G
the derivation acts on or what match
m

was chosen.

Functoriality.

For the identity derivation
\mathrm{id}_{G}
,
U_{4}(\mathrm{id}_{G})=\mathrm{id}_{U_{4}(G)}

since
\mathrm{id}_{G}
implements the trivial (empty) generator.
For sequential composition
d_{2}\circ d_{1}
:

U_{4}(d_{2}\circ d_{1})=U_{4}(d_{2})\circ U_{4}(d_{1})

by the definition of
U_{4}
on composites and the functoriality
of composition in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

Strict monoidality.

U_{4}(G_{1}\sqcup G_{2})=U_{4}(G_{1})+U_{4}(G_{2})
:
the species count of a disjoint union is the sum of the
individual counts (the
\spec
maps are independent on
disjoint components).

U_{4}(\emptyset)=\mathbf{0}
: the empty graph has no
components, hence contributes zero to every species count.
For morphisms,
U_{4}(d_{1}\sqcup d_{2})=U_{4}(d_{1})\otimes U_{4}(d_{2})
:
parallel derivations on disjoint graphs map to the monoidal
product of the corresponding
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
-morphisms.

Symmetry.

U_{4}
sends the symmetry isomorphism

\tau_{G_{1},G_{2}}:G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}\xrightarrow{\sim}G_{2}\sqcup G_{1}

in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
to the symmetry isomorphism

\tau_{U_{4}(G_{1}),U_{4}(G_{2})}
in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
,
since both simply swap the two summands.
∎

What
U_{4}
forgets and retains

Retained
: which Petri-net generator the DPO rule
realises (via its label
\gamma
), and therefore which
species are consumed and produced (stoichiometry).

Forgotten
: the molecular graphs of reactants and
products; which bonds formed or broke; the sequence of
elementary DPO steps; the identity of the reaction centre;
the presence or absence of intermediate molecular graphs
in stepwise mechanisms; all stereochemical information.

For the forcing pair of Section
6.1
,
the concerted-
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
-P DPO rule and the stepwise A–E
DPO rule
(realising identity substitution at phosphorus through
distinct mechanisms) carry distinct Petri-net labels

r_{\text{concerted}}
and
r_{\text{stepwise}}
when both
appear as parallel generators of
P
.
Their
U_{4}
-images are different but
parallel

generators in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
: distinct morphisms sharing source
and target complexes.

U_{4}
thus preserves the information that the two mechanisms
yield identical reactants and products, while discarding the
internal DPO structure that distinguishes them at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
and
justifies their existence as separate generators in the first
place.
The existence of parallel generators in
P
is unmotivated
at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
–
\mathcal{L}_{3}
(where it can be postulated only by
fiat) and finds its principled structural basis at
\mathcal{L}_{4}

(where it reflects genuinely distinct DPO derivations).

6.6.2.
U_{4}
and the full tower:
factorisation through intermediate levels

The functor
U_{4}:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
sends
\mathcal{L}_{4}

all the way down to the base of the tower.
We can also factor this descent through each intermediate
level: there are canonical forgetful functors

U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{k}}:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{k}(P)
for
k=1,2,3

that land at each decorator level,
and these are related by the adjacent-level forgetful
functors
V_{k}:\mathcal{L}_{k}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{k-1}(P)
.

Definition 6.30

(Intermediate forgetful functors)
.

For
k=1,2,3
, define the
intermediate forgetful
functor

U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{k}}:\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{k}(P)
to be the
functor that:

•

on objects and on the underlying stoichiometric
morphisms, agrees with
U_{4}

(i.e.
V_{1}\circ\cdots\circ V_{k}\circ U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{k}}=U_{4}
);

•

retains the decorating functor data available at
level
k
:

\displaystyle U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{1}}(d)

\displaystyle:=\bigl(U_{4}(d),\;F_{H}^{(4)}(d)\bigr),

\displaystyle U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{2}}(d)

\displaystyle:=\bigl(U_{4}(d),\;F_{H}^{(4)}(d),\;F_{S}^{(4)}(d)\bigr),

\displaystyle U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{3}}(d)

\displaystyle:=\bigl(U_{4}(d),\;F_{H}^{(4)}(d),\;F_{S}^{(4)}(d),\;F_{P}^{(4)}(d)\bigr),

where
F_{H}^{(4)}=F_{\!H}\circ U_{4}
,

F_{S}^{(4)}=F_{\!S}\circ U_{4}
,

F_{P}^{(4)}=\FP\circ U_{4}

are the lifted decorations of Proposition
6.32
.

Proposition 6.31

(Factorisation of
U_{4}
through the tower)
.

Let
V_{k}:\mathcal{L}_{k}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{k-1}(P)
denote the forgetful
functor that drops the topmost decoration at level
k

(i.e.
V_{1}
forgets
F_{\!H}
,
V_{2}
forgets
F_{\!S}
,

V_{3}
forgets
\FP
).
The following chain of equalities holds:

U_{4}\;=\;V_{1}\circ U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{1}}\;=\;V_{1}\circ V_{2}\circ U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{2}}\;=\;V_{1}\circ V_{2}\circ V_{3}\circ U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{3}}.

In particular,
U_{4}
factors through every intermediate
level of the tower.

Proof.

By Definition
6.30
, each
U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{k}}

retains the stoichiometric data
U_{4}
and adds the
decorating functor values.
Each
V_{k}
drops the topmost decoration, so

V_{k}\circ U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{k}}=U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{k-1}}
(with

U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{0}}:=U_{4}
).
Chaining gives the stated equalities.
∎

The following commutative diagram displays the full tower
of forgetful functors from
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
:

The commutativity of each triangle
(e.g.
V_{3}\circ U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{3}}=U_{4}^{\mathcal{L}_{2}}
)
follows from Proposition
6.31
.

The decorating functors
F_{\!H}
,
F_{\!S}
,
\FP
factor
through
U_{4}
as three additional commutative triangles:

Each triangle commutes by definition of the lifted
decoration (
F_{H}^{(4)}:=F_{\!H}\circ U_{4}
, etc.).
The three triangles together say: every piece of numerical
data at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
is obtained from
\mathcal{L}_{0}
-level data by
first forgetting the DPO structure (via
U_{4}
) and then
applying the appropriate functor.
No new
primitive
numerical functor enters at
\mathcal{L}_{4}

beyond those lifted from
\mathcal{L}_{3}
via
U_{4}
; the new
information lives entirely in the morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.

6.6.3. Lifting previous decorations to

\mathcal{L}_{4}

Proposition 6.32

(Lifting)
.

Define

F_{H}^{(4)}\;:=\;F_{\!H}\circ U_{4},\qquad F_{S}^{(4)}\;:=\;F_{\!S}\circ U_{4},\qquad F_{P}^{(4)}\;:=\;\FP\circ U_{4}.

Each is a strict SMC functor from
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
to the
respective target (
B\mathbb{R}
or
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
).

Proof.

Composition of strict SMC functors is a strict SMC functor.
∎

Remark 6.33

(No new numerical functor at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
)
.

Proposition
6.32
is the categorical
statement that
no new primitive numerical functor

enters at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
: every numerical functor on
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)

factors through
U_{4}
as
F^{(4)}=F\circ U_{4}
for some
functor
F
on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
The extension from
\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)
to
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
adds
structural information — the bond-change mechanism —
but not a new real-valued or stochastic-valued label
generated independently of the
\mathcal{L}_{3}
data.
This contrasts with
\mathcal{L}_{1}
–
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, where each level
added exactly one new functor into
B\mathbb{R}
or
\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{S}}
.

A chemist might expect the activation energy
E_{a}
to
enter at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, since bond breaking and forming are
precisely the mechanism-level events that set the
energy barrier.
However,
E_{a}
is the minimax of the potential energy
surface
V:\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)\to\mathbb{R}
along the
intrinsic reaction coordinate — a quantity that requires
the full
geometric
configuration space

\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)=\mathbb{R}^{3n}/(\mathrm{SE}(3)\ltimes\mathrm{Aut}(G))

at
\mathcal{L}_{5}
, not merely the bond-change graph at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.
A DPO rule specifies
which
bonds break and form,
but the same rule can correspond to different values of

E_{a}
depending on the 3-dimensional arrangement of atoms
(e.g. a bulky substituent at the phosphorus centre raises

E_{a}
for an
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
-P step relative to an unhindered
analogue, even though both go through the same DPO rule).

E_{a}
is therefore not functorial at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
; it enters
the tower at
\mathcal{L}_{5}
as the minimax of
V
along the
IRC (Section
8
).

Remark 6.34

(The
\mathcal{L}_{4}
quadruple)
.

Putting together Definition
6.22
,
the universal property Proposition
6.25
,
and the lifting Proposition
6.32
,
the mechanistic level is the quadruple

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\;=\;\bigl(\,\mathcal{L}_{4}(P),\;F_{H}^{(4)},\;F_{S}^{(4)},\;F_{P}^{(4)}\,\bigr),

where the first component is the underlying free SMC on
DPO rules and the remaining three are the lifted
thermochemical, entropy, and kinetic decorations.
The forgetful functor
U_{4}
embeds this quadruple into
the tower via the factorisation of
Proposition
6.31
: going from

\mathcal{L}_{4}
to any lower level amounts to applying
U_{4}

(to recover
\mathcal{L}_{0}
) and then using the appropriate
decorator inclusion or forgetful functor to reach the
desired level.

§6.7. Layer 1 and Layer 2 at
\mathcal{L}_{4}

The Layer 1/Layer 2 split established at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
–
\mathcal{L}_{3}
recurs
at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, but with a structurally different character.
At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
–
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, the split distinguishes the free assignment
of a numerical functor (Layer 1) from the coherence condition that
links it to lower tower levels (Layer 2).
At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, no new
primitive
numerical functor enters:
the decorating functors
F_{H}^{(4)}
,
F_{S}^{(4)}
,
F_{P}^{(4)}

are all lifted from below via
U_{4}

(Proposition
6.32
), so they are already fixed.
The split instead constrains the
choice of DPO rules
:
which bond-change patterns, together with their Petri-net
labelling, yield molecular graphs on which the lifted
decorations remain well-defined.

6.7.1. Layer 1: valid DPO rules

Layer 1 for
\mathcal{L}_{4}
admits any chemical DPO rule

p=(s,\gamma(p))
in the sense of
Definition
6.14
: a valence-conserving,
stoichiometrically consistent span

s=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)
in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
together
with a generator label
\gamma(p)\in\mathcal{R}
, subject to the
dangling condition (Proposition
6.17
) for all
intended matches.
The free parameter at Layer 1 is the choice of reaction-centre
graphs
L
,
K
,
R
— the specific bond-change pattern —
for a given generator label
\gamma(p)
.
For some Petri-net labels there are multiple Layer 1-valid
rules, corresponding to different mechanisms by which a
single reaction can proceed; for other labels, there may be
no single-span Layer 1 rule at all, and the only realisations
are as composites of other rules through intermediate species.
The forcing pair of Section
6.1
—

r_{\text{concerted}}
versus
r_{\text{stepwise}}
for identity
substitution at phosphorus — exhibits exactly this
asymmetry:
r_{\text{concerted}}
is the
U_{4}
-image of a
single Layer 1 rule
p_{\text{concerted}}
, while

r_{\text{stepwise}}
admits no single-span realisation and
arises at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
only as the composite

p_{\text{elim}}\circ p_{\text{add}}
through the
trigonal-bipyramidal intermediate.

6.7.2. Layer 2: valence coherence

A Layer 1 rule (Definition
6.14
) already
guarantees stoichiometric consistency between the span and its
generator label, and valence conservation at every context
atom in
K
.
What remains to check is the
product side
: atoms in

R\setminus r(K)
acquire new labels
(\mathrm{el},q^{\prime},\rho^{\prime})

and new incident bonds during the reaction, and these must
combine to give a valid molecular graph.
Layer 2 imposes this one remaining condition.

Definition 6.35

(Layer 2 condition at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
)
.

A chemical DPO rule

p=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R,\gamma(p))

(Definition
6.14
) satisfies Layer 2 if every
vertex of the product graph has a non-negative integer
lone-pair count:

\ell(v)\in\mathbb{N}\quad\text{for all }v\in V(R),

where
\ell(v)
is the lone-pair component of
v
’s vertex
label — determined by the basic valence formula of
Definition
6.4
at non-hypervalent atoms, and
supplied as part of the label at hypervalent atoms (the
pentacoordinate trigonal-bipyramidal phosphorus of the
forcing pair being a representative case).

Layer 2 as inter-level coherence

Where the condition lives.

The context atoms in
K
satisfy the valence constraint
automatically: by definition,
K
contains atoms whose labels
and bonds are unchanged between
L
and
R

(Remark
6.15
), so their lone-pair counts
are preserved trivially.
The genuine content of Layer 2 is at the reaction-centre
atoms in
R\setminus r(K)
: their post-reaction labels

(\mathrm{el},q^{\prime},\rho^{\prime})
together with their new bond
orders must combine to give
\ell(v)\geq 0
as a
non-negative integer.

Why it matters: linkage to
\mathcal{L}_{1}
–
\mathcal{L}_{2}
.

Enthalpy and Gibbs free energy are state functions evaluated
on valid molecular graphs.
A product atom with
\ell(v)<0
or non-integer
\ell(v)
is
not part of a valid molecular graph: a lone-pair count is an
electron count, which must be a non-negative integer.
This rules out two kinds of failure — the basic valence
formula of Definition
6.4
forcing
\ell

negative or fractional at a non-hypervalent atom, or a
hypervalent atom being supplied with an
\ell
outside
\mathbb{N}
.
The DPO derivation
d:G\Rightarrow H
would then have
no valid target
H
in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, so the lifted
decoration
F_{H}^{(4)}(d)=F_{\!H}(U_{4}(d))
is undefined at
the level of
\mathcal{L}_{4}
even before composition with
F_{\!H}
.
The Layer 2 condition guarantees that every product of a
valid rule is a well-formed element of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, keeping

F_{H}^{(4)},F_{S}^{(4)},F_{P}^{(4)}
well-defined throughout
any derivation.

What Layer 2 does
not
see.

The forcing pair of Section
6.1
—

r_{\text{concerted}}
versus
r_{\text{stepwise}}
for
identity substitution at phosphorus — involves two
chemical DPO rules that both satisfy Layer 2: both produce
valid molecular graphs at every step.
The pentacoordinate TBI intermediate of the stepwise pathway
is hypervalent (the basic valence formula of
Definition
6.4
would give
\ell(\mathrm{P})=-1/2
); under the hypervalent-vertex remedy of
Remark
6.37
in
Section
6.8
,
\mathrm{P}
in the
TBI carries a supplied
\ell=0\in\mathbb{N}
, satisfying the
Layer 2 condition.
The lifted decorations on both rules are accordingly
well-defined.
The distinction between them — whether the rule is a
single concerted DPO span or a composite span through the
TBI intermediate molecular graph — is a Layer 1 degree of
freedom, invisible to the valence check that defines Layer 2.
This is as it should be: Layer 2 asks only that each rule
be chemically well-formed, not that it be mechanistically
distinguished.
The mechanistic distinction is recovered by the
DPO-derivation structure itself in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, not by any
additional tower-layer condition.

Observation 6.36

(Layer 2 at each level: a universal pattern)
.

The Layer 2 conditions across the tower follow a common pattern.
In each case, Layer 1 is the unconstrained categorical choice
(functor, rate assignment, or DPO rule), and Layer 2 is the
coherence condition linking it to all lower levels.

Level

Layer 1

Layer 2

\mathcal{L}_{1}

Any functor
F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}\to B\mathbb{R}

Coboundary:
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h_{f}

(Hess’s Law cycle condition)

\mathcal{L}_{2}

Any pair
(F_{\!H},F_{\!S})
of functors

Thermodynamic Wegscheider:
both
F_{\!H}=\delta^{0}h_{f}
and
F_{\!S}=\delta^{0}s_{f}

hold simultaneously,
equivalently
F_{G}^{T}(c)=0
for every cycle
c

at all
T

\mathcal{L}_{3}

Any rate assignment
k_{r}

Kinetic Wegscheider: loop-balance conditions
on rate constants
(Section
5.5
)

\mathcal{L}_{4}

Any chemical DPO rule
p=(s,\gamma(p))

per Definition
6.14

Valence coherence:
\ell(v)\in\mathbb{N}
at every atom
of the product graph
R

(Definition
6.35
)

The progression from
\mathcal{L}_{1}
to
\mathcal{L}_{4}
reveals a shift in
what Layer 2 constrains: at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
–
\mathcal{L}_{2}
it constrains
the values of numerical functors on stoichiometric cycles;
at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
it constrains ratios of rate constants on those
cycles; at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
it constrains the graph structure of the
product molecules themselves, via the lone-pair count
condition of Definition
6.35
.
In each case, the Layer 2 condition is precisely what is
needed to keep the tower’s numerical data well-defined on
the new data introduced at that level.

§6.8. The forcing-pair derivations and their distinctness

Section
6.1
identified the

\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
forcing pair: identity nucleophilic
substitution at phosphorus, realisable either by a single
concerted
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
-P transition state or by stepwise
addition–elimination through a pentacoordinate
trigonal-bipyramidal intermediate (TBI).
Both pathways carry the same source and target complexes in

\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
and (under steady-state on the TBI) the same

\mathcal{L}_{3}
propensity; what distinguishes them is the
DPO-derivation structure at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.
This subsection makes that distinction precise.

Throughout,
\mathrm{P}
denotes the central phosphorus atom
of the substrate methyl ethylphenylphosphinate,
written
\mathrm{Et(Ph)P(=O)OMe}
.
We write
\mathrm{OMe}
for the leaving methoxide and

\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe}
for the isotopically labelled incoming
methoxide.
The ethyl group, phenyl group, and doubly-bonded oxygen
retain their labels and their bonds to phosphorus throughout
every rule below, and sit in
K
together with phosphorus
itself (Remark
6.15
).
The two methoxides change charge between
L
and
R

(neutral when bonded to P,
-1
when free), so each appears
outside
K
at any step where its bonded/free status changes.

Remark 6.37

(On hypervalent phosphorus)
.

The pentacoordinate phosphorus in the TBI is hypervalent:
its incident bond-order sum is
\sum_{e}b(e)=6
(Et, Ph,
P=O, plus two single P–O bonds to the methoxides), giving

\ell(\mathrm{P})=(5-0-0-6)/2=-1/2
from the basic
valence formula of Definition
6.4
.
The basic formula assumes octet-like electron counting and
does not accommodate the three-centre four-electron bonding
characteristic of hypervalent main-group atoms.
A standard remedy is to extend the formalism so that, at
hypervalent vertices,
\ell
is supplied as part of the
vertex label rather than computed from

(v_{\text{el}},q,\rho,\sum b)
; the basic formula is then
recovered as the special case where the supplied
\ell

matches the octet-derived value.

Example 6.38

(Concerted
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
-P as a single DPO rule)
.

The concerted rule has phosphorus unchanged in label

(\mathrm{P},0,0)
; the bonds to the two methoxides change
(P–OMe broken, P–
\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe}
formed), and the
methoxide vertex labels change accordingly under the
bonded/free charge convention recorded above.

L
:

P with three spectator bonds (to Et, Ph, and
the doubly-bonded O) plus one P–OMe bond;

\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe^{-}}
as a free isolated component.

K
:

P with the three spectator bonds only.
Both methoxides are excluded from
K
because their
formal charge changes between
L
and
R
.

R
:

P with three spectator bonds plus one
P–
\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe}
bond;

\mathrm{OMe^{-}}
as a free isolated component.

The rule fires as a single DPO step

G\Rightarrow_{p_{\text{concerted}},m}H
with no
intermediate molecular graph; phosphorus is tetracoordinate
in both source and target, and the rule passes from
L
to

R
without introducing a pentacoordinate species.
The generator label is
\gamma(p_{\text{concerted}})=r_{\text{concerted}}
.

Example 6.39

(Stepwise addition–elimination through the TBI)
.

The stepwise rule is the sequential composite

p_{\text{elim}}\circ p_{\text{add}}
of an addition step
followed by an elimination step, going through the
pentacoordinate intermediate.

Step 1 (Addition).

\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe^{-}}
adds to phosphorus, expanding it
from tetracoordinate to pentacoordinate.

L_{1}
:

P with the three spectator bonds plus one
P–OMe bond (the substrate);

\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe^{-}}
as a free isolated component.

K_{1}
:

the substrate alone, with all four bonds at

\mathrm{P}
preserved (P–Et, P–Ph, P=O, P–OMe);
the free
\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe^{-}}
component is excluded
because its formal charge changes between
L_{1}
and
R_{1}
.

R_{1}
:

P with three spectator bonds, one P–OMe
bond, and one P–
\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe}
bond.
This is the TBI.

Intermediate graph
G_{1}
(the TBI).

Phosphorus carries label
(\mathrm{P},0,0)
with five
incident bonds.
This is the pentacoordinate TBI; it is hypervalent in the
sense of Remark
6.37
and is absent from
any concerted derivation.
The TBI is itself an element of
\mathcal{S}
, distinct from the
substrate and product.

Step 2 (Elimination).

\mathrm{OMe^{-}}
leaves from the TBI, returning phosphorus
to tetracoordinate.

L_{2}
:

P with all five bonds — three to
spectators, plus P–OMe and P–
\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe}
.
This is the TBI.

K_{2}
:

P with three spectator bonds plus one
P–
\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe}
bond.
OMe is excluded because its formal charge changes
between
L_{2}
and
R_{2}
.

R_{2}
:

K_{2}
together with
\mathrm{OMe^{-}}
as a
free isolated component (the bonded structure at

\mathrm{P}
is unchanged from
K_{2}
).

The full stepwise derivation is

G\Rightarrow_{p_{\text{add}},m_{1}}G_{1}\Rightarrow_{p_{\text{elim}},m_{2}}H
.
The component rules carry generator labels

\gamma(p_{\text{add}})=r_{\text{add}}
and

\gamma(p_{\text{elim}})=r_{\text{elim}}
in
\mathcal{R}
.

Together with the concerted pathway, the two derivations
assemble into a triangle in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
:

where
G=\mathrm{Et(Ph)P(=O)OMe}+\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe^{-}}

is the substrate complex,

G_{1}=\mathrm{TBI}
is the pentacoordinate intermediate,
and
H=\mathrm{Et(Ph)P(=O){}^{18}OMe}+\mathrm{OMe^{-}}
is
the product complex.

Proposition 6.40

(The forcing-pair triangle does not commute)
.

The direct edge
p_{\text{concerted}}
and the composite

p_{\text{elim}}\circ p_{\text{add}}
of the triangle above are
distinct morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, both having source
G

and target
H
.

Proof.

Same source-target.

By inspection of Examples
6.38

and
6.39
: the source for both
derivations is the substrate plus the labelled methoxide,

G\;=\;\mathrm{Et(Ph)P(=O)OMe}+\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe^{-}},

and the target for both is the labelled product plus the
departing methoxide,

H\;=\;\mathrm{Et(Ph)P(=O){}^{18}OMe}+\mathrm{OMe^{-}}.

Distinctness in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.

The three DPO rules
p_{\text{concerted}}
,
p_{\text{add}}
,
and
p_{\text{elim}}
are pairwise distinct: their spans
differ in the contents of the context
K

(concerted: P plus three spectator bonds only; addition:
P plus spectators plus
\mathrm{OMe}
; elimination:
P plus spectators plus
\mathrm{{}^{18}OMe}
).
By Proposition
6.23
,
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
is a free
strict SMC on the chemical DPO rules, and the multiset of
rules appearing in any expression for a morphism is
invariant under the strict SMC equational theory
(associativity and unitality of both
\circ
and
\otimes
,
the interchange law

(g_{1}\otimes g_{2})\circ(f_{1}\otimes f_{2})=(g_{1}\circ f_{1})\otimes(g_{2}\circ f_{2})
,
and the naturality and coherence axioms for the symmetry

\tau
); each axiom rearranges or inserts identities without
changing the multiset of chemical generators that appear.
The direct edge has rule-multiset
\{p_{\text{concerted}}\}
,
while the composite has rule-multiset

\{p_{\text{add}},p_{\text{elim}}\}
; the two multisets are
disjoint, so the morphisms are distinct.
∎

§6.9. Four mechanisms as distinct morphisms in

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)

Section
6.1
established the forcing pair
for
\mathcal{L}_{4}
: concerted vs stepwise mechanisms at a single
heteroatom centre (the phosphorus identity-substitution
example), the only kind of pair
\mathcal{L}_{3}
genuinely conflates.
The classical mechanism pairs
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
vs
\mathrm{S_{N}2}

and
\mathrm{E1}
vs
\mathrm{E2}
are not forcing pairs in
this sense — their different propensity forms
(
v=k_{1}[\mathrm{RX}]
vs
v=k_{2}[\mathrm{RX}][\mathrm{Nu}]
,
and analogously for E1/E2) separate them already at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.
What
\mathcal{L}_{4}
adds for these familiar pairs is a

structural
account that complements the kinetic
distinction at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
: each mechanism becomes a specific
DPO derivation, with intermediate molecular graphs that
appear (or fail to appear) according to whether the
mechanism is concerted or stepwise.
This section constructs explicit DPO derivations in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
for all four mechanisms and verifies pairwise
distinctness in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.

Throughout, atoms are labelled by
(\mathrm{el},q,\rho)

and bonds by their order
b
.
The Layer 2 valence check at each step verifies that every
atom of the product graph
R
satisfies
\ell(v)\in\mathbb{N}

(Definition
6.4
).
For consistency with
Remark
6.15
, atoms whose label

(\mathrm{el},q,\rho)
changes between
L
and
R
appear
in
L\setminus l(K)
and
R\setminus r(K)
separately;
only atoms with unchanged labels sit in
K
.

6.9.1. Substitution pair:

\mathrm{S_{N}1}
and

\mathrm{S_{N}2}

Both mechanisms realise the same net transformation

\mathrm{R{-}X}+\mathrm{Nu^{-}}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{R{-}Nu}+\mathrm{X^{-}},

and carry the same reactants and products in
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
They are distinguished at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
by their propensity forms
(
v=k_{1}\,[\mathrm{RX}]
for
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
,

v=k_{2}\,[\mathrm{RX}][\mathrm{Nu}]
for
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
).
The DPO derivations below show
why
the propensities
differ: the two mechanisms have different DPO-level
structure, with
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
passing through an
intermediate molecular graph that
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
does not.

6.9.3. All four mechanisms are distinct in

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)

Proposition 6.45

(Four mechanisms as distinct morphisms)
.

In
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, the DPO derivations of
Examples
6.41
–
6.44
are pairwise
distinct morphisms.

(i)

The
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
derivation
(Example
6.41
) and the
\mathrm{S_{N}1}

derivation (Example
6.42
) are distinct
morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
and project to distinct
morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
:

U_{4}(\mathrm{S_{N}2})=r_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
a single
generator,
U_{4}(\mathrm{S_{N}1})=\gamma(p_{2})\circ\gamma(p_{1})
a 2-step composite, parallel to the
postulated generator
r_{\mathrm{S_{N}1}}\in\mathcal{R}
but
distinct from it.
All have shared source
\mathrm{RX}+\mathrm{Nu^{-}}

and target
\mathrm{RNu}+\mathrm{X^{-}}
.

(ii)

The
\mathrm{E2}
derivation (Example
6.43
)
and the
\mathrm{E1}
derivation (Example
6.44
)
are distinct morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
;

U_{4}(\mathrm{E2})=r_{\mathrm{E2}}
a single generator,

U_{4}(\mathrm{E1})=\gamma(p_{2})\circ\gamma(p_{1})
a
2-step composite at
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, parallel to the
postulated generator
r_{\mathrm{E1}}\in\mathcal{R}
but
distinct from it.

(iii)

No substitution morphism coincides with any
elimination morphism: the four are pairwise distinct
in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
and project to four pairwise distinct
morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.

Proof.

(i) Substitution pair.

The
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
derivation is a single DPO step whose
intermediate graph
D
contains neither a carbocation nor
any other chemically distinguished non-substrate vertex.
The
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
derivation is the sequential composite

p_{2}\circ p_{1}
passing through the intermediate molecular
graph
G_{1}
, which contains a vertex with label

(\mathrm{C},+1,0)
— the carbocation.
In
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, a morphism is an equivalence class of DPO
derivations under SMC congruence (associativity, unitality,
symmetry); no SMC congruence can collapse a derivation
passing through a
(\mathrm{C},+1,0)
vertex to one that
never visits such a vertex.
Hence the two derivations represent distinct morphisms.

By Definitions
6.14
and
6.27
,

U_{4}(\mathrm{S_{N}2})=\gamma(p_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}})=r_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
is a single
\mathcal{L}_{0}
generator, while

U_{4}(\mathrm{S_{N}1})=\gamma(p_{2})\circ\gamma(p_{1})
is the
2-step composite of the elementary heterolytic-cleavage and
-capture generators (by functoriality of
U_{4}
).
A single generator and a 2-step composite of distinct
generators are distinct morphisms in the free SMC

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
, so
U_{4}(\mathrm{S_{N}2})\neq U_{4}(\mathrm{S_{N}1})

even though both share source
\mathrm{RX}+\mathrm{Nu^{-}}

and target
\mathrm{RNu}+\mathrm{X^{-}}
in
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
.
The composite
U_{4}(\mathrm{S_{N}1})
is parallel to the
postulated generator
r_{\mathrm{S_{N}1}}\in\mathcal{R}
but distinct
from it:
r_{\mathrm{S_{N}1}}
has no single-span
\mathcal{L}_{4}

realisation.

(ii) Elimination pair.

Analogous: the
\mathrm{E2}
derivation has no intermediate
graph, while the
\mathrm{E1}
derivation passes through the
carbocation vertex
(\mathrm{C},+1,0)
.
The two are distinct in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
;

U_{4}(\mathrm{E2})=r_{\mathrm{E2}}
is a single generator,
while
U_{4}(\mathrm{E1})=\gamma(p_{2})\circ\gamma(p_{1})
is a
2-step composite, parallel to the postulated

r_{\mathrm{E1}}\in\mathcal{R}
but distinct from it.

(iii) Cross-class distinctness.

The substitution generators and the elimination generators
have distinct source and target complexes in
\mathbb{N}^{|\mathcal{S}|}
:
substitution consumes
\mathrm{RX}+\mathrm{Nu^{-}}
and
produces
\mathrm{RNu}+\mathrm{X^{-}}
, while elimination
consumes
\mathrm{RX}+\mathrm{B^{-}}
and produces

\mathrm{alkene}+\mathrm{BH}+\mathrm{X^{-}}
.
In particular, the number of species produced differs.
Thus no substitution morphism coincides with any
elimination morphism at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
, and since
U_{4}
is
well-defined on
\mathcal{L}_{4}
morphisms, no substitution morphism
coincides with any elimination morphism at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
either
(else their
U_{4}
-images would coincide in
\mathcal{L}_{0}
).
∎

What
\mathcal{L}_{4}
expresses that
\mathcal{L}_{3}
cannot

The proposition shows how the four classical mechanism
types are pairwise distinguished as morphisms in

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.
This is not the forcing argument of
Section
6.1
(which concerns the

\mathcal{L}_{3}
-indistinguishable phosphorus pair); rather, it
demonstrates that the same DPO machinery automatically
separates mechanism types that
\mathcal{L}_{3}
also distinguishes
kinetically.
In each case,
\mathcal{L}_{3}
already distinguishes the two
mechanisms numerically via their different propensity forms,
but
\mathcal{L}_{3}
supplies no
structural
account.

\mathcal{L}_{4}
supplies that account: the two mechanisms correspond
to DPO derivations with genuinely different internal
structure — one single-step without intermediate graphs,
the other two-step passing through a carbocation vertex

(\mathrm{C},+1,0)
.

Substitution.

At
\mathcal{L}_{3}
:
r_{\mathrm{S_{N}1}}
and
r_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
are
distinct generators with propensity values

k_{1}x_{\mathrm{RX}}
and
k_{2}x_{\mathrm{RX}}x_{\mathrm{Nu}}

respectively.
These propensity forms suffice to separate the two morphisms
in
\mathcal{L}_{3}
but give no
structural
reason for the
difference.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
: the propensity difference is explained by the
different DPO derivation structures —
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
as a
single concerted rule,
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
as a composite through
the carbocation intermediate graph.
The structural distinction has familiar downstream
consequences (Walden inversion for
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
; partial
racemisation for
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
via planar carbocation
attack from either face), but these
stereochemical

consequences require three-dimensional data and enter the
tower at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
rather than at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.

Elimination.

At
\mathcal{L}_{3}
:
r_{\mathrm{E1}}
and
r_{\mathrm{E2}}
are
distinct generators with propensities

k_{1}x_{\mathrm{RX}}
and
k_{2}x_{\mathrm{RX}}x_{\mathrm{B}}
,
which separate them numerically but again give no
structural account.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
: the difference is explained by the DPO
derivation structures —
\mathrm{E2}
as a single
concerted rule with cyclic reaction-centre topology,

\mathrm{E1}
as a composite through the same carbocation
intermediate graph as
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
.
The stereochemical consequences (
\mathrm{E2}
’s required
anti-periplanar geometry, absent in
\mathrm{E1}
) again
live at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.

Summary.

\mathcal{L}_{4}
explains
why
the Petri net carries parallel
generators that
\mathcal{L}_{3}
distinguishes only by their
propensity values.
The explanation is structural: two DPO derivations with
different intermediate graphs.
Three-dimensional consequences of this structure
(stereochemistry, orbital-symmetry selection rules) are the
content of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
(Section
7
).

6.9.4.
\mathcal{L}_{4}
in action:
the Briggs–Rauscher oscillating reaction

The examples of Section
6.9
involved pairs of
mechanisms competing for a single substrate.
The Briggs–Rauscher (BR) oscillating reaction shows a richer
phenomenon: a network in which two categorically different
mechanism types compete and switch roles periodically, producing
macroscopic colour oscillations visible to the naked eye.
It illustrates how mechanism-level information — the
structural data of
\mathcal{L}_{4}
— governs the topology of
reaction networks in ways that rate constants alone do not
encode, and provides the first case in this monograph where
a
global
property of a reaction network (the
structural origin of oscillation) is exhibited as an

\mathcal{L}_{4}
-level predicate.

The Briggs–Rauscher reaction: physical description

Mixing aqueous
\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}
,
\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}
, malonic
acid
\mathrm{CH_{2}(COOH)_{2}}
,
\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}
, sulfuric acid,
and starch produces a solution that cycles through

\text{colourless}\;\to\;\text{amber}\;\to\;\text{deep blue}\;\to\;\text{colourless}\;\to\;\cdots

approximately ten to fifteen times before the reaction ends

[
52
]
.
The
amber
colour is free iodine (
\mathrm{I_{2}}
);
the
deep blue
is the
\mathrm{I_{3}^{-}}
–starch complex,
which requires
both

\mathrm{I_{2}}
and
\mathrm{I^{-}}

simultaneously.
The overall net stoichiometry is

\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}+2\,\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}+\mathrm{CH_{2}(COOH)_{2}}+\mathrm{H^{+}}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{ICH(COOH)_{2}}+2\,\mathrm{O_{2}}+3\,\mathrm{H_{2}O}.

This is the
U_{4}
-image of one full oscillation period: a
composite morphism in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
that conceals all mechanistic
structure.

The oscillation arises from two competing sub-processes for the
intermediate conversion of
\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}
to hypoiodous acid

\mathrm{HOI}

[
231
]
:

Process A (non-radical/ionic): active when

[\mathrm{I^{-}}]
is high.

A1.

\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}+\mathrm{I^{-}}+2\mathrm{H^{+}}\to\mathrm{HIO_{2}}+\mathrm{HOI}

(slow;
g_{2}
,
g_{1}
)

A2.

\mathrm{HIO_{2}}+\mathrm{I^{-}}+\mathrm{H^{+}}\to 2\,\mathrm{HOI}

(fast;
g_{2}
,
g_{1}
)

A3.

\mathrm{HOI}+\mathrm{I^{-}}+\mathrm{H^{+}}\to\mathrm{I_{2}}+\mathrm{H_{2}O}

(fast;
g_{1}
,
g_{2}
)

Intermediate molecular graphs:
G_{\mathrm{HIO_{2}}}
(iodous acid,

q(\mathrm{I}){=}{+3}
, arising from step A1) and

G_{\mathrm{HOI}}
(hypoiodous acid,
q(\mathrm{I}){=}{+1}
,
arising from steps A1–A2).
Process A consumes
\mathrm{I^{-}}
and produces
\mathrm{I_{2}}

(amber), driving
[\mathrm{I^{-}}]
downward.

Process B (radical): active when
[\mathrm{I^{-}}]

is low.

B1.

\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}+\mathrm{HIO_{2}}+\mathrm{H^{+}}\to 2\,\dot{\mathrm{IO}}_{2}+\mathrm{H_{2}O}

(
g_{5}
: homolytic O–I)

B2.

\dot{\mathrm{IO}}_{2}+\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}+\mathrm{H_{2}O}\to\mathrm{HIO_{2}}+\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}+\mathrm{OH^{-}}

(
g_{6}
: SET)

B3.

\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}+\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}\to\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}+\dot{\mathrm{HO}}_{2}+\mathrm{H^{+}}

(
g_{6}
: SET, with H
+
loss)

B4.

\dot{\mathrm{HO}}_{2}+\dot{\mathrm{IO}}_{2}\to\mathrm{HIO_{2}}+\mathrm{O_{2}}

(
g_{4}
: radical combination)

Intermediate molecular graphs:
G_{\dot{\mathrm{IO}}_{2}}
(iodyl
radical,
\rho(\mathrm{I}){=}1
),
G_{\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}}

(
q(\mathrm{Mn}){=}{+3}
), and
G_{\dot{\mathrm{HO}}_{2}}

(hydroperoxyl radical,
\rho(\mathrm{O}){=}1
).
All three are absent from any Process A derivation.
Process B regenerates
\mathrm{HIO_{2}}
autocatalytically (via
both B2 and B4), building the chain carrier rapidly; HOI is
then produced indirectly via A2 once
[\mathrm{I^{-}}]
recovers.

Iodination loop C: active throughout.

\mathrm{I_{2}}+\mathrm{CH_{2}(COOH)_{2}}\;\to\;\mathrm{ICH(COOH)_{2}}+\mathrm{H^{+}}+\mathrm{I^{-}}\qquad(g_{2},\,g_{1}\text{ on malonic acid})

Loop C is a slow ionic iodination that
regenerates

\mathrm{I^{-}}
, refuelling Process A once
[\mathrm{I^{-}}]

rises again.

The switch.

When
[\mathrm{I^{-}}]
is high: Process A dominates, consuming

\mathrm{I^{-}}
and building
\mathrm{I_{2}}
(amber).
When
[\mathrm{I^{-}}]
drops: Process B ignites autocatalytically,
rapidly raising
[\mathrm{I_{2}}]
and
[\mathrm{I^{-}}]

simultaneously, triggering the starch complex (deep blue).
Loop C slowly consumes
\mathrm{I_{2}}
and rebuilds

[\mathrm{I^{-}}]
, re-enabling Process A and clearing the blue.

The following observation makes this rigorous, showing that
the structural account of the oscillation — which
mechanism families compose into the period morphism, and
how — is an
\mathcal{L}_{4}
phenomenon.

Observation 6.46

(One BR oscillation period as a
composite morphism in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
)
.

Setup.

Let
P_{\mathrm{BR}}
be the Petri net containing all elementary
reactions of the BR mechanism.
Define three families of morphisms in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P_{\mathrm{BR}})
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{A}

\displaystyle:=\text{morphisms generated exclusively by }g_{1},\,g_{2}\text{ (heterolytic)}

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{B}

\displaystyle:=\text{morphisms generated exclusively by }g_{4},\,g_{5},\,g_{6}\text{ (radical / SET)}

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{C}

\displaystyle\subset\mathcal{M}_{A}:\text{the iodination sub-family (}g_{1},\,g_{2}\text{ on malonic acid)}

The claim is
\mathcal{M}_{A}\cap\mathcal{M}_{B}=\{\mathrm{id}\}
:
no non-identity morphism belongs to both families.
In a free SMC (Proposition
6.23
), every
morphism can be expressed as a finite composite of generators,
and the multiset of generators appearing in that composite
(counted with multiplicities) is invariant under the SMC
congruence.
Since the generator sets
\{g_{1},g_{2}\}
and

\{g_{4},g_{5},g_{6}\}
are disjoint, no non-identity morphism
expressible using only generators from one set can be
SMC-congruent to one using only generators from the other;
hence the two generated sub-SMCs intersect only in the
identity.

Objects.

Define four molecular graphs (objects of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
) representing
the system at chemically distinguished points in one period:

\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{ionic}}

\displaystyle:=\text{state with high $[\mathrm{I^{-}}]$;
Process~A poised to fire}

\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{radical}}

\displaystyle:=\text{state after A has consumed $\mathrm{I^{-}}$;
$[\mathrm{I^{-}}]$ below threshold}

\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{loop}}

\displaystyle:=\text{state after B has produced $\mathrm{I_{2}}$;
malonic acid iodination pending}

\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{restored}}

\displaystyle:=\text{state after C has restored $[\mathrm{I^{-}}]$;
cycle complete}

The period morphism.

Three composite morphisms fill the three segments:

\varphi_{A}\;:\;\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{ionic}}\;\Rightarrow\;\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{radical}},\quad\varphi_{B}\;:\;\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{radical}}\;\Rightarrow\;\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{loop}},\quad\varphi_{C}\;:\;\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{loop}}\;\Rightarrow\;\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{restored}},

with
\varphi_{A}\in\mathcal{M}_{A}
,

\varphi_{B}\in\mathcal{M}_{B}
,

\varphi_{C}\in\mathcal{M}_{C}\subset\mathcal{M}_{A}
.
One oscillation period is the composite:

\tau_{\mathrm{period}}\;:=\;\varphi_{C}\;\circ\;\varphi_{B}\;\circ\;\varphi_{A}\;:\;\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{ionic}}\;\Rightarrow\;\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{restored}}.

Diagram.

The following diagram shows one period as a sequence of DPO
derivations, with the intermediate molecular graphs named:

The isomorphism
\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{restored}}\cong\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{ionic}}
(equality of species counts up to
consumed reactants) closes the period:
\tau_{\mathrm{period}}

can be iterated.

Formal content.

We establish three properties:

(i)

\tau_{\mathrm{period}}\notin\mathcal{M}_{A}

and
\tau_{\mathrm{period}}\notin\mathcal{M}_{B}
.

Since
\varphi_{B}\in\mathcal{M}_{B}
and

\mathcal{M}_{A}\cap\mathcal{M}_{B}=\{\mathrm{id}\}
,
any morphism containing
\varphi_{B}
as a sub-derivation
cannot lie in
\mathcal{M}_{A}
.
Dually,
\varphi_{A},\varphi_{C}\in\mathcal{M}_{A}

cannot lie in
\mathcal{M}_{B}
.
Hence
\tau_{\mathrm{period}}
is irreducible to either
family alone:
the structural realisation of oscillation
requires both mechanism types to exist in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P_{\mathrm{BR}})
.

(ii)

\tau_{\mathrm{period}}
decomposes essentially uniquely
as
\varphi_{C}\circ\varphi_{B}\circ\varphi_{A}
in

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P_{\mathrm{BR}})
.

By Proposition
6.23
,
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P_{\mathrm{BR}})

is a free SMC.
In a free SMC, the only relations among morphisms are those
imposed by the SMC congruence (associativity, unitality,
symmetry); no relation can merge a
g_{1}/g_{2}
step with a

g_{4}/g_{5}/g_{6}
step.
The three-segment decomposition of
\tau_{\mathrm{period}}

is therefore unique up to the ordering of independent steps
within each segment.

(iii)

U_{4}(\tau_{\mathrm{period}})
as a morphism in

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is determined by the full sequence of
generators in the composite, not by the net stoichiometric
change

U_{4}(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{restored}})-U_{4}(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{ionic}})\in\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathcal{S}|}

alone.

Both the radical-containing trajectory and a hypothetical
all-ionic alternative consume one BR-stoichiometric unit, so
their source-and-target objects in
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
agree.
However, the morphism
U_{4}(\tau_{\mathrm{period}})
in

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
is a specific composite of Petri-net generators
that records which mechanism was used.
The
existence of oscillation
, which requires the
radical-containing trajectory, is not visible from the
source-target stoichiometry alone — this is the sense in
which it is invisible at the object level of
\mathcal{L}_{0}
.

Property (i) is the key: it shows that the structural
prerequisite for oscillation is an
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-level constraint
on the reaction network.
A network containing only one generator family —
say, only ionic steps
g_{1},g_{2}
— cannot form a

\tau_{\mathrm{period}}
containing
\varphi_{B}
, because

\varphi_{B}
requires radical generators absent from such
a network.
Oscillation becomes possible
exactly when
the
Petri net
P
contains generators from at least two
mechanism families whose DPO-derivations can be composed
into a cyclic trajectory in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.

The tower dissects the BR reaction

At
\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

The Furrow–Noyes model requires eleven elementary rate
equations with eleven rate constants to reproduce the
oscillation quantitatively
[
231
]
.
The CME generator
\Omega
for the net HOI-production step
is
\Omega=k_{\mathrm{eff}}(R_{r_{\mathrm{HOI}}}-I)
,
where
k_{\mathrm{eff}}
summarises the observed production rate
regardless of which process is active.
The rate-equation
\dot{[\mathrm{HOI}]}=k_{\mathrm{eff}}[\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}][\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}]
is the same whether
Process A or Process B runs: the switch is invisible.
The full Furrow–Noyes system does reproduce the oscillation, but
only after being given all eleven rate constants — kinetic data
attached to elementary reactions, several of which are
radical-mechanism steps and several of which are ionic; the
radical/ionic distinction is part of the
\mathcal{L}_{0}
generator
structure of
P_{\mathrm{BR}}
, with
\mathcal{L}_{4}
supplying the
explicit DPO derivation structure that makes it geometrically
visible.

Level

Content in the BR system

\mathcal{L}_{0}

Overall BR stoichiometric equation; generators for each
distinct reaction in the network, including separate
generators for the ionic and radical HOI-production
pathways

\mathcal{L}_{1}

\Delta H
of the net iodate-to-HOI transformation

\mathcal{L}_{2}

Equilibrium constant
K_{\mathrm{eq}}
for HOI
production; Wegscheider conditions

\mathcal{L}_{3}

Eleven rate constants of the Furrow–Noyes model;
oscillation dynamics via the CME

\mathcal{L}_{4}

Two distinct DPO morphism families
(
\mathcal{M}_{A}
ionic,
\mathcal{M}_{B}
radical);
period morphism
\tau_{\mathrm{period}}
; the
structural prerequisite for oscillation
(Observation
6.46
)

The Briggs–Rauscher reaction thus illustrates a general
principle that the tower makes precise:

the structural origin of oscillation is an
\mathcal{L}_{4}

predicate: it requires that the network contain morphisms
from at least two distinct mechanism families that compose
into a cyclic trajectory
.
A kinetic model at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
can fit the oscillation period
and amplitude to data once the reaction network is supplied,
but only
\mathcal{L}_{4}
provides the structural account of why the
network admits oscillatory dynamics in the first place.

§6.10. What
\mathcal{L}_{4}
cannot express:
forcing of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

The mechanistic level
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
was forced by the
concerted versus stepwise pathway at phosphorus: two
reactions sharing source, target, and (under steady-state on
the TBI)
\mathcal{L}_{3}
propensity, distinguishable only at the
level of DPO derivations
(Sections
6.1
,
6.8
).
The same machinery applies to the analogous mechanism pairs
of carbon chemistry —
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
versus

\mathrm{S_{N}2}
,
\mathrm{E1}
versus
\mathrm{E2}
, and
ionic versus radical pathways in oscillating networks —
though for these
\mathcal{L}_{3}
already provides kinetic separation;
what
\mathcal{L}_{4}
contributes is the structural account
(Section
6.9
).
It does so by replacing stoichiometric transitions with DPO
derivations: objects are molecular graphs, morphisms encode
the sequence of bond changes, and mechanistically distinct
reactions are distinct morphisms.

Yet
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
remains blind to
spatial orientation
.
The label set
(\mathrm{el},q,\rho)
records element type,
formal charge, and radical count; bond-order labels record
connectivity.
None of these encode the three-dimensional arrangement of
substituents around a stereocentre.
Two molecules that are mirror images of each other are
graph-isomorphic in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
— identical vertex labels,
identical edge labels, identical adjacency structure — and
are therefore identified by
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, which sees nothing
beyond graph isomorphism.
Any DPO rule that applies to one applies identically to the
other.
The following forcing pair makes this concrete.

Forcing pair for
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
:
enantiomers under
\mathrm{S_{N}2}

Consider the
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
reaction of 2-bromobutane with
hydroxide, which has a stereocentre at C
2

(bonded to H, CH
3
, CH
2
CH
3
, Br — four distinct
substituents).
The reaction can proceed from either enantiomer:

(R)\text{-2-bromobutane}+\mathrm{OH^{-}}\;\longrightarrow\;(S)\text{-2-butanol}+\mathrm{Br^{-}},

(S)\text{-2-bromobutane}+\mathrm{OH^{-}}\;\longrightarrow\;(R)\text{-2-butanol}+\mathrm{Br^{-}}.

Both reactions use the same DPO rule from
Example
6.41
: break C–Br, form C–OH, concerted
single step.
The molecular graphs of
(R)
- and
(S)
-2-bromobutane are
graph-isomorphic in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
: same element types, same
formal charges, same radical counts, same bond orders, same
adjacency.
No datum in
(\mathrm{el},q,\rho)
distinguishes
a left-handed from a right-handed arrangement of the four
substituents around C
2
.

Yet the reactions are physically distinct: their products are
different enantiomers, and a chiral agent (an enzyme, a
resolving agent, an asymmetric catalyst) reacts with one but
not the other.
The swap
(R)\leftrightarrow(S)
is an automorphism of

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
— it preserves all categorical structure at the
graph level — but corresponds to genuinely different
physical reactions.
It is a non-trivial element of
\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})
in the
exact sequence

1\to\ker\varphi_{4.5}\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P))\;\xrightarrow{\;\varphi_{4.5}\;}\;\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))\to\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})\to 1,

extending Proposition
6.26
to the next level.
The same pattern recurs throughout stereochemistry:

(E)
/
(Z)
alkene isomers,

cis
/
trans
cycloalkane diastereomers,

endo
/
exo
cycloadducts.
The next chapter develops a second, independent forcing
pair — the conrotatory/disrotatory selectivity of
pericyclic ring closures (Woodward–Hoffmann) —
manifesting the same
\mathcal{L}_{4}
blindness in a different
chemical setting (Section
7.1
).

The type of extension

\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.

The extensions
\mathcal{L}_{0}\to\mathcal{L}_{1}\to\mathcal{L}_{2}\to\mathcal{L}_{3}
were

decorator extensions
: the underlying free SMC

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
was retained and a new numerical functor was
appended at each step.
The extension
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
was a
structural
extension
: the underlying free SMC was replaced by a new
one generated by DPO rules, with no new numerical functor.
The extension
\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
is of a third type: an

equivariant extension
.
The free SMC of DPO derivations is retained; no new
numerical functor is added.
Instead, the category is equipped with an action of a group
encoding spatial orientation, and morphisms are required to
be equivariant with respect to that action.
Chirality, stereochemical descriptors, and orbital-symmetry
selection rules are then the orbit structure and
representation theory of this equivariant extension.
The construction is developed in the following chapter.

§7.
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
: The Stereochemical Level

§7.1. Forcing the extension: what
\mathcal{L}_{4}

cannot express

Section
6.10
introduced the enantiomer
swap as the forcing pair motivating
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
: the same
DPO rule applied to
(R)
- and
(S)
-substrates produces
different physical products that
\mathcal{L}_{4}
cannot distinguish.
This section develops that forcing rigorously and introduces
a second independent forcing pair — the conrotatory /
disrotatory distinction in pericyclic ring closure —
which manifests the same
\mathcal{L}_{4}
blindness in a different
chemical setting.
Both pairs are then resolved by a single discrete algebraic
datum: a chirality label

\sigma\colon\mathrm{Stereo}(G)\to\{+1,-1\}
at each
stereocentre (see Definition
7.6
), augmenting the molecular graph without
introducing 3D coordinates.
Throughout,
\varphi_{4.5}
denotes the restriction map

\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4.5})\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4})
in the automorphism exact
sequence of the tower.

Remark 7.1

(Why
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
: a symmetry layer over
\mathcal{L}_{4}
)
.

The fractional index
4.5
is not a notational convenience.
It encodes the mathematical relationship between this level
and its predecessor:
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)

is

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)

seen through a symmetry filter.
The objects are augmented molecular graphs — the same
combinatorial kind as
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, decorated with chirality
labels — and the morphisms remain DPO derivations;
but now only the
G^{*}
-equivariant derivations are admitted.

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
is a category over
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
via the
forgetful functor
U_{4.5}\colon\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)

that drops the chirality labels: its morphisms are

G^{*}
-equivariant DPO derivations on chirality-labelled
graphs, with the same DPO machinery as
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.
It is not a sub-SMC of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
in the literal sense —
its objects are augmented graphs
(G,\sigma)
, not bare
graphs — but neither is it a new category built from
scratch: the underlying combinatorics and rewriting
machinery are inherited from
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.

This places
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
in contrast with the two surrounding
transitions.
The extension
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
was a
structural
break
:
\mathcal{L}_{4}
introduced an entirely new class of
morphisms (DPO derivations in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
) that
\mathcal{L}_{3}
had
no access to.
The forthcoming extension
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}\to\mathcal{L}_{5}
will be a

geometric break
:
\mathcal{L}_{5}
introduces genuinely
continuous and geometric data — 3D atom positions and
the continuous potential energy landscape they define —
a qualitatively new mathematical structure.

By contrast,
\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
is a

symmetry enrichment
: the same DPO framework,
restricted to its
G^{*}
-equivariant part.
No new numerical functor is added; the underlying free SMC
is not rebuilt.
The fractional index
4.5
records exactly this: we are
still in the
\mathcal{L}_{4}
world, but looking at the part of it
that respects a discrete symmetry group.
Separating
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
from
\mathcal{L}_{5}
honours the bottom-up
forcing principle: each level is the unique minimal
extension resolving a specific pair of reactions, and the
two forcing pairs of this section are resolved by the
discrete
G^{*}
-datum alone.

Two forcing pairs for
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

Forcing pair 1: enantiomers under

\mathrm{S_{N}2}
.

Consider the bimolecular substitution of 2-bromobutane
(stereocentre at
\mathrm{C_{2}}
, bonded to four distinct
substituents:
\mathrm{CH_{3}}
,
\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}
,

\mathrm{H}
,
\mathrm{Br}
) by hydroxide, starting from
each enantiomer:

\displaystyle r_{R}\colon

\displaystyle\quad(R)\text{-2-bromobutane}+\mathrm{OH^{-}}\;\to\;(S)\text{-2-butanol}+\mathrm{Br^{-}},

\displaystyle r_{S}\colon

\displaystyle\quad(S)\text{-2-bromobutane}+\mathrm{OH^{-}}\;\to\;(R)\text{-2-butanol}+\mathrm{Br^{-}}.

Walden’s 1896 observation that nucleophilic substitution
at a stereocentre proceeds with inversion of configuration

[
293
]
was mechanistically explained in the
1930s: Hughes and Ingold
[
151
]
identified
back-side attack as the
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
mechanism, and
Cowdrey, Hughes, Ingold, Masterman, and Scott

[
67
]
established in 1937 that the clean
elementary
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
step at a configurationally
stable tetrahedral stereocentre proceeds with

complete
inversion; mixed mechanisms involving

\mathrm{S_{N}1}
contributions, neighbouring-group
participation, or ion-pair effects appear in the tower
as compositions of multiple
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-morphisms with

\mathcal{L}_{3}
-level rate weights, not as deviations from the
elementary
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
rule.
The question for the tower is whether this experimental
fact is visible as a theorem or only as an empirical
constraint.

In
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, the molecular graphs of
(R)
- and

(S)
-2-bromobutane are isomorphic: identical element
types, formal charges, radical counts, bond orders, and
adjacency.
No datum in
(\mathrm{el},q,\rho,b)
distinguishes
left-handed from right-handed arrangements of substituents
around
\mathrm{C_{2}}
.
This rests on a modelling convention: the
\mathcal{L}_{0}
species
set is not pre-refined by stereodescriptors. Inserting

(R)
- and
(S)
- as primitive species labels at
\mathcal{L}_{0}

would build into the model the very distinction

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
is constructed to derive. Under this
convention, both reactions apply the
same
DPO rule
(Example
6.41
) to graph-isomorphic substrates
and produce graph-isomorphic products:

r_{R}\;=\;r_{S}\quad\text{as morphisms in }\mathcal{L}_{4}(P).

The permutation
\pi_{\chi}
that exchanges the two
graph-isomorphic enantiomer copies at the
\mathcal{L}_{4}
level is
an automorphism of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
identifying the two
reactions — but the physical reactions are distinct:
their products differ in sign of optical rotation, binding
affinity to chiral receptors, and metabolism by enzymes.
The entire field of asymmetric synthesis rests on the
distinction being real.
Hence
[\pi_{\chi}]
is a non-trivial element of

\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})
.

Forcing pair 2: conrotatory vs. disrotatory electrocyclic ring closure.

Consider the
4\pi
-electron electrocyclic ring closure of

(E,E)
-hexa-2,4-diene to 3,4-dimethylcyclobutene.
(The
(E,E)
annotation is alkene stereochemistry, which
sits outside the tetrahedral-stereocentre scope of
Definition
7.6
; we treat it
informally here as a substrate descriptor and do not
attempt formal
E/Z
-handling in this chapter.)
The Woodward–Hoffmann orbital-symmetry rules

[
305
,
307
]
predict
that the stereochemical outcome depends on the electronic
state:

\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{thermal}}\colon

\displaystyle\quad(E,E)\text{-hexa-2,4-diene}\;\xrightarrow{\;\Delta\;}\;\mathit{trans}\text{-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene},

\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{photo}}\colon

\displaystyle\quad(E,E)\text{-hexa-2,4-diene}\;\xrightarrow{\;h\nu\;}\;\mathit{cis}\text{-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene}.

The thermal reaction proceeds via a conrotatory motion
(the two terminal carbons rotate in the same direction
as the new
\sigma
-bond forms), preserving the
C_{2}
-axis
of the diene — the symmetry element under which the
ground-state HOMO
\psi_{2}
is symmetric.
The photochemical reaction proceeds via a disrotatory
motion (rotations in opposite directions), preserving
the
\sigma
-plane — the symmetry element under which
the excited-state HOMO
\psi_{3}
is symmetric.
The motions themselves are continuous trajectories in 3D
configuration space and live properly at
\mathcal{L}_{5}
; what

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
records is their discrete product outcome
(
trans
vs.
cis
-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene).
The photochemical reaction proceeds disrotatorily (rotations
in opposite directions): this mode preserves the

\sigma
-plane, the symmetry element under which the
excited-state HOMO
\psi_{3}
is symmetric.
Hoffmann shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with
Fukui for the theoretical insight that orbital topology
governs reaction stereochemistry

[
109
,
143
]
.

At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, the two reactions are indistinguishable on
two independent grounds.
First, they apply the
same
DPO rule

p_{\mathrm{ec}}
to the same host graph: one new

\sigma
-bond
\mathrm{C_{2}{-}C_{5}}
forms, and two

\pi
-bonds (
\mathrm{C_{2}{=}C_{3}}
,
\mathrm{C_{4}{=}C_{5}}
)
reduce to single bonds:

\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{ec}}

\displaystyle:\mathrm{C_{2}{=}C_{3}{-}C_{4}{=}C_{5}}\text{ (open diene centre)},

\displaystyle K_{\mathrm{ec}}

\displaystyle:\{\mathrm{C_{2},C_{3},C_{4},C_{5}}\}\text{ with no bonds among them},

\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{ec}}

\displaystyle:\mathrm{C_{2}{-}C_{3}{=}C_{4}{-}C_{5}}\text{ plus new $\sigma$-bond }\mathrm{C_{2}{-}C_{5}}.

Second, the two products
trans
- and

cis
-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene are graph-isomorphic in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
: they share the same atom set, same bond orders,
same adjacency.
Their difference lies entirely in the three-dimensional
arrangement of the two methyl groups at

\mathrm{C_{3}}
and
\mathrm{C_{4}}
— data not present in

(\mathrm{el},q,\rho,b)
.
The vertices
\mathrm{C_{3}}
and
\mathrm{C_{4}}
are

ring
stereocentres: removing such a vertex from a
ring leaves fewer than four connected components, so the
literal form of Definition
7.6
does
not apply. We use throughout this chapter the standard
generalisation via the CIP hierarchical digraph, which
handles ring atoms by introducing phantom duplicates at
ring-closure points; see §
7.2
.
Consequently, under the same
\mathcal{L}_{0}
-species convention
adopted for forcing pair 1,

d_{\mathrm{thermal}}\;=\;d_{\mathrm{photo}}\quad\text{as morphisms in }\mathcal{L}_{4}(P).

Woodward–Hoffmann chemistry is invisible.

In any category that distinguishes the two products,
they carry distinct chirality labels: writing

\sigma_{\mathit{trans}}(\mathrm{C_{3}})\cdot\sigma_{\mathit{trans}}(\mathrm{C_{4}})=+1
for matching
orientations and
\sigma_{\mathit{cis}}(\mathrm{C_{3}})\cdot\sigma_{\mathit{cis}}(\mathrm{C_{4}})=-1
for opposed
orientations makes the two products different augmented
graphs
(G,\sigma)
, even though they share the same
underlying
G
.
The permutation that identifies the two products in

\mathcal{L}_{4}
— call it
\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}
— is an
automorphism of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
that does not lift to

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
, where the two products are distinct
objects.
Hence
[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]
is a non-trivial element of

\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})
, independent of
[\pi_{\chi}]
from
pair 1.

The exact sequence

1\;\to\;\ker\varphi_{4.5}\;\to\;\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P))\;\xrightarrow{\;\varphi_{4.5}\;}\;\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))\;\to\;\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})\;\to\;1

(7)

has a non-trivial cokernel containing at least two
independent elements
[\pi_{\chi}]
and
[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]

(Observation
7.4
).
The extension
\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
is therefore forced by
at least two independent classes of chemical phenomenon:
stereoselective nucleophilic substitution and orbital-symmetry
selection in pericyclic reactions.

What minimal structure resolves both
forcing pairs.

Both pairs are resolved by a single discrete algebraic datum:
a chirality label
\sigma\colon\mathrm{Stereo}(G)\to\{+1,-1\}

at each stereocentre, augmenting the molecular graph without
introducing 3D coordinates.
The precise objects — chirality-labelled molecular graphs

(G,\sigma)
and the chirality-symmetry group
G^{*}=\mathrm{Aut}(G)\ltimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
acting on them, where
k
is
the number of stereocentres of
G
— are introduced in
§
7.2
–
7.3
.
We use
G^{*}
throughout the chapter for this construction;
note that this is
not
the Longuet–Higgins
permutation–inversion group (often also written
G^{*}
in
the molecular-spectroscopy literature) but a tower-internal
group tailored to the chirality-label data introduced here.
The connection to the molecular-spectroscopy
G^{*}
is
discussed in §
7.2
.
Here we record only how each pair is resolved.

Remark 7.2

(Resolving forcing pair 1: enantiomers)
.

In
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
the objects are augmented molecular graphs

(G,\sigma)
(Definition
7.12
).
The two enantiomers
(G_{R},\sigma_{R})
and
(G_{S},\sigma_{S})

share the same underlying graph but carry opposite chirality
labels:
\sigma_{R}(\mathrm{C_{2}})=+1
and

\sigma_{S}(\mathrm{C_{2}})=-1
.
They are distinct objects, sitting in different orbits of
the
G^{*}
-action: the natural
G^{*}
-orbit of

(G_{R},\sigma_{R})
is the singleton
\{(G_{R},\sigma_{R})\}
at
the level of unrooted graphs, and likewise for
(G_{S},\sigma_{S})
.

The cokernel non-triviality of
[\pi_{\chi}]
now follows
directly.
The permutation
\pi_{\chi}
identifies
(G_{R},\sigma_{R})
with

(G_{S},\sigma_{S})
as objects of
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
(where they are
graph-isomorphic).
A lift
\widetilde{\pi}_{\chi}\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P))
would
have to identify them as objects of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
as well,
mapping
(G_{R},\sigma_{R})
to
(G_{S},\sigma_{S})
on the nose.
But these are distinct objects of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
, so no such
lift exists.
Hence
[\pi_{\chi}]\in\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})
is non-trivial.

A separate, stronger statement is that the

G^{*}
-equivariant lift of the
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
DPO rule
(Example
6.41
) produces only the inverted
product — the wrong-handed product is not in its image.
This is the categorical content of Hughes–Ingold complete
inversion, made rigorous in Theorem
7.27
.
For the present section we need only the weaker statement
above:
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
separates the two enantiomers as objects,
which suffices to make
[\pi_{\chi}]
a non-trivial cokernel
class.

Remark 7.3

(Resolving forcing pair 2: conrotatory vs. disrotatory)
.

In
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
the two ring-closure products carry
distinct chirality labels at the new stereocentres

\mathrm{C_{3}}
and
\mathrm{C_{4}}
:

\displaystyle(G_{\mathrm{cb}},\sigma_{\mathit{trans}})\colon

\displaystyle\quad\sigma(\mathrm{C_{3}})\cdot\sigma(\mathrm{C_{4}})=+1\quad\text{(same orientation on both)},

\displaystyle(G_{\mathrm{cb}},\sigma_{\mathit{cis}})\colon

\displaystyle\quad\sigma(\mathrm{C_{3}})\cdot\sigma(\mathrm{C_{4}})=-1\quad\text{(opposite orientations)}.

These are distinct objects in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
.

A
G^{*}
-equivariant DPO rule for electrocyclic ring closure
must map reactants to products consistently with the

G^{*}
-action: the conrotatory closure produces the

trans
product (matching orientations), while the
disrotatory closure produces the
cis
product
(opposed orientations), and these outcomes are controlled
by which symmetry element of the transition state the rule
respects (
C_{2}
for conrotatory,
C_{s}
for disrotatory).
The permutation
\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}
identifying the two
products in
\mathcal{L}_{4}
does not lift to an equivariant
morphism of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, because the two products have
different
\sigma
-signs at their stereocentres.
Thus
[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]\in\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})
is
non-trivial.

The Woodward–Hoffmann orbital-symmetry rule becomes a
candidate theorem at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
: a pericyclic DPO rule is
thermally allowed iff it is equivariant with respect to
the
C_{2}
or
C_{s}
subgroup of the transition-state
symmetry consistent with the ground-state orbital
occupation.
Theorem
7.37
states this precisely.

Observation 7.4

(Independence of the two classes in the
cokernel)
.

The cokernel classes
[\pi_{\chi}]
and
[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]

have disjoint support:
\pi_{\chi}
acts non-trivially on the
stereocentre
\mathrm{C_{2}}
of 2-bromobutane (and as the
identity elsewhere), while
\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}
acts
non-trivially on the stereocentres
\mathrm{C_{3}}
and

\mathrm{C_{4}}
of 3,4-dimethylcyclobutene (and as the
identity elsewhere).
The two automorphisms therefore commute as elements of

\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))
, and each squares to the identity (it is a
sign-flip of
\sigma
).
Their joint image in
\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})
is a quotient
of
(\mathbb{Z}/2)\times(\mathbb{Z}/2)
.

The four candidate elements

\{1,\,[\pi_{\chi}],\,[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}],\,[\pi_{\chi}]\cdot[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]\}
are pairwise distinct
in the cokernel.
Any non-trivial relation among them would, after
multiplication, exhibit one of
\pi_{\chi}
or

\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}
as a lift of the other modulo the image
of
\varphi_{4.5}
, equivalently a lift of
\pi_{\chi}\cdot\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}^{-1}
to
\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P))
.
But
\pi_{\chi}\cdot\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}^{-1}
still acts as

\pi_{\chi}
on the bromobutane stereocentre (since

\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}
is the identity there), and any lift to

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
would in particular have to identify

(R)
-2-bromobutane with
(S)
-2-bromobutane as objects of

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
— precluded by
Remark
7.2
.
The same argument with the roles reversed precludes the
remaining identifications.
Hence
|\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})|\geq 4
.

More generally, every reaction in
P
producing or
consuming a non-meso stereoisomer pair contributes an
independent class by the same argument; molecules whose

\mathrm{Aut}(G)
-action identifies
\sigma
with
-\sigma
(meso
forms) do not contribute, because their two sign
assignments are already identified at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.
Stereochemistry is thus a pervasive feature of organic
chemistry, with
|\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})|
scaling with the
number of independent enantiomer pairs in
P
rather than
with the raw stereocentre count.

The two datums at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

The minimal new structure at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
consists of two
datums, both discrete and algebraic:

•

Chirality labels

\sigma\colon\mathrm{Stereo}(G)\to\{+1,-1\}

on each stereocentre, augmenting the molecular graph.
Six decades of asymmetric synthesis encoded as a sign.

•

The chirality-symmetry group

G^{*}=\mathrm{Aut}(G)\ltimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}

(Definition
7.5
), acting on chirality-labelled
graphs by permuting atoms and flipping
\sigma
at subsets
of stereocentres.
The Woodward–Hoffmann selection rules are captured as

G^{*}
-equivariance of the DPO rules — no 3D geometry
required.

Both datums are discrete and algebraic: the hallmark of the
symmetry-enrichment character of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.
Three-dimensional consequences (specific molecular geometries,
activation barriers, vibrational modes) are deferred to

\mathcal{L}_{5}
.

§7.2. The chirality symmetry group

G^{*}

Section
7.1
showed that both forcing
pairs for
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
— enantiomer substrates under

\mathrm{S_{N}2}
and conrotatory/disrotatory electrocyclic
closures — are resolved by equipping molecular graphs with
discrete chirality labels
\sigma\colon\mathrm{Stereo}(G)\to\{+1,-1\}
and by letting a finite group
G^{*}
act on
these labels.
This section defines that group, identifies its two factors,
and verifies that it acts sensibly on chirality-labelled
graphs.
The
G^{*}
-action on
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
, projected through the
forgetful functor
U_{4.5}
, makes the forcing cokernel
classes
[\pi_{\chi}]
and
[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]
in

\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))
visible as obstructions that the symmetry
enrichment to
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
removes.

The group
G^{*}
has two factors.
The first,
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
, is the group of label-preserving graph
automorphisms of
G
: permutations of the vertex set
V
that
fix the labelling functions
\lambda_{V}
,
\lambda_{E}
and the
bond-order function
b
.
These are the physically meaningful relabellings —
permutations of identical-nucleus atoms that also respect
the bonding pattern — and form a graph-theoretic
restriction of the permutation part of the Longuet–Higgins
framework
[
205
]
, namely those nuclear
permutations expressible from the connectivity data

\mathcal{L}_{4}
has made available.
The second factor encodes orientation flips at stereocentres.
For a molecule with
k=|\mathrm{Stereo}(G)|
stereocentres,
the minimal group that can independently invert the
orientation at each centre is
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
.
A single global
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
suffices to relate the two members
of an enantiomer pair (via simultaneous flips at all centres)
but cannot relate an enantiomer to a diastereomer — e.g. no element of a global
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
takes
(R,R)
-tartaric acid
to meso-tartaric acid, since the latter requires flipping

\sigma
at one stereocentre but not the other.
The independent single-centre flips in
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
are required
for that distinction, as the tartaric acid example below will
make explicit.

Definition 7.5

(Chirality symmetry group)
.

Let
G\in\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
be a molecular graph with stereocentre
set
\mathrm{Stereo}(G)=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}\}

(Definition
7.6
).
The
chirality symmetry group
of
G
is the
semidirect product

G^{*}(G)\;:=\;\mathrm{Aut}(G)\;\ltimes\;\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k},

where:

•

\mathrm{Aut}(G)
is the group of label-preserving graph
automorphisms of
G
(permutations of vertices
preserving
\lambda_{V}
,
\lambda_{E}
, and bond orders).

•

\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}=\{(\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{k}):\epsilon_{i}\in\{+1,-1\}\}
is the group of
orientation flips, one per stereocentre.

•

Fixing an enumeration

\mathrm{Stereo}(G)=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}\}
, every

\pi\in\mathrm{Aut}(G)
induces a permutation

\bar{\pi}\in S_{k}
via
\pi(v_{i})=v_{\bar{\pi}(i)}

(since
\pi
preserves stereogenicity, it maps

\mathrm{Stereo}(G)
to itself). The semidirect product
structure is given by the action

\mathrm{Aut}(G)\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k})
,

\pi\cdot(\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{k})\;:=\;(\epsilon_{\bar{\pi}^{-1}(1)},\ldots,\epsilon_{\bar{\pi}^{-1}(k)}),

so that
(\pi_{1},\bm{\epsilon}_{1})(\pi_{2},\bm{\epsilon}_{2})=(\pi_{1}\pi_{2},\,\bm{\epsilon}_{1}\cdot(\pi_{1}\cdot\bm{\epsilon}_{2}))
.

The group
G^{*}(G)
acts on chirality-labelled molecular
graphs
(G,\sigma)
(Definition
7.12
) by

(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})\cdot(G,\sigma)\;:=\;\bigl(G,\;\bm{\epsilon}\cdot(\sigma\circ\pi^{-1})\bigr),

where
(\bm{\epsilon}\cdot\sigma)(v_{i}):=\epsilon_{i}\cdot\sigma(v_{i})
.
The element

E^{*}:=(\mathrm{id},(-1,\ldots,-1))\in G^{*}(G)

is the
abstract parity operation
: it flips all
chirality labels simultaneously.

What
G^{*}
knows and what it defers

Definition
7.5
requires no 3D coordinates.

\mathrm{Aut}(G)
is determined by the labelled graph structure of

G\in\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
(which atoms are bonded to which, with which
bond orders), and
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
is a finite discrete group.
Both are available at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.

The abstract parity
E^{*}
is defined as an algebraic element
of
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
, not as a geometric reflection.
Its physical realisation as a spatial inversion in
\mathbb{R}^{3}

is a statement about
\mathcal{L}_{5}
— where 3D coordinates exist
— not about
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
,
E^{*}
is purely an operation on discrete
orientation labels.

The stereocentres on which
G^{*}
acts are now identified.

Definition 7.6

(Stereocentre: graph-theoretic detection)
.

Let
v\in V(G)
be a vertex with exactly four neighbours

w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4}
. For each neighbour
w_{i}
, the

rooted CIP tree

T_{w_{i}}^{v}
is the labelled
rooted tree obtained from
G\setminus\{v\}
by
depth-first traversal outward from
w_{i}
, with any
back-edge (an edge that would close a ring within

G\setminus\{v\}
) replaced by a phantom leaf labelled
by the element type of its target vertex.

The vertex
v
is a
stereocentre
in
G
if:

(i)

v
has exactly four neighbours in
G

(tetrahedral valence), and

(ii)

the four rooted CIP trees

T_{w_{1}}^{v},T_{w_{2}}^{v},T_{w_{3}}^{v},T_{w_{4}}^{v}

are pairwise non-isomorphic as labelled rooted trees.

Condition (ii) is the graph-theoretic form of the
Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) distinctness
condition
[
54
]
: it is the precise
criterion that makes a priority ordering of the four
substituents unique and well-defined. For acyclic
neighbourhoods, the rooted CIP trees coincide with the
four connected components of
G\setminus\{v\}
rooted
at the respective
w_{i}
, and the criterion reduces to
the standard form. For ring stereocentres (e.g. ring
atoms in cyclobutenes, cyclohexanes), the phantom-leaf
construction handles ring closures and recovers the
standard CIP priority assignment.

Both conditions are decidable from

(\lambda_{V},\lambda_{E})
alone; no 3D information is
needed. The set of stereocentres of
G
is denoted

\mathrm{Stereo}(G)
.

Remark 7.7

(CIP priorities and the chirality label)
.

The Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules
[
54
]

assign a total priority order to the four substituents of a
stereocentre based on atomic number and then on graph
topology (the “hierarchical digraph” algorithm).
This order is computable from
G\in\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
alone: atomic
numbers are part of
\mathrm{el}
, and topology is the graph
structure.

Given the CIP priority order, a chirality label

\sigma(v)\in\{+1,-1\}
determines the stereodescriptor:

\sigma(v)=+1
corresponds to the
(R)
-configuration
(priority sequence
1>2>3>4
runs clockwise when
substituent 4 points away) and
\sigma(v)=-1
to
(S)
.

At
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, however,
\sigma(v)
is an
abstract
binary label
: it records that a stereocentre has an
orientation and that the two orientations are distinct,
without committing to which spatial arrangement

\sigma=+1
realises.
The CIP rules establish that the label is well-defined and
graph-computable; which physical enantiomer it corresponds
to is a statement deferred to
\mathcal{L}_{5}
.

Observation 7.8

(
G^{*}(G)
acts on chirality labellings)
.

The group
G^{*}(G)
acts on the set of chirality
functions
\sigma\colon\mathrm{Stereo}(G)\to\{+1,-1\}

in two qualitatively different ways corresponding to its
two factors:

•

\pi\in\mathrm{Aut}(G)
relabels stereocentres:

\sigma\mapsto\sigma\circ\pi^{-1}
.
This relates labellings that differ only by atomic
relabelling; they represent the
same
molecule
in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
(Definition
7.12
).

•

\bm{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
flips
orientations:
\sigma\mapsto\bm{\epsilon}\cdot\sigma
with

(\bm{\epsilon}\cdot\sigma)(v_{i})=\epsilon_{i}\sigma(v_{i})
.
This relates labellings representing
chemically
distinct
stereoisomers.

Within the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
-action, the chemistry distinguishes
two group-theoretic signatures:

•

Enantiomers
are related by the global flip

E^{*}=(\mathrm{id},(-1,\ldots,-1))
, which
simultaneously inverts every stereocentre.

•

Diastereomers
are related by a partial flip

(\mathrm{id},\bm{\epsilon})
with some but
not all
\epsilon_{i}=-1
.

The combination of the two factors is why
G^{*}
is
the right group:
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
quotients out labelling
ambiguity, and
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
encodes the two independent
kinds of stereoisomer relation.

G^{*}
for tartaric acid: why
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
and
not
