\mathbb{Z}_{2}

Tartaric acid
\mathrm{HOOC{-}CH(OH){-}CH(OH){-}COOH}
has
two stereocentres at
\mathrm{C_{2}}
and
\mathrm{C_{3}}
,
giving
k=2
.
The graph
G
has a non-trivial automorphism
\tau\in\mathrm{Aut}(G)
swapping
\mathrm{C_{2}}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{C_{3}}

(together with the two COOH groups and the two OH groups);
the remaining automorphisms are generated by
\tau
, giving

\mathrm{Aut}(G)=\langle\tau\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}
.
The full chirality symmetry group is

G^{*}(G)=\langle\tau\rangle\ltimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}
, with

\tau
acting on
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}
by exchanging the two coordinates
(since
\tau
swaps the stereocentres at
\mathrm{C_{2}}
and

\mathrm{C_{3}}
); concretely,

\langle\tau\rangle\ltimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}\cong D_{4}
, the
dihedral group of order
8
. Its underlying set is
indexed by

Three stereoisomers, two orbits.

Tartaric acid has three physically distinct stereoisomers,
each an object in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
:

•

(R,R)
-tartaric acid: labelling
(+,+)
.

•

(S,S)
-tartaric acid: labelling
(-,-)
.

•

meso
-tartaric acid: labelling
(+,-)
, which
equals
(-,+)
as an object in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
because

\tau
provides an isomorphism between these two
labellings (the two halves of the molecule are
interchangeable).

Under the
G^{*}
-action these objects organise into two
orbits:

•

\{(R,R),(S,S)\}
: the enantiomer pair, related by
the global flip
E^{*}=(\mathrm{id},(-,-))
.
Orbit size 2.

•

\{\text{meso}\}
: a singleton orbit.
The meso compound is its own image under
E^{*}
because

E^{*}\cdot(+,-)=(-,+)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tau}}{{=}}(+,-)
as
objects; equivalently, meso-tartaric acid is achiral
(superimposable on its mirror image).

Why
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
alone is insufficient.

Replacing
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}
with a single
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
(allowing only
the global flip
E^{*}
) would correctly relate the
enantiomers
(R,R)
and
(S,S)
but would leave the meso
compound entirely disconnected from the enantiomer pair
within the symmetry structure.
The partial flips
(+,-)
and
(-,+)
, which relate
enantiomers to diastereomers (e.g.
(R,R)
to meso via

(\mathrm{id},(+,-))
), would be absent.

\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
is thus the minimal factor allowing
G^{*}
to
express all stereoisomer relations among molecules with
multiple stereocentres.

The following proposition records how the
G^{*}
-action
accounts for the two forcing cokernel classes from
§
7.1
, and thereby characterises the
passage from
\mathcal{L}_{4}
to
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
as a symmetry
enrichment.

Proposition 7.9

(
G^{*}
separates the forcing cokernel
classes)
.

Let
[\pi_{\chi}],[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]\in\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{4.5})
be the two forcing classes from
§
7.1
.

(i)

Enantiomer resolution.

Let
G
be the underlying graph of 2-bromobutane,
with stereocentre
v_{\chi}=\mathrm{C_{2}}
.
The two labellings
(G,+1)
and
(G,-1)
are
distinct objects in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
by
Definition
7.12
.
They are related by the
G^{*}(G)
-element

E^{*}=(\mathrm{id},(-1))\in G^{*}
(for
k=1
),
which maps
(G,+1)\mapsto(G,-1)
.
The
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-automorphism
\pi_{\chi}
identifying the
two enantiomers at the
\mathcal{L}_{4}
level arises from this

G^{*}
-action together with the forgetful functor

U_{4.5}
: passing through
U_{4.5}
collapses

(G,\pm 1)
to
G
and makes
E^{*}
appear as the
automorphism
\pi_{\chi}\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))
.
Within
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
, no automorphism identifies

(G,+1)
with
(G,-1)
: the cokernel class

[\pi_{\chi}]
is therefore non-trivial, and
E^{*}

is its representative in
G^{*}
.

(ii)

Electrocyclic resolution.

Let
G_{\mathrm{cb}}
be the underlying graph of
3,4-dimethylcyclobutene, with stereocentres

\mathrm{C_{3}},\mathrm{C_{4}}
(
k=2
).
The two labellings

(G_{\mathrm{cb}},\sigma_{\mathit{trans}})

with
\sigma(\mathrm{C_{3}})\cdot\sigma(\mathrm{C_{4}})=+1
and
(G_{\mathrm{cb}},\sigma_{\mathit{cis}})

with
\sigma(\mathrm{C_{3}})\cdot\sigma(\mathrm{C_{4}})=-1
are distinct objects in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
.
They are related by a partial flip in
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}\leq G^{*}(G_{\mathrm{cb}})
: for any fixed

\sigma_{\mathit{trans}}
, the element

(\mathrm{id},(+,-))\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}
maps

\sigma_{\mathit{trans}}\mapsto\sigma_{\mathit{trans}}^{\prime}
with the sign flipped at

\mathrm{C_{4}}
only, giving a labelling with

\sigma(\mathrm{C_{3}})\cdot\sigma(\mathrm{C_{4}})=-1
,
which is
\sigma_{\mathit{cis}}
(up to the

\tau
-isomorphism when
\tau\in\mathrm{Aut}(G_{\mathrm{cb}})

swaps the two ring carbons).
The
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-automorphism
\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}

identifying the conrotatory and disrotatory products
at the
\mathcal{L}_{4}
level arises from this partial-flip
action through
U_{4.5}
, by the same mechanism as
in part (i).
Within
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
, no automorphism identifies the
two products: the cokernel class

[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]
is therefore non-trivial.

Proof.

Both parts rest on the same mechanism.
The two labellings in question (
(G,+1)
vs.
(G,-1)

for part (i), and
(G_{\mathrm{cb}},\sigma_{\mathit{trans}})
vs.
(G_{\mathrm{cb}},\sigma_{\mathit{cis}})
for part (ii)) are distinct
objects in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
by
Definition
7.12
: two chirality functions
on the same underlying graph that are not related by any
element of
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
give distinct objects.
The
G^{*}
-element relating them (
E^{*}
in part (i), a
partial flip in part (ii)) is not an element of
\mathrm{Aut}(G)

alone, so the relation is not a
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
-isomorphism.
An automorphism of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
would have to send each
object to an isomorphic object; the labelling distinction
obstructs this, so the identification cannot lift.
Under
U_{4.5}
, which forgets the chirality labels, the
two objects collapse to the same underlying graph, and the

G^{*}
-relation becomes a non-trivial automorphism of

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
— the cokernel class.
∎

Remark 7.10

(Provenance: classical chemistry, new
categorical framing)
.

Proposition
7.9
records the
categorical form of a result that is well-established in
molecular symmetry theory.
The use of permutation-inversion groups in molecular
symmetry theory goes back to
Longuet-Higgins
[
205
]
, who introduced
the spectroscopic permutation-inversion group as the
symmetry group of the full molecular Hamiltonian under
feasible permutations of identical nuclei combined with
the parity operation
E^{*}
; Bunker and
Jensen
[
59
]
develop this framework
systematically for spectroscopic applications. This
spectroscopic group is not
G^{*}(G)
: the
Longuet-Higgins construction has a single global
E^{*}
,
whereas
G^{*}(G)
has
k
independent flips
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
,
the refinement needed to separate diastereomers from
enantiomers in molecules with multiple stereocentres.
That refinement was developed in the algebraic theory of
stereoisomerism due to Dugundji and
Ugi
[
81
]
and by Ruch
[
257
]
,
the latter introducing the “chirality function”

\sigma\colon\mathrm{Stereo}(G)\to\{+1,-1\}
used here.
The tartaric acid example of the chembox above is
classical, going back to van ’t Hoff’s original
demonstration of stereoisomerism in 1874.

What is specific to the tower construction is the
identification of
G^{*}
-elements with cokernel classes
of the automorphism exact sequence
\varphi_{4.5}
,
and the resulting characterisation of
\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
as a symmetry enrichment that removes
precisely the obstructions
[\pi_{\chi}]
and

[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]
identified in
§
7.1
.
The classical group-theoretic machinery is thus deployed
here to serve a specifically categorical purpose:
making the forcing argument of §
7.1

rigorous and showing that no smaller group-theoretic
datum would suffice.

Remark 7.11

(Minimality of the two factors)
.

Both factors of
G^{*}(G)=\mathrm{Aut}(G)\ltimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
are
necessary.
Without
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
, the action cannot identify equivalent
stereocentres: for instance, it would treat the two
labellings
(+,-)
and
(-,+)
of tartaric acid as distinct
objects, introducing spurious stereoisomers.
Without
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
in full (replacing it with a proper
quotient such as the single global
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
), the action
cannot relate enantiomers to diastereomers, as the
tartaric acid example makes explicit.
The semidirect product

\mathrm{Aut}(G)\ltimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
is therefore the smallest
group containing both factors with the required action
of
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
on
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
by index permutation,
and the action of Definition
7.5
realises
precisely the structure needed to separate the forcing
cokernel classes of §
7.1
while
identifying chemically equivalent relabellings.

Proposition
7.9
makes precise the
sense in which
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
is “
\mathcal{L}_{4}
with a symmetry
layer”: the
G^{*}
-action is exactly the additional
structure needed to separate the forcing cokernel classes,
and Remark
7.11
records that both
factors of
G^{*}
are independently required.
The chirality-labelled molecular graphs
(G,\sigma)
on
which this action operates are introduced in the next
section.

§7.3. Chirality-labelled molecular graphs and

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}

The forcing analysis of §
7.1
and the
group
G^{*}(G)=\mathrm{Aut}(G)\ltimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
of
§
7.2
together dictate the shape of

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
: its objects must carry a discrete chirality
datum at every stereocentre, and
G^{*}
must act on them
by symmetries of the category, not merely of the object set.
This section builds the ambient rewriting category in which

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
will operate — the chirality-aware refinement

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
— verifies adhesivity at the
ambient level (with chirality validity treated as an
admissibility predicate, so that DPO rewriting through
admissible rules carries over intact from
\mathcal{L}_{4}
), and
lifts the
G^{*}(G)
-action from objects to per-fibre
auto-equivalences of the category.
Section
7.4
will then define
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)

as the free strict SMC on
G^{*}
-equivariant DPO rules in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
.

Definition 7.12

(Chirality-labelled molecular graph)
.

A
chirality-labelled molecular graph
is a pair

(G,\sigma)
where
G\in\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
is a molecular graph
and
\sigma\colon\mathrm{Stereo}(G)\to\{+1,-1\}
is a

chirality function
assigning an orientation sign to
each stereocentre (Definition
7.6
).
The pair
(G,\sigma)
records exactly the datum absent
from
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
: a discrete orientation at every
stereocentre.
If
\mathrm{Stereo}(G)=\emptyset
, then
\sigma
has empty
domain and
(G,\emptyset)
is achiral.

Definition 7.13

(The category
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
)
.

The category
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
of chirality-labelled molecular
graphs has:

•

Objects
: chirality-labelled molecular graphs

(G,\sigma)
.

•

Morphisms
: label-preserving graph
monomorphisms
f\colon G\hookrightarrow H
that are

chirality-compatible
: for every stereocentre

v\in\mathrm{Stereo}(G)
, if
f(v)\in\mathrm{Stereo}(H)
then
\sigma_{H}(f(v))=\sigma_{G}(v)
.

•

Monoidal product
:
(G_{1},\sigma_{1})\sqcup(G_{2},\sigma_{2}):=(G_{1}\sqcup G_{2},\,\sigma_{1}\sqcup\sigma_{2})
, with chirality functions
concatenated over the disjoint union of stereocentre
sets.

•

Monoidal unit
:
(\emptyset,\emptyset)
.

Chemically: an object of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
is a molecule
together with a discrete orientation sign at each
stereocentre, and a morphism is a molecular-graph inclusion
that preserves those signs wherever it meets stereocentres.

The forgetful functor

U_{4.5}\colon\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}\to\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
,

(G,\sigma)\mapsto G
, is the tower-level bridge:

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
is
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
enriched by chirality data,
and
U_{4.5}
collapses that enrichment.
This is the categorical shadow of the
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}\rightsquigarrow\mathcal{L}_{4}
forgetful structure that will be
extended to full morphisms in §
7.4
.

Why chirality-compatibility is the right
morphism condition

A morphism
f\colon(G,\sigma)\to(H,\tau)
in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
is an
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
-monomorphism that preserves
every chirality label it transports.
Chemically: a reaction step that does not mechanistically
touch a stereocentre cannot change its configuration.
When
f(v)
remains a stereocentre in
H
, the label

\sigma_{G}(v)
must equal
\sigma_{H}(f(v))
; this is what
chirality-compatibility says.
Steps that
do
touch a stereocentre are handled by DPO:
the reactive vertex passes through the context graph
K

(where its reduced neighbour count makes it non-stereogenic
by Definition
7.6
(i)), so

\mathrm{Stereo}(K)
omits it, and it re-emerges in
R
with
a new chirality label assigned by the rule’s chirality lift.
The label change is a consequence of the pushout
construction, not of a morphism that flips
\sigma
in
transit.

Proposition 7.14

(Adhesivity at the ambient level;
admissibility for
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
)
.

Let
\widetilde{\mathbf{LGraph}}^{G^{*}}_{P}
be the typed attributed
graph category obtained from
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
by adjoining a
vertex attribute

\sigma\colon V(G)\to\{+1,-1,\star\}

to each graph, with the third value
\star
denoting
“no chirality datum”. This ambient category is adhesive
as a typed attributed graph category over the adhesive
base
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
in the sense of
Ehrig–Ehrig–Prange–Taentzer
[
84
]
.

The category
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
embeds as the full subcategory
whose objects
(G,\sigma)
satisfy the

chirality admissibility predicate
:
\sigma(v)\in\{+1,-1\}
for
v\in\mathrm{Stereo}(G)
and
\sigma(v)=\star

otherwise. DPO rewriting in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
is performed in
the ambient adhesive category, with admissibility verified
rule-by-rule: a rule
p=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)

is
admissible
when
L
,
K
, and
R
all satisfy
the predicate, and pushouts along admissible matches
preserve admissibility provided the rule’s chirality lift
specifies
\sigma
-values consistently with the

\mathrm{Stereo}
-pattern of
R
(cf. Remark
7.20
).

Proof.

Adhesivity of
\widetilde{\mathbf{LGraph}}^{G^{*}}_{P}
follows
directly from
[
84
]
Theorem 11.11: the
attribute category
\{+1,-1,\star\}
is discrete (hence
has all limits), and the typing functor assigning

\sigma\colon V(G)\to\{+1,-1,\star\}
to each graph is
a standard total vertex attribute, preserving pullbacks
trivially.

Admissibility preservation under pushouts along admissible
rules is verified locally: at every vertex of the pushout

H
, either
v
inherits its attribute from
G
(preserving
admissibility because
G
was admissible), or
v
inherits
from
R
via the rule (preserving admissibility because the
rule’s chirality lift was specified to match the

\mathrm{Stereo}
-pattern of
R
). No vertex inherits from both
sources unambiguously by the pushout property; agreement on
the overlap is enforced by the span morphisms’
chirality-compatibility.
∎

Remark 7.15

(Why admissibility rather than direct
adhesivity)
.

The full subcategory
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
is not in general
adhesive in isolation: pushouts in the ambient

\widetilde{\mathbf{LGraph}}^{G^{*}}_{P}
may yield graphs in which

\mathrm{Stereo}
has changed at some vertex (e.g. a 3-coordinate
vertex in
L
becoming 4-coordinate in
R
as new bonds
form), so a pushout of admissible objects need not be
admissible without an explicit chirality lift specifying
the new
\sigma
-values. Treating chirality validity as an
admissibility predicate inside the adhesive ambient
category, rather than seeking adhesivity of the validity-
restricted subcategory itself, parallels the treatment of
chemical validity in Chapter
6
and is the
standard pattern for attribute-dependent rewriting.

Remark 7.16

(Direct verification as a cross-check)
.

A direct construction of pullbacks and pushouts in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
confirms the abstract argument.
Given a cospan
(H_{1},\sigma_{1})\xrightarrow{f_{1}}(G,\sigma_{G})\xleftarrow{f_{2}}(H_{2},\sigma_{2})
, the pullback

(P,\sigma_{P})
has underlying graph
P=H_{1}\times_{G}H_{2}

(the
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
-pullback) and
\sigma_{P}(v):=\sigma_{1}(\pi_{1}(v))
for
v\in\mathrm{Stereo}(P)
; chirality-compatibility
of
f_{1},f_{2}
forces
\sigma_{1}(\pi_{1}(v))=\sigma_{2}(\pi_{2}(v))
whenever both projections are stereocentres, so

\sigma_{P}
is well-defined.
Pushouts along chirality-compatible monomorphisms are
constructed dually: the
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
-pushout carries a
chirality function obtained by gluing
\sigma_{1}
and

\sigma_{2}
, with agreement on the overlap enforced by the
span monomorphisms’ chirality-compatibility.
The Van Kampen condition in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
reduces to the
Van Kampen condition in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
via the comma-category
identification of the proof above.

Ambient adhesivity together with rule admissibility makes
DPO rewriting in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
behave as at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
: every
admissible rule
p=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)
in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
applied to a chirality-compatible match

m\colon L\hookrightarrow(G,\sigma)
has a unique pushout
complement
(D,\sigma_{D})
and a unique result
(H,\tau)

in the ambient adhesive category, with admissibility
preserved by the rule’s chirality lift specification.
The DPO machinery of
\mathcal{L}_{4}
thus carries over intact
to
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
; the tower-level novelty is only that
chirality labels now propagate deterministically through
every reaction step, rather than being absent.

Enantiomers as distinct objects in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}

In
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
, the graphs of
(R)
- and
(S)
-2-bromobutane
are
isomorphic objects
— the enantiomer swap

\pi_{\chi}
of §
7.1
is an isomorphism
witnessing this, and at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
it is an automorphism of

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
that conflates the two substrates.
In
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
they become
distinct non-isomorphic
objects

(G,+1)
and
(G,-1)
: any morphism between them
would have to map
\sigma(v_{\chi})=+1
to
\sigma(v_{\chi})=-1
at the stereocentre, violating chirality-compatibility.

The group element
E^{*}\in G^{*}
is not itself a morphism
of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
.
Rather,
E^{*}

induces
an endofunctor
E^{*}_{*}\colon\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}\to\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
(Remark
7.17

below) sending
(G,\sigma)\mapsto(G,-\sigma)
and
every chirality-compatible monomorphism to its

\sigma
-flipped counterpart.

E^{*}_{*}
relates the two enantiomers as objects in the same

G^{*}
-orbit but provides no morphism between them —
there is none.

This distinction is the passage from
\mathcal{L}_{4}
to
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

at the object level:
\pi_{\chi}
is an internal

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
-isomorphism but only an external

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
-endofunctor. Concretely, the endofunctor

E^{*}_{*}
projects through the forgetful functor
U_{4.5}
to
the automorphism
\pi_{\chi}\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))
via the
intertwining relation
U_{4.5}\circ E^{*}_{*}=\pi_{\chi}\circ U_{4.5}
, and the forcing cokernel class
[\pi_{\chi}]
is the
image of this projection.

The following diagram illustrates how chirality labels
propagate through a DPO derivation in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
.
The example is the
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
rule
(Example
6.41
) equipped with a specific
chirality lift
\sigma_{R}=-\sigma_{L}
at the reactive
carbon.

(8)

The rule’s left-hand side
(L_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}},+1)
carries
the substrate chirality label; the context

(K_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}},\emptyset)
has empty chirality function
because the reactive carbon in
K
has only three neighbours
(the C–X bond is broken, the C–Nu bond is not yet formed,
and the three substituent bonds are preserved through
K
),
hence fails condition (i) of
Definition
7.6
and lies outside

\mathrm{Stereo}(K)
; the right-hand side

(R_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}},-1)
carries the inverted chirality
label.
Given this chirality lift and a chirality-compatible match

m\colon L_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}\hookrightarrow(G_{R},+1)
,
adhesivity (Proposition
7.14
)
guarantees a unique pushout complement
(D,\sigma_{D})
and
a unique result
(H,-1)
.

The diagram establishes the
deterministic propagation

of chirality labels through a DPO derivation, given the
rule’s chirality lift.
It does not establish that the inverting lift

\sigma_{R}=-\sigma_{L}
is the
correct
chirality lift
for
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
rather than the retaining lift

\sigma_{R}=+\sigma_{L}
. Both lifts are

G^{*}
-equivariant; the selection of the inverting lift
is supplied by mechanism-specific input (back-side attack
geometry), as established in
Theorem
7.27
. The tower contribution at

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
is the
universal propagation
of the
chosen lift across
G^{*}
-orbits of substrates —
solvent-, temperature-, and substrate-independence —
not the selection of which lift to use.
The logical separation is tower-native: at the level of

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
, DPO machinery determines chirality
propagation once a chirality lift is given; which lift
realises a given mechanism is established in
§
7.4
–
7.5
.

Remark 7.17

(
G^{*}(G)
acts on the
G
-fibre of

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
by auto-equivalences)
.

The group
G^{*}(G)
acts naturally on the
G
-fibre of

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
— the full subcategory on objects

(G^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime})
with
G^{\prime}=G
as labelled graphs — via

(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}\colon(G,\sigma)\;\longmapsto\;\bigl(G,\;\bm{\epsilon}\cdot(\sigma\circ\pi^{-1})\bigr),

extended to morphisms within the fibre by composition with

\pi
on both source and target. This preserves
chirality-compatibility because the
\sigma
-action is
uniform across domain and codomain.
Each
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
is an equivalence of
the
G
-fibre with itself, with inverse

(\pi^{-1},\bm{\epsilon}^{-1})_{*}
; together these
form a strict
G^{*}(G)
-action on the
G
-fibre.

Globally, the per-graph actions assemble into a

groupoid action
of the stereochemical symmetry
groupoid
\mathcal{G}_{\rm st}
on
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
, with

\mathcal{G}_{\rm st}
having molecular graphs as objects
and
G^{*}(G)
as automorphism group at each
G
.
Equivalently, an element
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})\in G^{*}(G)
extends to an endofunctor of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}

acting non-trivially only on objects with underlying graph

G
, and as the identity on all other fibres.
Chemically:
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
relabels atoms
of
G
of the same element type according to
\pi
and
flips chirality at a subset of
G
’s stereocentres
determined by
\bm{\epsilon}
.
This lifts the object-level
G^{*}(G)
-action of
Definition
7.5
to a categorical action —
the data needed to formulate
G^{*}
-equivariance of DPO
rules in the next section.

Preview: equivariance as the content of

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

The auto-equivalences
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}

determine which DPO rules in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
are admitted as
morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
: a rule
p
is

G^{*}
-equivariant
if applying it commutes with
applying any
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
.
Equivariance does two things in the tower. First, it

propagates a chosen lift uniformly across

G^{*}
-orbits
, so that an
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
rule with the
inverting lift inverts every chirality-labelled substrate
in its orbit, regardless of solvent, temperature, or
substituent identity — the universality content of
Theorem
7.27
. Second, when a rule’s reaction
centre admits an involutive automorphism
\alpha
exchanging
new stereocentres,
\alpha
-equivariance
singles out
one of two possible product lifts
(Theorem
7.37
),
giving the categorical skeleton of the Woodward–Hoffmann
selection rules; the identification of the

\alpha
-equivariant lift with the thermally allowed product
is the content of Conjecture
7.39
.
The condition is defined precisely in
Definition
7.18
; its consequences
are the theorems of
§
7.5
–
7.6
.

The ambient rewriting category
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
is now in
place: chirality-labelled molecular graphs as objects,
chirality-compatible monomorphisms as morphisms, ambient
adhesivity together with admissibility guaranteeing
well-defined DPO rewriting through admissible rules, and a
per-fibre
G^{*}(G)
-action by auto-equivalences ready to
impose equivariance on the DPO rules.
The stereochemical level
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
, built as the free
SMC on
G^{*}
-equivariant DPO rules in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
, is
constructed in §
7.4
.

§7.4. Definition of

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)

Sections
7.2
–
7.3
assembled the
two pieces needed to define
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
: the
chirality symmetry group
G^{*}(G)=\mathrm{Aut}(G)\ltimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
and its action on the ambient rewriting category

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
by auto-equivalences.
This section imposes the
G^{*}
-equivariance condition on
DPO rules, defines
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
as the free strict symmetric
monoidal category those rules generate, and records the
universal property and tower coherence structure that follow.
The stereochemical theorems — Walden inversion, racemisation,
Woodward–Hoffmann — are then obtained in
§
7.5
–
7.6
as consequences of
the equivariance condition imposed here.

7.4.1.
G^{*}
-equivariant DPO rules

Definition 7.18

(
G^{*}
-equivariant DPO rule)
.

A DPO rule
p=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)
in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
is
G^{*}
-equivariant
if for every
object
(G,\sigma)\in\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
, every
chirality-compatible match
m\colon L\hookrightarrow(G,\sigma)
, and every element

(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})\in G^{*}(G)
, the
equivariance square below commutes; here the right-vertical
action of
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
on
(H,\tau)

denotes the corresponding element of
G^{*}(H)
obtained
by transporting
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})
through the
rule’s chirality lift (via the bijection of preserved
stereocentres
\mathrm{Stereo}(L)\cap\mathrm{Stereo}(R)\to\mathrm{Stereo}(H)

induced by
m
and the rule, extended to new stereocentres
of
R
by the rule’s specification of
\sigma_{R}
):

where
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}(m)\colon L\hookrightarrow(G,\,\bm{\epsilon}\cdot(\sigma\circ\pi^{-1}))
is the match obtained by applying the
endofunctor
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
to
m

(trivial on
L
since
L
is not the underlying graph
G
,
non-trivial on the codomain).
Equivalently: applying a
G^{*}
-action before the rule
fires gives the same result as applying the rule first and
then the
G^{*}
-action.
Since
\pi\in\mathrm{Aut}(G)
preserves
G
as a labelled graph
(it permutes vertices but preserves all edges and labels),
the underlying bond-graph transformation of
p
is identical
on both paths; only the chirality function transforms.

Remark 7.19

(Stereocentre creation and destruction under
the action)
.

For rules that preserve every stereocentre through the
derivation —
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
inversion is the principal
case — the bijection
\mathrm{Stereo}(G)\to\mathrm{Stereo}(H)
induced
by
m
and the rule is unambiguous, and the right-vertical
action of
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
on
(H,\tau)

acts on the corresponding stereocentre indices. For rules
that create new stereocentres in
R
(pericyclic ring
closures, addition reactions) or destroy stereocentres in
passing to
K
(the
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
ionisation step), the
chirality lift’s specification of
\sigma_{R}
at new
stereocentres or the absence of
\sigma_{K}
at destroyed
ones determines how
\bm{\epsilon}
extends to or
restricts from the product fibre. The equivariance
condition is verified rule-by-rule in
§
7.5
–
7.6
; in every case the
transport is determined by the rule’s data.

Remark 7.20

(Chirality lifts and the status of mechanism
specification)
.

Every DPO rule
p_{0}=(L_{0}\leftarrow K_{0}\rightarrow R_{0})

in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
admits a
chirality lift
: a DPO rule

\tilde{p}=(\tilde{L}\leftarrow\tilde{K}\rightarrow\tilde{R})
in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
such that

U_{4.5}(\tilde{p})=p_{0}
, where
U_{4.5}\colon\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}\to\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
is the forgetful functor of
Definition
7.13
.
The lift is constructed by taking
\tilde{K}=(K_{0},\emptyset)
— the context graph has empty chirality
function because its reactive atoms have reduced neighbour
count (the bonds being broken in
L\setminus K
leave
those atoms with fewer than four neighbours in
K
), so
they fail Definition
7.6
(i) and

\mathrm{Stereo}(K_{0})
excludes them — and by choosing
chirality functions
\sigma_{L}\colon\mathrm{Stereo}(L_{0})\to\{+1,-1\}
and
\sigma_{R}\colon\mathrm{Stereo}(R_{0})\to\{+1,-1\}
subject to the compatibility condition that

\sigma_{L}
and
\sigma_{R}
agree on vertices that appear in
both
L_{0}
and
R_{0}
unchanged (via
K_{0}
).

The pair
(\sigma_{L},\sigma_{R})
encodes the stereochemical
action of the rule.
Different lifts correspond to different stereochemical
behaviours of the same bond-graph mechanism:

•

A lift with
\sigma_{R}(v)=-\sigma_{L}(v)
at a reactive
stereocentre
v
encodes a
back-side attack

(inversion) mechanism.

•

A lift with
\sigma_{R}(v)=+\sigma_{L}(v)
encodes a

front-side attack
(retention) mechanism, as in

\mathrm{S_{N}i}
substitution.

The forgetful functor
U_{4.5}
collapses all lifts of
p_{0}

to the same
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-rule — confirming that
\mathcal{L}_{4}
is
blind to this stereochemical refinement.
This is the precise categorical sense in which
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

refines
\mathcal{L}_{4}
: the same bond-graph mechanism is enriched
with a chirality assignment, and different assignments
correspond to physically distinct stereochemical outcomes.

Which lift corresponds to a given mechanism is not
determined at this level.

Specifying a chirality lift records a stereochemical
hypothesis about the mechanism; both the inverting lift
(
\sigma_{R}=-\sigma_{L}
) and the retaining lift
(
\sigma_{R}=+\sigma_{L}
) are
G^{*}
-equivariant DPO rules
in the sense of Definition
7.18

(Theorem
7.27
). The selection between them
for a given physical mechanism is supplied by external
input: back-side attack geometry selects the inverting
lift for
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
, front-side attack selects the
retaining lift for
\mathrm{S_{N}i}
. The tower-level
separation is precise:
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
provides the ambient
data for chirality lifts;
G^{*}
-equivariance ensures
that any chosen lift propagates uniformly across every

G^{*}
-orbit of substrates; mechanism-specific input
selects which lift to use. The resulting morphisms of

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
are the
G^{*}
-equivariant DPO rules
together with their chirality lifts.

Equivariance as commutation with the

G^{*}
-action

Equivariance (Definition
7.18
)
is the condition that the DPO rule and the
G^{*}
-action
commute as operations on
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
: for every element

(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})\in G^{*}(G)
and every match

m
, applying the rule then the
G^{*}
-action yields the
same result as applying the
G^{*}
-action first (with its
induced match
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})\circ m
) and
then the rule.
The rule’s stereochemical behaviour is thus required to
be uniform across every element of every
G^{*}
-orbit.

Example.

Take the
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
rule
p_{\mathrm{SN2}}
with the
inverting chirality lift (
\sigma_{R}=-\sigma_{L}
) and the

G^{*}
-element
E^{*}=(\mathrm{id},(-1))
acting on a
single-stereocentre substrate.
The equivariance square reads:

Both paths yield the same result: the rule inverts
whichever enantiomer it is applied to.

E^{*}
-equivariance is precisely the condition that

both enantiomeric substrates are inverted, neither
privileged
.
The specific chirality labels in each box come from the
chirality lift
\sigma_{R}=-\sigma_{L}
; the equivariance
condition then forces the uniform behaviour across the

E^{*}
-orbit.
These two pieces together — chirality lift plus

G^{*}
-equivariance — determine the rule’s
stereochemical content.

Example 7.21

(Achiral reactions are automatically
equivariant)
.

If a DPO rule
p
has reaction centre avoiding every
stereocentre — formally,
m(L_{0}\setminus K_{0})\cap\mathrm{Stereo}(G)=\emptyset
for every match
m\colon L_{0}\hookrightarrow G
— then
p
is automatically

G^{*}
-equivariant.
The
\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
-factor of
G^{*}
acts only on chirality
labels at stereocentres, none of which are touched by
p
;
the
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
-factor permutes vertices of
G
, and applying
it before or after
p
gives equivalent results because

p
’s match is insensitive to the permutation’s action
outside the reaction centre.
Many simple organic transformations — proton transfer,
esterification at non-stereogenic centres,
\beta
-elimination
producing non-stereogenic alkenes — satisfy this vacuously.
Reactions that create new stereocentres (aldol condensation,
nucleophilic addition to prochiral carbonyls, pericyclic ring
closures) do not: they are equivariant only after a chirality
lift at the new stereocentre is specified, and selecting that
lift is the substantive content of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
analysis.
The non-trivial content of
G^{*}
-equivariance appears
precisely at rules that create, destroy, or invert a
stereocentre.

7.4.2. The categorical construction

Definition 7.22

(The stereochemical level
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
)
.

The
stereochemical level

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
is the free
strict symmetric monoidal category with:

•

Objects
: finite disjoint unions

(G_{1},\sigma_{1})\sqcup\cdots\sqcup(G_{n},\sigma_{n})

of chirality-labelled molecular graphs.

•

Generating morphisms
:
G^{*}
-equivariant
DPO rules in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}

(Definition
7.18
).

•

Morphisms
: composable sequences of

G^{*}
-equivariant DPO derivations, modulo the
free strict SMC congruence.

•

Monoidal product
: disjoint union

(G_{1},\sigma_{1})\sqcup(G_{2},\sigma_{2})
.

•

Monoidal unit
:
(\emptyset,\emptyset)
.

•

Symmetry
: component-swap isomorphisms

(G_{1},\sigma_{1})\sqcup(G_{2},\sigma_{2})\xrightarrow{\sim}(G_{2},\sigma_{2})\sqcup(G_{1},\sigma_{1})
.

The
forgetful functor

U_{4.5}\colon\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
sends every chirality-labelled object

(G,\sigma)\mapsto G
and every
G^{*}
-equivariant DPO
derivation to its underlying
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-derivation.
The
G^{*}
-action
on
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
is the
extension of the object-level action of
Remark
7.17
to morphisms:
for
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})\in G^{*}(G)
and any
generating morphism
p\colon(G,\sigma)\Rightarrow(H,\tau)
,
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}(p)
is the
image-rewritten derivation

(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}(G,\sigma)\Rightarrow(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}(H,\tau)
,
which is again a morphism of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
by equivariance
of
p
.

Proposition 7.23

(
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
is a strict SMC with

G^{*}
-action by SMC automorphisms)
.

Definition
7.22
yields a well-defined strict
symmetric monoidal category.
Moreover, for each
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})\in G^{*}(G)
,
the functor
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}\colon\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
is a strict SMC
automorphism, and the assignment

(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})\mapsto(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
is, for each labelled graph

G
, a group homomorphism

G^{*}(G)\to\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{SMC}}(\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P))
acting
non-trivially only on the
G
-fibre. Together these per-graph
homomorphisms assemble into a groupoid action of

\mathcal{G}_{\rm st}
on
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
.

Proof.

Category.

Composition of
G^{*}
-equivariant derivations is

G^{*}
-equivariant: given equivariance squares for

r_{1}\colon(G,\sigma)\Rightarrow(H,\tau)
and

r_{2}\colon(H,\tau)\Rightarrow(I,\upsilon)
, paste them
vertically along the common middle edge
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}(H,\tau)
; the pasted rectangle
commutes, giving the equivariance square for

r_{2}\circ r_{1}
.
The identity derivation (empty rewriting sequence) is
trivially equivariant.

Monoidal structure.

Disjoint union of chirality-labelled graphs is strictly
associative and unital with unit
(\emptyset,\emptyset)
,
inheriting these properties from disjoint union in

\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
.
The component-swap symmetry isomorphism commutes with the

G^{*}
-action because the action on a disjoint union is
defined componentwise:
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}

applied to
(G_{1},\sigma_{1})\sqcup(G_{2},\sigma_{2})

operates on each component independently, so swapping
components and then acting agrees with acting and then
swapping.
Hence the component swap is
G^{*}
-equivariant and is a
morphism of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
.

G^{*}
-action.

Each endofunctor
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
is an
SMC automorphism by Remark
7.17
:
it respects composition (because equivariance squares
compose, as in the category argument above), monoidal
product (by distributivity of the action over disjoint
union), and the component-swap symmetry (by the monoidal
structure argument above).
The action is strict:
(\pi_{1},\bm{\epsilon}_{1})_{*}\circ(\pi_{2},\bm{\epsilon}_{2})_{*}=(\pi_{1}\pi_{2},\,\bm{\epsilon}_{1}\cdot(\bm{\epsilon}_{2}\circ\pi_{1}^{-1}))_{*}
, which is
the group multiplication in
G^{*}
per
Definition
7.5
.
∎

Remark 7.24

(Tower extension type)
.

The extension
\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
is a

symmetry enrichment
: neither a decorator extension
(
\mathcal{L}_{0}\to\mathcal{L}_{1}
and its successors, which add a
numerical functor without changing the underlying SMC) nor
a structural extension (
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
, which rebuilds
the underlying SMC from scratch on DPO rules), but a third
pattern in which the underlying combinatorial data of

\mathcal{L}_{4}
are augmented with a group-equivariance condition
imposed on the rule set, with the resulting free SMC
fibred over
\mathcal{L}_{4}
via the forgetful functor
U_{4.5}
.
This type is introduced at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
and motivated in
Remark
7.1
; it will recur at
\mathcal{L}_{5}

(Euclidean-group enrichment of the configuration space)
and
\mathcal{L}_{6}
(
U(1)
-gauge enrichment of the electronic
Hilbert bundle), so it is worth naming here as one of the
three organising patterns of the tower.

Proposition 7.25

(Universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a strict symmetric monoidal category
equipped, for each labelled graph
G
appearing as the
underlying graph of some object in
\mathcal{C}
, with a
strict
G^{*}(G)
-action by SMC automorphisms on the

G
-fibre of
\mathcal{C}
. Equivalently,
\mathcal{C}

carries an action of the stereochemical symmetry groupoid

\mathcal{G}_{\rm st}
whose objects are labelled graphs
and whose automorphism group at each
G
is
G^{*}(G)
.
Any pair of assignments

•

objects of
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}

\to
objects of

\mathcal{C}
, respecting the per-graph

G^{*}(G)
-actions;

•

G^{*}
-equivariant DPO rules in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}

\to
morphisms of
\mathcal{C}
that are

G^{*}(G)
-equivariant on each fibre, compatible with
source and target assignments;

extends uniquely to a strict groupoid-equivariant SMC
functor
F\colon\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)\to\mathcal{C}
.

Proof.

By the universal property of the free strict SMC
(the analogue for
\mathcal{L}_{4}
is
Proposition
6.25
), any generator assignment
extends uniquely to a strict SMC functor.
The assumption that the generator assignment respects the

G^{*}
-actions, together with the compatibility with
source and target, ensures that the extended functor
intertwines the two
G^{*}
-actions: applying

(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
and
then
F
yields the same morphism in
\mathcal{C}
as
applying
F
first and then
(\pi,\bm{\epsilon})_{*}
in
\mathcal{C}
.
The free-SMC congruence preserves this intertwining because
it is closed under composition and monoidal product, both
of which are
G^{*}
-equivariant by
Proposition
7.23
.
Hence
F
is
G^{*}
-equivariant.
∎

7.4.3. Tower coherence

The universal property of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
locks its position
in the tower: every construction on the lower levels lifts
coherently.

Proposition 7.26

(Vertical tower coherence)
.

The chain of forgetful functors

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)\;\xrightarrow{U_{4.5}}\;\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)\;\xrightarrow{U_{4}}\;\mathcal{L}_{3}(P)\;\xrightarrow{U_{3}}\;\mathcal{L}_{2}(P)\;\xrightarrow{U_{2}}\;\mathcal{L}_{1}(P)\;\xrightarrow{U_{1}}\;\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

consists of strict SMC functors, each of which forgets the
extension data introduced at its source level.
The composition
U_{1}\circ U_{2}\circ U_{3}\circ U_{4}\circ U_{4.5}
sends every chirality-labelled reaction network
in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
to its stoichiometric shadow in

\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)
.
Dually, any functor
F\colon\mathcal{L}_{j}(P)\to\mathcal{C}
for

j\leq 4
has a canonical lift to a functor

\tilde{F}\colon\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)\to\mathcal{C}
given by
precomposition with the forgetful chain:

\tilde{F}\;=\;F\circ U_{j+1}\circ\cdots\circ U_{4.5}.

This is the unique lift that is
G^{*}
-trivial on the new
chirality data — i.e., that sends an object

(G,\sigma)\in\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
to the same image in

\mathcal{C}
regardless of the value of
\sigma
. Lifts
that distinguish
(G,+1)
from
(G,-1)
in
\mathcal{C}

require additional structure on
\mathcal{C}
and are not
unique.

Proof.

Each
U_{k}
is a strict SMC functor by construction at its
level (decorator extensions via functor forgetting,
structural extension
U_{4}
via DPO-derivation forgetting,

U_{4.5}
via chirality-function forgetting). Strict SMC
functors compose to strict SMC functors, so the full chain

U_{1}\circ U_{2}\circ U_{3}\circ U_{4}\circ U_{4.5}
is a
strict SMC functor. The canonical lift

\tilde{F}=F\circ U_{j+1}\circ\cdots\circ U_{4.5}

is then a strict SMC functor as a composition of strict SMC
functors; uniqueness as a
G^{*}
-trivial extension is
immediate from
U_{4.5}
’s definition (it identifies all
chirality assignments on a given underlying graph).
∎

Proposition
7.26
has a direct
consequence for tower-native computation: thermodynamic
data
F_{H},F_{S}^{G}
(from
\mathcal{L}_{1},\mathcal{L}_{2}
), kinetic data

F_{P}
(from
\mathcal{L}_{3}
), and mechanistic data (from
\mathcal{L}_{4}
)
all remain valid and consistent when the stereochemical
level is added above them.
No lower-level theorem needs to be reproved at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
:
the strict SMC functoriality of the forgetful chain

U_{4.5},U_{4},\ldots,U_{1}
ensures that every

\mathcal{L}_{j}
-datum extends canonically to
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
by
precomposition with
U_{j+1}\circ\cdots\circ U_{4.5}
.
This is what allows stereochemical statements at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

to be stated against the background of all the numerical and
structural data already available at lower levels, without
additional reconstruction.

The stereochemical theorems of §
7.5

— Walden inversion, racemisation, and net retention
through double inversion — can now be stated and proved
using the
G^{*}
-equivariance condition imposed here
(which propagates a chosen chirality lift uniformly across

G^{*}
-orbits) together with mechanism-specific input
(which selects the chirality lift), against the
tower-level machinery established in this section.

§7.5. Stereochemistry as theorems at

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

Sections
7.2
–
7.4
built

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
to resolve the two forcing cokernel classes

[\pi_{\chi}]
and
[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]
of
§
7.1
.
This section collects the payoff.
Four classical results of stereochemistry — Walden
inversion (§
7.5.1
), racemisation via

\mathrm{S_{N}1}
(§
7.5.2
), net retention
via double inversion (§
7.5.3
), and the
categorical structure of enantiomers
(§
7.5.4
) — become theorems at

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, deducible from the
G^{*}
-equivariance
condition and the DPO machinery alone.
No quantum mechanics, no 3D coordinates, and no
experimental postulates beyond the chirality lift of each
rule and the graph-theoretic detection of stereocentres
(Definition
7.6
) are invoked.

The tower-level contribution of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
is the

orbit-uniformity
of stereochemical outcome:

G^{*}
-equivariance propagates a given mechanism’s
stereochemistry uniformly across every chirality-labelled
substrate in each
G^{*}
-orbit, with the mechanism’s
directional choice (inversion vs retention) supplied as an
external input via the chirality lift. Solvent- and
temperature-invariance, where empirically observed, falls
outside
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
’s modelling scope; the level provides
the orbit-uniform shadow of those invariances, not their derivation.

7.5.1. Walden inversion

In 1896 Paul Walden observed that malic acid could be
converted to chlorosuccinic acid and back through a sequence
of reagents, with the recovered malic acid displaying

flipped
optical rotation: the configuration had been
inverted somewhere in the cycle without any obvious
cause
[
293
]
.
The mechanism remained contested for four decades.
Hughes and Ingold’s systematic kinetic work in the
1930s
[
151
]
established that bimolecular
nucleophilic substitution (
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
) proceeds by
back-side attack: the nucleophile approaches from the face
opposite the leaving group, forcing a “Walden inversion”
of the four substituents around the reactive carbon.
Cowdrey, Hughes, Ingold, Masterman, and Scott provided the
definitive stereochemical evidence in
1937
[
67
]
: every
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
reaction
gives
complete
inversion of configuration, on every
substrate, in every solvent, at every temperature.

This empirical universality demands a structural explanation
that is insensitive to the continuous parameters
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

does not know about (solvent, temperature, conformer).
At
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, universality is a theorem.

Theorem 7.27

(Walden inversion at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
)
.

Let
p_{0}^{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
be the
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-level
\mathrm{S_{N}2}

rule (Example
6.41
).
In
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
, this rule admits exactly two chirality
lifts at the reactive stereocentre
v
:

•

the
inverting
lift

\tilde{p}_{-}\colon\ \sigma_{R}(v)=-\sigma_{L}(v)
;

•

the
retaining
lift

\tilde{p}_{+}\colon\ \sigma_{R}(v)=+\sigma_{L}(v)
.

Both lifts are
G^{*}
-equivariant
(Definition
7.18
), and each,
together with its
G^{*}
-orbit, defines a family of DPO
rules in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
acting uniformly across all
chirality-labelled substrates.

The empirical back-side-attack topology of the

\mathrm{S_{N}2}
transition state selects the inverting lift.
With this selection, for every chirality-labelled substrate

(G,\sigma)
admitting a chirality-compatible match

m\colon L_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}\hookrightarrow(G,\sigma)

with reactive stereocentre
v
, the product satisfies

\sigma^{\prime}(f(v))\;=\;-\sigma(v),

where
f\colon R_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}\hookrightarrow H
is the “comatch".

Proof.

Identification of the two lifts.

The
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-level rule has
L_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
,
K
, and

R_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
with fixed bond-graph structure
(Example
6.41
).
The reactive carbon
v
has four distinct substituents in
both
L_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
and
R_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
(three
from the R-group, plus either X or Nu), so
v\in\mathrm{Stereo}(L_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}})\cap\mathrm{Stereo}(R_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}})
with a single value

\sigma_{L}(v),\sigma_{R}(v)\in\{+1,-1\}
each.
In the context graph
K
the carbon has reduced neighbour
count (the bond to X has been removed without the bond to
Nu being added), hence
v\notin\mathrm{Stereo}(K)
by
Definition
7.6
(i).
A chirality lift of
p_{0}^{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
is thus a choice
of
(\sigma_{L}(v),\sigma_{R}(v))\in\{+1,-1\}^{2}
, modulo
overall sign (a global flip at
v
produces the same rule
up to
G^{*}
-relabelling).
The quotient gives exactly two lifts:
\tilde{p}_{-}
with

\sigma_{R}(v)=-\sigma_{L}(v)
(opposite signs) and

\tilde{p}_{+}
with
\sigma_{R}(v)=+\sigma_{L}(v)
(same
signs).

Each lift is
G^{*}
-equivariant.

The equivariance square for
\tilde{p}_{-}
with

E^{*}=(\mathrm{id},-\mathbf{1})\in G^{*}(G)
(for
k=1
,
this is
(\mathrm{id},(-1))
) is verified as follows.
Taking any substrate
(G,+1)
, applying
\tilde{p}_{-}

yields
(H,-1)
.
Applying
E^{*}
to both sides:

E^{*}\cdot(G,+1)=(G,-1),\qquad E^{*}\cdot(H,-1)=(H,+1).

Applying
\tilde{p}_{-}
to
(G,-1)
yields
(H,+1)
by the
lift’s definition (
\sigma_{R}=-\sigma_{L}
).
Both paths around the equivariance square give
(H,+1)
:
the square commutes.
An analogous verification holds for
\tilde{p}_{+}
: applying

\tilde{p}_{+}
to
(G,+1)
yields
(H,+1)
, and
E^{*}_{*}(H,+1)=(H,-1)
; applying
\tilde{p}_{+}
to
E^{*}_{*}(G,+1)=(G,-1)
yields
(H,-1)
.
Squares commute for both lifts.

Universality of the inverting family.

Fix the inverting lift
\tilde{p}_{-}
.
For any chirality-compatible match
m\colon L_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}\hookrightarrow(G,\sigma)
,
chirality-compatibility forces

\sigma(m(v))=\sigma_{L}(v)
, and the DPO pushout in the
ambient adhesive category for
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}

(Proposition
7.14
; admissibility
of the rule’s chirality lift is direct from

\sigma_{R}(v)=-\sigma_{L}(v)
at the unique reactive
stereocentre) produces a unique comatch

f\colon R_{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}\hookrightarrow H
with
\sigma^{\prime}(f(v))=\sigma_{R}(v)=-\sigma_{L}(v)=-\sigma(v)
.
The uniform relation
\sigma^{\prime}(f(v))=-\sigma(v)
thus holds
on every substrate
(G,\sigma)
and every chirality-compatible
match, without substrate-, solvent-, or temperature-dependent
caveats.
∎

Remark 7.28

(Tower reading of Walden inversion)
.

Theorem
7.27
decomposes cleanly along the tower:

•

At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
: a single rule

p_{0}^{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
exists, carrying no stereochemical
information.
The inversion/retention distinction is

\mathcal{L}_{4}
-invisible.

•

At
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
: two chirality lifts exist,

\tilde{p}_{-}
and
\tilde{p}_{+}
, collapsing to the same

p_{0}^{\mathrm{S_{N}2}}
under
U_{4.5}
.
The choice between them is a mechanism-specific
input (back-side vs. front-side attack).

•

Given the back-side-attack input,
G^{*}
-equivariance
of
\tilde{p}_{-}
propagates the inversion uniformly
across every chirality-labelled substrate in every

G^{*}
-orbit.

The tower contribution is thus
universality of
propagation
, not
selection of direction
.
The direction comes from the mechanism’s topology;

G^{*}
-equivariance supplies orbit-uniformity over

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-substrates, which is the level’s shadow of
the empirically observed solvent- and temperature-independence.
Below
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, the forgetful functor
U_{4.5}
strips
the chirality label and both lifts collapse to the same

\mathcal{L}_{4}
-derivation; above
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, any tower-coherent
extension preserves the universality, since the higher-level
construction (which extends
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
by additional
data: 3D coordinates at
\mathcal{L}_{5}
, electronic structure at

\mathcal{L}_{6}
) embeds every
G^{*}
-equivariant

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-morphism as a corresponding equivariant
morphism at the higher level by construction, with the
forgetful functor down to
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
recovering the original.

Walden inversion: tower content and
empirical universality

Theorem
7.27
explains the universality of
Cowdrey et al.’s 1937 empirical observation

[
67
]
once back-side attack is supplied as
the mechanism-specific input. Its two inputs are:

•

the back-side-attack topology of
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
,
encoded as the chirality lift
\sigma_{R}=-\sigma_{L}
;

•

G^{*}
-equivariance, enforcing uniform behaviour
across
G^{*}
-orbits of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-substrates.

The categorical content is the uniform
\sigma^{\prime}(f(v))=-\sigma(v)
relation across every chirality-compatible
match. Solvent- and temperature-independence of the
empirical observation falls outside
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
’s
modelling scope (the level has no parameter for either),
so the theorem cannot directly establish it; what the
theorem provides is the consistent shadow at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

of an empirically solvent- and temperature-independent
phenomenon. No solvent model, no potential energy
surface, no quantum treatment of the transition state is
used — not because
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
proves their irrelevance,
but because the universality content visible at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

is the orbit-uniform sign relation, and that content is
solvent- and temperature-agnostic.

Mechanisms violating universality — those whose
stereochemical outcome depends on solvent, temperature, or
substrate type — are not single
G^{*}
-equivariant

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-morphisms; they are mixtures of two or more

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-morphisms whose relative weights require

\mathcal{L}_{3}
-level data (rate constants).
The
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
mechanism (next subsection) is an
example: it is not a single equivariant rule but two
equivariant rules sharing an achiral intermediate.

7.5.2. Racemisation via

\mathrm{S_{N}1}

Remark 7.29

(Racemisation, for mathematicians)
.

A
racemic mixture
is an equal-parts mixture of the
two enantiomers of a chiral molecule.
It has zero net optical rotation because the contributions
of
(G,+1)
and
(G,-1)
cancel.

Racemisation
is a process that converts an
enantiomerically pure starting material into a racemic
mixture; it destroys stereochemical information.
In tower language: racemisation is the passage from a
non-
E^{*}
-symmetric state (pure enantiomer) to an

E^{*}
-symmetric state (racemic mixture).
The
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
mechanism achieves this by passing
through a planar intermediate in which the reactive carbon
is no longer a stereocentre.

Theorem 7.30

(Racemisation at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
)
.

Let
p_{\mathrm{S_{N}1}}=p_{2}\circ p_{1}
be the two-step

\mathrm{S_{N}1}
derivation of Example
6.42
,
lifted to
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
.
The step
p_{1}
is the ionisation (C–X heterolysis); the
step
p_{2}
is the nucleophilic attack on the carbocation.
The following hold:

(i)

p_{1}
is stereochemistry-destroying.

The
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-level
L
of
p_{1}
contains the reactive
carbon
v
at four neighbours (three R-group bonds and
the C–X bond), so
v\in\mathrm{Stereo}(L)
. The product
side
R
has
v
at three neighbours (the cation, with
C–X removed), so
v\notin\mathrm{Stereo}(R)
and
\sigma_{R}

is undefined at
v
. Consequently
p_{1}
admits exactly
two
G^{*}
-equivariant chirality lifts at
v
, one
with
\sigma_{L}(v)=+1
and one with
\sigma_{L}(v)=-1
;
each lift applies via chirality-compatibility to the
corresponding substrate enantiomer, and both yield the
same achiral carbocation intermediate

p_{1}(G,+1)\;=\;p_{1}(G,-1)\;=\;(G_{1},\emptyset).

The chirality datum is destroyed in passing to
R

because
v
ceases to be a stereocentre.

(ii)

p_{2}
admits two
G^{*}
-equivariant
chirality lifts.

The
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-level
R
of
p_{2}
restores the reactive
carbon to four neighbours (bonded to the R-group and to
Nu), making it a stereocentre again.
The chirality lift
\sigma_{R}(v)\in\{+1,-1\}
is a
free choice; both values yield
G^{*}
-equivariant
DPO rules in
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
(by the argument of
Theorem
7.27
).
Neither lift is distinguished by any
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-datum,
so both are valid morphisms of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
from

(G_{1},\emptyset)
.

Consequently: starting from either pure enantiomer, the
composite
p_{2}\circ p_{1}
produces both product enantiomers
as valid morphism targets in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
.
In chemical terms:
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
gives racemisation.

Proof.

Part (i): stereochemistry-destruction.

In the
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-level rule
p_{1}
, the reactive carbon
v

has four neighbours in
L
(three R-group bonds plus the
C–X bond) and three in
R
(the carbocation, after C–X
removal). By Definition
7.6
(i),

v\in\mathrm{Stereo}(L)
but
v\notin\mathrm{Stereo}(R)
, so the
chirality lift specifies
\sigma_{L}(v)\in\{+1,-1\}
but
imposes no constraint on
\sigma_{R}
at
v
. Two

G^{*}
-equivariant chirality lifts of
p_{1}
thus exist,
one with
\sigma_{L}(v)=+1
and one with
\sigma_{L}(v)=-1
;
each lift is G*-equivariant trivially (the action on

\sigma_{R}
at
v
is vacuous), and each applies via
chirality-compatibility to the substrate enantiomer with
matching
\sigma(m(v))
. Both lifts produce the same
intermediate
(G_{1},\emptyset)
: the chirality datum is
lost when
v
ceases to be a stereocentre.

Part (ii): two lifts of
p_{2}
.

In
p_{2}
, the
R
-side has the reactive carbon at four
neighbours (bonded to the R-group and to Nu).
If Nu is distinct from the three R-group neighbours,
v\in\mathrm{Stereo}(R)
, and the chirality lift specifies a
value
\sigma_{R}(v)\in\{+1,-1\}
.
The
L
-side of
p_{2}
has the carbocation, three-coordinated
(
v\notin\mathrm{Stereo}(L)
), so
\sigma_{L}
is not
constrained.
Choosing
\sigma_{R}(v)=+1
gives one DPO rule

\tilde{p}_{2}^{+}
; choosing
\sigma_{R}(v)=-1
gives another,

\tilde{p}_{2}^{-}
.
Both are
G^{*}
-equivariant by the argument of
Theorem
7.27
(with the retaining/inverting
labelling playing no role, since the
L
-side has no

\sigma_{L}
to compare).
Neither is distinguished by any datum available in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
: the achiral intermediate
(G_{1},\emptyset)

carries no information about which product chirality is
“preferred”.
Both
(G_{1},\emptyset)\Rightarrow(H,+1)
and
(G_{1},\emptyset)\Rightarrow(H,-1)
are valid morphisms of

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
.

Consequence.

The composite
p_{2}\circ p_{1}
has two valid completions
from any starting enantiomer.
Starting from
(G,+1)
:
p_{1}
produces
(G_{1},\emptyset)
,
and
p_{2}
produces either
(H,+1)
or
(H,-1)
, each a
valid
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
-morphism.
Analogously from
(G,-1)
.
Thus both product enantiomers are reachable from either
starting enantiomer.
∎

Remark 7.31

(Categorical content vs. chemical corollary)
.

The correct categorical statement of
Theorem
7.30
is deterministic:

the
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
mechanism at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
provides
two valid morphisms from
(G_{1},\emptyset)
to the product
enantiomers, with no
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-datum preferring one over
the other
.
The
50{:}50
ratio of the racemic product mixture is a
corollary requiring
\mathcal{L}_{3}
-level data: the rate constants

k^{+}
and
k^{-}
for the two
p_{2}
-completions must be
equal.
Equality of these rates follows from the
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-level
symmetry (both lifts are in the same
G^{*}
-orbit of
rules at the achiral intermediate), but the quantitative
ratio is a
\mathcal{L}_{3}
computation, not a
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
one.

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
supplies the structural claim
(indistinguishability of the two products at the category
level);
\mathcal{L}_{3}
converts it into population statistics.

Remark 7.32

(Tower reading of racemisation)
.

Racemisation is the tower’s account of
loss of
stereochemical information
at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.
Part (i) says that
p_{1}
collapses the
G^{*}
-orbit

\{(G,+1),(G,-1)\}
to a single object
(G_{1},\emptyset)

— the chirality datum is destroyed because the
intermediate has no stereocentre.
Part (ii) says that
p_{2}
is then non-deterministic from
the intermediate: both elements of the product

G^{*}
-orbit
\{(H,+1),(H,-1)\}
are reachable.
The chirality datum is regenerated, but without memory of
what it was before
p_{1}
.

Contrast with the
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
case
(Theorem
7.27
): there,
the rule is injective on
G^{*}
-orbits (
(G,+1)\mapsto(H,-1)
and
(G,-1)\mapsto(H,+1)
, a bijection
between source and target orbits) and fully deterministic.
Stereochemical information is
conserved but
transformed
: a signed datum in, a signed datum out, with
the sign flipped.
The contrast between
\mathrm{S_{N}2}

(information-preserving, sign-inverting) and

\mathrm{S_{N}1}
(information-destroying, then
information-regenerating without memory) is visible at

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
as the difference between an injective and a
non-injective map on
G^{*}
-orbits of substrates.

7.5.3. Net retention via double inversion:
neighbouring group participation

The previous two subsections treated single-step
stereochemical events:
\mathrm{S_{N}2}
preserves and
inverts the chirality label in one rule application
(Theorem
7.27
);
\mathrm{S_{N}1}
destroys and
regenerates it across two rules
(Theorem
7.30
).
A third case, due to Winstein
[
208
]
, combines
two inversion steps to give
net retention
: the
reaction proceeds with inverted configuration at the
intermediate and inverted again at the product, so the
initial and final configurations match.
This mechanism is neighbouring group participation (NGP),
also called anchimeric assistance.

Remark 7.33

(Neighbouring group participation,
for mathematicians)
.

In NGP, the substrate carries a nucleophilic heteroatom or

\pi
-bond positioned close to the reactive carbon — for
example, a
\beta
-acetoxy group on a cyclohexyl tosylate,
Winstein’s classical system.
When the leaving group departs, the neighbouring
nucleophile attacks the reactive carbon
from the
opposite face
, forming a bridged intermediate (in
Winstein’s case, a five-membered acyloxonium ring).
The reactive carbon remains four-coordinated throughout:
it loses the bond to the leaving group but immediately
forms a bond to the bridging nucleophile, hence is a
stereocentre in the bridged intermediate.
An external nucleophile then attacks the bridged
intermediate, again from the opposite face, opening the
ring and giving the final product.
The classical experimental observation is that the reaction
gives
complete retention
of configuration at the
reactive carbon, despite involving two nucleophilic attack
steps
[
208
]
.
Historically this was puzzling because neither step
individually retains: each inverts.
Two inversions give retention.

Theorem 7.34

(Net retention via double inversion at

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
)
.

Let
(G,\sigma)
be a chirality-labelled substrate with
stereocentre
v
, and let
r_{1},r_{2}
be
G^{*}
-equivariant
DPO derivations such that:

•

r_{1}
has the inverting chirality lift at
v

(back-side attack by the neighbouring nucleophile);

•

r_{2}
has the inverting chirality lift at
v

(back-side attack by the external nucleophile on the
bridged intermediate).

Then the composition
r_{2}\circ r_{1}
satisfies

\sigma_{\mathrm{final}}(v)\;=\;\sigma(v),

i.e. the net stereochemical outcome at
v
is retention of
configuration.

Proof.

By Theorem
7.27
applied to
r_{1}
, the
intermediate chirality label satisfies

\sigma_{\mathrm{int}}(v)=-\sigma(v)
.
Applying Theorem
7.27
to
r_{2}
with
substrate
(\cdot,\sigma_{\mathrm{int}})
:

\sigma_{\mathrm{final}}(v)=-\sigma_{\mathrm{int}}(v)=-(-\sigma(v))=\sigma(v)
.
∎

The following diagram tracks the chirality label through
the two-step sequence in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
:

(9)

The chirality label at
v
begins at
\sigma
, is inverted
to
-\sigma
by the internal displacement
r_{1}
(formation
of the bridged intermediate), and is inverted back to

\sigma
by the external opening
r_{2}
.
The composition
r_{2}\circ r_{1}
is a morphism of

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
that preserves the chirality label at
v

while making new bonds: a retention mechanism built from two
inversion steps.

What the theorem says about NGP chemistry

Theorem
7.34
recovers, in two lines, a result that
historically required careful experimental design to
establish.
Winstein’s evidence
[
208
]
included: rate
acceleration (the neighbouring group assists the
ionisation, giving first-order kinetics despite formal
bimolecular reactants), racemisation in the absence of
external nucleophile (the bridged intermediate can open
from either face, analogous to
Theorem
7.30
(ii)), and
complete
retention
when the external nucleophile is present in
excess (the two sequential back-side attacks dominate the
kinetics).

At
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, the argument is structural and does not
require the ion-pair analysis that made Winstein’s original
treatment subtle.
Two
G^{*}
-equivariant back-side-attack DPO rules
compose to a rule that preserves the chirality label at

v
.
The bridged intermediate is a valid object in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)

because the reactive carbon remains four-coordinated
throughout — the bond to the leaving group is replaced
by the bond to the bridging nucleophile — so the carbon
is still a stereocentre in the intermediate, with its
chirality label inverted by the first step.

The theorem generalises immediately to longer sequences:
any sequence of
2n
back-side-attack steps at
v
gives
net retention; any sequence of
2n+1
gives net inversion.
This is the
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-level parity rule for nucleophilic
substitution sequences, recovered from
Theorem
7.27
by composition.

7.5.4. Enantiomers in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

The three previous subsections demonstrated the tower at
work on known chemistry.
This subsection turns the direction around: using the
tower construction, the
definition
of enantiomers
that the construction makes available is given, and shown
to capture the classical chemical notion.

Definition 7.35

(Enantiomers in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
)
.

Two objects
(G,\sigma)
and
(G^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime})
of

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
are
enantiomers
if:

(i)

U_{4.5}(G,\sigma)=U_{4.5}(G^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime})
: they
share the same underlying molecular graph (
G=G^{\prime}
);
and

(ii)

(G^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime})=E^{*}\cdot(G,\sigma)
as

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
-objects, i.e.
\sigma^{\prime}=-\sigma
as
chirality functions on
\mathrm{Stereo}(G)
.

A chirality-labelled molecular graph
(G,\sigma)
has a

distinct
enantiomer iff no
\pi\in\mathrm{Aut}(G)

satisfies
\sigma\circ\pi^{-1}=-\sigma
, equivalently,
iff
-\sigma
is not in the
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
-orbit of
\sigma
;
otherwise
(G,\sigma)\cong(G,-\sigma)
in

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
via
\pi
and the molecule is its own
enantiomer (
achiral
). Two paradigm cases:

•

\mathrm{Stereo}(G)=\emptyset
: trivially

(G,\emptyset)=E^{*}\cdot(G,\emptyset)
— achiral
without stereocentres.

•

Meso compounds.

\mathrm{Stereo}(G)\neq\emptyset

but the graph automorphism group
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
contains an
element
\pi
mapping
\sigma
to
-\sigma
— achiral
despite stereocentres. The textbook example is
meso-tartaric acid (§
7.2
), where the
centre-of-symmetry exchange of the two stereocentres
maps
(+1,-1)
to
(-1,+1)
.

A molecule is
chiral
iff it has a distinct
enantiomer.

Proposition 7.36

(Properties of enantiomers)
.

Let
(G,+1)
and
(G,-1)
be enantiomers in

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
(single stereocentre,
k=1
).

(i)

Distinct, non-isomorphic objects.

(G,+1)\not\cong(G,-1)
in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
:
there is no isomorphism between them.

(ii)

Same
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-image.

U_{4.5}(G,+1)=U_{4.5}(G,-1)=G
: enantiomers are
indistinguishable at every level below
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.

(iii)

Same
G^{*}
-orbit.

(G,-1)=E^{*}\cdot(G,+1)
: the two enantiomers are
related by the abstract parity, and their
G^{*}
-orbit
has exactly two elements.

(iv)

No chirality-neutral interconversion.

No morphism
(G,+1)\to(G,-1)
in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)

leaves the underlying molecular graph unchanged.

(v)

G^{*}
-equivariant transport.

Every
G^{*}
-equivariant DPO derivation

r\colon(G,+1)\Rightarrow(H,\tau)
determines a
derivation
E^{*}_{*}(r)\colon(G,-1)\Rightarrow(H,-\tau)
on the enantiomeric substrate, giving the
enantiomeric product.
The two derivations are in the same
G^{*}
-orbit.

Proof.

(i).

Suppose for contradiction that a morphism
r\colon(G,+1)\to(H,-1)
in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
exists with
G=H
as
labelled graphs. Since morphisms compose, it suffices to
consider a single DPO rule application
p=(L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R)
with match
m\colon L\hookrightarrow(G,+1)
and comatch
f\colon R\hookrightarrow(G,-1)

that achieves this on the reactive stereocentre
v
;
chirality-compatibility then forces
\sigma_{L}(v)=+1
and

\sigma_{R}(v)=-1
, so the rule has
\sigma_{R}(v)=-\sigma_{L}(v)
as its chirality lift.

The rule must also have
L=R
as labelled graphs (since
applying
p
via
m
produces
H=G
as labelled graphs,
and
f
matches
R
into
H
). Apply
E^{*}=(\mathrm{id},-\mathbf{1})\in G^{*}(G)
to the equivariance square of

p
. Path 1:
p
applied to
(G,+1)
yields
(G,-1)
,
then
E^{*}_{*}
yields
(G,+1)
. Path 2:
E^{*}_{*}
applied to

(G,+1)
yields
(G,-1)
, then
p
applied to

(G,-1)
yields — by
\sigma_{R}(v)=-\sigma_{L}(v)
and
the new
\sigma_{L}(v)=-1
— the object
(G,+1)
.

The two paths agree on the underlying graph but the
intermediate objects
E^{*}_{*}(G,-1)=(G,+1)
(Path 1) and

E^{*}_{*}(G,+1)=(G,-1)
(Path 2) are distinct. Thus

G^{*}
-equivariance of
p
requires

(G,+1)=(G,-1)
as
\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
-objects, which is
false. Therefore no such rule
p
is
G^{*}
-equivariant,
and no chirality-flipping morphism exists in

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
with
G
fixed.

(ii).

U_{4.5}
forgets
\sigma
, so
U_{4.5}(G,\pm 1)=G
by
definition.
Enantiomers are therefore indistinguishable at all lower
tower levels: their thermodynamic data
F_{H}
,
F_{S}^{G}

(from
\mathcal{L}_{1},\mathcal{L}_{2}
), kinetic data
F_{P}
(from
\mathcal{L}_{3}
),
and bond-graph mechanisms (at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
) are all identical.

(iii).

E^{*}=(\mathrm{id},-\mathbf{1})\in G^{*}(G)
sends

(G,+1)\mapsto(G,-1)
by Definition
7.5
.
The orbit
\{(G,+1),(G,-1)\}
has size at most two (two
labellings at a single stereocentre); it has size exactly
two because
(G,+1)\neq(G,-1)
as objects of

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}^{G^{*}}
(different chirality functions).

(iv).

The argument given for (i) above proves the stronger
statement that no morphism
(G,+1)\to(G,-1)
with
G

fixed exists in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
, equivariantly or not —
not just no isomorphism. Statement (iv) is therefore
established already by the proof of (i).

(v).

By
G^{*}
-equivariance of
r

(Definition
7.18
):

E^{*}_{*}\bigl(r((G,+1))\bigr)\;=\;r\bigl(E^{*}_{*}((G,+1))\bigr)\;=\;r\bigl((G,-1)\bigr).

The
E^{*}
-image of the original product is
E^{*}_{*}(H,\tau)=(H,-\tau)
; by
G^{*}
-equivariance this equals the
result of applying
r
to
(G,-1)
.
Hence
r((G,-1))=(H,-\tau)
: the enantiomeric substrate
yields the enantiomeric product.
∎

Enantiomers: the tower account

Properties (i)–(v) together reproduce, from the tower
construction, the full chemical concept of a pair of
enantiomers.

Property (ii) encodes why enantiomers have identical
achiral physical properties: same boiling point, same
melting point, same NMR spectrum in an achiral solvent,
same reaction rates with achiral reagents.
All of these are
\mathcal{L}_{k}
-level data for
k<4.5
, and
they are identical for the two enantiomers because

U_{4.5}
collapses the pair to a single object.

Property (iv) encodes the categorical statement that

within
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, no morphism flips the chirality
label at a bond-graph stereocentre while leaving the
underlying graph fixed. This captures the chemistry of

configurational chirality
at tetrahedral
stereocentres — the case where four distinct substituents
at
sp^{3}
carbon define the chirality datum.

Several real interconversion mechanisms fall outside this
framework because they are not visible at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
:
amine inversion (umbrella flipping at nitrogen via a
planar transition state), atropisomer interconversion
(rotation around a single bond), and helical inversion in
helicenes all interchange “enantiomeric” stereoisomers
without breaking the bond graph. These phenomena require
3D-coordinate data (transition-state planarity), barrier
heights (whether the inversion is thermally accessible at
room temperature), or both — inputs that enter the tower
only at
\mathcal{L}_{5}
and above. Property (iv) is the

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
-level shadow of configurational chirality
specifically; the broader physical concept of
“stereochemical interconvertibility” lives at higher levels.

Property (v) encodes the central principle of asymmetric
synthesis.
A
G^{*}
-equivariant reaction treats both enantiomers
uniformly, producing enantiomeric products in equal
amounts.
To produce one enantiomer preferentially, a reaction must

break
the
G^{*}
-symmetry — by using a chiral
catalyst or reagent modelled as a fixed object

(C,\sigma_{C})
in the reaction network.
When the catalyst appears explicitly with a fixed chirality
label
\sigma_{C}
, the two combined substrates

(G,+1)+(C,\sigma_{C})
and
(G,-1)+(C,\sigma_{C})

have different sources in
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P)
and are genuinely
distinct morphisms of the composite system.
The
G^{*}
-symmetry is broken not by violating
equivariance, but by holding one component of the reaction
fixed.
This is the categorical account of enantioselective
catalysis at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
.

The four theorems of this section — Walden inversion,
racemisation, net retention via double inversion, and the
enantiomer properties — together exhibit
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
’s
characteristic contribution to the tower:
universal
propagation of mechanism-selected stereochemical
outcomes across
G^{*}
-orbits of substrates
.
The next section (§
7.6
) applies the same
framework to pericyclic reactions, where the

\mathrm{Aut}(G)
-factor of
G^{*}
supplies the combinatorial
content of the Woodward–Hoffmann selection rules.

§7.6. Pericyclic stereochemistry at

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
: a theorem and a
Woodward–Hoffmann conjecture

The stereochemical theorems of §
7.5

treated reactions at a single stereocentre.
The present section takes up the second forcing obligation
of §
7.1
— the
electrocyclic forcing pair
[\pi_{\mathrm{ec}}]
— and
asks what
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
can say about the pericyclic
selection rules more generally.
The answer has two parts: a
theorem
providing the
categorical content (
\alpha
-equivariance selects one
chirality lift from two), and a
conjecture

identifying the equivariant lift with the thermally allowed
Woodward–Hoffmann product.
The theorem is established here; the conjecture is
accompanied by verification in the principal case
(electrocyclic) and a discussion of its scope and
limitations.

7.6.1. Background

A
pericyclic reaction
is a concerted reaction —
bond-making and bond-breaking occur simultaneously, with
no ionic intermediate — whose transition state has a
cyclic arrangement of the participating atoms and bonds,
allowing electron reorganisation around a closed
loop
[
307
]
.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, pericyclic reactions are DPO rules whose
reaction centre
L\setminus K
together with
R\setminus K
traces a cyclic subgraph topology
[
138
]
.
The three principal families are electrocyclic ring
closures/openings, cycloadditions, and sigmatropic shifts.

Woodward and Hoffmann discovered in
1965
[
305
,
307
]
that
the
stereochemical
outcome of every pericyclic
reaction is governed by a single principle: the symmetry
of the molecular orbitals must be conserved along the
reaction path.
For ground-state (thermal) reactions, this means the
orbitals of the reactant must flow continuously into those
of the product without crossing a symmetry-imposed barrier.
Reactions that satisfy this are
thermally allowed
;
reactions that would require a barrier crossing are

thermally forbidden
(but photochemically allowed,
since the barrier vanishes upon electron promotion).

The resulting selection rules depend only on electron
count:

Reaction type

Thermal

Photochemical

Electrocyclic,
4n
electrons

conrotatory

disrotatory

Electrocyclic,
4n{+}2
electrons

disrotatory

conrotatory

[4+2] cycloaddition (Diels–Alder)

supra-supra

antara-supra

[2+2] cycloaddition

forbidden

supra-supra

Conrotatory
means the two terminal groups rotate in
the same direction;
disrotatory
means they rotate
in opposite directions.

Suprafacial
(supra) means the new bond forms on
the same face of the
\pi
system;
antarafacial

(antara) means it forms on the opposite face.
The work earned Hoffmann the 1981 Nobel Prize in Chemistry,
shared with Fukui for related frontier-orbital
analysis
[
143
,
109
]
; Woodward
had died in 1979 and the prize could not be awarded
posthumously.

Pericyclic reactions are about stereochemistry — which
product isomer is produced and through which
transition-state geometry — and this is exactly the
content that lives at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
as chirality labels and
nowhere lower in the tower. At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, the
thermally allowed and thermally forbidden outcomes of a
pericyclic reaction share the same bond-graph DPO rule
(
L\leftarrow K\rightarrow R
); the distinction between
them is purely stereochemical (which face of the

\pi
-system the new bond forms on, and the resulting
relative configuration of the new stereocentres) and
invisible until
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
. At
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, the rate
constants of allowed and forbidden processes are different
in practice (forbidden reactions face higher activation
barriers), but
\mathcal{L}_{3}
does not explain
why
they
differ; the structural reason —
\alpha
-equivariance
or its failure at the chirality lift — is a
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}

fact.
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
is thus the first tower level where the
allowed/forbidden distinction can be
stated
structurally
, not merely registered as a numerical rate difference.

7.6.2. The categorical theorem

The connection between WH and
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
rests on a single
graph-theoretic observation.
A pericyclic reaction centre is a cyclic subgraph, and
cyclic graphs admit non-trivial automorphisms —
specifically, the reflections that swap pairs of
stereogenic terminal atoms.
These automorphisms project from the 3D symmetry elements
(
C_{2}
axes,
\sigma_{v}
planes) of the transition state to
the graph level, where they act on the vertex set by
permuting the reaction-centre atoms.
Call such an automorphism a
reaction-centre
automorphism
of the rule.

Theorem 7.37

(
\alpha
-equivariance distinguishes
pericyclic product lifts (ring-closure direction))
.

Let
p_{0}
be a pericyclic ring-closure DPO rule in

\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}
— a rule whose reactant side
L
has the
participating atoms in an open-chain
\pi
-system (sp
2

hybridisation at the termini) and whose product side
R

has the new
\sigma
-bond closing those termini into a
ring (sp
3
at the new stereogenic positions). Let

\alpha
be a reaction-centre automorphism of
p_{0}
—
that is, an involutive graph automorphism
\alpha\in\mathrm{Aut}(L)\cap\mathrm{Aut}(R)
that exchanges a pair of stereocentres

\{v_{1},v_{2}\}\subset\mathrm{Stereo}(R)
. Then:

(i)

p_{0}
admits exactly two chirality lifts

\tilde{p}^{+},\tilde{p}^{-}
distinguished by the
relative sign of
\sigma_{R}(v_{1})
and
\sigma_{R}(v_{2})
:

\tilde{p}^{+}\colon\ \sigma_{R}(v_{1})=\sigma_{R}(v_{2}),\qquad\tilde{p}^{-}\colon\ \sigma_{R}(v_{1})=-\sigma_{R}(v_{2}).

(ii)

Exactly one of the two lifts is

\alpha
-equivariant:
\tilde{p}^{+}
is

\alpha
-equivariant and
\tilde{p}^{-}
is not.

Proof.

(i).

The reaction produces the two stereocentres
v_{1},v_{2}\in\mathrm{Stereo}(R)
from sp
2
atoms in
L
(hence

v_{1},v_{2}\notin\mathrm{Stereo}(L)
: at the
L
-side these
vertices have three neighbours each, failing
condition (i) of Definition
7.6
).
A chirality lift of
p_{0}
is therefore a choice of

(\sigma_{R}(v_{1}),\sigma_{R}(v_{2}))\in\{+1,-1\}^{2}
at the
product side — four options in total. Identifying lifts
related by the
E^{*}
action
(\sigma_{R}\mapsto-\sigma_{R})
,
which produces the enantiomeric product and hence the same
stereochemical content up to overall enantiomer choice,
the four options collapse into two equivalence classes:

•

\tilde{p}^{+}=\{(+,+),(-,-)\}
: the lifts with

\sigma_{R}(v_{1})=\sigma_{R}(v_{2})
.

•

\tilde{p}^{-}=\{(+,-),(-,+)\}
: the lifts with

\sigma_{R}(v_{1})=-\sigma_{R}(v_{2})
.

(ii).

The
\alpha
-equivariance square
(Definition
7.18
) for

\tilde{p}^{\pm}
with
\alpha
acting on chirality
functions by
\sigma\mapsto\sigma\circ\alpha^{-1}

requires
\sigma_{R}\circ\alpha^{-1}=\sigma_{R}
on

\{v_{1},v_{2}\}
.
Since
\alpha
exchanges
v_{1}\leftrightarrow v_{2}
:

(\sigma_{R}\circ\alpha^{-1})(v_{1})=\sigma_{R}(v_{2}),\qquad(\sigma_{R}\circ\alpha^{-1})(v_{2})=\sigma_{R}(v_{1}).

\alpha
-equivariance thus requires
\sigma_{R}(v_{1})=\sigma_{R}(v_{2})
: exactly the condition defining

\tilde{p}^{+}
.
Hence
\tilde{p}^{+}
is
\alpha
-equivariant;

\tilde{p}^{-}
, with
\sigma_{R}(v_{1})=-\sigma_{R}(v_{2})
,
fails the equivariance condition.
∎

Remark 7.38

(What the theorem says, tower-natively)
.

Theorem
7.37
separates a pericyclic
rule into two chirality-lift classes defined by the
relative sign pattern at the new stereocentres.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, both lifts collapse under
U_{4.5}
to the
same bond-graph rule: the distinction is

\mathcal{L}_{4}
-invisible.
At
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
, the reaction-centre automorphism
\alpha

is a non-trivial element of
\mathrm{Aut}(G)\leq G^{*}(G)
, and

\alpha
-equivariance singles out exactly one of the two
lifts.
The tower contribution is the
classification
of
pericyclic product lifts by
\alpha
-parity, not the
