states, eigenvalues
V_{n}(\mathbf{R})
for

n=0,\ldots,N-1
, and connection coefficients

A_{mn}^{\mu}(\mathbf{R})
— sufficient to determine the
Hilbert bundle
{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{el}}}^{(N)}
and its
U(N)
-connection.
The hypothesis is that
(\Theta,f_{\theta})
has output type

\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
: at each
\mathbf{R}
, only the ground-state
energy
V_{0}
and its gradient
\nabla V_{0}
.
The base-level forgetful functor

U_{6}\colon\mathcal{L}_{6}\to\mathcal{L}_{5}
projects
\mathbf{HilbBund}
to

\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
by extracting the lowest eigenvalue and its
gradient, discarding excited-state energies, off-diagonal
connection coefficients, and topological class — none of
which appears in the
\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
output of

(\Theta,f_{\theta})
.

A reparametrisation
r\colon I\to\Theta
in

\mathrm{Para}(\mathcal{L}_{5}(P))
specialises the architecture to a parameter
value
\theta^{*}\in\Theta
via

f_{\theta^{*}}=f_{\theta}\circ(r\otimes\mathrm{id}_{X})
.
This operation fixes the source object
{C_{e}}(G)
and the
target object of
f_{\theta}
;
it cannot change the output type.
Hence if
f_{\theta}(\mathbf{R})
lies in
\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
for all

(\mathbf{R},\theta)
, then
f_{\theta^{*}}(\mathbf{R})
does
too.

Therefore no reparametrisation of
(\Theta,f_{\theta})

produces output in
\mathbf{HilbBund}
, and in particular none yields
the Berry connection
A_{mn}^{\mu}
, the multi-sheet PES

(V_{0},V_{1},\ldots,V_{N-1})
, or any topological invariant
of the bundle (
[\gamma_{B}]
for real molecular Hamiltonians;

c_{1}
in the SOC case).
The architecture remains in
\mathcal{L}_{5}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
:
parameter choice cannot supply the missing bundle data.
∎

Observation 11.20

(Empirical confirmation: models approaching
electronic topology move beyond
\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
)
.

Proposition
11.19
predicts
that capturing Berry phase and topological invariants requires
a change of output type from
\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
to
\mathbf{HilbBund}
.
The recent ML literature pursues this in two architecturally
distinct ways.
The
operator-level
route predicts the full electronic
Hamiltonian matrix
H_{\mathrm{el}}(\mathbf{R})
in a fixed
atomic-orbital basis; diagonalisation then recovers the bundle
fibres pointwise.
The
section-level
route predicts the connection
coefficients
A_{mn}^{\mu}
as a genuine vector section
directly.
The two are orthogonal sub-categories of
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para}}

(Section
11.3
); both escape the

\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
codomain, but only the operator-level route has so
far produced explicit topological demonstrations on
experimentally relevant systems.

ML Hamiltonian models.

PhiSNet
[
289
]
and
DeepH-E3
[
125
]
predict

H_{\mathrm{el}}(\mathbf{R})
as a Hermitian matrix field over

{C_{e}}(G)
, placing them in the operator-level sub-category

\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para},\mathrm{op}}(P)
defined in
Section
11.3
: the

SE(3)
-equivariance of the operator-valued map is
architectural, and the Hilbert-bundle fibres of

{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{el}}}^{(N)}\to{C_{e}}(G)
are recoverable pointwise by
diagonalising
H_{\mathrm{el}}(\mathbf{R})
.
The fixed atomic-orbital basis, however, provides a global
trivialisation that freezes the
U(N)
fibre gauge, and no
architectural enforcement of
[\gamma_{B}]
-consistency is in
place around loops encircling
\mathcal{X}_{01}
— the topological
data is recovered post-hoc rather than constrained during
training.
Full
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
membership would require both
operator-level fidelity and section-level gauge covariance;
these architectures provide only the former.
DeepH-E3 nonetheless demonstrates prediction of a topological
quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer Bi
2
Te
3
: as
spin–orbit coupling increases, the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
topological
invariant changes from
0
to
1
, confirmed by Brillouin-zone
integration of the predicted Berry connection and curvature.
This demonstration is possible precisely because the output
object escapes
\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
— the model predicts the operator
from which topological invariants are derived, not a scalar
that has already discarded that information.
Independently, Daggett, Yang, Liu, and
Muechler
[
71
]
construct a model
system whose two regimes share an
identical

ground-state potential energy surface yet carry

different
values of the Euler-class topological
invariant —
directly establishing that
\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
output cannot
distinguish topologically inequivalent electronic structures.

Neural non-adiabatic coupling models.

SchNarc
[
297
]
predicts excited-state
energies, forces, and non-adiabatic coupling vectors (NACs),
parametrising the NAC vectors as

d_{ij}^{\mu}(\mathbf{R})=\nabla_{\mu}s_{ij}
for learned
scalar functions
s_{ij}
.
This ansatz spans only exact 1-forms, so for every closed
loop
\gamma\subset{C_{e}}(G)\setminus\mathcal{X}_{01}
the integral

\oint_{\gamma}d_{ij}^{\mu}\,dR_{\mu}=\oint_{\gamma}ds_{ij}=0

vanishes by construction; the Berry-phase class

[\gamma_{B}]
is identically trivialised regardless of the
underlying physics, and the model cannot represent loops on
which
[\gamma_{B}]\neq 0
.
SPAINN
[
212
]
lifts this exact-form
obstruction by predicting equivariant vector NACs directly on
a PaiNN backbone, so the output is a genuine section of

A_{mn}^{\mu}
rather than a gradient of a scalar.
However, no
U(N)
-gauge equivariance is enforced on the
state indices
(m,n)
, no diabatic Hamiltonian is provided,
and no topological loss enforces
[\gamma_{B}]
-consistency.
SPAINN therefore reaches only a partial (connection-level)
approximation toward the section-level sub-category

\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para},\mathrm{sec}}(P)
, while making no attempt at
the operator-level axis.
Neither SchNarc nor SPAINN reaches full
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
,
which would require both sub-categories simultaneously.

ML diabatisation.

Neural-network quasi-diabatic Hamiltonians (Truhlar
group
[
311
]
; Zhang–Guo
group
[
145
]
; Shen and
Yarkony
[
270
]
) learn multi-state diabatic
potential-energy matrices that smooth the conical-intersection
singularity.
In tower language, this is a partial realisation of the blowup
resolution of Conjecture
10.45
: the result is a
function on the blown-up space near
\mathcal{X}_{01}
.
However, whether ML-fitted diabatic matrices preserve the
correct Berry-phase class
[\gamma_{B}]
in regions outside the
training set is largely unresolved in the literature — no
paper provides a formal guarantee of topological correctness as
an architectural constraint.
The Shen–Yarkony work handles at least three coupled
electronic states simultaneously (not a simple
2\times 2

system), demonstrating the geometric-phase effect in aniline
photodissociation as a physical consequence of the
conical-intersection structure — but does not formulate this
in terms of a Berry-phase or Chern-class invariant.

The topological gap is architectural, not
empirical

Proposition
11.19
is not a
statement about training-set size, model capacity, or
distribution coverage.
The Berry-phase class

[\gamma_{B}]\in H^{1}({C_{e}}(G)\setminus\mathcal{X}_{01},\mathbb{Z}_{2})
assigns
a
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-value to each homology class of loops encircling

\mathcal{X}_{01}
; the analogous
c_{1}\in H^{2}(-,\mathbb{Z})
in the
spin–orbit-coupled case is similarly a cohomology class.
These are not pointwise functions on
{C_{e}}(G)
at all — they
are global topological invariants of the eigenbundle. The
Berry connection
A_{mn}^{\mu}
is a
u(N)
-valued
1
-form on

{C_{e}}(G)
with state indices
(m,n)
, again not extractable
from a pointwise scalar. A model with output type

\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
produces, at every geometry
\mathbf{R}
, a real
number and a covariant vector: a scalar field on
{C_{e}}(G)
,
nothing more. The gap is type-theoretic. The proof of
Proposition
11.19
is just
the categorical observation that a reparametrisation

r\colon I\to\Theta
acts on the source by

r\otimes\mathrm{id}_{X}
, leaving the target object —
hence the output type — fixed. Increasing body order,
expanding the training set, or widening the network leaves
the gap untouched because none of these is a change of
output type.

The gap requires an
architectural
change of output
type. The operator-level route predicts the full electronic
Hamiltonian
H_{\mathrm{el}}(\mathbf{R})
, from which

A_{mn}^{\mu}
and
[\gamma_{B}]
(or
c_{1}
) can be extracted by
diagonalisation; the section-level route predicts a

U(N)
-gauge-equivariant section of the eigenbundle directly,
carrying
A_{mn}^{\mu}
as a connection 1-form.
Either route escapes the
\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
codomain, and full

\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
membership requires both simultaneously —
operator-level fidelity and section-level gauge covariance.
No published architecture provides both.
A separate question, beyond strict membership, is whether
the
trained
values of
[\gamma_{B}]
on loops encircling

\mathcal{X}_{01}
are correct outside the training distribution. No
current ML framework enforces this architecturally; a
topological-loss term on the Berry holonomy is the natural
candidate mechanism, but it is a training-time penalty
rather than an architectural constraint.

§11.8. Synthesis: the tower as design specification

This chapter has done three things.
It has located each major ML molecular architecture as a
parametric morphism in some
\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
by the membership
condition
(E_{k})
and the output type of its function class —
a precise address independent of training data or parameter
count.
It has established three tower-incompleteness results of
distinct character: a proposition with formal proof (the
topological output-type obstruction at the

\mathcal{L}_{5}\to\mathcal{L}_{6}
boundary) and two literature-survey
observations (the Eyring TST coherence gap between
\mathcal{L}_{3}
and

\mathcal{L}_{5}
, the Wegscheider consistency gap between
\mathcal{L}_{2}
and

\mathcal{L}_{3}
).
And it has shown that the Para enrichment provides a verifiable
structural criterion for the question “what can this model
represent?”, replacing benchmark intuition with a statement
about the model’s function class.

The central finding is that the vast majority of mainstream ML
molecular models operate at
\mathcal{L}_{5}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
or below.
A small number of ML Hamiltonian models —
PhiSNet
[
289
]
,
DeepH-E3
[
125
]
— reach the operator-level
sub-category
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para},\mathrm{op}}(P)
defined in
Section
11.3
;
SPAINN
[
212
]
offers the audit’s only
partial connection-level approach toward the section-level
sub-category
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para},\mathrm{sec}}(P)
.
No architecture occupies both sub-categories, and none reaches
full
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
.
The statement is about function-class representability, not
about accuracy or training coverage: the models cannot represent
certain tower objects regardless of how they are trained.

11.8.1. What category theory uniquely provides

Two general consequences of the Para enrichment deserve naming.

Equivariance as a theorem, not a design choice.

In every non-categorical treatment of ML for chemistry, symmetry
equivariance is either an empirical observation or a design
principle.
The Para enrichment makes it a theorem: an ML model is an object
of
\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
if and only if it satisfies the membership
condition
(E_{k})
.
This applies level-by-level:

SE(3)\rtimes\mathrm{Aut}(G)
-equivariance at
\mathcal{L}_{5}^{\mathrm{Para}}
,

G^{*}
-equivariance at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}^{\mathrm{Para}}
(the reflection-
inclusive factor that ML-literature
“
E(3)
-equivariance” implicitly invokes), the
Markov-category morphism condition at
\mathcal{L}_{3}^{\mathrm{Para}}
, and the
bundle-gauge condition at
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para}}
.
The correct inductive bias for a model targeting level
k
is
therefore not a design choice but a categorical necessity,
determined by the group and monad structure at that level.
A model claiming to predict chirality-sensitive reaction
outcomes must satisfy
(E_{4.5})
under the full
permutation-inversion group
G^{*}
; a model claiming to
predict Berry-phase effects must satisfy
(E_{6})
with respect to
the bundle gauge.
Failing the membership condition places the model at a lower
level regardless of benchmark performance.

Completeness as an architectural diagnostic.

Classical ML benchmarks measure accuracy on held-out data at a
fixed trained parameter setting.
Definition
11.5
provides a sharper criterion:
a model
(\Theta,f_{\theta})
is complete at level
k
on a
target morphism
\varphi\in\mathcal{L}_{k}(P)(X,Y)
if and only if

\varphi
lies in the function class

\mathsf{Func}(\Theta,f_{\theta})\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{k}(P)(X,Y)
—
equivalently, if some reparametrisation

r\colon I\to\Theta
instantiates
f_{\theta}
to
\varphi

exactly.
Completeness is a property of the model’s
function class
,
independent of training data.
A model that cannot express the Berry connection
A_{mn}^{\mu}

as part of its output type will fail at predicting
geometric-phase effects in ultracold reactions,
photodissociation branching ratios, and conical-intersection
dynamics — not because it was trained on too little data, but
because the relevant structure is not representable within the
function class at all.
The diagnostic therefore distinguishes failure modes that more
data can fix from those it cannot.

11.8.2. Three research targets forced by the tower

The tower is not only a classification of what exists.
Turned around, it is a
design specification
: each level
specifies, via its membership condition and forgetful functor
structure, what a model must do architecturally to represent the
chemistry at that level faithfully.
The three gaps identified in
Section
11.7
define three concrete
research targets — not aspirational goals, but consequences
forced by the tower’s structure, in the same sense that each
tower level was forced bottom-up by reaction pairs the previous
level could not distinguish.

Target 1: topologically complete
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)

models for non-adiabatic chemistry.

The tower forces this target on any model claiming to predict
photochemical reactivity, non-adiabatic dynamics, or electronic
topology.
Reaching full
\mathcal{L}_{6}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
membership requires two
architectural commitments simultaneously: operator-level
fidelity, provided by PhiSNet and DeepH-E3 through
Hamiltonian-matrix output in a fixed atomic-orbital basis;
and section-level gauge covariance on the eigenbundle,
approached partially by SPAINN at the connection level.
No published architecture provides both.
A separate concern, beyond strict membership, is whether the

trained
values of
[\gamma_{B}]
on closed loops
encircling
\mathcal{X}_{01}
are correct outside the training
distribution — the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-valued Berry-phase class for real
molecular Hamiltonians, or the integer-valued
c_{1}
in the
spin–orbit-coupled case. No current ML framework enforces
this architecturally; a topological-loss term on the Berry
holonomy, computed during training on geometries near conical
intersections, is the natural candidate mechanism but is a
training-time penalty rather than an architectural constraint.
The Daggett–Yang–Liu–Muechler
classification
[
71
]
supplies the
mathematical vocabulary — a model system whose two regimes
share an identical ground-state PES yet carry different
Euler-class topological invariants — and thereby establishes
empirically that
\mathbf{Orb}^{\mathrm{Morse}}
output cannot distinguish
topologically inequivalent electronic structures.
The tower specifies the architectural home those invariants
require.

Target 2: thermodynamically consistent neural
kinetics.

The tower forces this target on any model claiming to predict
reversible chemical kinetics at thermal equilibrium.
The categorical requirement is that the parameter space
\Theta

carry a dagger involution
\sigma\colon\Theta\to\Theta

satisfying

k_{\sigma(\theta)}(r)\;=\;k_{\theta}(r^{\dagger})\quad\text{for all reactions }r,

paired with a thermodynamic data channel that feeds

\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}
into the constraint.
This is not a regularisation term; it is the specification of
the type that
\Theta
must instantiate to guarantee detailed
balance at every reaction in every network.
The De Donder strategy of Kircher, Döppel, and
Votsmeier
[
254
]
demonstrates one
viable implementation by eliminating independent parameterisation
of the reverse rate constant and deriving it from a tabulated

K_{\mathrm{eq}}
.
The categorical generalisation shifts the primary parametric
commitment one level lower — from
\mathcal{L}_{3}^{\mathrm{Para}}
(independent
forward and reverse rate constants) to
\mathcal{L}_{2}^{\mathrm{Para}}
—
parameterising only the stoichiometry and a free-energy profile

\Delta G^{\circ}_{r}
per reaction, deriving rate constants
structurally via the dagger constraint above, with the
van’t Hoff relation

d(\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}})/dT=\Delta H^{\circ}/(RT^{2})
enforced
analytically through the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
-level enthalpy channel.
Such an architecture would extrapolate correctly in both
temperature and composition outside the training distribution —
a practical requirement for combustion modelling, heterogeneous
catalysis, and pharmaceutical kinetics.

Target 3: functorially separated topology–geometry
models for reactive dynamics.

The tower forces this target on any model claiming to predict
bond-breaking and bond-forming events in reactive molecular
dynamics: the forgetful functor

U_{4.5}\circ U_{5}\colon\mathcal{L}_{5}(P)\to\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
must be
realised as an explicit architectural boundary.
Current MLFFs lack any module for outputting
\mathcal{L}_{4}
graph
labels (bond order, formal charges, lone pairs); neighbour
graphs are defined by distance cutoffs rather than by chemical
bonding, so bond identity can be reconstructed only post-hoc
from distances via extrinsic criteria.
Proposition
11.9
formalises this for the
MACE family specifically.
A two-stage architecture would realise the separation
explicitly: Stage 1 predicts the DPO graph
G\in\mathbf{LGraph}_{P}

(bond order, formal charges, lone pairs) from the local atomic
environment, using a graph-valued output type consistent with

\mathcal{L}_{4}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
; Stage 2 takes the fixed topology
G
as input
and predicts the
SE(3)\rtimes\mathrm{Aut}(G)
-equivariant PES

V_{0}(\mathbf{R};G)
on the configuration orbifold, consistent
with
\mathcal{L}_{5}^{\mathrm{Para}}(P)
.
Bond-breaking events then correspond to transitions between
topologically distinct DPO graph objects in
\mathcal{L}_{4}(P)
, not to
continuous deformations of a cutoff-based graph.
The resulting architecture enables reactive MD in which the
model knows, at every step, which chemical bonds are present —
a capability with direct applications to combustion, catalysis,
and materials degradation.

In each of the three targets, the framework specifies not only
what is missing but what type the missing component must be —
a precision that benchmark comparison alone cannot provide, and
that makes the tower practically useful as a design tool rather
than merely a classification scheme.

§12. The lower tower in executable form:
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
on the Briggs–Rauscher oscillator

The preceding chapters have constructed a categorical tower that stratifies
chemistry by level of structure: stoichiometry at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
, thermodynamics
at
\mathcal{L}_{1}
–
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, kinetics at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, mechanism at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, with

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
stereochemistry and higher levels above. The tower’s content
is not mere vocabulary: at every level it delivers theorems. At
\mathcal{L}_{3}
,
Feinberg’s Deficiency Zero Theorem forces weakly-reversible mass-action
networks with deficiency
\delta=0
to admit a unique positive
stationary measure per stoichiometric class — which is precisely why
oscillating networks like the Briggs–Rauscher reaction must have

\delta>0
. At
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, the parameter projection
\pi_{4}

(§
12.8
) constrains exactly which mechanism data can
survive into the
\mathcal{L}_{3}
rate constants, making the gap between
mechanism-resolved and rate-resolved descriptions explicit rather than
tacit. These are not modelling choices that could have gone differently;
they are categorical consequences of the tower’s construction. If the
tower is to be more than a formal scaffold, those consequences have to
survive contact with an executable implementation evaluated against a
specific chemistry.

This chapter closes the tower at the bottom by constructing a functor

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}\;:\;\mathrm{Para}\!\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{0}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{2}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{3}\bigr)\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask}),

(37)

where
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
is the Para construction over Hask

[
70
]
with parameter type

W=\mathtt{Word64}
, the PRNG seed (§
12.2
). The
image of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
at the De Kepper–Epstein skeleton of the
Briggs–Rauscher oscillator
[
74
]
—

briggsRauscherDE
in the chapter’s Haskell implementation,
12 reaction channels with all rate constants tagged
Measured

(§
12.8
, Remark
12.29
) —
admits two operational realisations: the stochastic simulation
algorithm (SSA) at parameter dimension
n=1
, sampling from a

\mathtt{Word64}
-indexed family of continuous-time-Markov-chain
trajectories, and the deterministic ODE at
n=0
, realising the

V\to\infty
Kurtz limit of the species-mean process. A denotational
companion

F\;:\;\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})\;\longrightarrow\;\mathbf{BorelStoch}

[
105
]
marginalises over the PRNG seed and lands in
the Markov category
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
; the composite
F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}

sends a network to its canonical kernel

F_{\mathrm{BR}}:=F(\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathtt{briggsRauscherDE}))\in\mathbf{BorelStoch}
.
To our knowledge this is the first explicit application of the Para
construction to chemistry (§
12.7
,
Corollary
12.25
) and the first published categorical
semantics of the Gillespie next-reaction method
(§
12.5
, Theorem
12.12
).

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
and
F
in one diagram

Operational semantics
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
(running Haskell, parametric in

W=\mathtt{Word64}
) and denotational semantics
F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}

(Markov kernels on Borel spaces) related by the functor
F
that
marginalises over the PRNG seed (Proposition

,
§
12.2
).
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
is a strict 2-functor of bicategories
(§

, Proposition
12.22
); its

\gamma_{\mathrm{ODE}}
2-cell in
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
measures the deviation
of the ODE Kurtz limit from
F_{\mathrm{BR}}
itself and becomes
empirically visible at finite
V
(§

). The

\gamma_{\mathrm{SSA}}
2-cell vanishes in total variation modulo PRNG

.

What the instrument delivers, evaluated at

at

(§

), is the kernel

F_{\mathrm{BR}}
visible through two operationally distinct routes:

directly, and the ODE realises its
species-mean Kurtz limit as a Dirac kernel at the deterministic
trajectory. Both routes exhibit a relaxation-oscillator attractor, in
agreement to within a factor of two on spike-peak amplitudes across all
six dynamical species. They diverge in the low-copy quiescent phase:
the SSA shows integer-valued populations of
\mathrm{HIO}_{2}
,

\mathrm{IO}_{2}\bullet
, and
\mathrm{MnOH}^{2+}
fluctuating between

0
and a few molecules; the ODE shows smooth analytic floors at

–

that translate to sub-unity
ensemble-mean counts at this volume. This is the
\gamma
-cell
decomposition made empirically operational:
\gamma_{\mathrm{SSA}}=0

in total variation throughout,
\gamma_{\mathrm{ODE}}
non-trivial in
state-space/Wasserstein-1 metric in low-copy regions. At macroscopic
volumes the two realisations would converge in TV by the Kurtz theorem

[
179
]
; the deliberately small
V
chosen here makes the
distinction visible rather than asymptotically suppressed.

The framework provides three concrete deliverables beyond confirmed
predictions. First, an explicit vocabulary (§

)
for separating simulator-output features into three categories:

(the oscillation onset itself, tied to

\mathcal{L}_{3}

data), and

§12.1. The Briggs–Rauscher reaction as a forcing ladder

12.1.1. The empirical problem

The Briggs–Rauscher (BR) reaction
[
52
]
is the
clock reaction in which an acidic batch of iodate, hydrogen peroxide,
malonic acid, and a manganese(II) catalyst oscillates visibly between
colourless, amber, and dark blue before settling into equilibrium.
Its net stoichiometry,

\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}+2\,\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}+\mathrm{CH_{2}(COOH)_{2}}+\mathrm{H^{+}}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{ICH(COOH)_{2}}+2\,\mathrm{O_{2}}+3\,\mathrm{H_{2}O},

(38)

contains no information about the oscillation: it is
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data,
identical to that of a hypothetical non-oscillating reaction with the
same input and output complexes.

Two parallel skeleton mechanisms were proposed in 1982 by Noyes and
Furrow
[
231
]
and independently by De Kepper and
Epstein
[
74
]
in the same volume of JACS.
Both decompose the dynamics into two pathways for hypoiodous-acid
production:
Process A
(ionic, dominant at high

[\mathrm{I^{-}}]
), through sequential heterolytic O–I bond
formations via
\mathrm{HIO_{2}}
and
\mathrm{I_{2}}
intermediates;
and
Process B
(radical, dominant at low
[\mathrm{I^{-}}]
),
through homolytic

\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}+HIO_{2}\to 2\,IO_{2}^{\bullet}}
with Mn(II)/Mn(III)
cycling supplying single-electron transfer. Process A consumes

\mathrm{I^{-}}
; the iodination of malonic acid by
\mathrm{I_{2}}

regenerates it. The system switches between A and B across a
threshold in
[\mathrm{I^{-}}]
, and that switching is the mechanical
content of the oscillation. The implementation in

BR.Mechanism
(§
12.3
) follows the De
Kepper–Epstein variant with two explicit reverse channels (R3-rev
and R4-rev), giving twelve reactions in total.

A and B are indistinguishable below
\mathcal{L}_{4}
: they share the
\mathcal{L}_{0}

net stoichiometry of (
38
), and their bulk net
HOI-production rates share the form
\dot{c}_{\mathrm{HOI}}=k_{\mathrm{eff}}\,[\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}]\,[\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}]
with only

k_{\mathrm{eff}}
differing. Their distinction — heterolytic
versus homolytic bond character — is recorded in the DPO graph of
each elementary step and is
\mathcal{L}_{4}
data. The simulation in
§
12.7
is provably blind to the A/B distinction;
the main tower’s
\mathcal{L}_{4}
chapter
(Observation
6.46
) develops this blindness as
a categorical theorem.

12.1.2. The forcing hierarchy

The tower
\mathcal{L}_{0}\hookrightarrow\cdots\hookrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{7}
was
constructed level-by-level, each transition forced by an explicit
reaction pair the previous level cannot distinguish. The BR system
presents this ladder at every transition
\mathcal{L}_{0}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
.

\mathcal{L}_{0}\to\mathcal{L}_{1}
.

\mathcal{L}_{0}
records stoichiometric vectors only. Atom and charge
conservation across every reaction are the
\mathcal{L}_{0}
structural
integrity tests, realised in
BR.Invariants
as element-wise
and total-charge linear checks on the stoichiometric matrix.

\mathcal{L}_{1}
adds the monoidal functor
F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{1}\to(\mathbb{R},+)
whose
functoriality
F_{\!H}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})=F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2})
is Hess’s
Law.

\mathcal{L}_{1}\to\mathcal{L}_{2}
.

Iodate oxidation of
\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}
has
\Delta H^{\circ}\approx 0
at
standard conditions but proceeds spontaneously; the entropy gain on

\mathrm{O_{2}}
release controls the sign of
\Delta G^{\circ}
.
\mathcal{L}_{2}

adds the entropy functor
F_{\!S}
, the temperature-dependent

F_{\!G}^{T}=F_{\!H}-T\,F_{\!S}
, and the
\dagger
-structure identifying each
reaction with its reverse. The codebase realises the dagger
structure explicitly through paired reactions: the iodine
hydrolysis pair
R3
/
R3-rev
and the

\mathrm{IO_{2}^{\bullet}}
recombination pair

R4
/
R4-rev
appear as separate
Reaction

values whose rate-constant ratios satisfy Wegscheider’s relation

\prod_{i}k_{+,i}=\prod_{i}k_{-,i}
on each closed cycle. In this
implementation the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
and
\mathcal{L}_{2}
functors enter
through

the
\mathcal{L}_{3}
rate constants via Wegscheider, rather than as separate
fields of
Reaction
(§
12.4
).

\mathcal{L}_{2}\to\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

The BR system never reaches its
\Delta G^{\circ}
-determined equilibrium
during the oscillatory phase; dynamics are kinetically controlled
by rate constants spanning twelve orders of magnitude across the
elementary steps.
\mathcal{L}_{3}
adds the functor

F_{P}:\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\Stoch
sending each network to a Markov kernel on
populations. The simulation realises
F_{P}

twice
from the
same
Network
value: by the Gibson–Bruck next-reaction
method in
BR.SSA
(§
12.5
), and, in the
large-volume limit, by the implicit-midpoint mass-action ODE in

BR.ODE
. Together they form a cospan out of the
\mathcal{L}_{3}

object.

\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
: the BR forcing pair.

Processes A and B share
\mathcal{L}_{0}
stoichiometry and the bulk
HOI-production rate form, but the elementary bond changes —
heterolytic in A, homolytic in B — live in the DPO graph at

\mathcal{L}_{4}
. No observable computable from the
\mathcal{L}_{3}
rate equations
distinguishes them. This is the canonical
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
forcing
pair of the main tower
(Observation
6.46
), and it provides the chemical
motivation for the present chapter rather than its own subject of
study: this chapter constructs the simulation functor
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
at

\mathcal{L}_{0}
through
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, where the A/B distinction is invisible by
construction.

The BR forcing hierarchy in one line

\mathcal{L}_{0}\;\xrightarrow{F_{\!H}}\;\mathcal{L}_{1}\;\xrightarrow{F_{\!G}^{T}}\;\mathcal{L}_{2}\;\xrightarrow{F_{P}}\;\mathcal{L}_{3}\;\xrightarrow{U_{4}}\;\mathcal{L}_{4}

At each arrow lies a physical phenomenon inexpressible one level
below:
route-independence of heats
,
entropy-controlled
spontaneity
,
kinetic control
far from equilibrium, and
finally
ionic-versus-radical mechanism identity
— the
Process A/B forcing pair that motivates this chapter.

\mathcal{L}_{3}

§12.2. Target category:
Hask
and
\mathbf{BorelStoch}

A categorical interpretation of the simulation must fix a category
for total Haskell — the
operational
layer in which the
program runs — and a target category for the stochastic content
of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
— the
denotational
layer in which distributions
live — and a functor sending the first to the second. The
payoff is concrete: every claim about the simulator’s accuracy
will attach to a specific morphism in one of these categories and
to a specific user-controllable parameter
(§
12.5
onwards). This section fixes the two
categories; §
12.7
builds the functor.

12.2.1. Why not naive
Hask

The naive category with Haskell types as objects and all Haskell
functions as morphisms fails the identity law: Bauer

[
38
]
observes that
\mathtt{seq}\,\bot\,()
differs
from
\mathtt{seq}\,(\bot\mathbin{\texttt{.}}\mathtt{id})\,()
,
so
\mathrm{id}
is not a categorical identity under composition.
Danielsson, Hughes, Jansson, and Gibbons
[
72
]

prove that the
total
fragment of a partial language forms a
bicartesian closed category in which equational reasoning is
sound. By
Hask
in the rest of this chapter we mean that total
fragment.

Assumption 12.1

(Totality and purity of the simulation core)
.

Every function in the simulation core — the L0 invariants

atomConservation
,
chargeConservation
; the
constructors
mkReaction
,
mkNetwork
; the L3
realisations
BR.ODE.simulate
with
stepAdaptive
, and

BR.SSA.simulate
with
step
— is total and pure on
its domain. Stochasticity in
BR.SSA
is supplied entirely
by the vendored
BR.PRNG
(a state-threaded SplitMix64), so
the
IO
monad never appears in the call graph: no

System.Random
, no
unsafePerformIO
, no FFI, no
exceptions. File I/O is confined to
BR.Output
, which acts
only at the simulation boundary and is not invoked by any function
below it.

Remark 12.2

(Why no
\mathbf{Kl}(\mathsf{IO})
)
.

With
BR.PRNG
pure and explicit, both the ODE and SSA
realisations of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
live in
Hask
, not in a Kleisli category
of a probability monad in the sense of monadic semantics for
computational effects
[
226
]
. Introducing

\mathbf{Kl}(\mathsf{IO})
, the Kleisli category of the Haskell
IO

monad, would therefore add no structure here: the simulator would use
only the pure Kleisli arrows

A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{\mathrm{return}}\mathsf{IO}\,B,

i.e. the wide subcategory

\{\mathrm{return}\circ f:f\in\textbf{Hask}(A,B)\}\subseteq\mathbf{Kl}(\mathsf{IO})(A,B).

We therefore target
Hask
directly.

12.2.2. Two-layer semantics: operational and denotational

The stochastic content of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
requires a Markov category.

Definition 12.3

(Markov category;
\mathbf{BorelStoch}

[
105
]
)
.

A
Markov category
is a semicartesian symmetric monoidal
category
(\mathbf{C},\otimes,I)
in which every object
X

carries a natural commutative comonoid
(\mathrm{copy}_{X},\mathrm{del}_{X})
and every morphism
f
is counital,

\mathrm{del}_{Y}\circ f=\mathrm{del}_{X}
.
Equivalently, it is a category in which the algebra of probability —
sampling, copying, discarding, composing — is expressible as pure
morphism manipulation, without making measure-theoretic integrals part
of the primary syntax.

\mathbf{BorelStoch}
is the Markov category whose objects are
standard Borel spaces

(measurable spaces arising from a Polish topology, i.e. a complete
separable metric — countable sets,
\mathbb{R}^{n}
, and finite products
thereof) and whose morphisms are measurable Markov kernels. It is
a Borel restriction of the Kleisli category

\mathbf{Kl}(\mathcal{G})
of the
Giry monad

\mathcal{G}

[
123
]
, the
probability-measure monad sending each measurable space to its
space of probability measures.

Hask
is Cartesian and
deterministic
: any morphism in

Hask
between standard Borel spaces embeds into
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
as
a
Dirac kernel
— the degenerate Markov kernel placing all
mass on a single point, i.e. the embedding of a deterministic
function as a distribution concentrated at
f(a)
. All Haskell
types appearing in this chapter (
Word64
,
Double
,

Map Species Int
, lists thereof) are countable or Polish,
so this restriction is automatic. Two categories are necessary
because the stochastic content lives in
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
(where one
states theorems and accuracy bounds), but the simulator runs in

Hask
(where one debugs, profiles, and extends). The functor

F
below keeps the two pictures in sync: the seed-marginal of any
executable Haskell program is the Markov kernel it samples from.

Proposition 12.4

(Seed-marginalisation functor)
.

F
formalises the operation “run the simulator with random
seeds, infinitely many times, and read off the distribution of
outputs” as a functor. Concretely, let
W=\mathtt{Word64}
with
the uniform distribution
\mu_{W}
, and let

\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})\subseteq\mathrm{Para}(\textbf{Hask})
denote the sub-bicategory
of 1-morphisms whose parameter object is a (finite) power of
W

and whose source and target are standard Borel spaces. For a
1-morphism
(W^{n},f)
in
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
with

f:W^{n}\times A\to B
(
n\geq 0
), define

F\bigl(W^{n},\,f\bigr)(a,\cdot)\;:=\;\mathrm{law}_{w\sim\mu_{W}^{n}}\bigl(f(w,a)\bigr).

This extends to a (pseudo)functor
F:\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})\to\mathbf{BorelStoch}
, with sequential composition in
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})

taken on
W^{n+m}
(independent seed draws at each stage).
Identities (
n=0
) go to Dirac kernels; preservation of
composition is the Fubini factorisation

\mathrm{law}_{(w,w^{\prime})}\bigl(g(w^{\prime},f(w,a))\bigr)=\int F(g)(b,\cdot)\,F(f)(a,db)
.

Instantiation for BR.

f_{\mathrm{SSA}}
sits at

n=1
: its sole Para parameter is the
Word64
seed stored
in
ssaConfig
. The trajectory-dependent number of internal

nextWord
draws made by the Gibson–Bruck algorithm
(§
12.5
) is consumed
within

f_{\mathrm{SSA}}
as part of the underlying-morphism computation,
not as additional Para parameters.
f_{\mathrm{ODE}}
sits at

n=0
: the implicit-midpoint integrator is deterministic and
carries no seed. Both lie in
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
.

Remark 12.5

(BR.PRNG implementation and seed independence)
.

The marginalisation in Proposition
12.4
treats

\mu_{W}^{n}
as the law of
n
independent uniform draws on
W
. BR’s

BR.PRNG
delivers these draws via a single SplitMix64 state
threaded through
SSAState
, advancing via
nextWord

at each random draw: a single seed deterministically generates the
full stream of draws that
f_{\mathrm{SSA}}
consumes during a
trajectory, and the implementation of sequential composition reuses
the evolved state rather than drawing a fresh independent seed.
Functoriality of
F
on this implementation therefore holds only

statistically
— under the standard PRNG-quality assumption
that successive SplitMix64 outputs are independent for
distributional reasoning, satisfied to BigCrush (L’Ecuyer and
Simard’s empirical battery of independence and uniformity tests) by
SplitMix64
[
281
]
at the scales relevant to this
chapter.

The two-layer semantics is the diagram below.
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
is a
pseudofunctor with the documented laxity
\gamma
of the next
subsection;
F
is a (pseudo)functor by
Proposition
12.4
;
\Phi_{\mathrm{den}}:=F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}

supplies the Markov-category target that the stochastic content of

\mathcal{L}_{3}
requires.

Figure 1:
Operational and denotational semantics for the BR
simulator.
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
is operational (the pure Haskell program with
PRNG seed in scope as a Para parameter);
F
is denotational
(marginalise over the seed);
\Phi_{\mathrm{den}}=F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
lands in

\mathbf{BorelStoch}
.
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
denotes the sub-bicategory of

\mathrm{Para}(\textbf{Hask})
of
W
-parameterised pure morphisms between standard
Borel spaces.

12.2.3. One genuine laxity:
\gamma

In an IO-based formulation of this story (a

System.Random
-style codebase),
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
would carry three
lax cells: a unit
\alpha
, an IO-sequencing
\beta
, and a
truncation/numerical
\gamma
. Two of the three collapse for
BR. In pure
Hask
, Cartesian product is strictly associative
and commutative on the nose, so the parallel composition of two
seed-parameterised morphisms is invariant under sequencing:

\beta
is strict, not lax. The unit cell
\alpha
becomes the
parameter-tensor unit isomorphism of the Para bicategory

\mathrm{Para}(\textbf{Hask})
, treated as canonical coherence data
(§
12.6
) rather than as a laxity of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
. The
only cell that remains is
\gamma
:

The
\gamma
-cell: truncation

\gamma
is the gap between what the simulator returns and the
exact stochastic dynamics it approximates. The two branches behave
differently: SSA’s
\gamma
-component reduces to PRNG- and
floating-point-level numerical artifacts (no separate user knob);
ODE’s
\gamma
-component is a deterministic step-size error driven
to zero by a user-specified tolerance.

SSA branch (total-variation metric).

The Gibson–Bruck NRM in
BR.SSA
terminates when (a)

ssaTime
exceeds
ssaTimeMax
(a safety guard,
unreachable after any successful step), (b) all putative firing
times are infinite (genuine absorption), or (c) the next firing
would overshoot the horizon. Theorem
12.12
of
§
12.5
establishes that, for
\tau
encoded as

ssaTimeMax
in
ssaConfig
, the state at termination
agrees with the exact CTMC state at
\tau
in distribution under
all three termination paths: no events occur in the half-open
interval between any case-(c) termination time and
\tau
.
Writing
F_{P}
for the exact CTMC kernel of
\mathcal{L}_{3}

(Theorem
12.12
), in the
total variation

norm
\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|
on
probability measures,

\bigl\|F\bigl(\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}^{\mathrm{SSA}}(\mathcal{N})(\mathbf{x}_{0},\tau)\bigr)-F_{P}(\mathcal{N})(\mathbf{x}_{0},\tau)\bigr\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\;=\;0

modulo (i) SplitMix64’s deviation from i.i.d. uniform draws on

[0,1)
(Remark
12.5
above; bounded statistically
by the BigCrush results cited there), and (ii) IEEE-754
floating-point representation of inverse-CDF samples (per-draw
error
\lesssim 2^{-53}
). Neither qualification is a user knob
in the ordinary sense; the SSA branch of
\gamma
is effectively
zero in distribution.

ODE branch (state-space metric).

The implicit-midpoint integrator in
BR.ODE
produces a
deterministic trajectory; its discrepancy from the true
mass-action trajectory is measured in state-space sup norm rather
than TV. The local truncation error is
O(h^{3})
per step,
controlled adaptively by step doubling to a user-specified
tolerance — the user knob is the integration tolerance. Embedded
as Dirac kernels in
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
, the discrepancy is invisible to
the TV metric (which collapses to 0 or 1 between distinct Diracs);
the relevant metric on the ODE side of
\gamma
is therefore
Wasserstein-1 (or directly state-space) rather than TV.

The two branches differ in both the
form
of
\gamma

(effectively zero in distribution on SSA, deterministic step-size
error on ODE) and the metric in which it is measured (TV on SSA,
state-space on ODE). The asymmetry is structural: SSA’s exactness
modulo numerical artifacts is intrinsic to the Gibson–Bruck NRM
(§
12.5
), whereas the ODE branch carries a
genuine numerical laxity controllable by
odeRTol
and

odeATol
.

Remark 12.6

(Para is base-portable)
.

The Para construction applies over any symmetric monoidal base
category; varying the base gives different applications
(
\mathbf{Smooth}
for backpropagation in machine learning,
Hask

here for executable simulation,
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
for fully
probabilistic kernels). Capucci and Myers
[
57
]

show that all these incarnations are instances of a single
two-categorical pattern, so transferring techniques between them is
structural rather than ad hoc. The seed-marginalisation functor

F
above realises this bridge from the
Hask
incarnation to a
Markov-category target for our specific choice of uniform seed
distribution on
W
; other distributions would yield other
functors with the same shape.

§12.3.
\mathcal{L}_{0}
in Haskell:
Multiset Species
as free commutative monoid

Level
\mathcal{L}_{0}
is the tower’s stoichiometric foundation. Its
objects are elements of the free commutative monoid
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
on
the finite species set
\mathcal{S}
(Equation (
1
));
its morphisms are stoichiometric changes (reaction vectors in

\mathbb{Z}^{\mathcal{S}}
); its functorial invariants are the combinatorial data

(n,\ell,s)
— the number of distinct complexes, the number of
linkage classes (connected components of the reaction graph), and
the rank of the stoichiometric matrix — and the

deficiency

\delta=n-\ell-s
. Two
\mathcal{L}_{0}

structural integrity tests
— atom and charge conservation
— attach to every reaction and must pass before any
\mathcal{L}_{3}

dynamics are simulated. This section shows how the BR codebase
realises each of these pieces concretely.

12.3.1. The free commutative monoid in Haskell

The set
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
of Equation (
1
) carries a commutative
monoid structure under pointwise addition with the universal
property that any function
\varphi:\mathcal{S}\to M
to a commutative
monoid
M
extends uniquely to a homomorphism

\bar{\varphi}:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to M
. The BR implementation realises
both in a single newtype.

Proposition 12.7

(
\mathcal{L}_{0}
implementation)
.

The newtype

of

exactly implements
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
as an object of
\mathcal{L}_{0}
:

(i)

(Bijection.)
The invariant that the underlying

Map Species Int
has no entries with value
\leq 0
,
maintained by every smart constructor, puts

Multiset Species
in bijection with
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
.

(ii)

(Monoid.)

munion
is pointwise addition;

empty
is the identity.

(iii)

(Universal property.)
For any Haskell commutative
monoid
M
and any
\varphi:\texttt{Species}\to M
, the
unique extending homomorphism

\bar{\varphi}:\texttt{Multiset Species}\to M

is given by

\bar{\varphi}

= foldMap (\(s, n) -> stimes n (phi s)) . toList
.

12.3.2.
\mathcal{L}_{0}
structural integrity: atom and charge conservation

A multiset
r\in\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
has only multiplicity data. Attaching
it to a reaction
r_{\mathrm{src}}\to r_{\mathrm{tgt}}
as a

\mathcal{L}_{0}
morphism, two linear conditions on the reaction vector

r_{\mathrm{tgt}}-r_{\mathrm{src}}\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathcal{S}}
must hold for the
reaction to represent a physically meaningful elementary step:
conservation of each chemical element, and conservation of total
formal charge.

Definition 12.8

(Atom and charge conservation at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
)
.

For each element
a\in\{\mathrm{H,\,C,\,O,\,I,\,Mn}\}
, let

\varphi_{a}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{N}
be the function

s\mapsto\texttt{M.findWithDefault 0 a (formula s)}

(the
a
-coefficient of the species formula), and let

q:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{Z}
be
charge
. Their canonical
monoid-homomorphism extensions to
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]

(Proposition
12.7
(iii)) are denoted

\bar{\varphi}_{a}:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to\mathbb{N}
and

\bar{q}:\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]\to\mathbb{Z}
.

A reaction
r_{\mathrm{src}}\to r_{\mathrm{tgt}}
is

atom-balanced
if

\bar{\varphi}_{a}(r_{\mathrm{tgt}})-\bar{\varphi}_{a}(r_{\mathrm{src}})=0
for every element
a
, and
charge-balanced
if

\bar{q}(r_{\mathrm{tgt}})-\bar{q}(r_{\mathrm{src}})=0
. A
network is
\mathcal{L}_{0}
-
integral
if every reaction in it is both.

12.3.3. Deficiency and the
\mathcal{L}_{0}\!\to\!\mathcal{L}_{3}
structure of DZT

The deficiency
\delta=n-\ell-s
is entirely an
\mathcal{L}_{0}

invariant: it is computed from the stoichiometric matrix
\bm{\nu}\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{R}}
— the matrix of
\mathcal{L}_{0}
-morphism data —
without reference to rate constants, thermodynamics, or mechanism.
Theorem
2.29
states the L0 consequence of
\delta=0
;
Theorem
5.26
strengthens this to assertions about the
mass-action vector field once a rate functor
\FP
is supplied at

\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

Remark 12.9

(Cross-level structure of DZT)
.

The
hypotheses
of Theorem
2.29
(weak reversibility,

\delta=0
) are pure
\mathcal{L}_{0}
data; the
conclusions
become
assertions about the mass-action flow only once a rate functor

\FP
is chosen, at which point the statement strengthens to
Theorem
5.26
. This is the tower’s reading of the Feinberg
programme: DZT and DOT are
\mathcal{L}_{0}\!\to\!\mathcal{L}_{3}
theorems whose
content straddles the combinatorial and kinetic levels. A fully
categorical proof would make the straddling functorial.

\mathcal{L}_{0}
data of the Briggs–Rauscher network

The De Kepper–Epstein implementation
(
BR.Mechanism.briggsRauscherDE
, §
12.1
)
has
|\mathcal{S}|=15
species and twelve reactions (the ten elementary
steps R1–R10 plus explicit reverses R3-rev, R4-rev). Hand
enumeration of distinct source/target multisets gives
n=20

complexes distributed over
\ell=10
linkage classes (each
elementary forward/reverse pair occupies its own class, since no
two elementary steps share a source or target complex); the rank

s
of the stoichiometric matrix is computable by Gaussian
elimination but plays no role below. Running the L0 checks gives

atomConservation briggsRauscherDE == True
(each of H, C,
O, I, Mn balanced in every reaction) and

chargeConservation briggsRauscherDE == True
(net charge
zero in every reaction), so the network is
\mathcal{L}_{0}
-integral in
the sense of Definition
12.8
.

Why the deficiency theorems are silent on BR.

Of the twelve reactions, only the two pairs R3/R3-rev and R4/R4-rev
carry explicit reverses; the remaining eight elementary steps
(R1, R2, R5–R10) are unidirectional in the implementation. The
network is therefore
not weakly reversible
, and the
hypotheses of both Theorem
2.29
and the Deficiency One
Theorem fail regardless of the value of
\delta
.
\mathcal{L}_{0}
alone
cannot predict the BR steady-state structure — and indeed, no
steady state exists during the oscillatory phase: the system is
held far from equilibrium by the buffered substrate pool
(
\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}
,
\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}
, MA,
\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}
) and
cycles between Process A and Process B without converging. This
is the chapter’s first concrete demonstration that L0 data alone is
insufficient: the dynamical content lives strictly at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
and
requires the simulator built in subsequent sections.

§12.4.
\mathcal{L}_{1}
–
\mathcal{L}_{2}
: detailed-balance constraints on rate constants

Levels
\mathcal{L}_{1}
(enthalpies) and
\mathcal{L}_{2}
(free-energy and
reversibility) extend
\mathcal{L}_{0}
by a monoidal functor
F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{1}\to(\mathbb{R},+)
, an entropy extension giving
F_{\!G}^{T}=F_{\!H}-T\,F_{\!S}

at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
, and a
\dagger
-structure identifying each reaction
with its reverse. In the BR implementation these data are not
stored:
BR.Reaction
carries only
\mathcal{L}_{0}
stoichiometry
(

,

) and
\mathcal{L}_{3}

(

,

,

),
plus metadata (

,

,

). The full record:

and

\dagger
-paired reactions of

. The rate-law
saturation field deserves comment: when non-empty,

rxnSaturation
divides the mass-action rate by a rational
factor
1+\sum_{i}C_{i}[S_{i}]
, the De Kepper–Epstein 1982 form for
the iodine–malonic-acid step (R9), where saturation by
\mathrm{I_{2}}

closes the negative feedback essential to the batch limit cycle

[
74
]
. Saturation is an
\mathcal{L}_{3}
extension of
pure mass action; it plays no role in detailed balance. The
remainder of this section explains how detailed balance enters the
simulation via the two paired reactions, and what BR’s choice to
leave eight of ten elementary steps unidirectional means for the
cross-level structure.

12.4.1.
\mathcal{L}_{1}
: the enthalpy functor
F_{\!H}

At
\mathcal{L}_{1}
, every reaction
r
carries an enthalpy
F_{\!H}(r)\in\mathbb{R}

and
F_{\!H}
is a monoidal functor:

F_{\!H}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})\;=\;F_{\!H}(r_{1})+F_{\!H}(r_{2})\quad\text{(Hess's Law)},\qquad F_{\!H}(\mathrm{id})\;=\;0.

F_{\!H}
is not a field of
BR.Reaction
; the implementation
stores no per-reaction enthalpies, nor can
F_{\!H}
be reconstructed
from the rate constants alone — a single rate ratio
k_{+}/k_{-}

at one temperature determines
\Delta G^{\circ}(T)
, not the splitting

\Delta G^{\circ}=\Delta H^{\circ}-T\Delta S^{\circ}
. Hess’s Law

\sum_{i}F_{\!H}(r_{i})=0
on closed cycles is a non-trivial constraint
only when the reaction graph contains a cycle of length
\geq 3

(for example, a triangle

\mathrm{A}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{B}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{C}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{A}
); on a trivial 2-cycle

r\circ r^{-1}
it reduces to
F_{\!H}(r)+F_{\!H}(r^{-1})=0
, which
is already enforced by the
\dagger
-structure (below). In BR’s
implemented network the only cycles are the two trivial
reverse-pair cycles

\mathrm{R3}\circ\mathrm{R3\text{-}rev}
and

\mathrm{R4}\circ\mathrm{R4\text{-}rev}
, so Hess’s Law adds no
information beyond the dagger structure. The substantive

\mathcal{L}_{1}
/
\mathcal{L}_{2}
content of the network enters at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
via the
free-energy/rate-constant connection treated next.

12.4.2.
\mathcal{L}_{2}
: dagger structure via paired reactions

Level
\mathcal{L}_{2}
adds an entropy
F_{\!S}(r)
and the
temperature-dependent free-energy functor

F_{\!G}^{T}(r)=F_{\!H}(r)-TF_{\!S}(r)
, together with a

\dagger
-structure: each reaction has a reverse
r^{\dagger}

satisfying
F_{\!H}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{\!H}(r)
,
F_{\!S}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{\!S}(r)
,
and hence
F_{\!G}^{T}(r^{\dagger})=-F_{\!G}^{T}(r)
. The equilibrium locus
is
\ker F_{\!G}^{T}=\{r:F_{\!G}^{T}(r)=0\}
.

In the BR codebase the
\dagger
-structure is realised

explicitly only for two of the ten
elementary steps, by
including their reverses as separate
mkReaction
calls
with reactant and product multisets swapped:

•

R3
/
R3-rev
: iodine hydrolysis

\mathrm{HOI}+\mathrm{I^{-}}+\mathrm{H^{+}}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{I_{2}}+\mathrm{H_{2}O}
with

k_{\mathrm{R3}}=3.1\times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}}

and

k_{\mathrm{R3\text{-}rev}}=0.73\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}

(the latter first-order in
\mathrm{I_{2}}
after

[\mathrm{H_{2}O}]
is folded into
k
).

•

R4
/
R4-rev
: iodine-dioxide-radical
generation

\mathrm{HIO_{2}}+\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}+\mathrm{H^{+}}\rightleftharpoons 2\,\mathrm{IO_{2}^{\bullet}}+\mathrm{H_{2}O}

with

k_{\mathrm{R4}}=7.35\times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}}

and

k_{\mathrm{R4\text{-}rev}}=8.0\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}}
.

The remaining eight elementary reactions (R1, R2, R5–R10) are
unidirectional in the implementation: no reverse
Reaction

value is paired with them. The
\dagger
-structure is therefore
incomplete on the implemented network — consistent with BR being
not weakly reversible (§
12.3
chembox). The
implementation reads each missing reverse as “physically present
but kinetically negligible on the simulation timescale,” an
approximation we revisit empirically in
§
12.9
.

12.4.3. Wegscheider and detailed balance on the two BR pairs

Detailed balance requires that for any reaction cycle
r_{1}\circ\cdots\circ r_{n}=\mathrm{id}
,

\prod_{i=1}^{n}k_{+,i}\;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{n}k_{-,i}.

(39)

On a trivial 2-cycle
r\circ r^{-1}
, (
39
)
is the tautology
k_{+}k_{-}=k_{-}k_{+}
; it is non-trivial only when
the reaction graph contains a cycle of length
\geq 3
(for example
a triangle
\mathrm{A}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{B}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{C}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{A}
, which would
give a non-trivial product of three rate-constant ratios closing
to
1
). The cross-level content of the equation is the
substitution
k_{+}/k_{-}=\exp(-\Delta G^{\circ}/RT)
on each reversible
edge, which rewrites (
39
) as

\exp(-\Delta G^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cycle}}/RT)=1
: the cycle lies in

\ker F_{\!G}^{T}
at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
iff the rate-constant ratios close at

\mathcal{L}_{3}
. The hypothesis is at
\mathcal{L}_{2}
(cycle
\Delta G^{\circ}
); the
assertion is at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
(rate-constant closure). This is a
cross-level statement in the same spirit as DZT
(Remark
12.9
,
\mathcal{L}_{0}\!\to\!\mathcal{L}_{3}
), though
the level pair here is
\mathcal{L}_{2}\!\to\!\mathcal{L}_{3}
.

On the BR network the cycle equation (
39
)
is tautological — the two reverse-pair cycles are both 2-cycles.
What remains is the elementary
detailed-balance identity

applied separately to each pair:

k_{\mathrm{R3}}/k_{\mathrm{R3\text{-}rev}}\;=\;\exp(-\Delta G^{\circ}_{\mathrm{R3}}/RT),\qquad k_{\mathrm{R4}}/k_{\mathrm{R4\text{-}rev}}\;=\;\exp(-\Delta G^{\circ}_{\mathrm{R4}}/RT).

(40)

Each identity is non-trivial when
\Delta G^{\circ}
is fixed by
independent thermodynamic data, in which case the rate-constant
ratio is constrained to a single value rather than chosen freely.
The
\mathcal{L}_{1}
/
\mathcal{L}_{2}
thermodynamic content of the implemented
network at the simulation temperature is wholly carried by the two
ratios of (
40
); we check the constraint
empirically in the chembox below.

Remark 12.10

(The Wegscheider residual is not a lax cell of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
)
.

The single lax cell
\gamma
of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}

(§
12.2
) measures the operational truncation error
of the simulator. The Wegscheider residual — the distance of a
network’s rate constants from the equilibrium locus
(
39
) — is, by contrast, a property of

which network
the user constructs at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
, not a
functorial mismatch in
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
. Conflating the two would multiply
the chapter’s laxity vocabulary without corresponding functorial
content. Wegscheider is a parameter constraint;
\gamma
is a
truncation laxity.

The two
mkReaction
calls are the
operational

\dagger
-structure: the second has
rxnReactants
and

rxnProducts
swapped relative to the first. Detailed
balance on this pair reduces to a single ratio between the two

rxnRate
fields, which we check empirically below. The
R4/R4-rev pair is structurally identical with reactants

\mathrm{HIO_{2}}+\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}+\mathrm{H^{+}}
and

rxnRate

=7.35\times 10^{3}
forward,

8.0\times 10^{5}
reverse.

Detailed balance on the BR pairs

Cycle R3
\,\circ\,
R3-rev.

k_{\mathrm{R3}}/k_{\mathrm{R3\text{-}rev}}=3.1\times 10^{12}/0.73\approx 4.2\times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{M^{-2}}
.
With
RT\approx 2.48\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}
at
298\,\mathrm{K}
, the
detailed-balance identity (
40
) implies

\Delta G^{\circ}_{\mathrm{R3}}=-RT\ln K_{\mathrm{eq}}\approx-72\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}
. Direct computation of

\Delta G^{\circ}_{\mathrm{R3}}
from tabulated

\Delta G^{\circ}_{\mathrm{f}}
values
(
\mathrm{HOI(aq)}\approx-98
,
\mathrm{I^{-}(aq)}=-51.6
,

\mathrm{H^{+}(aq)}=0
,
\mathrm{I_{2}(aq)}=+16.4
,

\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}=-237.1
, all in kJ/mol) gives

-71\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}
. Agreement to
\sim 1\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}

— well inside the literature uncertainty on

\mathrm{HOI(aq)}
— so the R3/R3-rev pair satisfies detailed
balance against independent thermodynamic data.

Cycle R4
\,\circ\,
R4-rev.

k_{\mathrm{R4}}/k_{\mathrm{R4\text{-}rev}}=7.35\times 10^{3}/8.0\times 10^{5}\approx 9.2\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M^{-1}}
, implying

\Delta G^{\circ}_{\mathrm{R4}}\approx+11.6\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}
. Unlike
R3, this is not independently verified: no tabulated

\Delta G^{\circ}_{\mathrm{f}}
of
\mathrm{IO_{2}^{\bullet}}(\mathrm{aq})

is available, so the
+11.6\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}
is a value

inferred
from the rate ratio rather than checked against
external data. The sign and magnitude are consistent with
chemical expectation (radical-producing direction mildly
endergonic), but this is consistency-with-expectation, not
verification.

The eight unidirectional reactions.

For R1, R2, R5–R10 the implementation supplies no reverse, so the
implemented network contains no cycles involving these reactions.
(
39
) is tautological on the cycles that do
exist (the two 2-cycles), and (
40
) is silent on
the unidirectional steps because
k_{-}
is not represented.
Physically these steps have reverses; omitting them is a

modeling decision
expressing the empirical claim that those
reverses have rate constants negligible on the oscillation
timescale (
\tau\sim 10^{1}\,
s). This decision matches the BR
mechanism’s published treatment

[
231
,
74
]
and is exactly what
makes BR
not weakly reversible
at
\mathcal{L}_{0}

(§
12.3
chembox). The
\mathcal{L}_{1}
/
\mathcal{L}_{2}
thermodynamic
content of the BR network is therefore confined to the two
detailed-balance identities of (
40
).

The discussion has so far been about individual
Reaction

values; the
Network
record that aggregates them into

briggsRauscherDE
is small:

Remark 12.11

(Level stratification of
BR.Reaction
)
.

The
Reaction
record of
BR.Reaction
carries

\mathcal{L}_{0}
data (stoichiometric reactant and product multisets) and

\mathcal{L}_{3}
data (rate constant, rate-active subset, rate-law
saturation) in a single record; it carries no
\mathcal{L}_{1}
or
\mathcal{L}_{2}

fields. The thermodynamic content of the network nevertheless
enters the simulation indirectly, through the rate-constant ratios
of the two
\dagger
-paired reactions. Categorically, a

Network
value is a point in

\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{0}}\otimes\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{3}}
subject to the two detailed-balance
identities of (
40
) at the
\mathcal{L}_{2}
/
\mathcal{L}_{3}

interface; the
\mathcal{L}_{2}
functor
F_{\!G}^{T}
at the simulation
temperature is recoverable on the two paired reactions from these
identities, but recovering the
\mathcal{L}_{1}
enthalpy
F_{\!H}
and the
entropy
F_{\!S}
separately would require temperature variation
(
\partial\ln K/\partial T=\Delta H^{\circ}/RT^{2}
), which the
fixed-temperature simulation does not provide.

§12.5.
\mathcal{L}_{3}
in
Hask
: exact SSA and adaptive ODE as parallel operational realisations

The stochastic content of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
is carried by a functor
\FP

that sends each reaction network
\mathcal{N}
with rate constants
to the
\tau
-indexed family of time-
\tau
transition kernels of
its continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) on population states. We
write
\FP(\mathcal{N})_{\tau}\in\mathbf{BorelStoch}
for the kernel at
horizon
\tau
; it is this family that the operational arrows
below realise. The BR codebase implements
two simulators in
Hask
:
BR.SSA.simulate
samples

\FP(\mathcal{N})_{\tau}
exactly (for
\tau
set as

ssaTimeMax
), and
BR.ODE.simulate
integrates the
deterministic large-volume shadow of
\FP
.

•

BR.SSA.simulate
: an exact Gibson–Bruck next-reaction
method (NRM) that samples the CTMC at the molecule-count level.
Its denotational image, after marginalising over the PRNG seed,
is
\FP(\mathcal{N})_{\tau}

exactly
— modulo SplitMix
PRNG quality and floating-point precision; there is no
step-budget or
\tau
-leap truncation.

•

BR.ODE.simulate
: an adaptive implicit-midpoint
Newton integrator that produces the deterministic large-volume
mass-action flow, the
V\to\infty
Kurtz limit of the CTMC

[
179
]
, with a local truncation error controlled by
step-doubling.

Both arrows share their
\mathcal{L}_{0}
+
\mathcal{L}_{3}
input — a

Network
record (§
12.4
) plus an initial
counts or concentrations map — and both are
purely
functional
: no
IO
, no global mutable state, no impurity
at the type level. The SSA threads its SplitMix64 PRNG through
the
ssaPRNG
field of
SSAState
; the ODE is
deterministic and uses no PRNG. The
\gamma
-cell of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}

(§
12.2
) specialises here to zero in distribution
for SSA and to the implicit-midpoint local truncation error for
ODE.

12.5.1. The CTMC and its master equation

Given a reaction network
\mathcal{N}
with rate constants

(k_{r})_{r\in\mathcal{R}}
and a population state

\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}
, the
propensity
of reaction
r
in
state
\mathbf{x}
at volume
V
(litres) is

a_{r}(\mathbf{x};V)\;=\;\frac{k_{r}}{(VN_{A})^{n_{r}-1}}\,\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{a}}_{r}}x_{s}\,(x_{s}-1)\,\cdots\,(x_{s}-m_{rs}+1),

(41)

where
\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{a}}_{r}\subseteq\mathcal{S}
is the support of the
rate-active multiset
rxnRateActive
,
m_{rs}
the
multiplicity of species
s
in that multiset,

n_{r}=\sum_{s}m_{rs}
the rate-law order, and

N_{A}
Avogadro’s constant. The volume scaling

(VN_{A})^{1-n_{r}}
converts a concentration-units rate constant
(
\mathrm{M}^{1-n_{r}}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}
) to a propensity
(events per second). When
rxnSaturation
is non-empty the
propensity is divided further by the rational denominator

1+\sum_{\ell}C_{\ell}\,[S_{\ell}]
, with concentrations

[S_{\ell}]=x_{S_{\ell}}/(VN_{A})
.

Writing
\nu_{r}\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathcal{S}}
for the net stoichiometric change of

r
(products minus reactants), the
chemical master equation

(CME) for
p(\mathbf{x},t)=\Pr[\mathbf{X}(t)=\mathbf{x}]
is

\tfrac{d}{dt}p(\mathbf{x},t)\;=\;\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\bigl[\,a_{r}(\mathbf{x}-\nu_{r};V)\,p(\mathbf{x}-\nu_{r},t)\,-\,a_{r}(\mathbf{x};V)\,p(\mathbf{x},t)\,\bigr],

(42)

under the convention that
\nu_{r,s}=0
for every
pool
species

s
in
P\subseteq\mathcal{S}
(those listed in

netPoolSpecies
, modelling bath reservoirs at fixed counts).
Pool counts thus remain frozen and enter the propensity
(
41
) as fixed parameters — implemented by
the pool-set argument to
applyReaction
in
BR.SSA

and by
poolMask
in
BR.ODE
. For BR,
P
typically
contains
\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}},\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}},\mathrm{MA},\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}
at canonical pH.

For each
\tau>0
, the solution of (
42
) defines a
Markov kernel

\FP(\mathcal{N})_{\tau}\;:\;\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}\quad\text{in }\mathbf{BorelStoch},\qquad\FP(\mathcal{N})_{\tau}(\mathbf{x}_{0},\cdot)\;=\;p(\,\cdot\,,\,\tau\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}),

the
time-
\tau
transition kernel
of the CTMC (with pool
components of the output equal to those of
\mathbf{x}_{0}
by the
convention above). The CTMC construction is functorial in the
network argument by standard chemical-master-equation theory; the
new content below is its realisation as the denotational image of a
pure-Haskell function under the seed-marginalisation of
§
12.2
.

12.5.3. The categorical Gillespie theorem and the
\gamma
-cell

Theorem 12.12

(Categorical Gillespie for BR: exact sampling)
.

Let
\mathcal{N}
be a finite-rate reaction network with rate
constants
(k_{r})_{r\in\mathcal{R}}
, let
\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}
be
the initial population, and let
\tau>0
be the time horizon
encoded as
ssaTimeMax
in
ssaConfig
. Let

\mu_{\tau}(\mathbf{x}_{0},\cdot)
be the push-forward distribution
on
\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{S}}
obtained by sampling

\texttt{ssaSeed}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(\{0,1\}^{64})
, iterating

step
from the resulting initial
SSAState
until

step
returns
Nothing
, and reading the

ssaCounts
field of the last
Just
-state.
2
2

2

This reads the state directly from the iteration, bypassing

simulate
’s
ssaSampleEvery
filter: if

ssaSampleEvery > 0
, the final entry of the trajectory
returned by
simulate
can predate termination, but

ssaCounts
of the last
Just
-state always gives the
state at termination.
Under the para-monoidal seed-marginalisation
of §
12.2
,

\mu_{\tau}(\mathbf{x}_{0},\cdot)\;=\;\FP(\mathcal{N})_{\tau}(\mathbf{x}_{0},\cdot)\qquad\text{exactly}

(43)

in the sense of TV distance, modulo (i) SplitMix64’s deviation
from an i.i.d.
\mathrm{Uniform}([0,1))
source over the PRNG
draws the trajectory consumes (an
|\mathcal{R}|
-sized initialisation
plus one draw per firing under Gibson–Bruck’s draw-per-firing
update) and (ii) the floating-point representation of the
inverse-CDF exponential and uniform draws.

Proof.

By the Doob–Gillespie theorem
[
121
]
, at any

SSAState
with time
t
and counts
\mathbf{x}
, one call
to
step
samples the next firing

(\mu^{\star},\,T_{\mu^{\star}}-t)
from

(\mathrm{Cat}(a_{\mu}/A),\,\mathrm{Exp}(A))
with

A=\sum_{\mu}a_{\mu}(\mathbf{x};V)
— exactly the transition
kernel of the CTMC. At the post-firing time
t^{\prime}
, the
Gibson–Bruck update
[
120
]
sets, for the fired
channel,
\tau_{\mu^{\star}}^{\mathrm{new}}=t^{\prime}+W
with

W\sim\mathrm{Exp}(a_{\mu^{\star}}^{\mathrm{new}})
a fresh draw,
and for each un-fired affected channel
j
,

\tau_{j}^{\mathrm{new}}=t^{\prime}+(a_{j}^{\mathrm{old}}/a_{j}^{\mathrm{new}})(\tau_{j}^{\mathrm{old}}-t^{\prime})
; the latter preserves the exponential
distribution of the residual wait by the memorylessness of

\mathrm{Exp}
. Together, both updates ensure that after each step
the conditional joint distribution of
\{\tau_{\mu}-t\}_{\mu}
given
the current state remains the correct product of
\mathrm{Exp}(a_{\mu})

distributions. The
step iteration terminates only when (a) all putative times
are infinite (no firable reaction), or (b) the next firing time
exceeds
\tau
. Both are correct stopping rules for the
time-
\tau
kernel: in case (a) the chain has reached an absorbing
state and remains there through
\tau
; in case (b) no further
event occurs in
[t,\tau]
. Hence
ssaCounts
of the last

Just
-state equals the CTMC state at time
\tau
in both
cases. No truncation is introduced. The qualifications (i) and (ii) above
are the only departures from exactness: SplitMix64 passes BigCrush

[
281
]
, and
exponential
(in

BR.PRNG
) clamps the input to the inverse-CDF
-\log(u^{\prime})/a

at
u^{\prime}=2^{-53}
whenever a draw underflows to
u=0
; this
replaces only a probability-
2^{-53}
tail event with the maximum
draw
\log(2^{53})/a\approx 37/a
, leaving the exponential
distribution unchanged elsewhere.
∎

Remark 12.13

(The
\gamma
-cell of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
, made concrete)
.

The lax cell
\gamma
of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
(§
12.2
) is the
TV-metric laxity for the stochastic arrow and the state-space
local truncation error for the deterministic arrow.
Theorem
12.12
states that for SSA the TV
component of
\gamma
vanishes (up to qualifications (i)–(ii)):
BR.SSA has no
\tau
-leap, no step-budget, and no fixed-step-size
approximation. The remaining content of
\gamma
lives entirely
on the ODE arrow: the implicit-midpoint scheme with step-doubling
control bounds the per-component local truncation error in
species
s
by
\texttt{odeATol}+\texttt{odeRTol}\cdot|c_{s}|

(BR.ODE uses a weighted max-norm of these component errors as its
step-control criterion), accumulated over the trajectory; this is
what Remark
12.15
below compares against the SSA’s
exact samples.

Remark 12.14

(Pure-functional rather than Kleisli semantics)
.

Most categorical-CRN expositions treat the rate-equation ODE only
(e.g. Baez–Pollard’s open dynamical systems

[
28
]
); a Haskell-side stochastic treatment of the
CME would naturally reach for a Kleisli category of
IO
or
a similar effect-type framework. The BR.SSA implementation chooses
neither: the PRNG state is a pure value in
SSAState
, and

step
and
simulate
are total functions in
Hask

with no Kleisli or monadic structure visible at the type level.
The stochastic semantics enters only via the para-monoidal lift of
§
12.2
, where the PRNG seed becomes the parameter
object
W=\{0,1\}^{64}
and seed-marginalisation produces the
Markov kernel. This is operationally minimal: no
IO
taint
propagates, replay is trivial (just store the seed), and the type

SSAState -> Maybe SSAState
of
step
carries no
effect markers beyond the totality-signalling
Maybe
.

12.5.4. The deterministic limit: BR.ODE

The same network admits a deterministic flow by replacing the CME
with the mass-action ODE on concentrations

\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{\mathcal{S}}
:

\dot{\mathbf{c}}\;=\;\bm{\nu}\,\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{c}),\qquad v_{r}(\mathbf{c})\;=\;\frac{k_{r}\,\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{a}}_{r}}c_{s}^{m_{rs}}}{1+\sum_{\ell}C_{\ell}\,c_{S_{\ell}}},

(44)

with
\bm{\nu}\in\mathbb{Z}^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{R}}
the stoichiometric
matrix (column
r
is the
\nu_{r}
of (
42
)),
v_{r}

the (saturated) mass-action rate, and the
\ell
sum running over
the species–coefficient pairs
(S_{\ell},C_{\ell})
in

rxnSaturation
. This is the large-volume
Kurtz limit
V\to\infty
of the CTMC
[
179
]
: the
CTMC’s scaled population
\mathbf{X}(t)/(VN_{A})
converges in
probability to the ODE solution on any finite time interval.

integrates (

) with an adaptive

\displaystyle\texttt{simulate}\;::

for counts). Kurtz’s limit
theorem predicts agreement between CTMC and ODE on macroscopic

12.5.5. The two
\mathcal{L}_{3}
arrows as parallel operational realisations

Remark 12.15

(SSA and ODE as parallel operational realisations of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
)
.

BR.SSA.simulate
and
BR.ODE.simulate
are two
Haskell functions running side-by-side over the same
\mathcal{L}_{0}
+
\mathcal{L}_{3}

input data — a
Network
record plus an initial counts or
concentrations map — though their precise source and target types
differ (see the haskellbox signatures above; the SSA takes one

SSAState
, the ODE takes a curried

ODEConfig
\to
ODEState
\to
Double
). The SSA delivers a
sampled trajectory of molecule counts, the ODE delivers a
deterministic trajectory of concentrations. Their denotational
images differ: the SSA’s (under the para-monoidal lift of
§
12.2
) is
\FP(\mathcal{N})_{\tau}
itself, by
Theorem
12.12
; the ODE evaluates the deterministic
large-volume shadow of
\FP
, realised via the Kurtz limit

\mathbf{X}/(VN_{A})\rightsquigarrow\mathbf{c}
. Both functions
nonetheless read the rate constants, saturation data, and
stoichiometry from a single
Network
value without
translation, and agree on observables well-defined in the

V\to\infty
limit while disagreeing on finite-population
fluctuations.

\mathcal{L}_{3}
on the BR network

The implementation
briggsRauscherDE
(§
12.3
)
is driven at canonical BR conditions:

[\mathrm{IO_{3}^{-}}]_{0},\;[\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}]_{0},\;[\mathrm{MA}]_{0},\;[\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}]_{0}
in the published ranges

\sim 10^{-2}
–
1\,\mathrm{M}
at pH
\,\sim 2

[
231
,
74
]
.

•

No step-budget truncation.

BR.SSA.step

terminates only on (a) all putative times being infinite (no
firable reaction) or (b) the next firing time exceeding

ssaTimeMax
. Both are exact stopping rules for the
time-
\tau
kernel, so the TV component of
\gamma

(Theorem
12.12
) is zero in distribution.
The qualifications are PRNG quality (SplitMix64) and
floating-point precision in
exponential
.

•

Volume choice.

ssaVolumeL = 1e-15
(one
femtolitre) is the default, chosen to keep molecule counts
tractable: at this volume, a millimolar species has

\sim 6\times 10^{5}
molecules and a 10
\upmu
M species

\sim 6\times 10^{3}
. Higher volumes amplify event rates
linearly in
V
; the iodine-equilibration channel R3/R3-rev
(rate constants
3.1{\times}10^{12}\,\mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}}

and
0.73\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}
; §
12.4
) is typically
the dominant event channel and the principal constraint on the
largest tractable simulation volume.

•

Stiffness for the ODE.
Numerical rate constants in

briggsRauscherDE
span roughly ten orders of magnitude
(R3 forward at
3.1{\times}10^{12}
down to R9 at

12.5
and R10 at
37
, with R3-rev at
0.73
in different
units). This forces
BR.ODE
to use an implicit scheme:
explicit Runge–Kutta would require step sizes too small to
integrate even one BR oscillation in reasonable wall-clock
time. The adaptive implicit-midpoint Newton method with
step-doubling is the source of the ODE component of
\gamma

(Remark
12.13
).

•

Where SSA and ODE should differ.
At the
simulator’s tractable volumes (
\sim 1
fL by default), the
SSA is expected to show fluctuations on whichever species are
held at low occupancy by the dynamics — typically radical
intermediates such as
\mathrm{IO_{2}^{\bullet}}
— which the
ODE smooths to its mean-field shadow. The rate constants in

briggsRauscherDE
(shared by both arrows via the

Network
record) have been tuned to reproduce the
experimental BR oscillation period under the deterministic ODE
(typically reported in the
\sim 10
–
50\,\mathrm{s}
range,
depending on initial conditions and temperature

[
231
,
74
]
); whether the SSA
at the simulator’s small volume also reproduces this period, or
shows drift from finite-population effects, is the empirical
question addressed in §
12.9
.

§12.6. The Para construction in
Hask

The Para construction
[
70
]
formalises a morphism parameterised by an
external object. For BR, the parameter is the SplitMix64 seed

\texttt{ssaSeed}\in W=\{0,1\}^{64}
that fixes the SSA’s random
trajectory, threaded purely through
ssaPRNG

(§
12.5
); for the ODE, the parameter is empty.
Para gives the categorical home for “a Haskell function plus its
stored parameter,” decoupling the parameter algebra (how seeds
compose) from the underlying-morphism algebra (how SSA and ODE
trajectories compose). We give the abstract definition, instantiate
it over
Hask
, and verify the coherence laws — which here separate
cleanly into a strict underlying layer (function composition in

Hask
is on the nose) and a bicategorical parameter-tensor layer
(tuple-isomorphism coherence).

12.6.1. Abstract Para

Definition 12.16

(Para construction

[
70
, Def. 3.1]
)
.

Let
(\mathbf{C},\otimes,I)
be a symmetric monoidal category with
a right actegory action
\mathbf{M}\curvearrowright\mathbf{C}
.
The bicategory
\mathrm{Para}(\mathbf{C})
has:

•

Objects
: those of
\mathbf{C}
.

•

1-morphisms

A\to B
: pairs
(P,f)
with

P\in\mathbf{M}
a
parameter object
and

f:P\otimes A\to B
a morphism of
\mathbf{C}
.

•

Composition
:

(Q,g)\circ(P,f)=(P\otimes Q,\,g\circ(\mathrm{id}_{Q}\otimes f))
;
parameter objects compose by tensor.

•

2-morphisms

(P,f)\Rightarrow(Q,g)
:
reparameterisations
r:P\to Q
in
\mathbf{M}
such that

g\circ(r\otimes\mathrm{id}_{A})=f
.

•

Identity
:
(I,\eta_{A})
with
\eta_{A}:I\otimes A\to A

the left unitor of the actegory.

The bicategorical coherence data (associator, left/right unitors for
composition) are inherited from
(\mathbf{M},\otimes,I)
and the
actegory action.

For BR’s pure-functional simulation, we take both
\mathbf{C}
and

\mathbf{M}
to be
Hask
(the total fragment, following
Assumption
12.1
in §
12.2
), with
Cartesian product as tensor and the actegory action
P\otimes A=(P,A)
(tuple type). A 1-morphism
(P,f):A\to B
then
corresponds, by currying, to a pair (a stored parameter value of
type
P
, a pure Haskell function of type
P\to A\to B
). The
distinction from the operationally-effectful target one might
naturally reach for in a Haskell-side stochastic treatment (Para
over
\mathbf{Kl}(\mathsf{IO})
) is exactly the distinction articulated in
Remark
12.14
: BR.SSA carries its PRNG state as
pure data, not as an
IO
effect.

explicitly. For pedagogical clarity we display the wrapper that
