12.6.3. Coherence of the Para laws: two layers

The bicategorical laws of
\mathrm{Para}(\textbf{Hask})
split into two layers. The

parameter-tensor layer
involves canonical Cartesian-product
isomorphisms of
Hask
that are non-identity at the type level:

\displaystyle\lambda_{P}

\displaystyle:\bigl((),P\bigr)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;P,\qquad((\,),p)\mapsto p,

\displaystyle\rho_{P}

\displaystyle:\bigl(P,()\bigr)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;P,\qquad(p,(\,))\mapsto p,

\displaystyle\alpha_{P,Q,R}

\displaystyle:\bigl((P,Q),R\bigr)\;\xrightarrow{\sim}\;\bigl(P,(Q,R)\bigr),\quad((p,q),r)\mapsto(p,(q,r)).

The
underlying-morphism layer
consists of strict equalities of
pure Haskell functions
A\to B
: ordinary
Hask
composition

g\circ f=\lambda a.\,g(f(a))
is strictly associative and unital
on the nose (no monad laws are invoked because no monad is present).

Proposition 12.17

(Para laws in
Hask
)
.

The Haskell implementation realises
\mathrm{Para}(\textbf{Hask})
as a bicategory:
for any 1-morphisms

f :: ParaMorphism p a b
,

g :: ParaMorphism q b c
, and

h :: ParaMorphism r c d
,

(i)

(Left unit.)

paraThen paraId f
and
f
agree
under the parameter-tensor iso
\lambda_{P}
, with underlying
morphisms strictly equal by the identity law of
Hask

composition.

(ii)

(Right unit.)

paraThen f paraId
and
f
agree
under
\rho_{P}
, with underlying morphisms strictly equal by the
identity law of
Hask
composition.

(iii)

(Associativity.)

paraThen (paraThen f g) h
and

paraThen f (paraThen g h)
agree under
\alpha_{P,Q,R}
,
with underlying morphisms strictly equal by the associativity of

Hask
composition.

The non-identity tuple isomorphisms make
\mathrm{Para}(\textbf{Hask})
a

bicategory
, not a strict 2-category; coherence data live
entirely at the parameter-tensor layer, and all non-coherence
equalities hold strictly.

Proof.

We give (iii); (i) and (ii) are simpler and analogous. Unfolding

paraThen
twice:

\displaystyle\texttt{pmApply}\bigl(\texttt{paraThen}\,(\texttt{paraThen}\,f\,g)\,h\bigr)\,\bigl((p,q),r\bigr)\,a

\displaystyle\qquad=\texttt{pmApply}\,h\,r\,\bigl(\texttt{pmApply}\,g\,q\,(\texttt{pmApply}\,f\,p\,a)\bigr),

\displaystyle\texttt{pmApply}\bigl(\texttt{paraThen}\,f\,(\texttt{paraThen}\,g\,h)\bigr)\,\bigl(p,(q,r)\bigr)\,a

\displaystyle\qquad=\texttt{pmApply}\,h\,r\,\bigl(\texttt{pmApply}\,g\,q\,(\texttt{pmApply}\,f\,p\,a)\bigr).

The two right-hand sides are syntactically equal Haskell expressions;
they differ only in the bracketing of the parameter tuple, which is
mediated by
\alpha_{P,Q,R}
. Hence the two Para 1-morphisms agree
under the parameter-tensor associator, with strictly equal underlying
morphisms.
∎

Remark 12.18

(Why no monad laws appear)
.

The corresponding result for
\mathrm{Para}(\mathbf{Kl}(T))
over a Kleisli category
invokes the monad’s left-/right-unit and associativity laws to verify
the underlying-morphism equalities. In
\mathrm{Para}(\textbf{Hask})
no monad is
present: composition is plain function composition, and the
underlying-morphism equalities are strict identities of Haskell terms.
The bicategorical coherence remains at the parameter-tensor layer.
This is the Para counterpart of the
“pure-functional rather than Kleisli” choice articulated in
Remark
12.14
.

Remark 12.19

(Structural unity, continued)
.

Capucci–Myers
[
57
]
(discussed in
§
12.2
, Remark
12.6
) place

\mathrm{Para}(\mathbf{C})
and
\mathbf{Kl}(T)
as instances of a single abstract
construction. This shared structural placement is the reason a
functor
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}:\mathrm{Para}(\mathcal{L}_{3})\to\textbf{Hask}
(§
12.7
)
can be expected to exist naturally rather than as an ad-hoc
construction; we invoke this structural background implicitly but
do not develop it further here.

12.6.4. BR’s two arrows as Para 1-morphisms

The two operational realisations of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
(§
12.5
)
fit the Para shape as follows. Both lie in the sub-bicategory

\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})\subseteq\mathrm{Para}(\textbf{Hask})
of
§
12.2
, Proposition
12.4
:

f_{\mathrm{SSA}}
at
n=1
(parameter
W
) and
f_{\mathrm{ODE}}

at
n=0
(parameter
\mathbb{1}
).

SSA as a Para 1-morphism with
P=W
.

BR.SSA.simulate
fits the Para shape with parameter
space
W=\{0,1\}^{64}
(the PRNG seed stored in

ssaConfig
). Conceptually, we view it as a 1-morphism

\displaystyle\bigl(W,\;f_{\mathrm{SSA}}\bigr)

\displaystyle\;:\;\texttt{(Network, SSAConfig$\setminus$Seed, Map Species Int)}

\displaystyle\quad\;\longrightarrow\;\texttt{[(Double, Map Species Int)]}

in
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
, where
f_{\mathrm{SSA}}
is the curried form of

simulate
with the seed extracted from
ssaConfig
;
the remaining components of
SSAState
(network, volume,

\tau_{\max}
, sample interval, initial counts) sit in the second
argument. This is a categorical re-shaping, not a separately-named
BR function. Currying gives a function of type
W\to(\ldots)\to[\ldots]
matching the
pmApply
field of a

ParaMorphism W ……
. Sampling the seed from

\mathrm{Uniform}(W)
and reading
ssaCounts
of the last

Just
-state produces the Markov kernel

\FP(\mathcal{N})_{\tau}
of Theorem
12.12
; this
seed-marginalisation is the action of the denotational functor

F:\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})\to\mathbf{BorelStoch}
of
§
12.2
—
not
a
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
-internal
2-morphism, since
f_{\mathrm{SSA}}
at any single seed value
differs from the marginal kernel.

ODE as a Para 1-morphism with
P=()
.

BR.ODE.simulate
carries no Para parameter: its

ODEConfig
consists of tolerances and step bounds that are
fixed numerical-method choices, not stochastic parameters that the
denotational functor marginalises. Hence
BR.ODE.simulate

fits the Para shape as a
liftToPara
of an
unparameterised conceptual underlying-morphism

\displaystyle f_{\mathrm{ODE}}

\displaystyle\;::\;\texttt{(ODEConfig, ODEState, Double)}

\displaystyle\quad\;\to\;\texttt{([(Double, Map Species Double)], Maybe String)},

i.e. the Para 1-morphism

\bigl((),\,f_{\mathrm{ODE}}\bigr)
, which is the
n=0
case in

\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
. Like
f_{\mathrm{SSA}}
above,

f_{\mathrm{ODE}}
is the categorical re-shaping of the curried

BR.ODE.simulate
, not a separately-named BR function.

The asymmetry.

The two arrows sit at different powers of
W
within

\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
: the SSA at
n=1
(non-trivial seed parameter

W
), the ODE at
n=0
(unit parameter
\mathbb{1}
). This
asymmetry is the Para-side reflection
of the asymmetry in their denotational images established in
Remark
12.15
: the SSA’s denotational image

\FP(\mathcal{N})_{\tau}
is a non-trivial Markov kernel obtained by
seed-marginalisation, whereas the ODE’s denotational image is the
deterministic Kurtz limit, requiring no marginalisation.

Para parameters in BR

The Para parameters that appear in BR are:

•

Stochastic parameter
W=\{0,1\}^{64}
:
the
SplitMix64 seed of
BR.SSA.simulate
. Different seeds
yield different sampled trajectories; marginalising over

\mathrm{Uniform}(W)
recovers the CTMC kernel.

•

Trivial parameter
()
:
carried by

BR.ODE.simulate
and by any deterministic Haskell function
embedded via
liftToPara
.

Numerical-method choices such as
odeRTol
,
odeATol
,

odeHMin
,
odeHMax
sit
inside
the

ODEConfig
record and travel as ordinary inputs to the
underlying morphism — not as Para parameters — because the
denotational reading of the ODE does not marginalise over them; they
control the deterministic integrator’s local truncation error
(the ODE component of
\gamma
,
Remark
12.13
) rather than a stochastic
ensemble. The BR
Network
record’s stoichiometries,
rate-active multisets, saturation data, rate constants, and
pool-species set are likewise ordinary inputs, not Para parameters:
they fix the kinetic model that the kernel
\FP
acts on, and the
chapter’s tower already accounts for them across
\mathcal{L}_{0}
through

\mathcal{L}_{3}
(§§
12.3
,
12.4
,

12.5
).

§12.7. The simulation functor
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
: construction and properties

With
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
established in §
12.6
and the
seed-marginalisation functor

F:\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})\to\mathbf{BorelStoch}
in place
(Proposition
12.4
), the operational functor
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}

closes the diagram of Figure
1
.

12.7.1. Construction of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}

Definition 12.20

(Simulation functor)
.

The
simulation functor

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}\;:\;\mathrm{Para}\!\left(\mathcal{L}_{0}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{2}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{3}\right)\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})

(45)

sends an object
\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}]
(a free commutative monoid on
species) to its
Hask
realisation
Map Species Int

(Proposition
12.7
, §
12.3
). On
1-morphisms at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
,
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
realises a Para 1-morphism

(\Theta,f_{\theta})
as
(\Theta,\tilde{f}_{\theta})
in

\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
, where
\tilde{f}_{\theta}
is the
underlying-morphism realisation of
f_{\theta}
in
Hask
obtained
from the
\mathcal{L}_{k}
realisations of §
12.3
–§
12.5
; the parameter object
\Theta
is
unchanged because both source and target take their parameter
actegory from the same Cartesian fragment of
Hask
. BR’s two
operational realisations of
\mathcal{L}_{3}
(§
12.5
)
instantiate the two parameter classes of
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
:

\mathcal{L}_{3}
realisation

Para parameter

Image in
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})

SSA (Gibson–Bruck NRM)

W=\mathtt{Word64}

(W,\,f_{\mathrm{SSA}})
,
n=1

ODE (implicit midpoint)

\mathbb{1}

((),\,f_{\mathrm{ODE}})
,
n=0

On 2-morphisms,
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
acts as the identity on the underlying
reparameterisation
r:\Theta\to\Theta^{\prime}
(the parameter actegory
is shared), and the Para 2-morphism condition

g\circ(r\times\mathrm{id}_{A})=f
in the source transports to
its
Hask
counterpart in the target by strict functoriality of
the
\mathcal{L}_{k}
realisations.

Remark 12.21

(
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
between bicategories)
.

Both the domain

\mathrm{Para}(\mathcal{L}_{0}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{2}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{3})
and the
codomain
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
are bicategories with non-identity
parameter-tensor coherence data
\lambda,\rho,\alpha
inherited
from
Hask
’s Cartesian product (§

).
Proposition
12.22
below shows that
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
is
a strict
2
-functor between them: its own unit and composition
constraints are identity
2
-cells, and the target’s
parameter-tensor coherence is inherited verbatim.

12.7.2. Main proposition

Proposition 12.22

(Properties of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
)
.

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
is a strict
2
-functor between bicategories: all its
unit and composition constraints are identity
2
-cells, and the
parameter-tensor coherence of the target is inherited from

\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
unchanged. Explicitly:

(i)

Strict on objects.

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathbb{N}[\mathcal{S}])=\mathtt{Map\ Species\ Int}
on the
nose, by Proposition
12.7
.

(ii)

Strict on identities.

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathrm{paraId}_{A})=\mathrm{paraId}_{\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(A)}
on the
nose. The Para identity at
X
is
(I,\eta_{X})
with
I=()

the shared actegory unit and
\eta_{X}
the left unitor at
X
;

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
preserves both components.

(iii)

Strict on composition.

For composable Para 1-morphisms
f,g
in the source,

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}\bigl(g\circ_{\mathrm{Para}}f\bigr)\;=\;\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(g)\circ_{\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})}\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(f)

on the nose.

(iv)

Target coherence inherited.

The parameter-tensor associator, left unitor, and right unitor
of
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
(Proposition
12.17
) act as
the bicategorical coherence data of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
’s codomain;

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
introduces no additional
2
-cells at this layer.

Proof.

(i): Proposition
12.7
.
(ii): unfold
\mathrm{paraId}_{A}=(I,\eta_{A})
. The parameter
component
I=()
is identical in source and target because the
parameter actegory is shared (Cartesian fragment of
Hask
;
clause (iv)). The underlying component
\eta_{A}
is a left unitor
in the source’s underlying category, sent by the
\mathcal{L}_{k}

realisations to the left unitor
\eta_{\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(A)}
in
Hask
by
strict functoriality at the
1
-category level.
(iii): both
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(g\circ_{\mathrm{Para}}f)
and

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(g)\circ_{\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})}\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(f)
unfold via
Definition
12.16
to a Para 1-morphism with parameter

\Theta_{f}\times\Theta_{g}
and underlying morphism

(\theta_{f},\theta_{g},a)\mapsto\mathrm{und}(g)(\theta_{g},\mathrm{und}(f)(\theta_{f},a))
at the underlying-morphism
layer; the
\mathcal{L}_{k}
realisations
(§
12.3
–§

) preserve this
expression strictly as
1
-category functors.
(iv): the parameter actegory is shared (both source and target use
the Cartesian fragment of
Hask
), so
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
acts as the
identity on parameter objects and inherits the target’s
parameter-tensor coherence data verbatim.
∎

Remark 12.23

.

§12.8.
\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{3}
projection: rate constants as scalar
coarse-grainings and model variants as comparable reductions

The most conceptually delicate aspect of the simulation functor of
§
12.7
is that
\mathcal{L}_{4}
mechanism data appears
inside the
\mathcal{L}_{3}
parameter space. At first sight this violates
the tower’s level stratification —
\mathcal{L}_{4}
bond-level information
is supposed to be invisible at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
. This section shows that
the appearance is a
parameter projection
: the BR simulation
retains only the part of
\mathcal{L}_{4}
data that survives as scalar rate
constants and, for channels with rate-limiting intermediates, the
saturation form of the rate law. The chapter’s several BR network
variants are correspondingly different
\mathcal{L}_{3}
reductions of the
same underlying mechanism, comparable in
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
via the
construction of §
12.2
.

12.8.1. The
\mathcal{L}_{4}
content of BR’s rate constants

Level
\mathcal{L}_{4}
is the category of open reaction networks with full
bond-level mechanism data: a morphism at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
specifies the
elementary-step mechanism (which bonds form and break), the
transition-state geometry, and the parameters determining kinetic
isotope effects, temperature dependence, and solvent dependence

[
84
]
.

The BR mechanism in
BR.Mechanism
encodes the
De Kepper–Epstein skeleton
[
74
]
as

briggsRauscherDE
(10 elementary steps plus two explicit
reverses; 12 channels). Each channel is recorded as a

Reaction
value (§
12.4
) carrying three
pieces of data relevant to the
\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{3}
projection:

•

rxnRate :: Double
— the scalar rate constant
used by both
BR.SSA
and
BR.ODE
.

•

rxnSaturation :: [(Species, Double)]
— an
optional rational denominator
1+\sum_{i}C_{i}[S_{i}]
in the
rate law, non-empty only on channels with a rate-limiting
intermediate (e.g., R9 of
[
74
]
, where

\mathrm{I}_{2}
saturation supplies the negative feedback that
closes the limit cycle).

•

rxnProvenance :: RateProvenance
— metadata
tagging each rate as either
Measured
(with a citation
key to an independent kinetic study) or

FitToOscillate
(the “judicious assignment” of

[
231
]
).

The first two fields enter the propensity (SSA) and ODE
right-hand side; the third is metadata visible to the framework
but not used by the rate formula.

12.8.2. A parameter projection

Definition 12.26

(Coarse
\mathcal{L}_{4}
parameter space for BR)
.

For a BR network
\mathcal{N}
with channel set
\mathcal{R}
, the

coarse
\mathcal{L}_{4}
parameter space
is

\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{4},\,\mathrm{coarse}}(\mathcal{N})\;:=\;\prod_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\,\bigl(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\;\times\;\mathrm{List}(\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0})\;\times\;\mathsf{Prov}\bigr),

one factor per channel, with components
(\mathtt{rxnRate},\mathtt{rxnSaturation},\mathtt{rxnProvenance})
.

Definition 12.27

(The
\mathcal{L}_{4}
parameter projection
\pi_{4}
)
.

The
\mathcal{L}_{4}
parameter projection
is the map

\pi_{4}\;:\;\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{4}}(\mathcal{N})\;\longrightarrow\;\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{4},\,\mathrm{coarse}}(\mathcal{N})

sending each full
\mathcal{L}_{4}
mechanism to its triple

(k_{r},\mathrm{sat}_{r},\mathrm{prov}_{r})_{r\in\mathcal{R}}
.
The projection is
lossy by construction
: it drops all
mechanism data beyond what the three retained fields encode —
bond-level elementary-step structure, transition-state geometry,
isotopic-substitution sensitivity, solvent and ionic-strength
dependence, pressure dependence, and any explicit temperature
dependence beyond what is already absorbed into
k_{r}
at the
reference conditions (Remark
12.31
).

Proposition 12.28

(
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-coarse augmentation of the BR parameter space)
.

The BR simulation is parameterised by

\Theta_{\mathrm{sim}}\;=\;\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{1}}\otimes\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{2}}\otimes\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{4},\,\mathrm{coarse}}(\mathcal{N}),

(46)

where
\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{1}},\Theta_{\mathcal{L}_{2}}
are the species- and
stoichiometry-level parameters of §
12.4
and the
third factor is the
\pi_{4}
-image of
\mathcal{L}_{4}
mechanism data.
Under
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
(§
12.7
), the third factor enters
the simulation only through the propensity formulas of
Theorem
12.12
(SSA) and the corresponding ODE
right-hand sides (§
12.5
); two
\mathcal{L}_{4}

mechanisms whose
\pi_{4}
-images agree map to the same morphism in

\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
.

Proof.

BR.SSA.simulate
and
BR.ODE.simulate
compute
propensities using the rate-law fields
rxnRateActive
,

rxnRate
, and
rxnSaturation
, and update state
using the stoichiometric multisets
rxnReactants
and

rxnProducts
. No other reaction data is consulted:

rxnName
is a label, and
rxnProvenance
is
metadata visible to the framework but not read by the rate or
update logic. Full
\mathcal{L}_{4}
mechanism data (transition states,
KIE-sensitivity, etc.) is not represented in the

Reaction
record at all. Two
\mathcal{L}_{4}
mechanisms for the
same network whose
\pi_{4}
-images agree — i.e., produce identical

(\mathtt{rxnRate},\mathtt{rxnSaturation})
per channel —
therefore yield identical propensities and identical ODE
right-hand sides, hence identical simulator outputs modulo PRNG
and IEEE-754 qualifications.
∎

Remark 12.29

(Provenance as a discriminator of
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-strength)
.

The
rxnProvenance
tag is
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-strength metadata: not
used by the rate formula but visible to the framework. A network
all of whose rate constants are tagged
Measured

(independent kinetic citations) is
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-strong
: the
simulation’s qualitative behaviour is not tuned by free
parameters. The 12 channels of
briggsRauscherDE
are
currently all
Measured
, making BR an
\mathcal{L}_{4}
-strong test
bed within the chapter’s framework; oscillating reactions
requiring
FitToOscillate
constants would sit at a
correspondingly weaker
\mathcal{L}_{4}
strength.

12.8.3. Model variants as comparable
\mathcal{L}_{3}
reductions

BR.Mechanism
provides several network variants beyond

briggsRauscherDE
:
bufferedH
(with
\mathrm{H}^{+}

pooled),
broCODENetwork
(the BROCODE 2025 reduction),

broCODE5VarNetwork
(a five-dynamical-variable reduction
designed for Hopf bifurcation analysis), and

furrowLikePoolNetwork
(a Furrow-style variant pooling
several intermediates). Each variant is obtained from

briggsRauscherDE
by some combination of
(i) restricting the channel set
\mathcal{R}
, and
(ii) enlarging
netPoolSpecies
(the set of species held
constant during simulation;
ssaCounts
for these species
are frozen, per the pool-species convention of
§
12.5
).

Each variant
V
thus determines a different point of

\Theta_{\mathrm{sim}}
, and via
F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
a different Markov kernel
in
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
:

F_{V}\;:=\;F\bigl(\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(V)\bigr)\;\in\;\mathbf{BorelStoch},

(47)

sending each initial state
\mathbf{x}_{0}
and horizon
\tau
to a
probability measure
F_{V}(\mathbf{x}_{0},\tau,\cdot)
over
trajectories.

Proposition 12.30

(Canonical embedding of BR model variants)
.

The composition
F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
(§§
12.2
,

12.7
) embeds every well-formed BR network into

\mathbf{BorelStoch}
as a Markov kernel via
(
47
). The embedding is canonical in
the sense that the same
F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
applies to all variants;
comparison of variants is therefore comparison of Markov kernels
in a single category, with metric choices (total variation,
Wasserstein-1, relative entropy) available once the variants are
embedded in a common dynamical state space (extending each
variant’s kernel by Dirac mass on its pooled coordinates).

Proof.

F
and
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
are defined on
\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
regardless of
the network argument;
mkNetwork
validates each variant
as a well-formed value of type
Network
, on which both

BR.SSA.simulate
and
BR.ODE.simulate
are
total by Assumption
12.1
(§
12.2
),
so the resulting kernel is a probability measure on the
variant’s species support. Embedding into a common state space
(union of dynamical species sets) is by extension via Dirac mass
on each variant’s pooled coordinates.
∎

\mathcal{L}_{3}
reductions: predicted invariance and drift

The categorical framework predicts which BR observables should be
invariant under which
\mathcal{L}_{3}
reductions:

•

Onset preservation.
Oscillation
onset

(the Hopf bifurcation) depends on both the network’s
\mathcal{L}_{2}

stoichiometric topology and the sign-pattern of
\mathcal{L}_{3}

Jacobian eigenvalues at the fixed point. Reductions that
preserve the autocatalytic feedback channels of the
De Kepper–Epstein skeleton (in particular

broCODE5VarNetwork
, designed for Hopf bifurcation
analysis) preserve the capacity for oscillation, even if the
quantitative bifurcation point shifts.

•

Quantitative drift.
Oscillation
period
and

amplitude
are
\mathcal{L}_{3}
-quantitative: they depend on the
rate constants retained by
\pi_{4}
together with which
species are dynamical. Variants whose
netPoolSpecies

removes feedback-relevant species should show measurable drift
in these observables.

•

Falsification handle.
Replacing any

Measured
rate constant in

briggsRauscherDE
with a
FitToOscillate

surrogate of the same order of magnitude should preserve
oscillation onset but degrade quantitative agreement with the
experimental period and amplitude — the provenance
machinery makes this a structured test rather than an ad
hoc parameter sweep.

Proposition
12.30
grounds these claims
operationally: large TV distance between
F_{V}
and
F_{V^{\prime}}
at
horizon
\tau
flags variants disagreeing on observable
distributions at that horizon, even when both oscillate.

Remark 12.31

(What
\pi_{4}
cannot see, for BR)
.

By construction
\pi_{4}
retains only the scalar rate constant,
saturation list, and provenance tag per channel. It drops:

(i)

the full elementary-step mechanism (which bonds form and
break in each channel; concerted versus stepwise pathways;
radical versus closed-shell intermediates);

(ii)

kinetic isotope effects — the rate change under

\mathrm{H}\to\mathrm{D}
substitution at the methylene
hydrogens of malonic acid (predicted by transition-state
theory but invisible to a scalar
rxnRate
);

(iii)

solvent and ionic-strength dependence beyond the
reference conditions absorbed into
rxnRate
;

(iv)

pressure dependence and any temperature dependence not
captured by
rxnRate
at the reference temperature.

Any two BR mechanisms agreeing on the dynamical pair

(\mathtt{rxnRate},\mathtt{rxnSaturation})
per channel are
indistinguishable in the simulation, whether or not their
provenance tags agree (Proposition
12.28
;

rxnProvenance
is metadata, not consulted by the rate
or update logic). This is the
\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}
forcing pair of the main tower applied to
inorganic oscillating chemistry — an honest categorical
consequence of
\pi_{4}
’s range, not an implementation deficit.
Recovery of the dropped data requires either a higher-detail
simulator operating at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
(mechanism-resolved) or
experimental inputs (KIE measurement, pressure-jump kinetics)
whose results would re-parameterise the
\mathcal{L}_{3}
scalar at the new
reference conditions.

This closes the theoretical development of the chapter. The
operational functor
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
(§
12.7
) is
parameterised by (
46
), with
\pi_{4}

projecting all
\mathcal{L}_{4}
information through a three-component
coarse representation; BR’s network variants are different

\mathcal{L}_{3}
realisations comparable as Markov kernels via
(
47
). The simulation results of
§
12.9
test these constructions against the

briggsRauscherDE
network running under the conditions of

[
74
]
.

§12.9. Simulation results:
F_{\mathtt{briggsRauscherDE}}
in
\mathbf{BorelStoch}

With the theoretical development closed at
§
12.8
, we display the empirical realisation of

F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
applied to
briggsRauscherDE
. The exact
stochastic kernel

F_{\mathrm{BR}}\;:=\;F\bigl(\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathtt{briggsRauscherDE})\bigr)\;\in\;\mathbf{BorelStoch}

is sampled directly by the SSA (modulo PRNG and IEEE-754
qualifications, Theorem
12.12
). The deterministic
ODE trajectory realises the
V\to\infty
Kurtz limit of
F_{\mathrm{BR}}
’s
species-mean process (§
12.5
); the

\gamma_{\mathrm{ODE}}
2-cell of §
12.2
measures
the
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
-level deviation between this deterministic Kurtz
limit and
F_{\mathrm{BR}}
itself. Both simulators evaluate the same network
and parameters at the same point of
\Theta_{\mathrm{sim}}

(§
12.8
, eq. (
46
)); the
visible difference between their outputs at finite
V
is the
chapter’s
\gamma
-cell decomposition made concrete.

The empirical question is not whether the framework runs — by
construction
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
and
F
apply to any well-formed

Network
— but whether its predictions acquire visible
empirical content. We verify three predictions of the preceding
sections:

(P1)

The oscillator emerges.
Both simulators — the
SSA sampling
F_{\mathrm{BR}}
and the ODE realising its Kurtz limit —
exhibit relaxation-oscillator dynamics. This is the base case
for §
12.8
’s onset-preservation framework:
network reductions can subsequently be compared to this base.

(P2)

The
\gamma
-cell distinction is operational.
The
SSA samples and the ODE trajectory agree where the
rate-equation representation is faithful (high-copy spike
phase) and diverge where it is not (low-copy quiescent phase
at finite
V
), matching the form of
\gamma_{\mathrm{SSA}}=0

in total variation and
\gamma_{\mathrm{ODE}}
in
state-space/Wasserstein-1 metric predicted in
§
12.2
and §
12.5
.

(P3)

The divergence is structurally interpretable.
Where
the two simulators differ, the framework supplies the reason:
the ODE realises the
V\to\infty
Kurtz limit, and at

V=10^{-15}~\mathrm{L}
this limit represents quiescent
populations of low-copy species as fractional ensemble means
that do not correspond to any state of an individual
realisation.

12.9.1. Simulation parameters

Network.

briggsRauscherDE
(§
12.4
),
12 reaction channels encoding the De Kepper–Epstein skeleton

[
74
]
(10 elementary steps plus 2 explicit
reverses). Every rate constant carries a
Measured

rxnProvenance
tag with an independent kinetic citation
(§
12.8
, Remark
12.29
); no
constant is tuned to fit oscillatory behaviour.

Volume.

V=10^{-15}~\mathrm{L}
(femtoliter scale).
At this volume one molecule corresponds to a concentration of

1/(V\,N_{A})\approx 1.66\times 10^{-9}~\mathrm{M}
, where
N_{A}

is Avogadro’s number. The volume is chosen deliberately to keep
individual molecules resolvable and the SSA-versus-ODE distinction
empirically visible; at macroscopic volumes (e.g.
1~\mathrm{mL}
) the SSA distribution converges to the ODE limit
by the Kurtz theorem
[
179
]
and the two simulators become
indistinguishable in total variation.
V
is a user-chosen
simulation parameter (entering propensities via the

k_{\mathrm{micro}}=k_{\mathrm{macro}}/V^{\,n-1}
scaling for

n
-th order reactions); it is not part of
\Theta_{\mathrm{sim}}

(§
12.8
, eq. (
46
)) and not
derived from the framework.

Horizon.

\tau=1800~\mathrm{s}
, encoded as

ssaTimeMax
. The rate constants in

briggsRauscherDE
are parameterised for an inter-spike
interval near
10^{3}~\mathrm{s}
; the simulation horizon captures
between one and two complete cycles.

Ensemble.

For the SSA,
N=6
realisations with
independent
Word64
seeds. The ODE is deterministic and
run once. The ensemble size is sufficient for qualitative display
of timing, amplitude envelope, and quiescent-phase chatter;
quantitative kernel comparisons
(Proposition
12.30
) require

N\gtrsim 100
.

Initial state.

[\mathrm{I}^{-}]=10^{-5}~\mathrm{M}
,

[\mathrm{I}_{2}]=10^{-6}~\mathrm{M}
, all other species near
their analytic floors. These conditions sit off the limit cycle;
the first
\sim 250~\mathrm{s}
of every trajectory is transient
relaxation toward the attractor.

12.9.2. Deterministic view: the ODE Kurtz limit

Figure 2:
ODE trajectory for
\mathtt{briggsRauscherDE}
at the
chosen parameterisation: the
V\to\infty
Kurtz limit of

F_{\mathrm{BR}}

\sim 1100~\mathrm{s}

\approx 1250~\mathrm{s}
. Dashed

\mathrm{HOI}

absolute-tolerance floor (not chemistry); the analytic

.

Projection of the ODE trajectory onto

([\mathrm{I}^{-}],[\mathrm{I}_{2}])

The ODE trajectory exhibits the qualitative signature of a

,

[\mathrm{HOI}]\approx 10^{-6}~\mathrm{M}

[\mathrm{HIO}_{2}]\approx 10^{-5}~\mathrm{M}
,

[\mathrm{IO}_{2}\bullet]\approx 3\times 10^{-6}~\mathrm{M}
, and

[\mathrm{MnOH}^{2+}]\approx 10^{-8}~\mathrm{M}
;

[\mathrm{I}^{-}]
reaches a transient peak near

2\times 10^{-5}~\mathrm{M}
at spike onset before being consumed.
This confirms (P1) for the base network: the
\mathcal{L}_{2}
stoichiometric
topology together with the
\mathcal{L}_{3}
rate constants of

briggsRauscherDE
supports a relaxation-oscillator
attractor in the Kurtz limit.

The SSA realisations show the same qualitative oscillator
structure as the ODE, with three concrete and framework-predicted
differences:

•

Period shift.
The SSA mean inter-spike interval
(
\approx 1050~\mathrm{s}
) is approximately
15\%
shorter
than the ODE’s (
\approx 1250~\mathrm{s}
). In a given
realisation, rate-limiting integer transitions in the slow
recharge phase can fire earlier than the deterministic
species-mean trajectory predicts, advancing spike onset. The
direction is consistent with
\gamma_{\mathrm{ODE}}
’s
state-space-level deviation between the Kurtz limit and the
exact CTMC at low copy (§
12.2
,
§
12.5
); the magnitude is a phase-statistic
that requires
N\gg 6
realisations for a quantitative
kernel-level estimate.

•

Spike-peak agreement.
Peak molecule counts in the
SSA, converted to concentration, agree with ODE peak
concentrations to within a factor of two across all six
species (Table
8
). The systematic SSA-low
bias of the ensemble-mean peak relative to the ODE is the
expected consequence of
phase scatter
across
N=6

realisations: stochastic variation in spike-onset time
desynchronises the realisations slightly, and averaging
desynchronised spikes reduces the peak height of the
ensemble mean below that of any individual realisation.

•

Quiescent-phase divergence.
Where the ODE shows
smooth analytic floors (
\mathrm{HIO}_{2}
at

\sim 10^{-10}~\mathrm{M}
,
\mathrm{IO}_{2}\bullet
at

\sim 4\times 10^{-11}~\mathrm{M}
,
\mathrm{MnOH}^{2+}
at

\sim 10^{-13}~\mathrm{M}
), the SSA shows integer-valued
populations fluctuating between
0
and a few molecules. At

V=10^{-15}~\mathrm{L}
the ODE floors correspond to
ensemble means of
0.06
,
0.024
, and
6\times 10^{-5}

molecules respectively — below unity, hence describing
ensembles in which most individual realisations have zero
molecules during the quiescent phase.

The third bullet is the most pedagogically informative observation
in the section. The ODE quiescent floors are not numerical
artifacts: they are the analytical solution of the rate equations
in the time-asymptotic limit between spikes, and they are

correct as Kurtz-limit ensemble means
. At

V=10^{-15}~\mathrm{L}
, however, an ensemble mean of

6\times 10^{-5}

\mathrm{MnOH}^{2+}
molecules represents a
distribution in which essentially every individual realisation
has zero molecules during quiescence, with rare single-molecule
visits. The SSA shows this directly: most realisations have zero

\mathrm{MnOH}^{2+}
molecules during the quiescent phase, with
occasional single-molecule excursions. The discrepancy between
the two simulators is therefore neither a bug in the ODE solver
nor a sampling artifact in the SSA but a framework-predicted
consequence of evaluating
\mathcal{L}_{3}
at finite
V
:

\gamma_{\mathrm{SSA}}
vanishes in total variation throughout
(§
12.5
, Theorem
12.12
), while

\gamma_{\mathrm{ODE}}
— small in the high-copy spike phase
where the Kurtz limit is faithful — becomes non-trivial in the
low-copy quiescent phase where discrete chemistry dominates. This
confirms (P2) and (P3): the SSA and ODE outputs are operationally
distinguishable in precisely the regime where the chapter predicts
they should be, and the structure of the divergence is interpretable
from the framework rather than from numerical accident.

12.9.4. What is confirmed; what remains open

Framework deliverables and open items

Confirmed empirically.

•

(P1) The base BR oscillator emerges from

briggsRauscherDE
via
F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
. Both
simulators (SSA sampling
F_{\mathrm{BR}}
; ODE realising its Kurtz limit)
exhibit relaxation-oscillator structure; oscillation is robust
across the two semantic layers of
\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
.

•

(P2) The
\gamma
-cell distinction between the SSA samples
and the ODE Kurtz limit is operational and visible in the
figures: the two agree in the high-copy spike phase (where the
Kurtz limit is faithful) and diverge in the low-copy quiescent
phase (where the discrete chemistry dominates).

•

(P3) The form of the divergence is interpretable through
the Kurtz theorem and the
\gamma
-cell structure of
§
12.2
: the framework explains
why

the ODE smooths the quiescent phase, and
why
this
smoothing produces fractional molecule counts at the chosen
volume.

Not tested at this stage.

•

Variant comparison.
The empirical content of
Proposition
12.30
is the comparison
of the kernels

F\!\circ\!\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathtt{briggsRauscherDE})
,

F\!\circ\!\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathtt{broCODE5VarNetwork})
,

F\!\circ\!\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathtt{bufferedH})
, and

F\!\circ\!\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathtt{furrowLikePoolNetwork})
in the
canonical
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
embedding. We have sampled only

F_{\mathrm{BR}}
here.

•

Kinetic isotope effect.

Remark
12.31
(ii) predicts that
replacing the methylene hydrogens of malonic acid by deuterium
would alter the
\mathrm{C}
–

by a primary KIE. This
\mathcal{L}_{4}

invisible to the present

•

Quantitative agreement with experiment.
Period
and spike amplitudes here are set by the parameterisation
(target period

•

Volume convergence.
The Kurtz theorem

[
179
]
predicts that the SSA distribution converges
to the ODE limit as
V
grows. A volume sweep at fixed
parameterisation would make this convergence empirically
visible and provide a quantitative measure of

\gamma_{\mathrm{ODE}}
as a function of
V
.

Ensemble size.

N=6
is sufficient for the
qualitative displays of timing, amplitude envelope, and
quiescent-phase chatter. Quantitative kernel-level comparisons
in
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
(TV distance, Wasserstein-1, relative entropy)
require
N\gtrsim 100
, a natural next step the present
framework is built to support.

12.9.5. Closing

The simulation results do not validate the framework in any
absolute sense: a framework with no empirical content can pass
unfalsified by any data. What the figures establish instead is
that the framework’s predictions for BR are structurally
distinguishable from the generic statement “the simulator
produces some output”. The kernel

F_{\mathrm{BR}}:=F(\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathtt{briggsRauscherDE}))\in\mathbf{BorelStoch}

is a specific mathematical object computed via the construction
of §§
12.2
–
12.8
; its SSA
samples and its ODE Kurtz limit are two operational evaluations
of this object (the SSA samples
F_{\mathrm{BR}}
directly; the
ODE realises its species-mean Kurtz limit), and their visible
structural difference at the chosen volume is the chapter’s

\gamma
-cell decomposition in concrete form.

The framework earns its keep here in three concrete ways:

(1)

It
predicts.
The SSA samples and ODE Kurtz limit
must differ in low-copy regions of state space, with the form
of the difference determined by which semantic layer (exact
CTMC vs.
V\!\to\!\infty
Kurtz limit) is being evaluated.
The figures confirm this. The prediction could have failed
in several ways — the two simulators could have agreed in
the quiescent phase, the ODE could have failed to oscillate
while the SSA succeeded (or vice versa), the peak amplitudes
could have differed by orders of magnitude — and none did.

(2)

It supplies
vocabulary.
Every numerical claim
in this section is locatable in the chapter’s framework
decomposition:
V
is a user-chosen simulation parameter
(separate from
\Theta_{\mathrm{sim}}
);
\Theta_{\mathrm{sim}}
contains the
parameterisation and network variant; the simulator type
selects between the SSA and ODE morphisms in

\mathrm{Para}_{W}(\textbf{Hask})
; the kernel
F_{\mathrm{BR}}
is the
derived
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
-object;
\gamma_{\mathrm{ODE}}
is the
Kurtz-limit deviation; the discrete quiescent-phase chatter
is
\mathcal{L}_{3}
-stochastic truth that the framework’s

\mathcal{L}_{3}
-deterministic representation cannot capture at finite

V
. This decomposition is tacit in standard simulation
practice; the framework makes it explicit.

(3)

It
equips.
Proposition
12.30

embeds every BR variant into
\mathbf{BorelStoch}
via the same

F\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}
; comparison is then comparison of Markov
kernels in a single category, with metric choices (TV,
Wasserstein-1, relative entropy) available. The variant
comparisons, KIE prediction, and volume sweep listed above
are the natural next steps; the machinery to perform them
is in place.

The classical chemical phenomena of the Briggs–Rauscher
oscillator — period, amplitude, autocatalytic feedback, the
distinction between the spike and quiescent phases — emerge
through this framework. What the framework adds is the discipline
of distinguishing three categories.
Essential features
—
such as the oscillation onset itself — are tied to the
\mathcal{L}_{2}

stoichiometric feedback topology and the
\mathcal{L}_{3}
Jacobian
sign-pattern; they survive across both simulators and would
survive across network variants retaining the autocatalytic
skeleton.
Tunable features
— the oscillation period
(
\sim\!10^{3}~\mathrm{s}
at the chosen parameterisation) and
spike amplitudes — are physical functionals of the
\mathcal{L}_{3}

rate constants and the
\pi_{4}
-coarse
\mathcal{L}_{4}
data of
§
12.8
; re-parameterising to classical batch BR
conditions would shift them continuously to the experimental

30
–
60~\mathrm{s}
regime.
Scale-dependent representational
artifacts
— the smooth ODE quiescent floors at

\sim 10^{-13}~\mathrm{M}
for
\mathrm{MnOH}^{2+}
, and the

\sim\!15\%
SSA-vs-ODE period shift — are not chemistry but
artifacts of evaluating an essentially-discrete process through
its continuous Kurtz limit. The floor values are valid ensemble
means at all
V
but acquire physical referents (as occupied
discrete states) only at sufficiently large
V
; at

V=10^{-15}~\mathrm{L}
they correspond to sub-unity counts
that no individual realisation can occupy. The
15\%
drift,
distinct in V-dependence, is a
\gamma_{\mathrm{ODE}}
residual
that vanishes as
V\to\infty
by the Kurtz theorem

[
179
]
. Both manifest at
V=10^{-15}~\mathrm{L}

because the volume is too small for the continuous limit to be
faithful to individual discrete trajectories.

This tripartite separation is tacit in standard simulation
practice; the framework makes it explicit. Simulator outputs
then become inputs to inference about chemistry — the
essential-versus-tunable boundary is what falsification tests
should target; the scale-dependent representational artifacts
are what should be disregarded — rather than illustrations of
dynamics in which all three categories are silently conflated.

§13. Conclusion

§13.1. The tower in retrospect

This monograph constructed a canonical tower

\mathcal{L}_{0}\to\mathcal{L}_{1}\to\mathcal{L}_{2}\to\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathcal{L}_{4}\to\mathcal{L}_{4.5}\to\mathcal{L}_{5}\to\mathcal{L}_{6}\dashrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{7}

of categorical levels for chemical reactions, each step forced from
the one below by a non-trivial cokernel in the automorphism exact
sequence

1\to\ker\varphi_{k}\to\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{k})\xrightarrow{\varphi_{k}}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{k-1})\to\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{k})\to 1:

each non-trivial cokernel class names a pair of reactions that
physics distinguishes but the lower-level forgetful functor
U_{k}

collapses (Proposition 6.26 at
k=1,\ldots,4
;
§7.1, §8.7, §9.7, §10.1 at the remaining levels).
A perpendicular Para dimension (Chapter 11) classifies
machine-learning architectures for chemistry as parametric morphisms
over the same levels, with zero-parameter inclusions

\gamma_{k}:\mathcal{L}_{k}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}
recovering the
exact tower.

Three rules from undergraduate chemistry became provable theorems
within the tower.
Hess’s Law is the functoriality of
F_{\!H}:\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)\to(\mathbb{R},+)
:
the equality
F_{\!H}(r_{2}\circ r_{1})=F_{\!H}(r_{2})+F_{\!H}(r_{1})
is the
monoidal-functor condition, not an empirical observation
(Chapter 3).
Walden inversion is the statement that the permutation

\pi_{\chi}\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4}(P))
exchanging the
(R)
- and

(S)
-enantiomers has no preimage in
\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{L}_{4.5}(P))

under
\varphi_{4.5}
: the chirality-flipping generator

E^{*}\in G^{*}(G)=\mathrm{Aut}(G)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
separates
the enantiomers as objects of
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
(Theorem 7.27).
The Longuet–Higgins sign change is the non-vanishing of the first
Stiefel–Whitney class

w_{1}(L_{R_{0}})\in H^{1}(\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)\setminus\Sigma_{\mathrm{CI}},\mathbb{Z}/2)
of the real ground-state eigenline on loops linking
the codimension-2 conical-intersection seam (§9.3); the complex
Chern class
c_{1}(L_{0})\in H^{2}
is the codimension-matched companion.

The forcing argument is structural.
At each level, the unique minimal categorical extension with
non-trivial
\mathrm{coker}(\varphi_{k})
for the relevant reaction
pair produces, as a theorem, what was previously only a rule.
The rules did not become theorems because the mathematics was
sharpened.
They became theorems because the level was made explicit.

§13.2. A taxonomy of extension types

The nine constructions
\mathcal{L}_{0},\mathcal{L}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{L}_{7}
are not nine
independent acts of imagination.
With the full tower in view, they fall into seven types,
distinguished by the kind of categorical operation each performs;
this classification could not be stated before all levels were
available.

The seven extension types

I (Free construction).

\mathcal{L}_{0}
is the free symmetric monoidal category on the Petri net of
a reaction system (Meseguer–Montanari).
Every subsequent level is an extension of this base.

II (Functor decoration).

\mathcal{L}_{1}
,
\mathcal{L}_{2}
,
\mathcal{L}_{3}
each add a monoidal functor on
\mathcal{L}_{0}(P)

without changing its objects or morphism type:
F_{\!H}
,
F_{\!S}
and the
Gibbs functor
F_{G}^{T}
, and the kinetic functor

F_{P}:\mathcal{L}_{3}\to\mathbf{Stoch}
respectively.

III (Mechanism rebuild).

\mathcal{L}_{4}
replaces
\mathcal{L}_{3}
morphisms (Markov kernels) with DPO
derivation spans in
\mathbf{LGraph}
.
This is the only transition in the tower where the underlying
category changes rather than being decorated; SN1 and SN2 coincide
at
\mathcal{L}_{3}
and split at
\mathcal{L}_{4}
(Examples 6.41, 6.42).

IV (Symmetry enrichment).

\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
equips the mechanism level with the

G^{*}(G)=\mathrm{Aut}(G)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{k}
-equivariant
structure (Definition 7.5); discrete, no continuous parameter
introduced.

V (Geometric decoration).

\mathcal{L}_{5}
adds the configuration orbifold

\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)=\mathbb{R}^{3n}/(\mathrm{SE}(3)\rtimes\mathrm{Aut}_{\mu}(G))
and the PES

V:\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)\to\mathbb{R}
.
Continuous: nuclear geometry, point groups, and transition-state
theory enter the structure (§8.2.2).

VI (Topological enrichment).

\mathcal{L}_{6}
adds the rank-
N
active Hilbert bundle

\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{el}}^{(N)}\to\mathcal{C}_{e}(G)
with Berry
connection, carrying the primary invariant

w_{1}(L_{R_{0}})\in H^{1}(\cdot,\mathbb{Z}/2)
and its companion

c_{1}(L_{0})\in H^{2}(\cdot,\mathbb{Z})
.

VII (Algebraic deformation).

\mathcal{L}_{7}
deforms the algebra: a continuous field

\{A_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon\in[0,1]}
of
C^{*}
-algebras with
classical fibre
A_{0}=C_{0}(\mathcal{C}_{e}(G))
and non-commutative
quantum fibre
A_{\varepsilon}
for
\varepsilon>0
.

Types I–VI admit Para enrichments
\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{Para}}
via

\gamma_{k}
(Chapter 11); Type VII does not, because the deformation
parameter
\varepsilon
is physical, not learnable.
This cleanly separates ML-for-chemistry (Types I–VI) from
mathematical physics (Type VII).

§13.3. Open constructions

Five constructions raised in the body remain open; each has a
precise statement, identified ingredients, and known obstructions.

C1: The continuous field for molecules.

Construct
\{A_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon\in[0,1]}
with

A_{0}=C_{0}(\mathcal{C}_{e}(G))
and
A_{\varepsilon}
the full molecular

C^{*}
-algebra, satisfying the Rieffel conditions
[
252
]
.
The Panati–Spohn–Teufel space-adiabatic perturbation
theory
[
238
]
, the Hagedorn–Joye asymptotic
theory
[
130
]
, the Landsman tangent groupoid
construction
[
185
]
, and the Georgescu–Iftimovici

N
-body framework
[
117
]
are all in place; no paper
has assembled them into a single
C^{*}
-algebraic framework for
molecules.

C2: The groupoid
C^{*}
-algebra for molecular symmetry.

Construct the transformation-groupoid algebra

C^{*}(G^{*}(G)\rtimes Q^{\mathrm{reg}}_{\mathrm{lab}}(G))
(§10.7)
and show that its representation theory recovers simultaneously the
permutation-inversion selection rules, the Woodward–Hoffmann
orbital-symmetry rules, and ortho/para nuclear-spin statistics.
Renault’s groupoid algebra theory
[
248
]
supplies the
abstract framework.

C3: The
K
-theoretic obstruction at conical intersections.

Promote
w_{1}(L_{R_{0}})\in H^{1}(\cdot,\mathbb{Z}/2)
and

c_{1}(L_{0})\in H^{2}(\cdot,\mathbb{Z})
to classes in the algebraic

K
-theory of
\{A_{\varepsilon}\}
, generalising the formal
Emmrich–Weinstein result
[
85
]
to the
strict
C^{*}
-setting via a blow-up of the algebra at

\Sigma_{\mathrm{CI}}
.

O1: A categorical Deficiency Zero Theorem.

Prove that the deficiency
\delta=n-\ell-s
equals the
negative Euler characteristic of the stoichiometric chain complex

\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{C}]\xrightarrow{\partial_{1}}\mathbb{Z}^{S}
,
and derive Feinberg’s Deficiency Zero
Theorem
[
94
]
from this homological identity.

O2: Open mechanistic reaction networks.

Construct the symmetric monoidal bicategory

\mathrm{Csp}(\mathcal{L}_{4}^{\mathrm{Para}})
of cospans of open DPO derivations in

\mathbf{LGraph}
, extending the Baez–Pollard open Petri net
framework
[
28
]
from
\mathcal{L}_{3}
to
\mathcal{L}_{4}
.
The Lack–Sobociński adhesive structure on

\mathbf{LGraph}

[
180
]
guarantees the required
pushout complements.

Proximity to resolution

O1 and O2 are within reach with currently available tools:
ingredients in place, construction pending.
C2 needs a single synthesis step.
C3 requires a new technical ingredient — the seam blow-up — but
the surrounding framework is clear.
C1 is the deepest: it requires C2, C3, and a resolution of the
Coulomb singularity problem, and is the correct formulation of what
it would mean to complete the
\mathcal{L}_{6}\dashrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{7}
step.

§13.4. Outlook

The tower has implications for three communities not previously in
close contact.

For chemical reaction network theory.

The Feinberg deficiency theory and the Craciun–Yu and
Anderson–Shiu multistationarity results sit entirely within

\mathcal{L}_{0}
(combinatorial hypotheses) and
\mathcal{L}_{3}
(dynamical
conclusions).
The tower makes this level gap explicit for the first time and
suggests, via O1, a homological proof of the Deficiency Zero
Theorem that would place these landmark results inside a
categorical framework rather than leaving them as isolated facts.
The open mechanistic network construction O2 extends Baez–Pollard
grey-boxing from
\mathcal{L}_{3}
to
\mathcal{L}_{4}
, giving an algebraic foundation
for compositional analysis of reaction mechanisms.

For machine learning in chemistry.

The Para dimension answers a question that becomes urgent as
ML models for chemistry scale: what does it mean for a model to be
physically correct at a given level?
The answer is architectural: a model is physically correct at

\mathcal{L}_{k}
if and only if the level-
k
exact functor factors through
it.
The equivariance groups grow monotonically through the tower:

\mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{S})
at
\mathcal{L}_{0}
,
\mathrm{Aut}(G)
at

\mathcal{L}_{4}
,
G^{*}(G)
at
\mathcal{L}_{4.5}
,
\mathrm{SE}(3)\rtimes\mathrm{Aut}_{\mu}(G)
at
\mathcal{L}_{5}
, and the
U(N)
structure of the
active Hilbert bundle at
\mathcal{L}_{6}
.
A model whose architecture respects only the
\mathcal{L}_{5}
group cannot
represent
\mathcal{L}_{6}
phenomena: there is no slot for the line-bundle
holonomy that distinguishes adiabatic from non-adiabatic dynamics
— this is the architectural barrier currently separating
photocatalysis and conical-intersection chemistry from the
mainstream ML-for-chemistry stack.
Chapter 12 supplies one concrete executable instance: the
simulation functor

\Phi_{\mathrm{op}}:\mathrm{Para}(\mathcal{L}_{0}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{2}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{3})\to\mathbf{Kl}(\mathsf{IO})
composed with the denotational
realisation
F
into the Markov category
\mathbf{BorelStoch}

(Fritz
[
103
]
), applied to the Briggs–Rauscher
oscillator with the
\varphi
-cell distinction between exact CTMC
and Kurtz-limit ODE made operational (§12.9).

For mathematical chemistry and mathematical physics.

The constructions C1–C3 would collectively provide the first
rigorous categorical treatment of the Born–Oppenheimer
approximation as a limit rather than an ansatz.
The Landsman–Rieffel–Georgescu–Hagedorn–PST literature has
reached a point where all ingredients are available; the obstacle
is synthesis rather than any single missing result.
O1, conversely, would connect classical CRNT to homological algebra
in a way that has been suspected since Feinberg’s earliest papers
but never made precise.

§13.5. Coda

A hydrogen atom transfers from carbon to oxygen in an enzyme active
site.
Whether that transfer is governed by classical barrier-crossing or
by quantum tunnelling depends on which level of the tower the
question is posed at.
The enzyme does not know which level the chemist is using.
It operates at all of them simultaneously.

The tower does not add new chemistry.
Hess’s Law was not more true after
F_{\!H}
was defined.
Walden inversion was not more real after the cokernel argument
identified it as a non-trivial automorphism class.
The retinal photoisomerisation was not faster because the
Stiefel–Whitney class was computed around the conical-intersection
seam.
What the tower adds is precision: each chemical fact is now located
at the unique level where it can be expressed, and the tools
available at that level are exactly those needed to prove it.

Chemistry’s rules are not wrong.
Their exceptions are not failures.
They are coordinates.
The tower is the coordinate system.

The central result of this monograph is negative in form but
positive in content.
Negative: no single category suffices to express all of chemistry.
Positive: the minimal number of categories needed, their order, and
the unique forcing pair that makes each one necessary — this is
determined, not chosen.

The map is forced.
